Cover inset figure: Courtesy of Maude Guillier. 

Regulation of gene expression in bacteria plays a key role in their adaptation to ever-changing environments. Transcription is the first level of control that has been described and decades of research have led to a thorough characterization of the transcriptional network, at least for some of the model bacteria such as Escherichia coli. However, it is now clear that many genes are subject to post-transcriptional control as well, and small RNAs are a major class of post-transcriptional regulators. Many functions are in fact controlled by mixed regulatory circuits encompassing both transcriptional and post-transcriptional control mediated respectively by proteins or RNAs. The properties of such circuits are just starting to be elucidated. In the regulatory scheme shown on the cover, the involvement of Hfq-binding sRNAs in control of motility and adhesion in enterobacteria is depicted. Positive and negative controls are shown with normal and blunt-end arrows respectively. Asterisks indicate regulatory interactions presumed to be direct. Green triangles highlight feedforward regulatory motifs. The regulatory scheme is found in Figure 5.1.1 in Chapter 5.1 by Maude Guillier et al. For more details see Chapter 5.1.

The field of stress and environmental control of gene expression in bacteria is a very active field, moving rapidly and in multiple directions. An extensive overview book has existed since 2011, when the excellent Bacterial Stress Responses book of reviews (ASM Press) appeared. This book is an update and extension of that volume, with chapters mainly based on publications post 2010 or from de novo contributions; it is thus a complementary rather than competitive work, which focuses on original research papers and reviews in a large variety of different organisms, rather than reviewing model systems only. The large outline covers 23 different topics and provides selected new reviews as well as a series of research chapters for each topic. Altogether, it provides a detailed and broad overview of the field and emphasizes differences and commonalities in different organisms. 

As mentioned, this book contains not only reviews but also many recent, original research chapters. The authors have been asked to provide succinct materials and methods, and to refer back to their original publication when deemed appropriate. This book provides an extensive Index to facilitate the search for key terms. Special attention has been given to cross-referencing the chapters in the book. The book appears in print as well as in electronic format at the Wiley website, in order to facilitate downloading of particular chapters. 

The primary audience is (clinical) microbiologists, biochemists, geneticists, and microbial ecologists working in the field of stress and environmental control of gene expression and adaptation to stress conditions. 

These books are in principle research-intensive books, but they could be used in upper level undergraduate and graduatelevel courses in Microbiology, Molecular Genetics, Biochemistry, and Microbial Ecology. These books are particularly useful for instructors who want to integrate aspects of environmental control of gene expression (response to stresses) in their upper level courses, and they can assign particular chapters to students to present back to the class. It is particularly useful for postdocs and for graduate or advanced undergraduate students who are working in laboratories focused on environmental control of gene expression and adaptation in bacteria to broaden their horizons. It is also very useful for those wanting to familiarize themselves with this field of study. 

Frans J. de Bruijn

Bacteria in various habitats are subject to continuously changing environmental conditions, such as nutrient deprivation, heat and cold stress, UV radiation, oxidative stress, desiccation, acid stress, nitrosative stress, cell envelope stress, heavy metal exposure, osmotic stress, and others. In order to survive, they have to respond to these conditions by adapting their physiology through sometimes drastic changes in gene expression. In addition, they may adapt by changing their morphology, forming biofilms, fruiting bodies or spores, filaments, or viable but nonculturable (VBNC) cells, or moving away from stress compounds via chemotaxis. Changes in gene expression constitute the main component of the bacterial response to stress and environmental changes, and they involve a myriad of different mechanisms, including (alternative) sigma factors, bior tri-component regulatory systems, small noncoding RNAs, chaperones, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR)–Cas systems, DNA repair, toxin–antitoxin systems, the stringent response, efflux pumps, alarmones, and modulation of the cell envelope or membranes, to name a few. Many regulatory elements are conserved in different bacteria; however, there are endless variations on the themes, and novel elements of gene regulation in bacteria inhabiting particular environments are constantly being discovered. Especially in (pathogenic) bacteria colonizing the human body, a plethora of bacterial responses to innate stresses such as pH, reactive nitrogen and oxygen species, and antibiotic stress are being described. Many of the regulatory systems being uncovered are specific, but there is also considerable “cross-talk” between different circuits. 

Stress and environmental regulation of gene expression and adaptation in bacteria is the topic of this book. The book consists of reviews and original research chapters, and for each topic several chapters on different bacterial systems are included to highlight both the common and unique aspects of the regulatory circuits operating in response to the specific stress or environmental condition. Most of the chapters will use molecular techniques and advanced biochemical analyses. An attempt is made to not only cover model systems but also give a broad overview of the stress-responsive regulatory systems in a variety of bacteria, including medically important bacteria, where elucidation of certain aspects of these systems could lead to treatment strategies for the pathogens. 

The book starts out with a series of key overview chapters to set the stage for the individual sections, each addressing a particular stress or environmental condition and the various genetic systems to respond to stress. Not included in the book, except for one overview chapter, is antibiotic resistance, since this topic cannot be covered adequately in a single section and other books and reviews on this topic are available in the literature. 

Section 3 will cover the role of one to three component regulatory systems in the response to changing environmental conditions. Section 4 will address the role of alternative sigma factors under stress conditions. Section 5 will cover the recent subfield of small noncoding RNAs in stress responses. The sixth section will review the role of toxin–antitoxin systems in stress responses in different bacteria. The seventh section will cover the canonical stringent response to stress in a variety of bacteria. Sections 8 and 9 will cover UV irradiation responses in different bacteria and the canonical SOS repair system, and Section 9 will also address the issue of double-stranded break repair. Sections 10 and 11 will discuss the response of a variety of bacteria to oxidative and osmotic stress environmental conditions. The twelfth section will cover desiccation tolerance and drought stress in bacteria. Sections 13, 14, and 15 will address the bacterial responses to heat and cold stresses, as well as the role of chaperones. Section 16 covers the adaptation of bacteria to acid stress, and Section 17 discusses the bacterial response to nitrosative stress. The eighteenth section deals with the adaptive response to cell envelope stress. Section 19 describes the process of iron homeostasis, and Section 20 covers the resistance mechanisms to (heavy) metals. Bacterial quorum sensing, biofilm formation, and the formation of VBNC cells are described in Sections 21, 22, and 23, respectively. 

This book is meant to be a thorough compilation of chapters dealing with the molecular genetics and “omics” of gene regulation systems in response to stress and varying environmental conditions, and it is meant for researchers in the field and also for students. 

## Key overview chapters

## Dvora Biran1 and Eliora Z. Ron1,2

1Department of Molecular Microbiology and Biotechnology, Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv, Israel 

2MIGAL – Galilee Research Institute, Kiriat Shemona, Israel 

## 2.1.1 Introduction

Exposure to stress requires fast adaptation of bacteria to the new environmental conditions. This adaptation is carried out by extensive changes in gene expression. Several regulatory mechanisms have been shown to play a role in changing the expression of stress-related genes. In many Gram-negative bacteria belonging to the gamma proteobacteria (i.e., Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa), most of the stress-related changes in gene expression involve utilization of stress-specific transcriptional activators, or sigma factors (see Chapters 2.3, 2.4, 2.6, 2.15; Section 4). As examples, sigma32 preferentially transcribes heat shock genes (Cowing et al., 1985; Grossman et al., 1984) when the temperature is elevated, and sigmaS transcribes general stress genes at starvation or a stationary phase (Weber et al., 2005). Gram-positive bacteria also have stress-induced regulatory mechanisms that involve sigma factors (Antelmann et al., 1997; Boylan et al., 1993). However, some of their heat shock genes are usually regulated by specific conserved inverted repeats (CIRCEs) that bind to a protein repressor (Zuber and Schumann, 1994). This repressor system is also present in the Gram-negative alpha proteobacteria (i.e., Agrobacterium tumefaciens and Bradyrhizobium japonicum) but not in all the heat shock genes (Segal and Ron, 1993, 1998). Thus, in bacteria, control of the expression of stress-induced genes is mainly carried out at the initiation of transcription of stress genes. 

However, during the last decade, it has become increasingly evident that posttranscriptional regulation of bacterial gene expression plays an important role in how bacteria respond to stress. Thus, additional control systems exist that operate posttranscriptionally by modifying transcript stability. Essentially, there are three regulatory mechanisms involved in changing transcript stability: 

1 RNA-based mechanisms at the level of RNA structure involving riboswitches and RNA thermometers (Coppins et al., 2007; Grundy and Henkin, 2006; Rasouly et al., 2007). 

2 Regulation in trans by specific small regulatory noncoding RNAs (sRNAs) (Gottesman, 2004; Storz, 1999; Vogel et al., 2014; Wassarman and Storz, 2000). So far, a very large number of small noncoding RNAs has been identified and their functions analyzed (see Section 5). 

3 Regulation in trans by RNA-binding proteins. Some of these proteins, such as Hfq, can act in coordination with a sRNA (Chao et al., 2012; Sharma et al., 2011; Sittka et al., 2008, 2009). 

One group of important RNA-binding proteins are the cold shock proteins (Csp’s), which have previously been shown to act as RNA chaperones and affect transcript stability (Goldstein et al., 1990; Inouye, 1999; Jones and Inouye, 1994; Lee et al., 1994; Phadtare and Inouye, 2001; Phadtare et al., 2006; Yamanaka and Inouye, 2001). Recent studies in E. coli indicate that during stress, the effect of CspC on transcript stability is global, controlling gene expression of at least two stress regulons – the heat shock response and the general stress response. Regulation of stress response in E. coli by Csp’s is the focus of this review. 

## 2.1.2 RNA chaperones – cold shock proteins

CspA was the first Csp to be discovered; it is a cold-induced protein shown to stabilize transcripts by protecting them from degradation by RNase E (Hankins et al., 2007). The other eight Csp family members have been identified based on their homology to CspA (Bae et al., 2000; see Section 15). Interestingly, these family members have different induction profiles suggesting disparate functions. In E. coli, five out of the nine CSPs are not cold inducible. Two of these RNA chaperones, CspC and CspE, are involved in modulating transcript stability during stress (Phadtare and Inouye, 2001; Phadtare et al., 2006). 

## 2.1.3 Stability of the general stress transcripts

The general stress response involves a very large number of genes, involved in carbon starvation, stationary phase, oxidative stress, acid stress, and more (Weber et al., 2005). During these stresses, the genes involved in the response are transcribed by a specific sigma factor, sigma S (Hengge, 2008), whose cellular concentration increases in response to the stress. One of the important factors contributing to the elevation of sigma S concentration is the increase in the stability of sigma S transcripts (Phadtare and Inouye, 2001). This increased stability is mediated by two Csp’s – CspC and CspE – that complement each other. Thus, a deletion of one of them has a minor effect, but a deletion of both abolishes the stabilization of sigma S transcripts during stress and results in a decreased level of sigma S and increased sensitivity to lethal stresses such as oxidative or acid stress (Shenhar et al., 2012; see Section 10 and 16). Actually, the poor stress survival of bacteria deleted for both CspC and CspE is similar to that of bacteria deleted for RpoS. 

## 2.1.4 Stress-induced change in transcript stability of heat shock response genes

One would expect that transcript stability of heat shock genes during heat shock would follow a similar pattern of the general stress response–specific transcripts. However, the situation is very different and unexpected (Shenhar et al., 2009; see Section 13 and 14). Thus, during heat shock, there is a significant decrease in the stability of specific heat shock gene transcripts. This decrease is independent of the heat shock– specific sigma factor, sigma 32, as the stability of its transcripts is highly increased. Yet, this change in transcript stability involves the cold shock RNA chaperones, but only one of them – CspC. Thus, CspC is essential for stabilizing the transcripts of heat shock genes. In its absence, the half-life of these transcripts decreases by about half. CspE does not appear to be significant for the stability of the transcripts of these genes. 

So why, then, is there a decrease in the stability of transcripts involved in the heat shock response? The answer lies in the fact that CspC, which is stabilizing transcripts of the heat shock response, is enzymatically proteolyzed upon heat shock. This heat shock–dependent proteolysis involves the GroE chaperone that subjects CspC to proteolysis by adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-dependent proteases (Lenz and Ron, 2014). As GroE is a heat shock protein, its concentration increases upon exposure to elevated temperatures resulting in increased proteolysis of CspC and a decrease in its cellular concentration. One of the consequences of this decrease is loss of protection of the messenger RNA (mRNA) of heat shock genes and their decreased stability. 

## 2.1.5 Physiological consequences of the decreased stability of heat shock gene transcripts

Understanding the role of decreased stability of heat shock gene transcripts has to take into account the fact that the heat shock response is transient. Thus, there is a strong induction of the heat shock genes that stops after a peak at about 2–5 min from the onset. The transient nature of the heat shock response depends on the decreased half-life of the heat shock gene transcripts. Thus, when the level of CspC is kept artificially high by introducing it on a multicopy plasmid, the decrease in the heat shock response is very slow, and the transient nature of the response is lost. The direct result is that the cellular levels of the heat shock proteins are much higher at the elevated temperature, and – consequently – the growth rate at the higher temperature is slower (Shenhar et al., 2009). 

## 2.1.6 The physiological roles of CspC and CspE

These two chaperones are similar but have different roles. While CspC appears to stabilize transcripts of the general stress response genes and of the heat shock response, CspE appears to stabilize only the transcripts of the general stress response and has no effect on the stability of heat shock gene transcripts. These two chaperones are differentially regulated – while the level of CspE is not significantly affected by the stress, the level of CspC undergoes significant changes. Thus, it goes up significantly during the general stress response and becomes very low during the heat shock response. These changes in the cellular concentration of CspE are largely responsible for the change in stability of the stress-involved gene transcripts (Shenhar et al., 2012). 

It appears that CspE, whose concentration is essentially steady during stresses, functions as a general maintainer of transcript stability (RNA stability “housekeeping”). In contrast, CspC apparently has the regulatory role of modulating the pattern of transcript stability during stress. 

## 2.1.7 Conclusions

- Stability of stress-related transcripts is modified during the stress. Transcripts of the general stress response are stabilized during the stress, and those of heat shock response have a decreased stability during the stress. 

- Transcripts involved in the general stress response and in the heat shock response are stabilized by the cold shock RNA chaperones CspC and CspE. 

- During the general stress response, or stationary phase, CspC and CspE can cover for each other, and only deletion of both results in loss of RNA stabilization. 

- For the heat shock response, only CspC is important. Its cellular concentration goes down significantly during the stress, 

due to ATP-dependent proteolysis mediated by the heat shock protein GroE. 

- The heat shock–dependent decrease in stability of heat shock transcripts is important for adaptation to elevated temperatures. 



Jones PG, Inouye M. 1994. The cold-shock response – a hot topic. Molecular Microbiology 11: 811–818. 



The concentration of CspC is reduced upon heat shock and increases upon the stationary phase, concurrently with changes in the stability of the relevant stress genes; however, it is not affected upon cold shock conditions. By contrast, the concentration of CspE remains relatively stable under all of these conditions, and current evidence suggests that it increases only upon cold shock (Uppal et al., 2008), where it has a role in transcription antitermination (Hankins et al., 2007). Taken together, it appears that CspC is the modulator of transcript stability upon exposure to environmental stress, while CspE acts as a “housekeeping RNA chaperone.”

Phadtare S, Hwang J, Severinov K, Inouye M. 2003. CspB and CspL, thermostable cold-shock proteins from Thermotoga maritima. Genes to Cells: Devoted to Molecular & Cellular Mechanisms 8: 801–810. 



- The two chaperones – CspC and CspE – stabilize transcripts of stress genes. However, the recognition sites have not yet been identified for any of them. In vitro studies indicate that the consensus sequences for binding of CspC and CspE are, respectively, AGGGAGGGA and AU/AT-rich regions, especially AAAUUU (Phadtare and Inouye, 1999). However, these sequences are not present in many transcripts that are clearly regulated by CspC. Therefore, it can be concluded that the in vivo recognition sites for these RNA chaperones are not yet fully identified. 



Phadtare S, Inouye M. 1999. Sequence-selective interactions with RNA by CspB, CspC and CspE, members of the CspA family of Escherichia coli. Molecular Microbiology 33: 1004–1014. 



While both chaperones are almost identical in amino acid sequences, they are disparately regulated and also seem to associate with different transcripts. Which molecular mechanism explains this? 



Phadtare S, Inouye M. 2001. Role of CspC and CspE in regulation of expression of RpoS and UspA, the stress response proteins in Escherichia coli. Journal of Bacteriology 183: 1205–1214. 



CspC and CspE are very similar. Yet these two RNA chaperones have very different physiological roles that are difficult to explain in view of their high sequence similarity. For example, what defines the differential binding to transcripts of heat shock genes, and what are the RNA motifs that are bound by CspC but not CspE? 



Phadtare S, Tadigotla V, Shin WH, Sengupta A, Severinov K. 2006. Analysis of Escherichia coli global gene expression profiles in response to overexpression and deletion of CspC and CspE. Journal of Bacteriology 188: 2521–2527. 



- How is the expression of cspC and cspE regulated? How is cspC induced upon the stationary phase? 



Rasouly A, Shenhar Y, Ron EZ. 2007. Thermoregulation of Escherichia coli hchA transcript stability. Journal of Bacteriolog y 189: 5779– 5781. 



CspE was recently shown to be critical for transcription antitermination in the cold (Phadtare et al., 2003), and three centrally located aromatic patch amino acid residues – Phe(17), Phe(30), and His(32) – are responsible for these activities (Bae et al., 2000; Phadtare et al., 2003). However, CspC also contains these three aromatic amino acids but does not play a role in the cold or in antitermination under these conditions. 



Segal G, Ron EZ. 1993. Heat shock transcription of the groESL operon of Agrobacterium tumefaciens may involve a hairpin-loop structure. Journal of Bacteriology 175: 3083–3088. 



- In terms of regulation of the chaperones, it has been established that CspA synthesis is controlled by a thermosensor in the 5′ UTR of the mRNA that results in cold induction 



Segal G, Ron EZ. 1998. Regulation of heat-shock response in bacteria. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences 851: 147–151.

(Giuliodori et al., 2010). However, it is not clear if CspE synthesis is controlled in a similar way or how CspC, which is not cold induced, is regulated. 

Clearly, our understanding of stress-induced regulation of transcript stability is rather limited at this point, especially in respect to the role of RNA chaperones. Broadening our perception is expected to advance our understanding of RNA-binding proteins and their role in determining transcript stability. This comprehension will also enhance our understanding of the stress responses, which is essential for bacterial survival under changing conditions.

## C H A P T E R 2.2

# StressChip for monitoring microbial stress response in the environment

## Joy D. Van Nostrand1, Aifen Zhou1 and Jizhong Zhou1,2,3

1Institution for Environmental Genomics and Department of Microbiology and Plant Biology, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, United States 

2Earth Sciences Division, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, CA, United States 

3State Key Joint Laboratory of Environment Simulation and Pollution Control, School of Environment, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China 

## 2.2.1 Introduction

Microorganisms are a highly diverse group of organisms, inhabit almost every environment on Earth, and play critical roles within their environment. As such, microbial ecology has spent much time attempting to understand the roles and impact that microorganisms have on their environment and how environmental conditions, in turn, impact microbial community functions. One important aspect of this is the constantly changing environmental conditions that microorganisms face. Both natural and artificial systems are prone to environmental perturbation, which can stress microbial communities, impact their activity, and have negative consequences for both natural and industrial bioprocesses. Numerous conditions can cause stress to bacteria, including changes in physiochemical and chemical parameters (e.g., temperature, pressure, turgor pressure, radiation, pH, osmolite–salt concentration, oxygen, and redox state), nutritional deprivation (e.g., carbon, phosphate, nitrogen, glucose, and amino acids), and the presence of toxic substances (e.g., toxins, antibiotics, heavy metals, and mutagens). Microbial cells have only a minimal ability to remove themselves from stressful environments or to modify their environments. Most of their stress response strategies are designed to limit exposure or the consequences of exposure to the cell. Microbes can eliminate the stressor by adjusting intracellular osmolarity to compensate, degrade, or secrete the stressor to get rid of it, or scavenge for missing nutrients. Microbes can also repair damage to DNA or proteins caused by the stressor. Finally, microbes can attempt to escape from the stressor by chemotactic movements toward or away from attractants or repellents, respectively, forming spores or capsules to await better environmental conditions, or adapting to the stressor through either morphological changes or developing resistance mechanisms. 

Extensive studies in microorganisms such as Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis (Schweder and Hecker, 2004; Wick and Egli, 2004) have demonstrated that the microbial stress response is controlled by a complex global regulatory network. Regulation at the transcriptional or posttranscriptional levels via DNA, RNA, protein, alternative sigma factors (regulatory subunits in the binding of the RNA polymerase complex to their promoter sequences), two-component systems (the basic stimulus– response coupling mechanisms allowing organisms to sense and respond to changes in the environment; see Section 3), and small-molecular-weight molecules such as (p)ppGpp (see Chapter 7.1) ensures an effective response to and survival in changing environmental conditions (Wick and Egli, 2004; Zhou et al., 2011). General stress responses or nonspecific protective stress responses have also been identified. 

There is great interest in better understanding how these stressors impact environmental processes since microorganisms are so important to ecosystem functioning and are involved in global biogeochemical cycling of carbon, nitrogen, sulfur, phosphorous, and various metals. However, their extraordinary diversity (estimates range from 2000 to 54,000 microbial species per gram of soil (Hong et al., 2006; Roesch et al., 2007; Schloss and Handelsman, 2006; Torsvik et al., 2002), 1400 phylotypes in the upper oceans (Rusch et al., 2007), and at least 500 phylotypes in the human intestine (Eckburg et al., 2005)) and the uncultivated status of most microorganisms (>99%; Amann et al., 1995; Fuhrman and Steele, 2008; Whitman et al., 1998) make it difficult to study environmental microorganisms using traditional culture-based methods. There are many culture-independent methods available from lowresolution analyses like denaturing gradient gel electrophoresis (DGGE) and terminal-restriction fragment length polymorphism (T-RFLP) to high-resolution, high-throughput methods such as next-generation gene amplicon sequencing and metagenomics sequencing. As cost has decreased and data output has increased, high-throughput sequencing has become a popular option for microbial community studies, has allowed an unprecedented look into community composition and makeup, and has allowed us to discover many unique species (Pace, 1997). However, while these so-called open-format technologies are ideal for the detection of novel species, they are also vulnerable to random sampling artifacts that result in low reproducibility and are biased toward dominant populations (Zhou et al., 2013, 2015). A “closed-format” technology, such as microarrays, is less susceptible to these problems and can be ideal for comparing two or more communities since this allows interrogating the communities against the same genes and species (Zhou et al., 2015). 

## 2.2.2 Microarrays

Microarrays are similar in concept to Northern and Southern blots where target nucleic acids are attached to a membrane and are then hybridized with a labeled probe. This is reversed in microarrays. Probes are attached to the array surface, and then labeled target nucleic acid is hybridized to the probes. The array surface is typically glass (Rhee et al., 2004; Taroncher-Oldenburg et al., 2003; Tiquia et al., 2004) since it has low background fluorescence (Schena et al., 1995, 1996) and allows a high probe density (Ehrenreich, 2006), although nylon can also be used (Steward et al., 2004). 

The first microarray was developed a couple of decades ago, and it was designed to monitor gene expression in the plant Arabidopsis thaliana (Schena et al., 1995). A later design from the same group demonstrated the potential of microarrays for use in environmental studies (Guschin et al., 1997). Several types of arrays have since been developed that can be used to examine microbial communities, including phylogenetic oligonucleotide arrays, which contain probes for conserved genes used for taxa detection; functional gene arrays (FGAs), which contain probes for key functional genes involved in various processes of interest; community genome arrays, which use whole-genomic DNA as probes; metagenomic arrays, which contain probes created from clone libraries of environmental DNA; and whole-genome open reading frame (ORF) arrays, which contain probes targeting all ORFs in one or more genomes. Currently available arrays can contain up to a million probes across an area less than the size of a microscope slide. 

## 2.2.3 Functional gene microarrays

The lack of cultured microorganisms, high microbial diversity, and metabolic flexibility of microbial communities has limited our ability to know the exact functions of most microorganisms (Fitter et al., 2005). As such, FGAs are particularly useful for environmental samples since they can provide detailed functional information for a given community. The first FGA proof-of-concept array used polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplicon probes to target N-cycling genes (nirS, nirK, amoA, and pmoA) (Wu et al., 2001). Later FGA versions switched to oligonucleotide probes, which have higher specificity (Zhou, 2003) and are customizable (Denef et al., 2003; Gentry et al., 2006; Zhou, 2003). Many different FGA designs have been reported over the past 15 years to target specific functions – such as antibiotic resistance (Call et al., 2003), organic contaminant degradation and metal resistance (Rhee et al., 2004), N-cycling (Jenkins et al., 2004; McGrath et al., 2008; Steward et al., 2004; Taroncher-Oldenburg et al., 2003; Tiquia et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2006), methanotrophs (Bodrossy et al., 2003, 2006; Stralis-Pavese et al., 2004), pathogens (Cleven et al., 2006; Jaing et al., 2008; Kostic´ et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2008; Palka-Santini et al., 2009), nodC variants (Bontemps et al., 2005), and stress response (A Zhou et al., 2013) – or specific environments, such as acid mine drainage sites (Yin et al., 2007) and human body sites (Tu et al., 2014a). A few designs have tried to encompass a greater functional diversity. The GeoChip arrays were initially designed to provide a truly comprehensive FGA probe set and one with sufficient probe specificity to distinguish between genes with high homologies (He et al., 2007). Several new versions of GeoChip have been reported (He et al., 2010; Tu et al., 2014a,b), including some new gene groups or environments, such as the human microbiome (Tu et al., 2014a), pathogens (Lee et al., 2013), and stress response genes (A Zhou et al., 2013). The remainder of this chapter will focus on the design and application of the StressChip FGA. 

## 2.2.4 The StressChip FGA

## 2.2.4.1 Design overview

The general gene selection and design process described throughout Section 2.2.4 is applicable to most FGA designs, but the details are specific to the GeoChip and related FGAs. The first step in FGA design is selecting what genes will be covered on the array. Ideally, the selected genes should code for proteins or enzymes that are specific to the process of interest, are vital to the process, and, if a multicomponent or multistep process, contain catalytic subunits or active sites. Once the gene has been selected, sequences can be obtained from public databases (e.g., GenBank) using keywords. The keywords should be chosen carefully because gene annotation can vary across microorganisms or be more general or specific, so broad keywords are generally best. The sequences are then downloaded and evaluated using HMMER alignment (http://hmmer.wustl.edu) with seed sequences, which are those sequences whose protein identity and function have been experimentally confirmed. Seed sequences are a critical component in the design process since they help filter out similar but incorrect sequences, and so they should be carefully selected. Sequences passing HMMER 2.3.2 (Ashburn, VA, USA) alignment are then used to design gene-specific or group-specific 50-mer oligonucleotide probes using an updated version of CommOligo (Li et al., 2005). Experimentally established probe design criteria include sequence homology (≤90% identity for gene-specific; ≥96% for group-specific), continuous stretch length (≤20 bases for genespecific; ≥35 for group-specific), and free energy $( \geq - 3 5$ k J mol−1 for gene-specific; $\leq - 6 0$ kJ mol−1 for group-specific) (He et al., 2005b; Liebich et al., 2006). The designed probes (50-mer) are then verified using ProbeChecker, an in-house software program, and then blasted against the GenBank database to confirm specificity. The final probe list can then be used for a commercially printed array or synthesized to produce in-house arrays. 

## 2.2.4.2 General microarray qualities

A great deal of progress has been made since 2000 with regard to microarray technology for studying environmental communities (Adey et al., 2002; Gao et al., 2007; He et al., 2007, 2010; He and Zhou, 2008; Liang et al., 2010; Liebich et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2011; Ning et al., 2009; Rhee et al., 2004; Tu et al., 2014b; Wang et al., 2011; Wu et al. 2001, 2006; Xie et al., 2012). However, several challenges and key issues remain. 

## 2.2.4.2.1 Specificity and sensitivity

Both specificity and sensitivity are important for microarray analysis of environmental samples. However, to increase one often results in decreasing the other. As such, a balance must be struck so that both are optimized within an acceptable range. Specificity is largely controlled by probe design, while sensitivity is primarily controlled by hybridization conditions. Design of specific probes can be difficult because so many environmental sequences are unknown and those that are known are highly similar (homologous genes). As mentioned in Section 2.2.4.1, experimentally determined criteria have been established based on similarity, stretch, and free energy (He et al., 2005a, 2007, 2010; Liebich et al., 2006; Tu et al., 2014b), which allows for highly specific probe design. Previous estimates suggest a detection limit of about 5% of the microbial community (Bodrossy et al., 2003). Sensitivity of both PCR amplicon–based probes and 50-mer oligo probes designed using the above criteria was 1 ng of pure genomic DNA or 25 ng of community DNA (Rhee et al., 2004; Tiquia et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2001). Sensitivity can be increased by using longer probes, (Denef et al., 2003; He et al., 2005a), although this decreases specificity (Relogio´ et al., 2002). Increasing the amount of probe per spot may increase sensitivity (Cho and Tiedje 2002; Relogio ´ et al., 2002; Zhou and Thompson 2002), although this may cause a lower signal intensity (Denef et al., 2003), which would effectively counteract any gain in sensitivity. 

Specificity and sensitivity also can be adjusted by altering hybridization conditions and therefore stringency. Hybridization stringency is generally controlled by temperature or formamide concentration. For example, at $6 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ hybridization occurred for sequences with similarities >87%, while at $4 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ hybridization occurred at 70–75% (Wu et al., 2001). 

Sensitivity can also be increased at the sample preparation stage. Whole-community genome amplification (WCGA) can increase the abundance of all community DNA (Wu et al., 2006). Representative amplification was observed using 1–250 ng of community DNA, but amplification bias was least when at least 100 ng of template was used. Various labeling techniques can also be used to increase sensitivity, including cyanine dye–doped nanoparticles (Liu et al., 2011; Zhou and Zhou, 2004) or tyramide signal amplification labeling (Denef et al., 2003), both of which increased sensitivity up to 10-fold. 

## 2.2.4.2.2 Quantitative ability

There is evidence that microarray results provide some quantitative data. Oligonucleotide probes (50-mer) provided a linear relationship $( r = 0 . 9 8 – 0 . 9 9 )$ over an 8–1000 ng concentration range (Tiquia et al., 2004). Similarly, RNA hybridization has also shown linearity over the range of 50–100 ng (Gao et al., 2007). Methods for improving the quantitative capability of microarrays are still needed. 

## 2.2.4.3 StressChip design

As mentioned in this chapter, stress responses can be difficult to monitor. Since it is important to understand how microbial communities respond to environmental perturbation, functional genes that are known to be involved in the transcriptional regulation of microbial stress response could be used as markers of stress response. A GeoChip-based StressChip has been designed to monitor functional gene changes related to stress response in order to monitor microbial community response to stress. Representative genes, including sigma factors, twocomponent system regulators, transcriptional factors, and key functional genes involved in specific or general stress responses, were chosen for inclusion on the StressChip FGA (Zhou et al., 2013). The gene coverage has since been expanded with additional genes and updated sequences. 

## 2.2.4.4 Gene selection

The first-generation StressChip, manufactured by Roche NimbleGen (Madison, WI, USA), contained 22,855 probes covering 79,628 gene sequences for 46 functional genes from 12 stress–regulator categories covering both general and specific stress responses from sequences downloaded in February 2010 (Zhou et al., 2013). Coverage included 46 genes targeting specific stress response pathways, including 9 for temperature shift, 4 for osmotic stress, 14 for oxidative stress or oxygen limitation, 11 for nutrient limitation, and 2 for protein stress along with 4 sigma factors and 1 gene each for stringent and general stress response. Coverage for the next-generation StressChip has been expanded to 26,325 probes for 99 functional genes covering 19 stress response categories (Table 2.2.1). The genes selected for inclusion are detailed in this subsection.

Chapters 2.3 to 2.5, 2.15 and Section 4), $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ (rpoN, the nitrogen limitation sigma factor), $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ (RpoS, which is induced during entry into the stationary phase and controls the general stress response in Gram-negative bacteria) (Weber et al., 2005), $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ (RpoH, the heat shock sigma factor), $\sigma ^ { 2 4 }$ (RpoE, the extracytoplasmic/extreme heat stress sigma factor), and extracytoplasmic function sigma factors (see Chapter 2.6). In addition, the antisigma factors, rseA $( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ factor negative regulatory protein) and rseB (a periplasmic negative regulator of σE), were included (see also Section 4). 

Temperature stress. Conditions in the environment, such as temperature, often fluctuate, so stress genes related to temperature stress were selected. Most of the heat shock genes are involved in repair or removal of denatured proteins and include molecular chaperones or ATP-dependent proteases (Schumann, 1996). Response to cold shock involves modification of the membrane via an increase in the proportion of unsaturated fatty acids (UFAs) in order to maintain membrane fluidity and induction of chaperone cold shock proteins (Csp’s) to eliminate secondary structures and restore RNA functionality (Phadtare et al., 1999). Chaperone genes dnaK, dnaJ, grpE, groES, and groEL; regulatory gene hrcA (Schulz and Schumann, 1996); the ATP-dependent protease complex genes, clpA, clpP, and clpX; and the ATPdependent protease, Lon, were selected for heat shock. Cold shock genes cspA, cspB, and cspG (Jiang et al., 1997; Mazzon et al., 2008) and the two-component regulatory system genes desK–desR (Aguilar et al., 2001) that exclusively control the cold induction of a desaturase enzyme were included in the StressChip (see Section 13). 

Osmotic stress. Microorganisms adjust to changes in osmotic pressure by regulating the cellular concentrations of osmolytes or compatible solutes (Kempf and Bremer, 1998; see Section 11). Genes from various transporter systems controlling uptake of the osmolytes and solutes were selected, including opuE (osmoprotectant uptake, a single component sodium–solute symporter with a high affinity for proline (Spiegelhalter and Bremer, 1998; von Blohn et al., 1997)); the ProU system genes proX, proV, and proW (broad substrate specificity for osmoprotectants with a preferential transport of glycine betaine and prolinebetaine (Gouesbet et al., 1994; Haardt et al., 1995)); as well as two-component sensor histidine kinase gene and transcriptional regulator pairs involved in osmoregulation, degS–degU, kdpD–kdpE, mtrB–mtrA, and envZ–ompR (regulates ompF and ompC expression; see Section 3). 

Oxidative stress. An imbalance in production and scavenging of reactive oxygen species (ROS) can cause oxidative stress (see Section 10). For this category, the ROS detoxification genes ahpCF (alkyl hydroperoxide reductase), katA (catalase), and sodA (superoxide dismutase), as well as the regulatory genes perR, oxyR, and soxR (Fuangthong et al., 2002; Pomposiello and Demple, 2001; Mostertz et al., 2004), were selected. 

Oxygen limitation. A decrease in oxygen is another typical stressor that microorganisms face. To manage this stress, they can adjust their energy metabolism to survive. For this category, cytochrome genes (cydA and cydB), activated when oxygen becomes limiting; regulatory genes for cydAB expression such as fnr and two-component system genes (arcA and arcB) (Govantes et al., 2000; Spiro and Guest, 1991); nitrate reductase genes (narG, narH, narJ, and narI), allowing nitrate to be used as an electron acceptor when under anaerobic conditions (Nakano and Zuber, 1998); and the nitrite-sensitive transcriptional repressor nsrR were selected. 

Nutrient limitation. Limited access to nutrients is a common stress encountered in the environment. For the StressChip, genes for glucose, phosphate, and nitrogen limitation were covered. 

Glucose and carbon limitation. For glucose limitation, microorganisms typically activate genes that allow the use of alternate carbon sources, such as bglP (aryl-beta-glucosidespecific enzyme II) and bglH (phospho-beta-glucosidase), for utilization of aryl-β-glucosides (Kruger and Hecker, 1995); or that limit the loss of or need for available carbon, like ccpA (catobolite control protein), which represses expression of carbohydrate utilization genes such as amyE (alpha-amylase) and acsA (acetyl-coenzyme A synthase) and represses genes involved in activating transporters that remove excess carbon from the cell. Disruption of ccpA also decreases the growth rate of some bacteria in order to limit the need for carbon. In addition, the genes csiD (carbon starvation-induced protein) and lrp (leucine-responsive regulatory protein) were included. 

Phosphate. Phosphate is essential for microbial metabolism because the majority of the cellular building blocks are phosphorylated. Pst is the main Pi uptake system under phosphate-limiting conditions, so genes involved in this phosphate-specific transport system, pstS, pstA, pstB, and pstC, were selected; as well as the alkaline phosphatase gene phoA involved in liberating free Pi from external sources and regulatory genes; phoB, the response regulator for these genes (Allenby et al., 2004; Fiedler et al., 2008; Fischer et al., 2006; N’Guessan et al., 2009; Nikata et al., 1996; Torriani, 1990; Webb et al., 1992); as well as the phosphate regulon sensory histidine kinase phoR. 

Nitrogen. There is a diverse array of N limitation regulators to control nitrogen metabolism, so only a few were selected for inclusion. These included glnA (glutamine synthase) since glutamine serves as a sensor of external nitrogen availability in enteric bacteria (Yan, 2007), and the regulatory genes (Wray et al., 1996) tnrA, glnR, ntrB, and ntrC (see Chapter 2.19). 

Other environmental stresses. Acid shock and alkaline shock proteins were included for pH stress (see Section 16). Trehalose synthase genes were included for drought tolerance in fungi and archaea. The trehalose acts as a protecting agent to maintain structural integrity of the cytoplasm under environmental stress. 

Protein stress. While not necessarily an environmental stress, overproduction of proteins such as recombinant proteins stimulates protein stress (Dong et al., 1995; Goff and Goldberg 1985) and induces the activation of the heat shock sigma factor $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ -dependent genes (Kosinski et al., 1992). In addition to these sigma factors, clpC (ATPase subunit in the Clp machinery) (Jurgen ¨ et al., 2001; Kruger et al., 2000), the regulator gene ctsR (Derre´ et al., 1999), and degP, a serine endoprotease, were selected for protein stress. 

Envelope stress. When the bacterial membrane is damaged in some way, envelope stress genes are upregulated in order to repair and maintain the cell integrity (see Section 18). Genes selected for this category include the two-component regulatory systems, baeR–baeS and cpxR–cpxA, and the periplasmic protein, cpxP, which combats stress by reducing the toxic effects of certain envelope-based protein malfunctions (Danese and Silhavy, 1998). Phage shock protein genes, pspA, pspB, pspC, pspD, and pspF, were also included. The main product of this operon is PspA, which helps maintain the proton motive force, while the other gene products serve as positive and negative regulators (Model et al., 1997). 

Other and general stress responses. Several additional genes involved in the general stress response or response to specific stressors, not related to the other categories in this list, were included as well. For a general stress response, katE (hemecatalase) (Engelmann et al., 1995) was selected, while obgE (encoding a GTPase involved in keeping low intracellular concentrations of ppGpp) and spoT ((p)ppGpp synthetase II) were selected for a stringent response (Persky et al., 2009; Raskin et al., 2007; Scott and Haldenwang, 1999; Wout et al., 2004; see Section 7). Siderophores from bacteria, archaea, and fungi were selected as antipathogen proteins; acc (1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate deaminase), which lowers plant ethylene levels and increases plant resistance to stress, and pec (pectic enzymes, which soften the middle lamellae and promote mineral and water uptake by plant roots) were selected for plant stress protection; and $h f q$ which regulates translation of some sigma factors $( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { S } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } } )$ , was selected. 

Control probes. Internal control probes were also included in the StressChip. Degenerate probes for the 16S rRNA gene as positive controls and probes for hyperthermophile hypothetical proteins as negative controls (He et al., 2010) and a 50-mer common oligonucleotide reference standard (CORS) (Liang et al., 2010) were arranged in a grid-like pattern in each array for quality control and data normalization, respectively. 

## 2.2.4.5 Evaluation of StressChip

The original StressChip design reported by Zhou et al. (Zhou et al., 2013) was evaluated using several methods. First, probe design was evaluated in silico to determine specificity. Then, gene inclusion was evaluated using metagenomic data to determine how well the selected genes were applicable in the environment. Finally, microbial communities from an oil-stressed environment were compared with a nearby community that was not impacted by oil to determine how well the array works with real environmental samples. 

## 2.2.4.5.1 Computational

To test the specificity of the designed probes, a computational analysis in terms of sequence identity, stretch length, and free energy of each probe to nontarget sequences was performed. No experimental testing was performed since the probe design method has been previously experimentally tested using synthesized oligonucleotide targets, and probes were shown to be highly specific (He et al., 2007, 2010; Liebich et al., 2006; Rhee et al., 2004; Tiquia et al., 2004). Most of the probes were well within the desired ranges of each criterion, and only a very few fell near the thresholds of 5–13% for gene-specific probes (Zhou et al., 2013). 

## 2.2.4.5.2 Gene inclusion

To determine how well the selected stress genes represent microbial community response to actual stress conditions, seven metagenomes, representing marine (stable, unstressed environment), freshwater (low-stress environment), nonmarine saline and alkaline (unstable, stressed environment), and desert soil (unstable, stressed environment), were downloaded from the Joint Genome Institute Integrated Microbial Genomes (IMG) database (http://img.jgi.doe.gov/cgi-bin/m/main.cgi), and the distribution of the 46 stress genes was examined (Figure 2.2.1). Gene distribution clustered by environment, with the unstressed samples in one clade and the stressed samples in a second clade, which in turn showed additional clustering by location (desert samples together). More stressful environments were enriched in regulatory genes, while the saline-water and marine environments were enriched in osmotic stress genes as would be expected due to the high salinity in these environments. The desert environments were enriched in nutrient limitation genes. 

## 2.2.4.5.3 Real-world sample

Several steps are necessary for StressChip hybridization and analysis. These steps are described in detail here and in Section 2.2.5. 

For target preparation and hybridization, high-quality nucleic acid is critical for microarray success. There are many DNA extraction kits available that will provide high-quality DNA, but a frequently used kit is the PowerSoil DNA Isolation kit (MoBio, Carlsbad, CA, USA). This has been used for many GeoChip studies and has provided good results. For soils that are difficult to extract or purify, a modified method is available (http://ieg.ou.edu/protocol.htm), and a well-established freezegrind method can also be used (Hurt et al., 2001; Zhou et al.,

1996). The freeze-grind protocol is especially useful if large fragments of genomic DNA are necessary or for increased coverage (e.g., Gram-positive bacteria can be difficult to lyse using some extraction methods). The final DNA should have $\mathrm { A } _ { 2 6 0 } { : } \mathrm { A } _ { 2 8 0 } { > } 1 . 8$ and $\mathrm { A } _ { 2 6 0 } { : } \mathrm { A } _ { 2 3 0 } { > } 1 . 7 { : }$ the $\mathrm { A } _ { 2 6 0 } { : } \mathrm { A } _ { 2 3 0 }$ is most important for microarray success (Ning et al., 2009), so obtaining highly pure DNA is critical. A high $\mathrm { A } _ { 2 3 0 }$ reading could indicate contamination with EDTA, carbohydrates, phenol, or guanidine HCL (NanoDrop, 2007). If additional purification is needed, several purification kits are available, and for samples that are difficult to purify using kit methods, such as those high in humics, an agarose gel purification followed by a phenol–chloroform–butanol extraction works well if there is a large amount of DNA available, as is often the case for soil samples (Xie et al., 2012). Any impurities remaining in the DNA can inhibit subsequent downstream applications such as amplification, labeling, and hybridization. 

For GeoChip-type arrays (including the StressChip), 1 μg of DNA is needed for hybridization. If there is insufficient DNA, 

WCGA can be used to increase the amount of DNA available for hybridization from small amounts of template (ideally, 100 ng) (Wu et al., 2006). WCGA provides a sensitive (10 fg detection limit) and representative amplification (<0.5% of amplified genes showed >twofold difference from unamplified ones) (Wu et al., 2006). 

Most FGA studies, including the GeoChip-type arrays, use DNA, which can provide a snapshot of the community structure and functional potential. Some activity information can be inferred from these data if comparing two or more communities, especially across a timeline, based on gene abundance. An increased abundance of one gene group under specific conditions or with time suggests that that population is increasing and likely active. However, to truly look at microbial activity, messenger RNA (mRNA) is necessary. However, environmental community mRNA is difficult to work with due to its relatively low abundance and short turnover rates. However, several methods are available for extraction of environmental community RNA (Burgmann et al., 2003; Hurt et al., 2001; McGrath et al., 2008). Much larger amounts of RNA are required for hybridization (∼10 μg) since mRNA accounts for only about 10% of total RNA. Purified RNA should have $\mathrm { A } _ { 2 6 0 } { : } \mathrm { A } _ { 2 8 0 } > 1 . 9 0$ and $\mathrm { A } _ { 2 6 0 } { : } \mathrm { A } _ { 2 3 0 } > 1 { . } 7 0$ . As with DNA, if insufficient RNA is available, whole-community RNA amplification (WCRA) (Gao et al., 2007) can be used. WCRA uses a fusion primer composed of a short (6–9) set of random nucleotides and a T7 promoter. Commercially available kits can also be used for this step. Amplification of 50–100 ng of total RNA resulted in a representative amplification that maintained the original relationship of mRNA (Gao et al., 2007). Stable isotope probing has also been used to monitor active community members (Leigh et al., 2007). 

The resultant nucleic acid is then labeled with fluorescent dyes $( \mathrm { e . g . , \ C y 3 }$ and Cy5). For DNA, random priming with the Klenow fragment of DNA polymerase is used (He et al., 2010; Tu et al., 2014a; Wu et al., 2006). RNA is labeled using SuperscriptTM II/III RNase H-reverse transcriptase (He et al., 2005b). The labeled nucleic acids are then purified and dried for hybridization. The labeled nucleic acid is suspended in hybridization buffer. GeoChip-type arrays (versions <5.0) are generally hybridized at $4 2 { - } 5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and 40–50% formamide (He et al., 2007, 2010; Tu et al., 2014b). The hybridization stringency can be modified by temperature and formamide concentration to detect more or less diverse sequences. For every 1% of formamide added, the effective hybridization temperature increases $0 . 6 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ GeoChip 5 and later arrays are manufactured by Agilent (Santa Clara, CA, USA). Agilent’s array chemistry, hybridization buffer composition, and hybridization mechanics (i.e., bubble mixing) require different temperature and formamide settings. For Agilent-produced FGAs, hybridizations are performed at $6 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and 10% formamide. A detailed description of the new Agilent GeoChip protocol is available in Van Nostrand et al. (2015) 

Depending on the design and manufacturer, FGA hybridization can be carried out across a range of instrumentation from fully manual methods to completely automated ones. Manual hybridizations can be performed using a water bath or hybridization oven and specially designed hybridization chambers. The Agilent arrays use a more manual method using a rotating hybridization oven to provide mixing. Other hybridization stations provide incubation at controlled temperatures and mixing (e.g., Mai $\operatorname { T a i } ^ { \circledast }$ from SciGene (Sunnyvale, CA, USA) and SlideBooster from Advalytix (Munich, Germany)) or are completely automated from prehybridization through posthybridization washes (e.g., Tecan HS4800Pro from TECAN US (Mannedorf, Switzerland)). ¨ 

After hybridization, the array is imaged using a microarray scanner with a resolution of 10 μm or better (GeoChip <4.0, 10 μm; GeoChip 4.0 and greater, 2–3 μm). The image is then digitally analyzed by quantifying the pixel density (intensity) of each spot using microarray-analysis software. The software can also be used to evaluate spot quality with predetermined criteria and flag poor- or low-quality spots for later removal. Distinguishing a positive spot from background noise is generally based on the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR; SNR = (signal mean − background mean) / background standard deviation). However, other calculations can be used instead of SNR. He and Zhou (2008) developed a signal-to-both-standard-deviations ratio (SSDR; SSDR = (signal mean − background mean) / (signal standard deviation − background standard deviation)), which resulted in fewer false positives and negatives than the SNR calculation. 

## 2.2.5 GeoChip data analysis pipeline

A GeoChip data analysis pipeline (http://ieg.ou.edu/entrance .html) is available to take the raw data and assess the quality of individual spots, evenness of control spots across the array, and background levels. Poor-quality spots and outliers (those positive spots with (signal – mean signal intensity of all replicate spots [from replicate arrays]) > three times the replicate spots signal standard deviation (He and Zhou, 2008)) are removed. The signal intensities are normalized first based on the CORS signal across the array to remove hybridization variation. Since the same amount of DNA is loaded on each array, the total signal of each array would be expected to be equal, so the arrays are then normalized by the total signal intensity of all sample probes (select the highest array value within the experimental group, and scale the other samples up to this same total signal sum). The data can then be stored for further statistical analysis using the data analysis pipeline. After normalization, poor spots, those with an SNR or signal below a given threshold, are removed. 

StressChip analysis. For the StressChip evaluation, the array was manufactured by Roche Nimblegen (Madison, WI, USA) on their 12-plex format. Water samples from the Gulf of Mexico were collected in 2010 from May 27 to June 2 at a depth of 1099–1219 m and filtered with 0.22 μm polyethylsulfone membrane filters (Hazen et al., 2010). Eight samples (BM053, BM054, BM057, BM058, BM064, OV201, OV401, and OV501) from the oil plume and five samples (OV003, OV004, OV009, OV013, and OV014) from a nonplume area were examined. Approximately 100 ng of the DNA was amplified using WCGA, and then 2 μg of the product (2.8–3.3 μg) was labeled with Cy3 and dried as described previously (Wu et al., 2006). Dried DNA was rehydrated with 2.68 μL sample tracking control (Roche NimbleGen) to confirm sample identity, incubated at $5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 5 min, and vortexed; and then hybridization buffer (7.32 μL; 40% formamide, 25% SSC, 1% SDS, 2% Cy5-labeled CORS target, and 2.38% Cy3-labeled alignment oligo; NimbleGen) was added and further incubated at $9 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 5 min, and then maintained at $4 2 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ until loading onto the array and hybridization at $4 2 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 16 hours on a MAUI hybridization station with mixing (BioMicro Systems, Salt Lake City, UT, USA). The hybridized arrays were scanned using a NimbleGen MS200 microarray scanner at 100% laser power photomultiplier tube settings. Spots with an SNR less than 2.0 or that were detected in only one sample were removed.

Figure 2.2.2 Canonical correspondence analysis of the relationship between the stress response genes of seawater microbial communities (symbols) and environmental factors (arrows). Reprinted with permission from Zhou et al. (2013). Copyright 2015 American Chemical Society.


StressChip evaluation of oil-impacted communities. Of the 22,855 probes on the StressChip, 1744 were positive in at least some of the samples. More stress genes were detected in the plume samples than in the nonplume samples. There was clear separation of plume and nonplume samples in the canonical correspondence analysis ordination plot (Figure 2.2.2). This was consistent with other studies of microbial communities exposed to the oil near the wellhead (Hazen et al., 2010; Kessler et al., 2011; Mason et al., 2012; Valentine et al., 2010). Indicators of oil presence (total volatile hydrocarbon, fluorometer detection of oil, 1,3,5- trimethylbenzene, and small particle concentrations) were strong drivers of community structure along with dissolved oxygen and nitrate. The number of probes for sigma factors, obgE (stringent response), katE (general stress), and genes related to heat shock, oxidative stress, oxygen limitation, phosphate limitation, and nitrogen limitation were significantly higher within the plume than outside the plume. This increased abundance was consistent with other studies of the same site or with known environmental conditions at the site. For example, a decreased oxygen concentration was present in oil plume samples taken at the same time (Hazen et al., 2010; Kessler et al., 2011; Valentine et al., 2010), and an enrichment of assimilatory N reduction and ammonia assimilation genes, inorganic polyphosphate degradation, and phytate degradation genes in the oil plume samples was previously reported (Lu et al., 2012). Greater numbers of Oceanospirillales probes were detected in plume samples (10 ± 2) compared to nonplume samples (5 ± 2), consistent with the observed enrichment of this species with hydrocarbon (Mason et al., 2012). In addition, methylotrophs were detected by StressChip in both plume and nonplume samples consistent with their detection in metatranscriptomics studies (Kessler et al., 2011; Mason et al., 2012). 

A few other studies have used the StressChip array to examine microbial communities. A study of microbial communities examined colonized soil, ventral quartz surfaces, cracks in sandstone and granite, and pore spaces of weathered sandstone in the Antarctic Dry Valleys (Wei et al., 2015). Communities in the cracks of granite and sandstone had the greatest abundance of stress genes. A similar study from this same group at a colder and drier location in the Dry Valleys found a greater abundance of stress-related genes (Chan et al., 2013) compared to the abundance observed by Wei et al. (2015), further showing the ability of the StressChip to provide valuable information regarding the stress conditions prevalent at a site. 

## 2.2.6 Conclusion and summary

These findings suggest the StressChip is a powerful tool for monitoring microbial community stress response in the environment. Results from computational, coverage, and a realworld sample analysis demonstrated the specificity of the array, the coverage of relevant stress response genes, and agreement between environmental conditions and the abundance of stress response genes. This could be a valuable tool for ecosystem management as it relates to global climate change, bioremediation, and environmental engineering.

# A revolutionary paradigm of bacterial genome regulation

Akira Ishihama 

Micro-Nano Technology Research Center and Department of Frontier Bioscience, Hosei University, Koganai, Tokyo, Japan 

## 2.3.1 Introduction

Bacteria constantly monitor physical, chemical, and biological conditions in their environment, and they respond for adaptation and survival by modifying the expression pattern of their genome. Transcription, the major step of regulation of the genome expression, is carried out by a single species of RNA polymerase (RNAP). The pattern of genome transcription is determined by controlling the utilization of a limited number of RNAPs within the genome (Ishihama, 2010, 2012). The RNAP core enzyme with the subunit composition $\alpha _ { 2 } \beta \beta ^ { \prime }$ ω carries the full activity of RNA polymerization, but lacks the ability of promoter recognition and transcription initiation. For promoter recognition, another subunit, referred to as the sigma subunit, is needed in addition to these RNAP core enzyme subunits. The fully active RNAP holoenzyme (or transcriptase) is formed between the core enzyme and the sigma subunit (Gross et al., 1992; Helmann and Chamberlin, 1988; Ishihama, 2000). The model prokaryote Escherichia coli harbors seven species of the sigma subunit, each recognizing a specific set of promoters (Gourse et al., 2006; Gruber and Gross, 2003; Paget and Helmann, 2003). Thus, RNAP core enzyme is functionally differentiated into seven species of the holoenzyme, each harboring a different recognition specificity of target promoters. 

The promoter selectivity of RNAP holoenzyme is further modulated through the interplay with another set of regulatory proteins, referred to transcription factors (TFs) (Ishihama, 2010, 2012). E. coli contains approximately 300 species of TFs, of which most associate with their DNA targets, usually located near promoters, and interact with the promoter-bound RNAP. The binding of TFs to RNAPs is generally weak, but once bound near the promoter, it leads to increasing the local concentration of TFs and thereby allows the molecular contact with RNAP. Some TFs are able to bind to RNAP in the absence of DNA, and these TFs remain bound with RNAP even after transcription initiation for control of transcription elongation and termination. 

DNA-bound TFs interact directly with promoter-bound RNAP at one of its subunits to function (Busby and Ebright, 1999; Ishihama, 1992, 1993) (Figure 2.3.1). There is a tight correlation between the mode of transcription regulation and the contact subunit (alpha subunit, contact class-I; sigma, contact class-II; beta, contact class-III; and beta prime, contact class-IV). 

Identification of the regulation targets for all seven sigma subunits and all 300 TFs is key to understanding the whole view of regulation of genome transcription in E. coli. For this ultimate purpose, we have long been involved in two lines of the research, one to identify the whole set of regulation target promoters by each sigma or TF and another to identify the whole set of sigma factors and TFs involved in regulation of each promoter. For these purposes, we have developed two experimental systems (Figure 2.3.2a). The Genomic SELEX (systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment) screening system allows the identification of regulation target promoters, genes, and operons under the direct control of each sigma and each TF. On the other hand, the PS-TF (promoter-specific TF) screening system allows identification of the whole set of TFs involved in the regulation of each promoter (Figure 2.3.2b). The aim of this report is to overview the current state of these two lines of our research. Progress reports of the initial stage of this research have been described in previous reviews (Ishihama, 2010, 2012). 

## 2.3.2 RNA polymerase sigma factors: search for recognition of target promoters

Each RNAP holoenzyme is able to recognize a specific set of promoters and initiate transcription from the promoters. The sigma-70 subunit encoded by the rpoD gene is the major sigma involved in regulation of the promoters that are associated with growth-related genes in exponentially growing cells (see Chapters 2.4, 2.5; Section 4). Upon entry into the stationary phase, RNAP-associated sigma is replaced by sigma-38 encoded

RNAP core enzyme with the subunit structure α ββ′ ω functionally differentiates in two steps: association with one of seven species of the s subunit at the first step; and interaction with one of about 300 species of the transcription factor (TF) at the second step. by the rpoS gene. The sigma replacement is an efficient and economical way for utilization of a limited amount of RNAP core enzyme (Jishage and Ishihama, 1995; Jishage et al., 1996; Maeda et al., 2000). In addition to these two major housekeeping sigma subunits, two species of the minor sigma, sigma-54 (the rpoN gene product) and sigma-28 (the rpoF gene product), are present, albeit at low concentrations, in growing E. coli cells. RpoN sigma is used for transcription of a set of genes for nitrogen assimilation, while RpoF sigma is involved in transcription of a group of genes for flagella formation and chemotaxis (Kundu et al., 1997). The other three minor sigma subunits – RpoH for transcription of the heat shock response genes, RpoE for transcription of extracytoplasmic stress response genes, and FecI for transcription of the genes for ferric citrate transport – are not present in steady-state growing cells, but induced under respective stress conditions (Maeda et al., 2000). 

The promoter selectivity of each sigma subunit has been analyzed in vitro and in vivo using representative promoters, but the identification in vivo of the whole set of promoters recognized by each RNAP holoenzyme is difficult because the majority of E. coli genes are not transcribed by RNAP alone but depend on supporting TFs to be transcribed. Transcription of these TF-dependent genes is, therefore, modulated by the level and activity of activator TFs that are involved in regulation of the target promoter. Sometimes, the binding in vivo of RNAP holoenzyme to target promoters is interfered with by repressor TFs. Recent studies indicate that multiple TFs are involved in regulation of a single and the same promoter (Ishihama, 2010, 2012). For transcription of these multifactor-regulated promoters, positive and negative TFs not only compete with each other for binding to promoters, but also sometimes collaborate to enhance the binding to the target promoters (Ishihama, 2012; Ogasawara et al., 2010).

(b) Genomic SELEX: E. coli genome DNA was sonicated into 200–300 bp long fragments, which were then inserted into a multicopy plasmid for construction of the E. coli DNA library. Figure 2.3.3 Mapping of the constitutive promoters on the E. coli genome. The distribution of constitutive promoters recognized by RpoD sigma was determined on the E. coli genome after mapping the binding sites of RNAP RpoD holoenzyme using the Genomic SELEX screening system. A total of 1975 sites are located within three types of intergenic spacer, shown on the right side: 403 type-A between bidirectional transcription; 585 type-B between one-direction transcription; and 87 type-C at the termini of both-side transcription. A total of 1626 sites are located inside open reading frames, but their possible regulatory roles remain unidentified.


One short-cut approach for identification of the whole set of “constitutive promoters” under the direct control of each sigma factor is to search in vitro for the promoters recognized by RNAP holoenzyme alone in the absence of activators and repressors. For this purpose, we employed the Genomic SELEX screening system that was developed for identification of TF-binding sites along the entire genome (Shimada et al., 2005). Up to the present time, the whole set of constitutive promoters has been determined for all seven sigma subunits. For instance, a total of 669 constitutive promoters have been identified, which are recognized by the RpoD sigma-saturated RNAP holoenzme alone (Shimada et al., 2014b) (Figure 2.3.3). The total of approximately 4500 genes of the E. coli genome are organized into about 2000 operons, but at least half of these operons are estimated to harbor two promoters on average. Thus, the total number of promoters in the E. coli genome is estimated to be approximately 3000, of which 20∼25% should be the constitutive promoters. The majority (75∼80%) of nonconstitutive or inducible promoters are expressed only in the presence of supporting TFs. Identification of the whole set of TFs involved in each promoter is, therefore, needed for identification of the whole set of both constitutive and inducible promoters on the E. coli genome. 

## 2.3.3 Transcription factors (TFs): search in vivo for regulation targets using transcriptome and ChIP–chip analyses

Complete genome sequences has allowed the prediction of a full repertoire of the TFs (Babu and Teichmann, 2003; Ishihama, 2010, 2012; Perez-Rueda et al., 2000). In E. coli, a total of approximately 300 TFs have been identified, of which more than 280 are DNA-binding TFs while about 20 TFs are able to form stable complexes with RNAP in the absence of DNA. The DNA-binding TFs are classified into 62 families based on DNAbinding motifs (Ishihama, 2009, 2012) (see Table 2.3.1 for the current list). Up to the present time, about 70–80% of the estimated TFs have been linked to at least one regulation target gene in the genome. At present, neither regulation targets nor regulatory functions remain unidentified for about 70 TFs, or about one-fifth of the total DNA-binding TFs. Even for the known TFs, our knowledge of the regulation target and mode is limited. At present, we have only fragmentary knowledge for TFs even for the best characterized model prokaryote, E. coli. 

After development of the microarray techniques for detection of mRNA levels for the whole set of genes in a single bacterial genome, the transcriptome analysis has been widely employed for monitoring the pattern of genome transcription (Hatfield et al., 2002; Selinger et al., 2000; Wei et al., 2001). The expression pattern of E. coli genome has been analyzed under various culture conditions, such as the addition or depletion of nutrients, increased or decreased temperature, after the addition of drugs and metals, upon exposure to oxidative stress, under acidic or alkaline conditions, under anaerobic conditions, inside biofilms, and within host animals. The DNA microarray system has also been widely employed to identify the whole set of regulation targets of each TF by comparing the transcriptome patterns between wild type and mutants lacking a test TF or after overproduction of the test TF.
