Microarray technology produces gene expression data of E. coli on a genome scale for an endless variety of conditions. The gene set thus identified, however, does not represent the regulation targets under the direct control of the test TF but instead includes large numbers of indirectly affected gene (Ishihama, 2010, 2012). Generally the direct targets of TFs represent only minor fractions of the genes detected by microarray analysis, because under the control of one specific TF, the genes for other transcription factors are organized, altogether forming a complex TF–TF network (discussed further in this chapter). 

To overcome the problems associated with the transcriptome analysis, chromatin immunoprecipitation coupled with promoter microarrays (i.e., ChIP–chip) has been employed for identification of the TF-associated sites along the E. coli genome. The ChIP–chip system has been successfully employed for identification of the localization of individual components of the transcription apparatus on the E. coli genome (Bulyk, 2006; Grainer and Busby, 2008; Wood, 2009). To achieve the ChIP–chip analysis of TFs, however, the growth conditions under which the TFs are present in functional forms and at a level high enough for detection by immunoprecipitation must be well defined. The expression level of most TFs in E. coli under the steady state of laboratory culture conditions is too low for reliable detection with ChIP–chip analysis (Ishihama et al., 2014). Furthermore, for ChIP–chip analysis, cells must be treated with a reagent, typically formaldehyde, which creates a covalent crosslink between proteins and genome DNA. Formaldehyde, a highly toxic carbonyl compound, reacts as an electrophile with the side chains of Arg and Lys, resulting in the formation of glycation end products, and causes protein–protein and protein–DNA crosslinks in vivo (Orlando et al., 1997). As a stress response to formaldehyde treatment, the distribution of TFs changes even during formaldehyde treatment (Huyen et al., 2009). The ChIP–chip system is being revised so as to minimize the time and concentration of formaldehyde treatment for application to bacterial systems (Ishihama, A., unpublished). 

## 2.3.4 Transcription factors (TFs): search in vitro for regulation targets using the Genomic SELEX screening system

The majority of genes that show altered expression pattern in TF mutants, however, represent the set of genes indirectly affected (Ishihama, 2010, 2012). One short-cut approach for the identification of regulation targets under the direct control of a test TF is to determine its binding sites on the genome because bacterial TFs generally bind to recognition sequences located near the regulation target promoters. Identification of the connections between TFs and their DNA-binding sites represents a major bottleneck for modeling transcriptional regulatory networks. Thus, the first step of a bottom-up approach toward understanding the regulatory network is to make the connection list of all TFs and their DNA recognition motifs in the genome. 

For a quick search of DNA sequences that are recognized by DNA-binding proteins, the elegant SELEX system was developed, in which DNA–protein complexes were isolated from mixtures of a test DNA-binding protein and a pool of synthetic oligonucleotides of all possible sequences, subsequently followed by sequencing of protein-bound DNA fragments (Ellington and Szostak, 1990; Tuerk and Gold, 1990). Typically, the starting DNA library used for screening contained 4n different sequences, where n represents the length of nucleotide residues of the DNA probes. Upon increase in the chain length, however, the number of probe species increase, and as a result, it becomes difficult to solve all the long-sized probes at the effective concentration needed for TF binding. To overcome the solubility problem, mixtures of genome DNA fragments can be used in place of synthetic oligonucleotide mixtures because the binding sites of test TFs are located on the E. coli genome (Gold et al., 1997; Shimada et al., 2005; Singer et al., 1997). 

In order to search for regulation targets of hitherto uncharacterized putative TFs as well as to identify the whole set of targets by known TFs, we have developed an improved method, Genomic SELEX (Figure 2.3.2b), and initiated a systematic search for DNA sequences recognized by each of all 300 species of the DNA-binding TF from E. coli. For determination of the sequences of protein-bound SELEX DNA fragments, two procedures are employed, SELEX-clos (cloning and sequencing) and SELEX-chip (mapping by a tilling array consisting of 43,450 species of a 60 base pair (bp) long oligonucleotide probe aligned at 160 bp intervals along the E. coli genome) (see Figure 2.3.2b). Genomic SELEX has been employed for identification of the whole set of regulation targets of each of seven sigma factors and each of approximately 300 TFs. The assembly of SELEX patterns indicates that TFs and their regulation target genes and operons are generally located near each other on the genome. Such distance constraints may arise from horizontal gene transfer (Mironov et al., 1999; Tan et al., 2007). The Genomic SELEX search supports the prediction that TFs and their regulated genes tend to evolve concurrently. The TF–target sets were then interconnected through cross-talks between different TF–target systems. 

The Genetic SELEX screening is particularly useful for identification of the regulation targets of uncharacterized TFs, for which no information is available for screening the mutant phenotype. In fact, through using the SELEX-chip system, the regulatory roles and regulation target genes have been identified for a number of uncharacterized TFs (Table 2.3.2).

Genomic SELEX screening is a useful short-cut system for identification of the regulatory functions of hitherto uncharacterized TFs. A systematic search is in progress, and some results have been published as listed in this table. PG, peptidoglycan; TF, transcription factor. 


Combination of the SELEX-clos and SELEX-chip patterns provides not only a more reliable set of regulation targets by the test TF but also the order of binding affinity between the predicted targets because both the number of SELEX-clos clones and the peak heights of SELEX-chips correlate with the affinity of TF to each target. The fraction of known targets successfully identified by Genomic SELEX screening varies depending on the test TFs, mainly because the current databases’ E. coli TFs such as RegulonDB (Gama-Castro et al., 2008; Salgado et al., 2006) include regulation targets with different levels of accuracy, some being predicted in silico simply based on the presence of sequences similar to the recognition sequence by TFs but without experimental confirmations. Genomic SELEX screening allows the identification of a whole set of potential binding sites for one specific TF, whereas the actual binding sites of the test TF under a given culture condition can be identified by ChIP–chip analysis. 

Identification of in silico transcription regulatory signals in bacterial genomes is still a difficult problem of bioinformatics because of the lack of algorithms capable of making reliable predictions. The initial computer analysis of TF-binding sequences produced a huge number of false positives. However, once the list of recognition and association sequences by TFs is established after Genomic SELEX, a more accurate consensus sequence can be deduced, which can afterward be used for in silico search of additional targets using the whole genome sequence. 

## 2.3.5 Functional classification of TFs

In classical molecular genetic studies, E. coli promoters were believed to be regulated by a single specific regulatory protein, either a repressor or an activator, as originally identified in the lac operon regulation by LacI repressor (Reznikoff, 1992). Accordingly, most of TFs in E. coli have been believed to be the “local” TFs that control transcription of one specific gene or a small number of transcription units (Martinez-Antonio and Collado-Vides, 2003). Until recently, only a small number of TFs have been classified as “global” regulators, which influence the expression of a large number of transcription units that belong to different metabolic pathways, thereby exhibiting pleiotropic phenotypes when mutated (Gottesman, 1984; Gutierrez-Rois et al., 2003; Perez-Rueda and Collado-Vides, 2000). The set of global TFs includes CRP (cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate) receptor protein), FNR (fumarate and nitrate reduction), ArcA (anoxic redox control), Fur (ferric uptake regulation), Lrp (leucine-responsive regulatory protein), and NarL (nitrate/nitrite response regulator) (Balderas-Martinez et al., 2013). After Genomic SELEX screening of TFs with known regulatory roles, however, the number of regulation targets were found to be more than those hitherto identified or predicted (Ishihama, 2010, 2012), ranging from single targets to more than several hundreds of targets. After Genomic SELEX screening, it became difficult to discriminate 300 TFs simply into two groups, “specific (local)” and “global” regulators. Instead, most TFs were found to regulate multiple genes or operons, and a linear gradient exists with respect to the number of regulation targets for each TF. 

Among a total of more than 200 TFs so far examined, the single-target TFs are very rare, approximately less than 20. One typical example is BetI (betaine inhibitor) that binds to only the spacer region between the betIBA operon encoding BetI itself and the enzymes for glycine betaine biosynthesis and the betT gene encoding the betaine transporter (Figure 2.3.4a), supporting the concept that BetI represses this bidirectional transcription (Lamark et al., 1996). BetI is an unusual repressor because it remains bound to DNA in the presence of inducer choline. The majority of TFs control more than 10 promoters. For instance, SutR (regulator of sulfur utilization) was found to regulate about 15 promoters (Figure 2.3.4b), which are all associated with the genes for a wide range of sulfur utilization (Yamamoto et al., 2015). 

In the current databases such as RegulonDB and EcoCyc (Gama-Castro et al., 2008; Salgado et al., 2004, 2006), the number of regulation targets for those global regulators ranges from 30 (NarL) to at most 150 (CRP). After a systematic Genetic SELEX screening, however, the number of predicted regulation targets have increased for most of the hitherto characterized TFs. As a result, a large number of promoters have been found to be controlled by one and the same TF, altogether forming the regulon. Moreover, the genes encoding TFs are under the control of different TFs, altogether forming a complex network of TFs. Taking these findings into account, the classification of TFs could be revised based on the hierarchic TF network. For instance, the genes involved in utilization of carbon sources are under the control of two global regulators, CRP and Cra. CRP, also called catabolite gene activator protein (CAP), is the global regulator involved in monitoring the carbon availability in the environment and regulating a large number of the genes for transport and utilization of carbon sources (Harman, 2001; Kolb et al., 1993; Krueger et al., 2003). In the absence of glucose, cAMP is synthesized, which associates CRP for its conversion into the active regulator in transcription. CRP is a dual regulator, acting as an activator or a repressor depending on the position of CRP binding relative to promoters (Kolb et al., 1993; Krueger et al., 2003). The DNA-bound CRP is the first transcription factor that was identified to directly interact with the promoter-bound RNA polymerase for its function (Busby and Ebright, 1999; Ishihama, 1992, 1993). After Genomic SELEX screening in the presence of cAMP, CRP was found to bind to a total of 378 promoters on the E. coli genome (Table 2.3.3) (Shimada et al., 2011b). The major role of cAMP–CRP is the control of the genes for uptake carbon sources and for the downstream metabolism of glycolysis, including the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and aerobic respiration. Most of the transporter genes for carbon sources are under the control of CRP. In contrast, a number of the genes for both glycolysis and gluconeogenesis are under the control of catabolite repressor activator (Cra), initially characterized as FruR (fructose repressor) (Geerse et al., 1989). Cra was later identified to regulate a set of genes for carbon metabolism (Ramseier, 1996; Saier and Ramseier, 1996). After Genomic SELEX screening, Cra was found to regulate a total number of 178 promoters associated with the genes in major pathways of carbon and energy metabolism (Table 2.3.3) (Shimada et al., 2005, 2011c). All the enzymes involved in the central carbon metabolism from glycolysis to the TCA cycle are under the control of Cra. Thus, CRP and Cra cooperate by sharing the regulation targets of the whole set of genes involved in the entire pathways of carbon utilization.

TF, transcription factor. 


Likewise, transcription of the genes for amino acid metabolism is controlled by two global regulators, LeuO and 

Lrp, both monitoring the availability of leucine as a metabolic signal controlling the level of amino acids. LeuO was originally identified as a regulator of the genes involved in leucine biosynthesis (Hertzberg et al., 1980). After Genomic SELEX screening, at least 140 LeuO-binding sites were identified on the E. coli genome (see Figure 2.3.4c for a SELEX-chip pattern; and see Table 2.3.3) (Shimada et al., 2009). Interestingly, 95% of the LeuO-binding sites overlap with the binding sites of H-NS, the universal silencer of stress response genes (Shimada et al., 2011a). This finding indicates that one important biological role of LeuO is antisilencing of H-NS-mediated repression of a set of genes, which are needed in the absence of amino acids. Lrp is another sensor of leucine level, and it regulates the genes for amino acid transport, biosynthesis, and catabolism (Calvo and Matthews, 1994; Newman and Lin, 1995). Using Genomic SELEX screening, we have identified as many as 506 genes as regulation targets of Lrp (Shimada et al., 2015) (Table 2.3.3). By sensing the leucine level, Lrp regulates the genes encoding the enzymes for not only amino acid metabolism but also nitrogen metabolism, nutrient transport, stationary-phase growth, and stress response. Most of these genes are repressed by the general silencer H-NS, implying the antisilencing role for Lrp. 

In the E. coli nucleoid, two groups of the nucleoid protein exist: universal nucleoid proteins (UNPs) that always stay in the nucleoid, and growth phase– and growth condition–specific nucleoid proteins (GNPs) that appear only at specific phases of cell growth (Ishihama, 1999, 2009). All these nucleoid proteins are bifunctional, playing both architectural roles in folding and packaging the genome DNA and regulatory roles of the genome functions. H-NS, an abundant UNP, is known as a general silencer of a large number of genes, with a strong preference for horizontally acquired genes (Atlung and Ingmer, 1997; Hengge-Aronis, 1999). Each of the genes silenced by H-NS could be activated by a specific regulatory protein with antisilencing activity. One major antisilencing player is LeuO (Shimada et al., 2009, 2011a). H-NS is present in a high level of molecules per cell in the log phase but decreases in the stationary phase (Dorman, 2004; Ishihama, 2009; Tending and Bertin, 2003). Based on the Genetic SELEX screening, the total number of H-NS binding sites on the E. coli genome was determined to be 987 (Figure 2.3.4d and Table 2.3.3). Concomitant with the decrease of H-NS in the stationary phase, StpA, another curved DNA-binding H-NS-like protein, increases in the stationary phase (Ishihama et al., 2014), implying that StpA plays a role in genome silencing in the stationary phase. 

Integration host factor (IHF), another UNP, is abundant during all the growth phases at concentrations ranging from 6000 dimers per cell at the log phase to 3000 dimers in the stationary phase (Azam et al., 1999; Ishihama et al., 2014). By using Genomic SELEX screening, a total of 813 IHF-binding sites were identified on the E. coli genome (Table 2.3.3). The list of IHFbinding targets supports its dual role model, that is, an architectural role for DNA supercoiling and DNA duplex destabilization and a regulatory role for genome functions controlling processes such as DNA replication, recombination, and the expression of a number of genes (Freundlich et al., 1992; Swinger and Rice, 2004; Ishihama, 2009). HU protein is also present at high levels in both the exponential-growth and stationary phases, and thus is classified as a UNP (Azam et al., 1999; Ishihama et al., 2014), playing a DNA architectural role (by forming high-affinity complexes with curved DNA) and being a regulatory factor in DNA replication and transcription (Dame and Goosen, 2002; Macvanin and Adhya, 2012; Swinger and Rice, 2004). 

Fis, Dps, and Dan are typical GNPs. These GNP-group nucleoid proteins also carry dual functions, playing both architectural roles for folding the genome DNA and regulatory roles in genome functions. Fis is the most abundant protein associated with the growing cell nucleoid, reaching concentrations as high as 75,000 copies per cell (Azam et al., 1999; Ishihama et al., 2014), and it plays an essential role for transcription of growthrelated genes (Ball et al., 1992; Ishihama, 2009; Sugimura and Crothers, 2006). Genomic SELEX screening identified a total of as many as 1269 Fis-binding sites in both intergenic spacers and open reading frames on the E. coli genome (Table 2.3.3), and ChIP–chip analysis indicated that Fis binds to 894 DNA regions in the genome (Cho et al., 2008). As a transcriptional regulator, Fis regulates the expression of a number of growth-related genes, such as the genes for translation (ribosomal RNA (rRNA), transfer RNA (tRNA), and r-protein genes), response to external environments, biofilm formation, motility, and chemotaxis (Ishihama, 2009). Accordingly, the microarray analysis indicated that transcription of approximately 21% of genes is modulated directly or indirectly by Fis (Cho et al., 2006). In stationaryphase cells, Fis decreases to a nearly imperceptible level (Azam et al., 1999; Ishihama et al., 2014). 

Concomitantly with the decrease in Fis level, Dps (DNAbinding protein under starved conditions) starts to increase in the stationary phase (Almiron et al., 1992; Azam et al., 1999; Ishihama et al., 2014), and it covers the entire genome in place of Fis. Dps is involved in protection of the genome role from multiple environmental stresses, including oxidative stress (Mendoza-Vargas et al., 2009; Nair and Finkel, 2004). Besides the induction of stress response genes, Dps plays a role as a ferritin-like iron collector that protects from oxidative damage by directly binding free iron (Andrews et al., 2003; Zeth, 2012). By Genomic SELEX screening, a total of 624 Dps-binding sites were identified (Ishihama et al., 2016), which covers the genome surface of stationary-phase cells. 

Dan (DNA-binding protein under anaerobic conditions) is a typical GNP induced only under aerobic growth conditions (Teramoto et al., 2010). Upon exposure to hypoxic and anaerobic conditions, the intracellular concentration of Dan increases more than 100-fold, reaching levels as high as those of UNPs such as HU and IHF. A systematic search for the regulation targets by Dan, using Genomic SELEX, indicated a total of more than 700 binding sites within the E. coli genome. At high concentrations, Dan covers the entire DNA surface through protein–protein interaction (Lim et al., 2013). Dan plays dual roles in both maintenance of the nucleoid architecture and expression of the nucleoid function under the anaerobic condition. One regulation target of Dan is the ttd operon encoding L-tartrate dehydratase and the L-tartrate–succinate antiporter (Oshima and Biville, 2006). 

## 2.3.6 Level control of TFs

The intracellular levels of RNAP sigma subunits, the first-step regulation of RNAP modification, vary depending on the culture conditions (Jishage and Ishihama, 1995; Jishage et al., 1996; Maeda et al., 2000). Likewise, the intracellular concentrations of TFs are also subject to growth condition– or growth phase– dependent control. The intracellular concentration of TFs has been reported for some TFs, but each determination was carried out using different E. coli strains grown under different conditions and using different measurement systems. Since the expression of E. coli genome is determined by the relative level of seven sigma factors and 300 TFs, it is absolutely necessary to measure all these regulatory proteins within the same E. coli cells grown under the same conditions and using the same qualification system. We therefore determined the intracellular concentrations of all sigma factors and all TFs in E. coli K-12 W3300 by the quantitative immune-blot analysis with use of a collection of specific antibodies. 

The first reports of this line research included the intracellular concentrations of more than 150 TFs, including 10 species of the bifunctional nucleoid proteins (Azam et al., 1999; Ishihama et al., 2014). The 10 species of the nucleoid proteins are involved in folding the single molecule of genome DNA into the compact nucleoid configuration. Each nucleoid protein, however, plays a different role in this process, and thus the compaction state changes depending on the composition of nucleoid proteins from the exponential-growing to the stationary phase. In growing wild-type E. coli cells, the level was the highest for Fis (75,000 molecules per genome), a growing-phase-specific GNP. High concentrations were also detected for all the UNPs, (HU, IHF, and H-NS), but upon entry into the stationary phase, the level decreased for DnaA, Fis, H-NS, Hu, Rob, and StpA. Concomitantly with the dramatic decrease of Fis level, another GNP, Dps, appeared, reaching the highest level in the late stationary phase. Under the anaerobic condition, the third GNP, Dan (a stationary-phase-specific GNP), plays a major role in controlling the structure and/or function of the nucleoid. The intracellular level was also high for the global regulators, including CRP, FNR, ArcA, Fur, Lrp, and NarL. Except for about 10 species of the nucleoid proteins and 10 species of the global regulator, the levels of most local TFs are less than 100 molecules per cell under steady-state cell growth under laboratory culture conditions. However, by changing the culture conditions, such as nutrients, salts, and temperature, some TFs exhibit unique changes at the intracellular level. For instance, two UNP homologs, H-NS and StpA, exhibit opposite responses for the temperature shift: the general silencer H-NS decreases with the increase in culture temperature, whereas the level of StpA, a homolog of H-NS, increases at high temperature (Ishihama et al., 2014), implying their different architectural and/or regulatory roles. 

In parallel with the measurement of TF levels, the systematic measurement is being carried out for the activity of TF gene promoters using reporter assay systems (Yamamoto et al., 2014). At the beginning of cell growth, high-level expression was observed only for a small number of TFs. In the exponential phase, approximately 80% TFs are expressed, but the expressed TF species change upon transfer to the stationary phase. 

## 2.3.7 Activity control of TFs

The intracellular levels of TF proteins do not necessarily represent the level of functional TF molecules. At present, the increasing number of TFs is recognized to be interconvertible between active and inactive forms after interaction with effectors. Genomic SELEX is a powerful experimental system but has potential pitfalls. For instance, to achieve Genomic SELEX screening for the uncharacterized TFs, the conditions or effectors to make the test TFs active need to be known prior to conducting experiments. More than 30 TFs are organized in two-component systems (TCSs) in E. coli (Mizuno, 1997; Yamamoto et al., 2005; see Section 3.1). Each TCS consists of a sensor protein–histidine kinase (HK) and a response regulator (RR), together forming a signal transduction pathway via a histidyl–aspartyl phospho-relay. Both self-phosphorylation of HKs and transphosphorylation of RRs by phosphorylated HKs take place in vitro using purified components (Yamamoto et al., 2005), but both the rate and level of phosphorylation and dephosphorylation are different between HK–RR pairs. Furthermore, transphosphorylation in vitro takes place for about 3% of noncognate HK–RR pairs, indicating cross-talk between TCSs. Since phosphorylation in vitro of some, but not all, RRs takes place in the presence of high concentrations of acetyl phosphate (AcP), in the absence of HKs, the activation in vitro of RR TFs can be achieved using AcP. 

Most of the uncharacterized putative TFs are activated by as-yet-unidentified effectors. The identification of effector ligands that affect TF activities was not easy, but one possible approach to identify specific effectors or conditions for TF activation, the phenotype microarray (PM), may be useful; with it, the growth of E. coli mutants lacking the genes for test transcription factors can be examined under up to 2000 different conditions to monitor the utilization of various C, N, P, and S sources; survival at different pH ranges or different osmolarity; and sensitivity to various drugs and chemicals (Bochner, 2009). In fact, we have succeeded in identifying effectors for some uncharacterized TFs (Ishihama, A., unpublished). Alternatively, sets of chemicals and natural products could be used for identification of effector molecules for TF activation. Until now, a small number of TFs have been identified that are controlled by two different effectors, such as AllR (allantoin and glyoxylate), ArgP (arginine and lysine), CysB (O-acetyl-L-serine and thiofulfate), IclR (glyoxylate and pyruvate), Lrp (alanine and leucine), PurR (hypoxanthine and guanine), and RutR (uracil and thymine) (Table 2.3.4). One exceptional TF is TyrR, which is controlled by three effectors, Phe, Trp, and Tyr (Pittard, 1996). Once the new screening system for effector identification is developed, TF systems under the control of multiple effectors should increase, ultimately contributing to the expansion of a regulation network. For instance, using a collection of analogs of homoserine lactone (HSL), the quorum-sensing signal for cell–cell communication, three species of the active effector were identified that activated SdiA, the regulator of the genes for cell division (Shimada et al., 2014a) (Table 2.3.4). Recently, the activity of Lrp has been reported to be controlled by most of the amino acids, some toward activation and others toward inhibition (Hart and Blumenthal, 2011) (Table 2.3.4). These findings indicate that both the level and the activity of TFs vary depending on the cell growth conditions, ultimately leading to regulation of the genome transcription at various levels. 

## 2.3.8 Promoter-specific (PS)-TF screening

After a Genomic SELEX search, we found that most of the E. coli promoters carry the binding sites for multiple transcription factors (Ishihama, 2010, 2012), each factor monitoring a different environmental condition or a metabolic state. In some extreme cases, such as the csgD gene encoding the master regulator of biofilm formation (Ogasawara et al., 2010) and the sdiA gene encoding the regulator of cell division and quorum sensing (Shimada et al., 2013a), more than 10 TFs are involved in promoter control. In these multifactor promoters, not only competitive but also collaborative interplays take place between TFs. The involvement of multiple TFs allows the fine regulation of genome transcription. The current promoter databases indicate that approximately 50% of the E. coli promoters are under the control of one specific regulator, whereas the other 50% of the genes are regulated by more than two transcription factors (Gama-Castro et al., 2008; Salgado et al., 2004, 2006). 

In order to directly identify the whole set of TFs involved in the regulation of a single promoter, we have developed a promoter-specific transcription factor (PS-TF) screening system in vitro (Shimada et al., 2013a) (see Figure 2.3.1a). In the PS-TF system, the binding of purified TFs to the test promoter can be easily detected after PAGE (polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis) analysis. For instance, as many as 30 TFs were found to specifically bind to the csgD promoter, but not to other, unrelated promoters. With the use of mixtures of promoter fragments of different sizes, the simultaneous PS-TF screening can be performed for different promoters. The PS-TF system can also be employed for identification of effectors affecting the activity and specificity of TFs.

Most of the effector-regulated TFs are under the control of single species of the effector, but some are controlled by more than two different effectors. TF, transcription. 


## 2.3.9 Hierarchical networks of TF–TF interplays

After systematic SELEX-chip analysis and PS-TF screening, increasing numbers of the promoters, genes, and operons have been identified to be under the direct control of multiple TFs. Noteworthy is that the genes encoding key regulators for the lifestyle of E. coli, such as the csgD gene encoding the master regulator of biofilm formation and the flhDC gene encoding the master regulator of motility control and planktonic growth, are under the control of 20–30 TFs. However, these key regulators for lifestyle control regulate a number of genes encoding varieties of TF. For instance, two global regulators for carbon utilization, CRP and Cra, regulate 70 and 32 TF genes, respectively (Figure 2.3.5). Likewise, two global regulators for

Figure 2.3.5 The interplay networks of TFs involving two global regulators, CRP and Cra, for utilization of carbon sources. Genomic SELEX screening indicated that a total of 70 TFs are under the direct control of CRP (cAMP receptor protein) and a total of 32 TFs are under the direct control of Cra (catabolite repressor and activator). The regulatory functions under the control of CRP and Cra are shown in different colors: regulation of the genes for carbon metabolism is shown in green, regulation of the genes for nitrogen metabolism is shown in brown, regulation of the stress response genes is shown in violet, and the uncharacterized TFs are shown under a black background.

Figure 2.3.6 The interplay networks of TFs involving two global regulators, LeuO and Lrp, for biosynthesis and utilization of amino acids. Genomic SELEX screening indicated that a total of 23 TFs are under the direct control of LeuO (leucine operon regulator) and a total of 19 TFs are under the direct control of Lrp (leucine responsive regulatory protein). The regulatory functions under the control of LeuO and Lrp are shown in different colors: regulation of the genes for carbon metabolism is shown in green, regulation of the genes for nitrogen metabolism is shown in brown, regulation of the stress response genes is shown in violet, and the uncharacterized TFs are shown under a black background.


nitrogen utilization, Lrp and LeuO, regulate 21 and 23 TF genes, respectively (Figure 2.3.6). These findings indicate that the genes downstream of these direct target TF genes are indirectly regulated by these global regulators, and thus the genes affected as detected by transcriptome analysis after depletion or overexpression of CRP, Cra, Lrp, and LeuO mostly represent the indirect targets. 

These findings also raised the presence of a complex network of TFs that together regulating the expression pattern of the genome. The genes organized in one regulon are, therefore, often a member of other regulons, together forming complex and hierarchic networks of TFs. The most important and unique point of this study is that all the data are obtained using a single and the same strain of E. coli, under the same experimental systems in a single research group. As a result, the regulatory interactions in E. coli can now be recognized to be more complicated than those hitherto understood, and probably as complex as those in eukaryotes, involving the multifactor promoters and multitarget regulators, together forming hierarchic regulation networks. The TF networks can be connected to yield the interaction networks consisting of a number of signaling pathways. These interacting pathways co-construct an intricate network that integrates diverse extracellular and intracellular signals to ensure the regulated expression of appropriate genes in the genome at the proper time and proper level. The TF network is dynamic depending on the conditions, reflecting variations in the level and activity of TFs. The elucidation of the dynamic interplay between TFs should be a key subject in the coming age of transcription research in bacteria.

# Role of changes in $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ -driven transcription in adaptation of E. coli to conditions of stress or starvation

Umender K. Sharma 

Bangalore, India 

## 2.4.1 Introduction

Regulation of gene transcription is one of the major strategies of bacteria to adapt to unfavorable environmental conditions. The sigma factors, which associate with core RNA polymerase (RNAP) to form a holo enzyme (referred to as a holo RNAP or Eσ), provide the necessary specificity for binding of RNAP to promoter DNA sequences (see Chapter 2.3). In bacteria, all the sigma factors are dependent on a single species of core RNAP for transcribing genes. The subunit composition of core RNAP is as follows: α2, β, β′ , and ώ (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). A number of DNA-binding proteins are known to control the rate of transcription initiation from bacterial promoters by binding to specific sequences on DNA (activators or repressors) (for reviews, see Balleza et al., 2009; Browning and Busby, 2004; Grainger and Busby, 2008), by interacting with the DNA in a nonspecific manner (nucleoid-associated proteins) (McLeod and Johnson, 2001), or by mechanisms in which the transcription factors are not known to have direct interaction with DNA (reviewed by Haugen et al., 2008). Continuing with the analysis of factors influencing the transcriptional efficiency especially availability of cognate Eσ (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010), the overall scenario and recent advances in the area are discussed in this chapter. 

## 2.4.2 Sigma factors compete for binding to core RNAP

The presence of multiple sigma factors in bacteria probably helps in adaptation to varied physiological conditions because the factors respond to a larger variety of environmental signals through changes in transcription. Escherichia coli carries the following seven sigma factors, generally designated by either numbers or letters: $\mathrm { \stackrel { \sim } { \sigma } } ^ { 7 0 } ( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { D } } ) , \sigma ^ { 5 4 } \ \mathrm { \stackrel { \sim } { ( } \sigma ^ { \mathrm { N } } ) } , \sigma ^ { 3 \dot { 8 } } \ ( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { S } } ) , \mathrm { \stackrel { \sim } { \sigma } } ^ { 3 2 } \ ( \mathrm { \sigma ^ { H } } ) , \sigma ^ { 2 8 } \ ( \mathrm { \sigma ^ { F } } ) , \sigma ^ { 2 4 } \ ( \mathrm { \sigma ^ { E } } )$ , and $\sigma ^ { 1 8 } \ ( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { F e c I } } )$ (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). The sigma factors can be broadly classified into two groups: the $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ and the $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ . The $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ family of sigma factors shares structural similarities with each other, whereas the $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ factors are structurally different from the $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ family (Wosten, 1998). Despite showing high similarity ¨ in their structures, various members of the $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ family of sigma factors are known to recognize different classes of promoters (Gruber and Gross, 2003). The core RNAP-binding surface on sigma factors is conserved across different classes and consists of multiple regions (Sharp et al., 1999). The housekeeping sigma factor, $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ , is essential for survival of E. coli and other bacteria. In contrast, the majority of the other sigma factors (the alternative sigma factors), which are required only for certain physiological roles, are not essential for cell survival. However, inactivation of genes coding for certain alternative sigma factors $( \mathrm { e . g . , } \sigma ^ { 2 4 }$ of E. coli) also has been found to lead to loss of viability (De Las Penas˜ et al., 1997). The intracellular abundance of core RNAP molecules is limited, and this amount remains almost constant under various physiological conditions (Grigorova et al., 2006; Piper et al., 2009; Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). Similarly, the number of molecules of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 } , \sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ , and $\sigma ^ { 2 8 }$ has been found to be constant in growing and stationary-phase E. coli cells (Jishage et $a l . ,$ 1996). In contrast, the levels of some of the alternative sigma factors $( \mathrm { e . g . , } \sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ and $\bar { \mathfrak { r } } ^ { 3 8 } )$ can vary significantly upon entry into physiological states such as stationary phase or heat shock (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). During the exponential phase, the housekeeping sigma factor $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ in E. coli is the most abundant, followed by $\sigma ^ { 2 8 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ (which are 50% and 10% as abundant of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ , respectively). Interestingly, the $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ levels are below the detection limits during this phase of growth (Jishage et al., 1996). Yet, during the stationary phase, the level of $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ reaches up to 30% of the $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ levels (Jishage et al., 1996; Piper et al., 2009). Apart from the intracellular concentration, what determines the probability of a sigma factor’s association with core RNAP is the 

affinity with which it associates with core RNAP. Using purified E. coli core RNAP and sigma factors in in vitro binding experiments, it has been observed that $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ has the highest affinity for core RNAP, whereas $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ has the lowest (Maeda et al., 2000). In Bacillus subtilis also, the housekeeping sigma factor, ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { A } }$ , has a higher affinity to core RNAP compared with ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ (Fujita and Sadaie, 1998) or sporulation-specific $: \sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ or $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ (Lord et al., 1999; Rollenhagen et al., 2003). However, the abundance of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ or $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ during stress or sporulation is not more than twofold higher than ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { A } }$ , which means that increased levels of these sigma factors alone will not be able to compensate for the lack of a higher affinity to core RNAP as compared with $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { A } }$ (Lord et $a l .$ , 1999). The idea of competition among sigma factors for limited amounts of core RNAP has been experimentally validated by varying the abundance of a particular sigma factor by regulating its expression or by generating sigma factor mutants with lower affinity to core RNAP (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). For example, a mutant of $\mathbf { \sigma } _ { \mathbf { 0 } } ^ { \cdot 3 2 }$ with lower affinity for core RNAP showed a reduced ability to transcribe heat shock genes in the presence of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ , implying that the mutant $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ probably was unable to compete with $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ for binding to core RNAP (Zhou et al., 1992). A mutant $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ with a fivefold reduction in transcriptional efficiency was found to suppress the heat shock gene transcription defect of the $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ mutant (Zhou and Gross, 1992). Similarly, it was found that a $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ -driven gene uspA was induced, whereas uspB, which is transcribed by $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ , was repressed in a σ38 mutant. A similar effect was seen upon overexpression of $\mathbf { \sigma } _ { 0 } ^ { \cdot }$ , whereas overexpression of $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ had the reverse effect, in which uspA was downregulated while uspB was upregulated (Farewell et al., 1998). It was shown that varying the abundance of the principal sigma factor in B. subtilis, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { A } }$ , resulted in association of lower or higher amounts of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ with core RNAP (Hicks and Grossman, 1996). To conclude, the abundance of a sigma factor and its affinity to core RNAP determine the outcome of sigma factor competition for association with core RNAP. 

## 2.4.3 Reallocation of RNAP to maintenance-related promoters during stress and starvation

When bacterial growth conditions change from those of nutrient abundance to nutrient starvation, the RNAP is reallocated to transcribe genes involved in maintenance and survival (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). Although the abundance of certain alternative sigma factors increases during the shift from “feast to famine” (Nystrom, 2004), the increased sigma factor levels alone cannot compensate for the lack of higher affinity of alternative sigma factors to the core RNAP. Due to this, the bacterial cells have evolved strategies to restrain the dominant $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ transcription activity in a reversible manner, which provides an opportunity for the alternative sigma factors to compete more effectively for association with core RNAP (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). The major effectors that facilitate the switchover of transcription from $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ to alternate sigma factors during starvation are Rsd, 6S RNA, (p)ppGpp, and DksA (Figure 2.4.1). The former two are involved in inhibiting $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ -driven transcription; ppGpp and DksA, in contrast, carry out their functions by varied mechanisms such as direct inhibition or activation of transcription, or indirectly by altering the competitiveness of sigma factors for binding to core RNAP. Because the actions of all the effectors listed above facilitate the transcription of genes involved in the maintenance of cell functions, understanding the contributions of all of them together will unravel a larger picture of transcriptional regulation during starvation. The biochemical characteristics of the effectors and their functional roles in transcriptional regulation are discussed below.
