Figure 2.4.1 Transcriptional switchover in Escherichia coli from proliferation-related genes during active growth to maintenanceand survival-related functions during nutrient starvation. During active growth $, \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ transcribes the majority of the genes involved in cellular proliferation, while during stress or starvation, alternative sigma factors shown in the figure contribute to major transcriptional activity. This switchover in transcription is facilitated by Rsd, 6S RNA, (p)ppGpp, and DksA. This is a simplified representation of bacterial growth and transcriptional switchover and does not show the abundance of the molecules shown at any time in growth cycle. Adapted from Sharma and Chatterji (2010).


## 2.4.4 Rsd: An Anti-??70 protein

Antisigma factors are proteins that are involved in regulating transcription by binding to the cognate sigma factors in a specific manner (reviewed by Hughes and Mathee, 1998; Osterberg ¨ et al., 2011). Some notable examples of biochemically and structurally well-characterized antisigma factors in Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria include SpoIIAB and RsbW of B. subtilis, RsrA of Streptomyces coelicolor, FlgM of Salmonella typhimurium, and RseA of E. coli (Campbell et al., 2008; Oster- ¨ berg et al., 2011). A large majority of the antisigma factors regulate the activity of the alternative sigma factors. However, an E. coli protein, Rsd (repressor of sigma D), is an interesting exception since it inhibits the activity of the housekeeping $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ . Rsd was recognized as a stationary-phase-induced protein that could be co-purified with $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ of E. coli (Jishage and Ishihama, 1998). Pseudomonas aeruginosa–encoded AlgQ, which shows a high degree of amino acid similarity to Rsd, also seems to be a functional equivalent of Rsd since loss of AlgQ in P. aeruginosa could be complemented by E. coli Rsd (Ambrosi et $a l .$ , 2005). From initial studies, it was concluded that the maximum intracellular abundance of Rsd during the stationary phase was only 20% of the $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ level (Jishage and Ishihama, 1998); however, recent studies suggest that during the stationary phase, the numbers of Rsd and $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ molecules in E. coli are in a similar range (Piper et al., 2009). A significantly higher amount of Rsd was found to be associated with $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ during the stationary phase compared with the active-growth phase, although the number of Rsd molecules had only doubled during this period (Piper et al., 2009). The absence of Rsd in E. coli did not show impaired growth during the stationary phase (Jishage and Ishihama, 1999), nor did it show a significant difference in the transcript levels of E. coli during the stationary phase as detected by DNA microarray analysis (Mitchell et al., 2007). However, overexpression of Rsd resulted in upregulation of certain genes, and a majority of them were shown to be $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ regulated (Mitchell et al., 2007). As the phenotypic effects of Rsd could only be seen in strains overexpressing Rsd, it suggests that higher abundance of Rsd favors stationary-phase transcription (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). The rsd gene is regulated by two promoters, P1 and P2, driven by $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ , respectively (Jishage and Ishihama, 1999). Mutational analysis of the promoters in a wild-type and $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ mutant background suggested that the P2 promoter makes the maximum contribution toward Rsd synthesis in E. coli cells (Piper et al., 2009). In E. coli, (p)ppGpp might play a role in Rsd synthesis as some reduction in the β-gal activity was observed in a rsd–lacZ fusion studied in a $( \mathrm { p } ) \mathrm { p p G p p } ^ { 0 }$ mutant background (Jishage and Ishihama, 1999). 

## 2.4.4.1 Rsd promotes transcription by alternative sigma factors

Although most of the work on Rsd has focused on its property to favor $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ -driven transcription, there are clear indications that Rsd has the ability to support transcription by other alternative sigma factors such as $\sigma ^ { 2 4 } , \sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ , and $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ (Costanzo et al., 2008; Jishage et al., 2002; Laurie et al., 2003). The experimental proof for a role of Rsd in promoting transcription by alternate sigma factors, especially $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ , has come from studies involving the transcription of $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ -specific promoters either in mutant E. coli lacking Rsd or $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ or in strains overexpressing Rsd or $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ . In transcriptional studies in vivo, involving lacZ fusions to $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ -driven promoters, it was found that an Rsd mutant of E. coli showed diminished β-gal activity as compared to the activity in wild-type cells (Jishage and Ishihama, 1999). Overexpression of either Rsd or $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ from a multicopy plasmid in E. coli led to an increase in β-gal activity (Jishage and Ishihama, 1999; Mitchell et al., 2007), suggesting that increased abundance of Rsd favors $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ -driven transcription during the stationary phase. In order to study the influence of Rsd on a $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ -specific ompF promoter in a ompF–lacZ fusion background, a mutant of E. coli lacking Rsd showed increased β-gal activity, which was reversed by overexpression of either Rsd or $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ (Jishage and Ishihama, 1999). Notably, these changes could only be observed during the stationary phase and not during the active-growth phase. Expression of a mutant Rsd in E. coli, which bound to $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ with a higher affinity, was found to further enhance transcription from $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ promoters, indicating that Rsd promotes the redistribution of RNAP to $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ -specific promoters by sequestering $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ (Mitchell et al., 2007). Overexpression of Rsd in E. coli has been shown to promote transcription by alternative sigma factors such as $\sigma ^ { 2 4 } , \sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ , and $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ in a $( \mathrm { p } ) \mathrm { p p G p p } ^ { 0 }$ background (Costanzo et al., 2008; Jishage et al., 2002; Laurie et al., 2003); however, there is no information on the influence of Rsd on the transcriptional ability of alternative sigma factors in wild-type cells (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). Compared to the potent inhibition of transcriptional activity of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ by the T4 phage-encoded antisigma factor AsiA, Rsd shows only modest effects on $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ transcription in vitro and in vivo (Jishage and Ishihama, 1998; Pineda et al., 2004; Sharma and Chatterji, 2008). However, Rsd has been shown to inhibit in vitro transcription from certain $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ promoters (e.g., alaS), yet there was poor inhibition or no inhibition of transcription from other promoters such as lacUV5 or puvsX (Jishage and Ishihama, 1999; Pineda et al., 2004). Along similar lines, the transcriptional profile of an Rsd overexpressing E. coli strain showed increased levels of transcripts only in a subset of $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ promoters, while other $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ -specific transcript levels remained unchanged (Mitchell et al., 2007). The reason for this selectivity is not known since the characteristic features of promoters inhibited by Rsd are not well understood (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). 

## 2.4.4.2 Mechanism of inhibition of $\bullet ^ { 7 0 }$ -driven transcription by Rsd

Binding studies have suggested that Rsd binds to region 4 of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ , though it has been shown to interact with regions 2 and 3 as well (Patikoglou et al., 2007; Sharma and Chatterji, 2008; Yuan et al., 2008). Structural studies of the Rsd–σ70 region 4 complex have suggested that binding Rsd to $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ interferes with the core binding and recognition of the -35 region of E. coli promoters (Patikoglou et al., 2007). Rsd’s ability to interact with multiple regions on $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ , including core binding regions, probably hampers the binding of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ to core RNAP, which in turn provides a better opportunity for alternate sigma factors (e.g., $\sigma ^ { 3 8 } )$ to form the Eσ complex. Thus, in terms of the mechanism of binding, Rsd behaves like other antisigma factors (e.g., FlgM, RseA, and SpoIIAB), which by interacting with multiple regions of the cognate sigma factors prevent the holo enzyme formation (Campbell et al., 2008). Biochemical and structural data suggest that Rsd enhances $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ transcription by sequestering $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). However, poor inhibition of in vitro transcription, lack of an observable phenotype, and no detectable change in the transcription profile of rsd mutants suggest that much more needs to be learned to decipher the precise role and mechanism of inhibition by Rsd (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). Also, the reported weak interaction of Rsd with core and holo RNAP (Ilag et al., 2004) adds further complexity to the story. 

## 2.4.5 6S RNA: a transcription-regulating small RNA

6S RNA, a species of small RNA, was discovered in 1970, but it took 30 years to unravel its function and physiological role in E. coli (reviewed by Wassarman, 2007). It has been shown that 6S RNA forms a specific complex with $\mathrm { E } \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ but not with E or $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ (Wassarman, 2007; Wassarman and Storz, 2000). Ms1, a small RNA recently identified in mycobacteria, interacts with core RNAP as against 6S binding to holo RNAP (Hnilicova´ et al., 2015), signifying differences in the mechanisms of action of small RNA molecules present in different bacterial species. 

Bioinformatics-based approaches have predicted the presence of 6S RNA coding genes in a number of genomes of enterobacterial species (Barrick et al., 2005; Trotochaud and Wassarman, 2005). Additionally, biochemical approaches involving total RNA analysis and co-immunoprecipitation with RNAP have identified 6S RNA from other bacterial species (Trotochaud and Wassarman, 2005). Partial sequencing of an abundant 185- nucleotide RNA species led to the identification of 6S RNA from Bordetella pertussis (Trotochaud and Wassarman, 2005). Two species of 6S RNA in B. subtilis, with both the species showing binding to the $\mathtt { E o } ^ { \mathrm { { A } } }$ holo enzyme, were identified by co-immunoprecipitation with RNAP (Trotochaud and Wassarman, 2005). 

## 2.4.5.1 6S RNA and survival of E. coli during the late stationary phase

Analysis of mutants of E. coli in which the 6S RNA coding gene (ssrS1) was inactivated did not show any clear phenotype under various growth conditions, including growth in log or early stationary phase and also at temperatures ranging from 23 to $4 2 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in the presence of a variety of carbon sources, due to which it was difficult to assign any physiological role to 6S RNA (Lee et al., 1985; Trotochaud and Wassarman, 2004). However, the ssrS1 cells were unable to compete with the wild-type cells beyond day 1 in growth competition experiments, which suggested that the lack of 6S RNA probably leads to a growth disadvantage (Trotochaud and Wassarman, 2004). Inactivation of the ssrS gene in Streptomyces coelicolor led to defects in growth rate and changes in transcription of the number of genes involved in antibiotic synthesis (Mikul´ık et al., 2014). Though the ssrS1 gene is transcribed throughout the life cycle of E. coli, the number of 6S RNA molecules increases from 1000 to 10,000 (10-fold) during the stationary phase (Wassarman and Storz, 2000). The corresponding increase in 6S RNA abundance in B. subtilis has been found to be 5–18-fold (Barrick et al., 2005). Contrary to (p)ppGpp and Rsd, which are upregulated during the early stationary phase (Jishage and Ishihama, 1998; Piper et al., 2009), maximum accumulation of 6S RNA takes place during the late stationary phase (Wassarman and Storz, 2000). Based on this finding, it can be speculated that 6S RNA probably influences transcriptional activity during the late stationary phase (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010), which is also reflected in the growth phenotype of the mutant cells lacking 6S RNA (Trotochaud and Wassarman, 2004). By analyzing the abundance of 6S RNA mutant E. coli cultures lacking global stress regulators such as FIS, H-NS, LRP, and StpA, and based on the results obtained from gel retardation and in vitro transcription assays, Neusser et al. (2008) concluded that these proteins might act as negative regulators of transcription from the ssrS1 promoter. It was also demonstrated that (p)ppGpp does not affect the synthesis of 6S RNA in E. coli under in vitro conditions (Neusser et al., 2008). However, in E. coli cells lacking 6S RNA, (p)ppGpp was found to be sufficiently upregulated during the early stationary phase to alter the expression of a number of genes driven by $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ , including those involved in amino acid and ribosomal RNA (rRNA) synthesis (Cavanagh et al., 2010). As in the case of the rsd gene, the ssrS1 gene is transcribed by $\sigma ^ { 7 0 } .$ - and $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ -specific P1 and P2 promoters generating 6S RNA of different lengths, which are subsequently cleaved by RNAseE and RNAseG to yield the mature 6S RNA (Kim and Lee, 2004). The differential mechanism of transcription and processing is thought to help in modulating the levels of 6S RNA in E. coli (Kim and Lee, 2004). Since the upregulation of 6S RNA during the stationary phase is not compromised in a $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ mutant (Wassarman and Storz, 2000), it suggests that the ssrS1 gene transcription is mainly transcribed by $\sigma ^ { 7 0 } .$ . Interestingly, 6S RNA associated with RNAP can act as a template to synthesize a product RNA, called pRNA (Gildehaus et al., 2007; Wassarman and Saecker, 2006). The process of pRNA generations is thought to be similar to RNA synthesis during transcription involving DNA templates in terms of abortive initiation, falling off of the sigma factor, and so on. The synthesis of pRNA has been shown to take place during outgrowth of cells from the stationary phase, indicating that the process involving synthesis of pRNA helps in the release of 6S RNA from $\mathrm { E } \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ , thus relieving the inhibition. It was observed that upon pRNA synthesis, the 6S $\mathrm { R N A - E } \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ complex disintegrates while 6S RNA and pRNA undergo degradation (Wurm et al., 2010). The synthesis of pRNA has been shown to be important for recovery of E. coli and B. subtilis cells from the stationary phase (Cavanagh et al., 2012). The signal for the release of 6S RNA is probably the higher concentration of NTP inside the cell during the transition from starvation to nutrient availability (Wassarman and Saecker, 2006). 

## 2.4.5.2 6S RNA inhibits $\bullet ^ { 7 0 }$ -mediated transcription

Binding studies by co-sedimentation and immunoprecipitation demonstrated that 6S RNA interacts with $\mathrm { E } \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ , while UV crosslinking indicated that it binds to regions of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 } ;$ , β, and β′ (Gildehaus et al., 2007; Trotochaud and Wassarman, 2005; Wassarman and Storz, 2000). Overexpression of 6S RNA, a mutant 6S RNA, and 5S RNA in 6S RNA–deficient E. coli showed that only 6S RNA co-immunoprecipitated with $\mathrm { E } \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ and inhibited transcription from a $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ -specific rsd P2 promoter in vivo and in vitro (Trotochaud and Wassarman, 2005). Although it has been suggested that 6S RNA can bind to and inhibit $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ -driven in vitro transcription in assays using purified RNAP preparations (Gildehaus et $a l .$ , 2007), it is not clear whether these observations are physiologically relevant. In studies involving overexpression of the ssrS1 gene in E. coli, inhibition of transcription from the rsd P2 promoter was observed, indicating that 6S RNA inhibits $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ -driven transcription (Wassarman and Storz, 2000). In the absence of 6S RNA, transcription from some other stationary-phase-specific promoters (e.g., bolA, hya, and rsd P1) was found to be reduced (Trotochaud and Wassarman, 2004). However, in some of these cases, 6S RNA overexpressionmediated reduction of transcription from $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ promoters did not lead to a simultaneous increase in $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ transcriptional activity (Kim et al., 2004), which suggested that other regulators might be involved in the transcription of certain σ38-specific promoters (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). Analysis of the data obtained from microarray-based experiments showed that almost half of the genes expressed in E. coli are regulated by 6S RNA, thus making 6S RNA a global regulator of transcription (Cavanagh et al., 2008). A large majority of the promoters inhibited by 6S RNA belong to the category of either an extended -10 class (promoters with a TGn motif upstream to the -10 consensus sequence) or those with a poor -35 consensus sequence. Since the intracellular abundance of 6S RNA in an E. coli cell is quite high (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010), it can be speculated that the majority of the Eσ70 complexes will be bound by 6S RNA. From the published data, it is not clear as to how 6S RNA helps in increasing the $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ transcription. At this moment, there is no evidence to suggest that binding of 6S RNA to $\mathrm { E } \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ leads to destabilization of holo RNAP or, alternatively, if trapping of $\mathrm { E } \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ by 6S RNA can increase the probability of binding of $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ to core RNAP. 

## 2.4.5.3 6S RNA competes with -35 promoter region for binding to region 4.2 of $\bullet ^ { 7 0 }$

The highly conserved secondary structure of 6S RNA is thought to be critical for its binding activity since it was found that mutants lacking the structure were deficient in interacting with $\mathrm { E } \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ (Trotochaud and Wasserman, 2005). All $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ -driven promoters are not equally sensitive to 6S RNA inhibition. A characteristic feature of the promoters of 6S RNA–regulated genes is the presence of a weak -35 region and an extended -10 region (Cavanagh et al., 2008). Yet, the inhibition of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ transcription by 6S RNA does not seem to be restricted to weak promoters alone (Cavanagh et al., 2008). It has been postulated that 6S RNA binds to the active site of RNAP and inhibits transcription by preventing the access of RNAP to the promoter regions on DNA (Gildehaus et al., 2007; Wassarman and Saecker, 2006). In vitro binding studies with truncated $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ fragments bound to RNAP showed that region 4.2 of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ is required for interaction with 6S RNA (Cavanagh et al., 2008), though earlier studies had indicated binding of 6S RNA to other regions of RNAP as well (Wassarman and Storz, 2000). Thus, 6S RNA competes with the -35 of the promoter region for binding to region 4.2 of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ . Further biochemical characterization of the interaction revealed that the 6S binding region of region 4.2 of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ consists of positively charged residues in the helix–turn–helix motif. Thus, the promoter recognition residues and 6S RNA-binding residues of region 4.2 seem to be distinct (Klocko and Wassarman, 2009). It is interesting to note that many of the 6S RNA–binding residues of $\mathbf { \sigma } _ { 0 } ^ { \cdot }$ are known to interact with protein activators, which regulate transcription by binding to region 4 of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ (Decker and Hinton, 2009). 

## 2.4.6 (p)ppGpp, DksA and CarD regulate transcription

Growth of bacteria under conditions of amino acid starvation results in shutting down the synthesis of rRNA and transfer RNA (tRNA) by a process known as the stringent response (Magnusson et al., 2005; Potrykus and Cashel, 2008; see Chapter 7.1). This response is primarily mediated by (p)ppGpp, whose intracellular levels are regulated by RelA and SpoT proteins in beta- and gammaproteobacteria, whereas in others, including many Gram-positive bacteria, a single Rel Spo homolog (RSH) protein, Rel (Mittenhuber, 2001), performs a similar function (Chatterji and Ojha, 2001; Potrykus and Cashel, 2008). In addition to amino acid starvation, depletion of iron, phosphorus, carbon source, and fatty acids can also induce the synthesis of (p)ppGpp (Srivatsan and Wang, 2008, and references therein). It has been observed that a mutant E. coli lacking both RelA and SpoT is unable to generate (p)ppGpp (called $\mathsf { p p G p p } ^ { 0 } )$ , and hence is unable to show stringent response and thus continues generating rRNA even during amino acid starvation (relaxed response), a phenomenon that has now been confirmed by proteome analysis and global transcription profiles of the mutant strains (Durfee et al., 2008; Magnusson et al., 2003). In the beginning, (p)ppGpp was thought to be the sole regulator of the physiological changes observed during the stringent response; however, with the discovery and biochemical characterization of DksA, a new dimension has been added to the story of the stringent response. DksA was first isolated by virtue of its property to suppress the thermotolerance defect in a DnaK mutant of E. coli (Kang and Craig, 1990). In later years, its role in the synthesis of $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ during the stationary phase and in stringent response became evident (Brown et al., 2002; Paul et al., 2004, 2005). CarD of Mycobacterium tuberculosis has been shown to be a functional homolog of DksA by virtue of its ability to complement the loss of DksA in E. coli (Stallings et al., 2009). CarD of M. tuberculosis, an essential protein compared to the non-essential nature of E. coli DksA in nutrient-rich media, was shown to be involved in stringent response, survival during nutrient starvation, and maintaining persistent infection in animals. Mutational studies involving functional domains of CarD showed that this protein plays an important role in pathogenesis and susceptibility of M. tuberculosis to antibiotics (Garner et al., 2014). 

## 2.4.6.1 (p)ppGpp, DksA and CarD interact with RNAP

By binding experiments and structural studies, it has been confirmed that (p)ppGpp interacts directly with RNAP (Artsimovitch et al., 2004; Chatterji et al., 1998). Based on the binding data and bioinformatics approach, a large number of cellular proteins falling into five categories have been proposed to be regulated by ppGpp (Kanjee et al., 2012). The impact of binding of (p)ppGpp to all these proteins on the physiology of E. coli during stress or starvation is not clearly understood. Mutations in DksA, which can suppress the auxotrophic requirement of (p)ppGpp0 cells, were shown to have increased their in vitro and in vivo activities because of their higher affinity to RNAP (Blankschien et al., 2009). Suppressor mutants of E. coli that have the ability to reverse the $( \mathrm { p } ) \mathrm { p p G p p } ^ { 0 }$ phenotype have been mapped to σ70, β, or $\beta ^ { \prime }$ subunits of RNAP (Hernandez and Cashel, 1995; Szalewska-Palasz et al., 2007). Studies conducted to decipher the role played by another RNAP subunit, ώ , in stringent response has not provided very clear answers (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). Studies involving in vitro transcription assays indicated that ώ was required for (p)ppGpp action in vitro (Vrentas et al., 2005), and the relA gene was also shown to be downregulated in strains lacking ώ (Chatterji et al., 2007). Yet, the stringent response was not altered in ΔrpoZ cells (Gentry et al., 1991), pointing toward the redundancy of a functional role of ώ in E. coli. Interestingly, it was observed that purified RNAP lacking the ώ subunit does not respond to (p)ppGpp in vitro; the responsiveness could be restored by DksA, which suggested that probably ώ was linked to the stringent response (Vrentas et al., 2005). Based on the structural studies of DksA and RNAP–(p)ppGpp complexes, it was suggested that DksA and (p)ppGpp interact with each other in the secondary channel of RNAP, and this interaction helps in stabilizing the (p)ppGpp–RNAP complex (Perederina et al., 2004). However, the mutational analysis of the predicted (p)ppGpp-binding amino acid residues in E. coli RNAP did not support the earlier findings (Vrentas et al., 2008). Rutherford et al. (2009) proposed that DksA by its ability to bind to the secondary channel of RNAP disrupts its interactions with promoter DNA allosterically and thus does not make any direct contact with DNA. CarD of M. tuberculosis, a functional homolog of DksA, in addition to binding to RNAP also interacts with promoter DNA and unlike DksA it promotes transcription activity from rRNA promoters (Srivastava et al., 2013). The differences in mechanism of action shown by these two functionally similar proteins pose a new challenge in understanding the intricacies of transcriptional regulation in bacteria. 

## 2.4.6.2 Complementary and opposing effects of (p)ppGpp and DksA

Both (p)ppGpp and DksA interact with RNAP to exert their transcriptional regulatory effects. Generally, (p)ppGpp and DksA enhance transcriptional activity from alternative sigma factor–driven promoters, while in the case of $\mathbf { \sigma } _ { 0 } ^ { \cdot }$ promoters, the regulation is more complex (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). In case of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 } ,$ , (p)ppGpp and DksA function by a differential regulatory mechanism in which growth-related $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ -driven genes (e.g., rRNA) are negatively regulated, while the maintenancerelated genes (e.g., amino acid biosynthesis) are positively regulated (Gourse et al., 2006; Paul et al., 2004, 2005; Potrykus and Cashel, 2008). The transcriptional activities of $\sigma ^ { 3 2 } , \sigma ^ { 3 8 } , \sigma ^ { 2 4 }$ , and $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ have been shown to be dependent on (p)ppGpp and DksA (Costanzo et al., 2008; Kvint et al., 2000; Szalewska-Palasz et al., 2007). Both (p)ppGpp and DksA have been found to be involved in upregulation of $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ synthesis during the stationary phase (Brown et al., 2002; Gentry et al., 1993). Although the critical features of stringently regulated promoters are not well understood, some features that seem to affect responsiveness to (p)ppGpp are -35 and -10 DNA sequence, spacer length, presence of a GC- or AT-rich sequence between the transcription start site and -10 sequence, and the supercoiling status (Figueroa-Bossi et al., 1998; Potrykus and Cashel, 2008; Travers, 1980). Since DksA was shown to influence (enhance) both negative and positive effects of (p)ppGpp on rRNA and amino acid synthesis promoters, respectively (Paul et al., 2004, 2005), these observations have helped explain some of the discrepancies observed between in vitro and in vivo effects of (p)ppGpp. Furthermore, the effects of (p)ppGpp and DksA on $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ -driven transcription were found to be complementary, and both DksA and (p)ppGpp were shown to contribute toward $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ transcription in an additive manner. In the absence of (p)ppGpp and DksA in the cell, transcription from $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ -dependent promoters in vivo was fully abolished (Bernardo et al., 2006). Since DksA had stimulatory effects on (p)ppGpp-mediated transcription inhibition or activation, it was considered to be a cofactor of (p)ppGpp (Paul et al., 2004, 2005; Potrykus and Cashel, 2008). However, later on, when it was found that overexpression of DksA can reverse a number of phenotypes of $\mathsf { a \ ( p ) p p G p p ^ { 0 } }$ E. coli mutant (Magnusson et al., 2007), it was realized that DksA can also play an independent (complementary to (p)ppGpp) role during the stringent response. Comparison of phenotypes of $( \mathrm { p } ) \mathrm { p p G p p } ^ { 0 }$ and DksA null mutants in E. coli suggests that these two effectors play complementary roles; however, the presence of divergent phenotypes suggests the presence of distinct regulatory functions as well. For example, overexpression of DksA could reverse the amino acid auxotrophy, motility defect, and filamentation phenotypes of a $( \mathrm { p } ) \mathrm { p p G p p } ^ { 0 }$ E. coli mutant, although contrasting effects were seen on the adhesion phenotype (Magnusson et al., 2007). Similarly, analysis of fimbriation in E. coli lacking (p)ppGpp or DksA showed opposing phenotypes, although both (p)ppGpp and DksA independently as well as when added together could enhance in vitro transcription from the $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ -driven fimB P2 promoter. The apparent contradiction observed here could be explained by the increased association of secondary channel-binding proteins GreA and GreB to RNAP in the absence of DksA, which led to the stimulation of transcription from the fimB promoter. The contrasting effect of (p)ppGpp and DdksA was also reflected in the transcriptional profile of (p)ppGpp0, ΔdksA, and $( \mathsf { p } ) \mathsf { p p G p p } ^ { 0 } - \Delta d k s A$ mutants; here, it was observed that despite a number of genes being affected similarly, some genes (e.g., chemotaxis and flagellum synthesis) showed contrasting effects as well (Aberg et al., 2008; 2009. Contrasting effects of (p)ppGpp and DksA on regulation of transcription have also been observed on a stringently regulated bacteriophage lambda pR promoter (Lyzen et al., 2009). In summary, DksA and (p)ppGpp can affect cellular transcription in E. coli in a similar, independent, additive, synergistic, or even antagonistic manner (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). 

## 2.4.6.3 Presence of (p)ppGpp or DksA favors transcription driven by alternate sigma factors

(p)ppGpp is required for efficient transcription of E. coli $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ , $\sigma ^ { 3 2 } ;$ , and $\sigma ^ { 2 4 }$ and Pseudomonas putida $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ regulons. It has been suggested that by employing processes that reduce the transcription activity of $\overleftarrow { \sigma ^ { 7 0 } }$ by disfavoring its association with core RNAP, the transcriptional activity of alternative sigma factors is upregulated (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). This indirectly suggests that the presence of (p)ppGpp increases the competitiveness of alternative sigma factors against $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ in binding to core RNAP. Jishage et al. (2002), showed that the ability of $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ to compete with $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ was diminished in a $( \mathrm { p } ) \mathrm { p p G p p } ^ { 0 }$ strain, thus providing evidence for this hypothesis. In the same study, they also showed that the presence of $\mathtt { a \ { \sigma } \mathfrak { c } ^ { 7 0 } }$ with a reduced affinity to core RNAP, underexpression of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ or overexpression of 

Rsd, could enhance the transcriptional activity of $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ in the absence of (p)ppGpp in vivo. The influence of (p)ppGpp and DksA on favoring the association of alternative sigma factors with core RNAP has been investigated using $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ -driven transcription of the Po promoter of P. putida (Bernardo et al., 2006; Laurie et al., 2003; Szalewska-Palasz et al., 2007; Sze and Shingler, 1999). Although (p)ppGpp and DksA do not affect $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ - driven transcription in vitro, the transcription from the Po promoter in vivo is considerably reduced in the absence of these molecules (Bernardo et al., 2006; Sze and Shingler, 1999). It was found that expression of two $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ mutants in E. coli, which were defective for competing with $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ for binding to core RNAP in vitro, could enhance transcription from Po promoters even in the absence of (p)ppGpp and DksA (Bernardo et al., 2006; Laurie et al., 2003). Also, underexpression of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ or overexpression of Rsd could bring back the transcriptional activity of $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ -driven Po promoters in the absence of (p)ppGpp (Laurie et al., 2003). However, the outcome of the competition between $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ for binding to RNAP in vitro was not influenced by the presence of (p)ppGpp (Laurie et al., 2003). Suppressor mutants with the ability to reverse the auxotrophic character of $( \mathrm { p } ) \mathrm { p p G p p } ^ { 0 }$ E. coli cells were found to map to β or β′ subunits of RNAP, and some of these mutants could support (p)ppGppindependent transcription from the Po promoter (Sze and Shingler, 1999). The same transcription-enhancing effect of these mutants on the Po promoter was also observed in ΔdksA mutant background (Szalewska-Palasz et al., 2007). In vitro biochemical characterization demonstrated that the mutant RNAP forms favored the association of $\cdot _ { \sigma ^ { 5 4 } }$ with core RNAP (Szalewska-Palasz et al., 2007). $\sigma ^ { 2 4 }$ of E. coli is another example of an alternative sigma factor that is regulated by (p)ppGpp–DksA under conditions of stress. Expression of low-affinity $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ mutants in a $( \mathrm { p } ) \mathrm { p p G p p } ^ { 0 }$ strain of E. coli makes the $\sigma ^ { 2 4 }$ transcription activity constitutive, whereas overexpression of Rsd in the same strain enhanced $\sigma ^ { 2 4 }$ -driven transcription during the stationary phase (Costanzo et al., 2008). As seen with $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ , a mutant $\beta ^ { \prime }$ that suppresses the $( \mathrm { p } ) \mathrm { p p G p p } ^ { 0 }$ phenotype in E. coli could restore the upregulation of $\sigma ^ { 2 4 }$ transcriptional activity upon entry into the stationary phase in a $( \mathrm { p } ) \mathrm { p p G p p } ^ { 0 }$ strain (Costanzo et al., 2008). The occurrence of DksA and (p)ppGpp stimulated transcription from $\sigma ^ { 2 4 }$ -driven promoters even under in vitro conditions suggests a direct mode of transcriptional activation (Costanzo et al., 2008). An inverse relationship between (p)ppGpp levels and growth-related $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ transcriptional activity at rRNA promoters could be established with the observations that $( \mathrm { p } ) \mathrm { p p G p p } ^ { 0 }$ cells show higher abundance of $\mathrm { E } \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ and that overexpression of $\mathrm { E } \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ results in enhanced transcription from rRNA promoters, whereas transcription from genes involved in stress and amino acid biosynthesis is downregulated (Gummesson et al., 2009). Thus, it can be argued that the processes that disfavor the association of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ with core RNAP stimulate the redistribution of RNAP from the housekeeping genes to those involved in maintenance (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). The actions of both (p)ppGpp and DksA also lead to similar physiological outcomes under conditions of stress or starvation. 

## 2.4.7 Concluding remarks

Though the majority of the core RNAP during active growth is utilized by $\sigma ^ { 7 0 } ;$ , E. coli cells upon entry into the stationary phase use numerous strategies to redistribute RNAP to promoters of maintenance and survival-related genes (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). This switchover primarily involves shifting the focus away from $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ -driven proliferation-related transcription toward transcription of maintenance-related genes. The relative changes in the abundance of core RNAP, sigma factors, and the effector molecules during starvation have been depicted in Figure 2.4.2a. The outcome of modulation of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ activity by these effectors, which leads to a shift toward transcription of maintenancerelated genes, has been diagrammatically represented in Figure 2.4.2b. Rsd prevents the binding of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ to core RNAP, thus facilitating transcription by $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ and probably other alternative sigma factors during stress or starvation. Although 6S RNA has been shown to inhibit transcription in a large number of $\mathbf { \sigma } _ { 0 } ^ { \cdot }$ promoters, the exact mechanism by which 6S RNA upregulates stationary-phase transcription is not understood. Since 6S RNA traps $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ -bound core RNAP during the stationary phase, the increase in transcription by $\varpi ^ { 3 8 }$ might not be because of the availability of increased amounts of core RNAP. (p)ppGpp and DksA can regulate transcription by direct inhibition and activation, yet there is evidence to suggest that a significant increase in the transcriptional activity of alternative sigma factors results from increased availability of core RNAP as a result of destabilization of $\mathrm { E } \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ complexes by (p)ppGpp and DksA. To know whether the presence of (p)ppGpp and DksA can affect the affinity of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ to core RNAP, kinetics of binding of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ to core RNAP in the presence of (p)ppGpp and DksA will have to be performed (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). It is interesting to note that unlike the severe defects in growth phenotype shown by $( \mathrm { p } ) \mathrm { p p G p p } ^ { 0 }$ or dksA mutants, the phenotypes of rsd and ssrS1 mutants are quite mild. It could mean that (p)ppGpp and DksA play major roles in the redistribution of RNAP during starvation, while Rsd and 6S RNA are only required for fine tuning the (p)ppGpp or DksA effects (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). Both 6S RNA and (p)ppGpp have been shown to be present in Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, whereas the presence of Rsd seems to be restricted to some Gram-negative bacteria only. As bioinformatics approaches may not be able to predict novel antihousekeeping sigma factors in Gram-positive bacteria, experimental approaches should be undertaken to detect these proteins. Currently, the interdependence and interactions of these effectors with each other are not understood. However, upregulation of these effectors during different phases of bacterial growth, ranging from the late exponential to the late stationary phase, suggests that the mechanism of transcriptional switching could be temporally regulated (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). Further studies on CarD in M. tuberculosis might reveal commonalities between transcriptional changes during starvation and those during infection by pathogenic bacteria. The study of ssrS1 and rsd deletion or overexpression phenotypes and transcription profiles in strains lacking (p)ppGpp and/or DksA will help in understanding the relative contributions of these effectors toward reducing $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ transcriptional activity (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). An integrated approach for studying the role of (p)ppGpp, DksA, Rsd, and 6S RNA in transcriptional regulation by virtue of their ability to subdue the proliferation-related $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ transcription will help in fine tuning the model of molecular mechanisms of adaptation of bacteria to conditions of stress or starvation.

# The distribution and spatial organization of RNA polymerase in Escherichia coli: growth rate regulation and stress responses

Ding Jun Jin, Cedric Cagliero∗, Jerome Izard, Carmen Mata Martin, and Yan Ning Zhou 

Transcription Control Section, Gene Regulation and Chromosome Biology Laboratory, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, Frederick, MD, USA 

∗Currently at: Jecho Laboratories Inc. Frederick, MD, USA 

## 2.5.1 Introduction

The control of cell growth and stress responses is of fundamental importance to all living organisms, from bacteria to humans. Remarkably, Escherichia coli is able to grow rapidly when nutrients are plentiful; however, its growth slows down or arrests when nutrients become limited and/or it is exposed to hostile environments, leading to stress responses. Because of its sophisticated genetics, advanced biochemistry, and amenability to physiological perturbations, E. coli has been used as a favorable simple model system for many decades and has thus significantly advanced our scientific knowledge of biology (Neidhardt et al., 1996). More than 50 years ago, researchers discovered that bacterial growth rate, as measured by cell mass and RNA level, is determined by growth media (Kjeldgaard et al., 1958; Schaechter et al., 1958). Subsequent studies found that the growth rate is a function of the rate of stable RNA (ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and transfer RNA (tRNA), although primarily rRNA) synthesis, as ribosomes are assembled onto rRNAs, which are key molecules for ribosome biogenesis, and the number of ribosomes in the cell is proportional to the growth rate in order to meet the demand for protein synthesis (Bremer and Dennis, 1996; Gausing, 1977; Keener and Nomura 1996; Nomura et al., 1984). Regulation of rRNA synthesis from rRNA (rrn) operon(s) has been extensively studied, and there are many comprehensive reviews on the subject (Condon et al., 1995a; Gourse et al., 1996; Jin et al., 2012; Paul et al., 2004; Potrykus et al., 2011; Ross et al., 2013; Wagner, 2002). 

Transcription is a key step in growth rate regulation and stress responses. Much knowledge has been accumulated from studies on the regulation of specific genes and/or operons involved in bacterial growth and stress responses as well as on the distribution of RNA polymerase (RNAP) on fragments of genomic DNA from broken cells (Grainger et al., 2005; Herring et al., 2005). However, using wide-field fluorescent microscopy and other “state-of-the-art” imaging techniques, we have recently begun to understand how changing environments influence the threedimensional distribution of RNAP inside intact cells. Emerging evidence has revealed that the transcription machinery is spatially organized and sensitive to environmental cues (Cabrera and Jin, 2003b; Cagliero and Jin, 2013; Cagliero et al., 2014). In addition, changes in the distribution of RNAP in cells accompany changes in nucleoid structure, indicating an important role of transcription in the organization of the bacterial chromosome (Cabrera et al., 2009; Cagliero et al., 2013; Jin and Cabrera, 2006; Jin et al., 2013). 

In this chapter, we discuss the features of the E. coli cell and its genome in the context of differential RNAP allocation in cells in response to changing environments. We also review the progress made in studying the distribution of RNAP both conceptually and technically. The emphasis is on co-imaging of RNAP and DNA in fast-growing cells and in cells undergoing stress responses. Visualization of RNAP inside the whole cell has provided many new insights into growth rate regulation and stress responses at the cellular and subcellular levels. 

## 2.5.2 Cell, genome, and growth rate regulation

E. coli cells, such as the prototype K-12 strain MG1655, are small, rod-shaped, Gram-negative bacteria. Their size, ranging from ∼0.4 to 1.7 μm (short axis) × ∼1.0 to 10 μm (long axis), is sensitive to growth media and conditions (Figure 2.5.1). 

The E. coli genome contains ∼4.6 million base pairs (bp). If fully extended, a single E. coli genomic DNA is ∼1600 μm long.

The nucleoid is stained with Hoescht 33342. The scale bar represents 2 μm. Adapted from Jin et al. (2013).

Figure 2.5.2 E. coli chromosome map. Positions of the rrn operons, with oriC and ter regions indicated. The red arrows represent each of the seven rrn operons, all of which are localized in the oriC proximal half of the chromosome; four are near the oriC, from which replication initiates and elongates bidirectionally, as indicated by black arrowheads. Transcription of rrn occurs in the same direction as replication.


Therefore, the genome must be compacted ∼1000-fold to fit in the cell. The genome encodes a total of 4453 genes, which are organized into about 2390 operons (Blattner et al., 1997; Riley et al., 2006). The growth-promoting genes and operons, most of which encode rrn, tRNA, and ribosomal proteins, are mainly involved in the translational machinery (for simplicity, hereafter they are called rrn collectively), and they are regulated similarly. There are seven nearly identical rrn operons (each ∼5.5 kb in length) per genome, and these represent only about 1% of the genome. The vast majority of the remaining 99% of the genome encodes mRNAs across the genome, and these are regulated differently. Thus, in terms of growth regulation (or growth rate regulation), E. coli genes may be broadly defined as falling into one of two classes: rrn and other genes. 

The E. coli chromosome map shows a circular DNA molecule with only one specific origin of chromosome replication (oriC) that replicates bidirectly toward the terminus region (ter) (Figure 2.5.2). 

A unique feature of the E. coli genomic map that is significant to growth rate regulation is the location of the rrn operons. All seven rrn operons are located in the oriC half of the genome, and, specifically, four of these are close to the oriC. In addition, transcription of rrn and most translational machinery is in the same direction as that of chromosome replication (Lin et al., 2010; McLean et al., 1998; Rocha and Danchin, 2003). This co-directionality has likely evolved to minimize replication–transcription conflicts in bacteria (Merrikh et al., 2012). 

Only cells growing very slowly in poor media, such as minimal medium containing glycerol as the carbon source at $3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (a doubling, or generation, time of 168 min), contain an average of one single genome per cell (Figure 2.5.1). Because of the simplicity in copy number of bacterial chromosome(s), poor growth conditions have been exploited in studying cell cycle parameters in E. coli, including the time required by the cell to replicate a single chromosome and for cell division. Under poor growth conditions, transcription from rrn is minimal (Bremer and Dennis, 1996). 

However, E. coli is capable of rapid growth in vivo (Poulsen et al., 1995) and in vitro. Under nutrient-rich and optimal conditions, a doubling time can be as short as ∼20 min. When cell doubling time is shorter than the combined time needed for the completion of one round of genome replication and cell division (∼70 to 120 min) (Stokke et al., 2012), additional initiation(s) from oriC in preceding generations is (are) necessary before the previous round is completed to ensure that at least one completed chromosome is inherited by each of the two newly formed daughter cells (Cooper and Helmstetter, 1968). Thus, a single E. coli cell can contain from 8 to 16 copies of the OriC (Nielsen et al., 2007). Consequently, in fast-growing cells, the copy number of genes will be higher near the oriC than near the terminus region. Because of the unique locations of rrn relative to oriC, as mentioned, the copy number (or gene dosage) of rrn amplifies as the growth rate increases. For a particular gene in the cell, the number of copies can be calculated based on the growth rate and the location of the gene on the genetic map (Bremer and Dennis, 1996; Condon et al., 1993). For example, when cells are growing in nutrient-rich Lennox broth (LB) at $3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ with a doubling time of 45 min, the copy number for rrn is 18 per cell, whereas with a doubling time of 20 min (LB, $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ , the copy number of rrn approaches 50 per cell, as there are about five genome equivalences in the cell. Under optimal growth conditions, transcription from rrn is maximal, accounting for more than 60% of transcription activity in the cell (Bremer and Dennis, 1996). 

The “thrive or survive” lifestyle reflects the two ends of the spectrum in growth rate regulation in E. coli and is manifested in E. coli’s amazing ability to rapidly adapt to environmental changes in the cell. Having multiple rrn operons is found to be advantageous for the cells because it enables them to rapidly respond to changing environmental conditions (Condon et al., 1995b; Stevenson and Schmidt, 2004). While a cell grows slowly in nutrient-poor media, it becomes fast-growing when nutrients are plentiful. This characteristic enables E. coli to compete with other bacteria in the same environments. When rapidly growing cells encounter a hostile environment, their growth usually decreases or stops (rrn is turned off) because cells redirect their transcription machinery from rrn to other stress-responsive genes genome-wide. There is an apparent inverse correlation between the growth potential of the environment and the number of genes expressed systematically genomewide, as is evident when cells are growing on different carbon sources (Liu et al., 2005). The poorer the quality of carbon source used, the larger the number of genes expressed genomewide. Similarly, when rapidly growing cells are subject to amino acid starvation, leading to the stringent response (Cashel et al., 1996), transcription of rrn decreases to a minimal level and leads to the cells’ growth arrests, whereas the number of other genes expressed across the genome increases systematically (Durfee et al., 2008; Traxler et al., 2008). This apparent inverse relationship between the expression of growth-promoting genes and the number of other genes expressed genome-wide in response to environmental cues indicates that the growth regulation and stress responses can be explained by genome-wide competition between rrn and other genes for limited RNAP in the cell (Jin et al., 2012).

The rest of the DNA (between rpoBC and rrnE) contains much less RNAP, with only 1 molecule per 10–20 kb. (B) Higher magnification of the rrnB operon and tufB gene. ## 2.5.3 Competition for limited RNAP between rrn and other broad, genome-wide genes in changing environments

Several additional lines of evidence have indicated that RNAP is limiting in the cell for the simultaneous active expression of rrn and the broad transcription of other genes genome-wide. 

First, genetic studies of a class of RNAP mutants, which are defective in growth rate regulation, have revealed that these mutants grow slowly in LB because of reduced transcription of rrn, as if those cells are partially starved for amino acids, even in a nutrient-rich medium. However, the expression of some other genes, which are activated only during starvation in wild type, increased in those mutants grown in LB (Zhou and Jin, 1997, 1998). Based on the studies of these RNAP mutants, it has been proposed that RNAP is limiting in the cell and thus redistributes from rrn to other genes in the genome during the stringent response induced by amino acid starvation (Zhou and Jin, 1998) 

Second, a calculation based on the estimated number of RNAP molecules in the cell can be made. Although these estimates vary based on the growth conditions and the methods used (Grigorova et al., 2006; Ishihama, 2000), for fast-growing, exponential-phase cells, values ranging from ∼2600 to 5000 RNAP molecules per cell have been reported either by quantitative Western blot (Piper et al., 2009) or by directly counting single molecules using photoactivated localization microscopy (Bakshi et al., 2012; Endesfelder et al., 2013). Theoretically, then, even with as many as 5000 RNAP molecules per cell, there are only ∼2 RNAP molecules per operon (a total of 2390 operons per genome) or ∼1 RNAP per gene (a total of 4453) in cells containing only a single genome. The average number of RNAP molecules per gene or operon would be far lower in fast-growing cells (in LB) containing multiple genome equivalents per cell, as described here. 

Third, because RNAP distribution is dictated by the expression of rrn, the limitation of RNAP for genome-wide transcription is further exacerbated in a fast-growing cell. The iconic “double Christmas tree” morphology is the signature of active rRNA synthesis on rrn from chromatin spreads of cells grown in LB, covering more than 600 kb of genomic DNA fragments (Figure 2.5.3). 

Such a feature is easily identified on electron micrographs from fast-growing cells (French and Miller 1989; Miller et al., 1970) but is absent from cells growing in minimal media (Hamkalo and Miller, 1973a,b). The rate of rRNA synthesis in a cell reaches one initiation per second per rrn operon, under optimal growth conditions (Bremer and Dennis, 1996; Condon et al., 1993), which correlates well with ∼65 RNAP molecules per rrn operon (∼5.5 kb) (or one RNAP molecule for every 85 bp) estimated from electron micrographic images (Condon et al., 1993; French and Miller, 1989; Voulgaris et al., 1999). As described here, in fast-growing cells (LB 37 ◦C, doubling time 20 min), there are ∼50 copies of rrn per cell, which will capture ∼3250 RNAP molecules, or ∼65% of the total RNAP (assuming ∼5000 molecules per cell) in the cell. In contrast, RNAP densities transcribing other genes in the genome are significantly reduced, ranging from one RNAP molecule per 1 kb to one for every 10–20 kb. Significantly, the chromosome is mostly transcriptionally inactive, and there are regions as long as 30 to 40 kb that are devoid of RNAP from cells grown in LB (French and Miller, 1989). Thus, owing to the extremely high initiation rate and the long transcripts of rrn, the majority of RNAP molecules in fast-growing cells are engaged in active rRNA synthesis; consequently, RNAP becomes limiting for broad genomewide gene expression. 

Note that, unlike the eukaryotic nucleosomal “beads-on-astring” morphology (Olins and Olins, 1974, 2003; Woodcock et al., 1976), the E. coli genomic DNA appeared to be mostly “naked” in electron micrographs of chromatin spreads, and the most easily identified nucleoid-associated proteins are RNAP. This feature suggests that, in addition to other major nucleoid-associated proteins, including FIS, H-NS, and HU, in fast-growing cells (Murphy and Zimmerman, 1997; Stonington and Pettijohn, 1971), RNAP, and thus transcription, plays a critical role in the organization of the bacterial chromosome (Jin et al., 2013). 

Fourth, studies of the genome-wide distribution of RNAP using chromatin immunoprecipitation and microarray (known as ChIP–chip) assays (Grainger et al., 2005; Herring et al., 2005) support the redistribution model for RNAP with much higher resolution than is available with chromatin spreads. In the ChIP–chip assays, it is necessary to use formaldehyde to fix E. coli cells before the genomic DNA is broken down to about or less than 500 bp. Formaldehyde is a cell-permeable, fouratom cross-linker that penetrates cells rapidly without causing “artificial” perturbations (Cabrera and Jin, 2003b; Davis et al., 2011); thus, it preserves a “snapshot” of RNAP distribution in the genome in either one dimension or three dimensions (imaging of RNAP in cells is discussed further in this chapter). When cells are grown in LB, most RNAP is associated with growth-promoting genes at ∼90 locations in the genome. However, after the addition of rifampicin, which inhibits promoter clearance but not transcription elongation and DNA binding, the number of binding sites for RNAP increases to 529 (Grainger et al., 2005). A greater than fivefold increase in the locations of RNAP genome-wide after rifampicin treatment reflects the increase in the number of free RNAP molecules that become available for broad genome-wide binding when active transcription of rrn is inhibited. 

Together, the above analyses suggest that the differential allocation of RNAP in the two operational classes of genes (rrn vs. other genes genome-wide) plays a critical role in the growth rate regulation and stress responses. However, chromatin spreads and ChIp–chip techniques are both in vitro assays that use DNA fragments from broken cells; thus, they are unable to fully address the questions regarding what really happens threedimensionally with RNAP and the nucleoid in a single cell. For example, (i) does RNAP transcribe each rrn independently in the nucleoids of fast-growing cells, and (ii) does differential allocation of RNAP influence the spatial organization of the nucleoids during growth and stress responses? These questions can be addressed only by developing tools for studying the cell biology of RNAP and DNA inside intact single cells. 

## 2.5.4 Imaging of RNAP in cells of changing environments

Several derivatives of the rpoC–gfp fusion in its normal chromosomal location in the MG1655 strain background have been constructed to study the cell biology of RNAP using fluorescence microscopy (Bakshi et al., 2012; Cabrera and Jin, 2003a,b, 2006; Cabrera et al., 2009; Cagliero and Jin, 2013; Endesfelder et al., 2013; Jin et al., 2013). A special challenge was encountered early on during the study: the distribution of RNAP is extremely sensitive to physiological perturbations, including the one caused by the sampling process, in which cells are sampled from a rapidly shaking flask and agarose embedded on coverslips. Rapid adaptation of the cells to changing environments such as the sampling process prevents the capture of the true state of RNAP in the particular growing conditions being studied. 

This dynamic property of RNAP is in contrast to most GFPfusion proteins, such as those of single-stranded DNA-binding protein (Reyes-Lamothe et al., 2008) and SeqA (Molina and Skarstad, 2004), two components at or near replication forks as their distributions are not affected significantly by changes in growth conditions. To overcome the problem of rapid bacterial adaptation, a breakthrough technique has been developed in which cells are rapidly fixed with formaldehyde to “freeze” RNAP and subcellular structures before imaging. Using this procedure, the dynamic nature of the distribution of RNAP in the cell can be captured as a snapshot, and the results have been shown to be consistent with the genetics and physiology of E. coli cells (Cabrera and Jin, 2003b). Subsequently, this procedure has been adapted and validated in ChIP–chip assays to study the distribution of RNAP genome-wide (Davis et al., 2011; Grainger et al., 2005; Herring et al., 2005), as described in this chapter. 

In the remainder of this chapter, we first summarize the advances in cell biology of RNAP in fast-growing cells, followed by analyzing the effects of rrn deletions and different stress responses on the distribution of RNAP and the nucleoid structure. The methods for imaging of RNAP and DNA using the MG1655 derivative strain containing either rpoC–gfp or rpoC– venus fusion have been described (Cabrera and Jin, 2003b; Cabrera et al., 2009; Cagliero and Jin, 2013; Cagliero et al., 2014), and experimental details are specified in the figure legends. 

## 2.5.5 Spatial organization of RNAP in fast-growing cells

To support growth in nutrient-rich media, RNAP is primarily allocated for rRNA synthesis from rrn, and the major transcription machinery is three-dimensionally organized and duplicated in each of the multiple nascent nucleoids in fastgrowing cells.

## 2.5.5.1 RNAP foci at clustering of rrn operons or bacterial nucleolus

The distribution of RNAP is sensitive to the growth rate as determined by the growth media (Jin et al., 2013) (Figure 2.5.4). When cells are growing in a poor medium (MOPS + glycerol; doubling time, 93 min), RNAP distributes relatively homogeneously across the nucleoid(s) in the cell. The nucleoid is relatively expanded in cells growing in a minimal medium, as measured by the relative nucleoid size (RNS), defined as the ratio of the nucleoid length to that of the cell (Cabrera et al., 2009; Manasherob et al., 2003). 

When cells are grown in LB at $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (doubling time, 20 min; estimated rrn copy number, 50), the majority of RNAP molecules are concentrated as major transcription foci, and there is an average of four foci per cell in a population of cells, as determined by wide-field microscopy (the foci numbers are doubled when using a super-resolution imaging system, as described further in this chapter). Because the number of foci identified by wide-field microscopy is far lower than the estimated copies of rrn in fast-growing cells, these predominant foci likely locate at the clustering of rrn operons, which are termed bacterial nucleolus-like structures (Cabrera and Jin, 2003b; Cagliero et al., 2014). Other subcellular hyperstructures in bacteria have been described (Norris et al., 2007). Superresolution imaging of RNAP in rapidly growing cells using photoactivated localization microscopy (PALM) shows both large clusters of RNAP (up to 800 molecules), which are likely engaging in rRNA synthesis from multiple rrn operons, and small clusters of RNAP (∼70 molecules), which are attributed to the transcription of a single rrn operon (Endesfelder et al., 2013). It remains to be determined experimentally whether rrn from different locations in the chromosome is clustered with transcription foci. The nucleoids are relatively compact in the fast-growing cells.

## 2.5.5.2 Requirement of multiple copies of rrn in the genome for RNAP foci formation

Using a set of chromosomal rrn deletions (Δ1rrn to Δ6rrn) constructed by Catherine Squires’ laboratory, the minimal copy numbers of rrn required for the formation of RNAP foci in cells growing in LB at $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ were determined (Figure 2.5.5). The prominent transcription foci are evident in both wild type and the Δ2rrn strain, which has a wild-type growth rate, but diminished in the Δ5rrn strain (only two copies of rrn remaining in the chromosome), which grows significantly slower compared to wild type. Thus, having five copies of rrn in the chromosome is sufficient for the major RNAP foci formation and optimal growth. This finding is in agreement with the previous observations that while E. coli cells are able to compensate for the loss of two copies of rrn by increasing the transcription frequency (or occupancy of RNAP per rrn) from the remaining rrn operons, the growth rate starts to decrease with fewer rrn copies remaining in the chromosome (Asai et al., 1999; Condon et al., 1995b). These results suggest that there is some redundancy for the rrn copy number in the genome to support rapid growth in E. coli. As indicated by the relative RNS values, the nucleoids in wild type and the Δ2rrn strain are relatively compact compared with those in the Δ5rrn strain. Apparently, multiple copies of rrn in the genome are required for the proper nucleoid organization and maximal rRNA synthesis in fast-growing cells.

## 2.5.5.3 Colocalization of RNAP foci with foci of NusA and NusB

Transcription of rrn is regulated by an antitermination mechanism during elongation (Morgan, 1986; Quan et al., 2005; Squires et al., 1993). NusA and NusB factors and the boxA sequence in the nascent rRNA are critical for the rrn antitermination system in E. coli (Li et al., 1984; Torres et al., 2004). NusA binds to RNAP during elongation (Greenblatt and Li, 1981). NusB, together with ribosomal protein S10, binds the boxA RNA (Greive et al., 2005; Nodwell and Greenblatt, 1993; Stagno et al., 2011), but NusB does not bind to RNAP in vitro. To determine whether NusA and NusB behave like RNAP in fast-growing cells, strains containing both rpoC–Venus and nusA–mCherry (or nusB–mCherry) fusions at the original chromosomal loci were constructed. Co-imaging of RNAP and NusA shows that NusA also forms foci, and 86% of the NusA foci colocalize with RNAP foci in fast-growing cells (Figure 2.5.6). 

Similarly, 87% of the NusB foci colocalize with RNAP foci in fast-growing cells (Figure 2.5.6). An almost complete colocalization of RNAP foci with foci of NusA and NusB demonstrates that, in fast-growing cells, the major transcription machinery includes RNAP and at least the two Nus factors (NusA and NusB), and it locates at the clustering of rrn operons and associates with nascent rRNA transcripts. 

## 2.5.5.4 Spatial compartmentation of RNAP foci

Co-imaging of RNAP with DNA using super-resolution structured illumination microscopy (SIM) reveals spatial compartmentation of the transcription machinery at the surface (DNA loops) of the nucleoid (Figure 2.5.7). An inverse relationship between the signal intensities of RNAP and DNA is apparent from the normalized $\mathrm { L o g } _ { 2 }$ (RNAP/DNA) density plot or heat map.

Figure 2.5.7 Spatial compartmentalization of transcription foci in fast-growing cells. (A) SIM images of RNAP, DNA (nucleoid), and an overlay of RNAP (green) and DNA (red) from a representative fast-growing E. coli cell (rpoC–venus) $( \mathrm { L B } , 3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ) .$ . The scale bar represents 2 μm. The log2 (RNAP–DNA) plot (heat map) is a quantitative representation of the relationship between RNAP and DNA, which is represented by a color scale bar with values ranging from −3 to 3. Note that regions enriched up to eightfold in RNAP over DNA are at the periphery of the nucleoid (red foci), and regions enriched up to eightfold in DNA over RNAP are in the center of the nucleoid (blue regions). (B) The histogram showing the distribution of apparent RNAP–Venus foci (transcription foci) in fast-growing cells. The red line indicates the median number of transcription foci (8) in the population of cells. Note that, compared with the images using wide-field microscopy (Figure 2.5.4), more RNAP foci are identified by SIM. Adapted from Cagliero et al. (2014).


Fast-growing cells (LB at $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ contain an average of eight RNAP foci per cell, as identified by SIM with its superresolution, compared with wide-field microscopy as described in Figure 2.5.4. The cells contain an average of four nascent nucleoids per cell, and each nascent nucleoid has an average of two foci. Thus, transcription machinery is maintained in each nascent nucleoid and “inherited” by newborn daughter cells without the need for de novo synthesis and/or assembly. This feature can explain in part why, in fast-growing cells, newly divided daughter cells maintain the same growth rate as the parental cells. 

Genome conformation capture analysis has shown that growth-promoting genes, which are downregulated during amino acid starvation, are in a highly interactive environment and present in large clusters (Cagliero et al., 2013). This suggests that transcription foci are likely to be networking hubs (Jin et al., 

2013) for the transcription of growth-promoting genes, most of which are rrn and some of which are located a distance away from rrn. The spatial organization of transcription machinery has logistical advantages, including reducing the transcription traffic jam and facilitating the coupling of rrn transcription and ribosomal assembly. 

## 2.5.6 Redistribution of RNAP during stress responses

When fast-growing cells are exposed to various stresses, RNAP rapidly disperses from the major foci and redistributes in the cell; such redistribution is coupled with changes in nucleoid structure. However, the manifestation of this effect depends on the particular stress-inducing agent. In the first four cases described in this section, RNAP released from the clustering of rrn redistributes across the genome for the expression of responsive genes, accompanying nucleoid expansion. In contrast, during hyperosmotic stress response, RNAP initially dissociates from the genome and then reassociates, and the nucleoid becomes hypercondensed temporarily during the response. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/dbd2e36b-966a-4745-a615-c0703cb42feb/d99ef0a10086a9c258a9291d9a34b4c821b95ce62cf8a846fdbb86e95315c0b7.jpg)



Figure 2.5.8 RNAP foci dispersion accompanied by nucleoid expansion during the amino acid starvation–induced stringent response in wild type (rpoC–venus). RNAP, nucleoid, and overlays of RNAP (green)–nucleoid (red) and nucleoid–cell (RNS value estimated from a population of cells is indicated) of cells grown in LB or in LB + serine hydroxamate (SHX, 30 min and 120 min) at 37 ◦C, after the induction of the stringent response. The scale bar represents 2 μm. Adapted from Jin et al. (2013).


Amino acid starvation. After the addition of serine hydroxamate (SHX) into a fast-growing culture in LB, cells become starved for serine (Tosa and Pizer, 1971), inducing the stringent response (Cashel et al., 1996). Major transcription foci disappear, and RNAP redistributes across the nucleoid relatively evenly for the expression of global genes located genome-wide (Durfee et al., 2008; Traxler et al., 2008). Such a change in RNAP allocation in the genome is accompanied by an apparent nucleoid expansion, as indicated by increased RNS values (Figure 2.5.8). 

Low pH. E. coli can survive when cells are exposed to a lowpH environment because of the acid stress response, during which global gene expression changes (Foster, 2004; Hansen et al., 2005). Lowering a fast-growing culture from pH 7.0 to pH 5.5 (acid stress) for 15 min causes major RNAP foci to disappear. RNAP redistributes to the nucleoid relatively evenly, and the nucleoid expands during the mild acid stress (Figure 2.5.9; see Section 10). 

Hydrogen peroxide. $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ causes DNA damage (Imlay, 2013; Imlay and Linn, 1987), which induces the SOS response (Walker, 1996) in E. coli cells, leading to reprogramming of global gene expression (see Section 10). After the addition of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (5 mM) into fast-growing cells for 15 min, no major RNAP foci are present and RNAP redistributes across the nucleoid (Figure 2.5.9). Concomitantly, the nucleoid expansion becomes evident. 

Methyl methanesulfonate (MMS). The alkylating agent MMS modifies DNA bases and induces cellular defense systems, including adaptive and SOS responses, the DNA repair pathway, and mutagenesis (Sikora et al., 2010; Uphoff et al., 2014; Wrzesinski et al., 2010). After fast-growing cells are treated with 20 mM MMS for 15 min, major RNAP foci are absent and RNAP relocates throughout the nucleoid (Figure 2.5.10). The nucleoid becomes elongated with regions of different DNA densities. 

Osmotic shock. When compared with the stress responses described in this chapter, RNAP behaves differently during the hyperosmotic stress response (Cagliero and Jin, 2013) (Figure 2.5.11; see Section 11). Initially, a significant number of RNAP molecules dissociate from the nucleoid into the cytoplasmic space owing to the transient accumulation of the cytoplasmic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , and, concomitantly, the nucleoid becomes hypercondensed. Subsequently, the free RNAP reassociates with DNA at the periphery of the nucleoid, probably for the expression of responsive genes during the osmoadaptation phase, when the cytoplasmic K+ levels decrease. During the osmoadaptation phase, the nucleoid gradually expands to a size approaching that prior to the salt shock.

## 2.5.7 Summary

Studying the cell biology of RNAP using state-of-the-art imaging technologies is a relatively new approach in the long-standing journey to understand growth rate regulation and stress responses in E. coli at the single cell level. Since the first report (Cabrera and Jin, 2003b), steady progress has been made in frontier research, revealing new insights into the distribution of RNAP and the spatial organization of transcription machinery in response to changing environments. Several key findings from the studies include the discovery of RNAP foci at clustering of rrn (bacterial nucleolus), and the composition and spatial organization of the transcription machinery in fast-growing cells (Figure 2.5.12).

The distribution of RNAP is dynamic and sensitive to environmental cues, and differential allocation of RNAP genome-wide influences nucleoid structure. When cells are grown in nutrient-poor media or undergo general stress responses excluding salt stress, transcription of rrn is minimal; RNAP distributes across the genome relatively homogeneously for the expression of stress-responsive genes genome-wide, and the nucleoid is expanded. # The ECF classification: a phylogenetic reflection of the regulatory diversity in the extracytoplasmic function ?? factor protein family

Daniela Pinto and Thorsten Mascher 

Technische Universitat Dresden, Institute of Microbiology, Dresden ¨ 

## 2.6.1 Extracytoplasmic function ?? factors

Regulation of gene expression is an essential step for every cell’s survival. The cells must activate or repress expression of specific sets of genes according to both external and internal signals. In bacteria, the RNA polymerase holoenzyme is the machinery responsible for gene transcription and consists of five subunits $\mathbf { \Sigma } - \mathbf { \alpha } \mathbf { \alpha } _ { 2 } , \mathbf { \beta } \mathbf { \beta } , \mathbf { \beta } ^ { \prime }$ ω, and σ. The σ factor is the subunit responsible for promoter recognition and hence RNA polymerase specificity (Helmann and Chamberlin, 1988; see Section 4). 

Of the two major families of bacterial σ factors, $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ , the latter is by far the more abundant and includes the housekeeping σ factors (group 1). Three additional groups were defined (Gruber and Gross, 2003; Helmann, 2002; Helmann and Chamberlin, 1988; Lonetto et al., 1992): group 2, which includes the nonessential paralogs of the housekeeping σ factors; group 3, which includes flagellar, heat shock, and sporulation-specific σ factors; and group 4, which includes the extracytoplasmic function (ECF) σ factors. 

While σ factors of groups 1 and 2 contain four conserved protein domains (designated regions ${ \mathfrak { O } } _ { 1 } , { \mathfrak { O } } _ { 2 } , { \mathfrak { O } } _ { 3 } ,$ and $\sigma _ { 4 } )$ , those of group 3 lack region ${ \mathfrak { o } } _ { 1 } ,$ , while ECF σ factors (group 4) contain only regions σ and $\sigma _ { 4 } .$ . These two regions are sufficient for interaction with both the RNA polymerase and the promoter. 

In addition to this domain architecture, the ECF σ factors are classically described as sharing the following hallmark features (Helmann, 2002) (see Section 2.6.6 for a more detailed discussion): 

1 They recognize alternative promoter sequences that are characterized by a highly conserved AAC motif in their -35 region and a CGT motif in their -10 region. 

2 Their activity is regulated by co-expressed anti-σ factors. In the absence of a signal, these anti-σ factors tightly bind the σ factors, thereby keeping them inactive. Once stimulated, 

the anti-σ factors release the σ factors to recruit the RNA polymerase core enzyme $( \alpha _ { 2 } \beta ^ { ' } \beta \omega )$ and initiate transcription from their specific alternative target promoter sequences. 

3 The ECF σ factor–encoding operon is normally under positive autoregulation. This allows for an enhancement of the activation effect it exerts on gene expression from its target promoters as long as the activation conditions are maintained. As soon as the activating stimulus ceases, the simultaneous upregulation of the cognate anti-σ factor activity ensures a rapid shutdown of σ factor activity. 

## 2.6.2 Regulation of ECF ?? factor activity

Several different modes of regulation of ECF σ activity have been described since the 2000s: 

1 The best understood mechanism of regulation of σ factor’s activity is the regulated proteolysis of the membraneanchored anti-σ factors (Figure 2.6.1a). This mechanism has been studied in great detail for two ECF paradigms, RpoE of Escherichia coli and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ of Bacillus subtilis, and has been summarized in detail elsewhere (Chaba et al., 2007; Heinrich and Wiegert, 2009; Ho and Ellermeier, 2012). Briefly, three successive proteolytic steps of the anti-σ factor are necessary to release the cognate σ factor from its inhibitory grip: First, the cleavage of the extracellular domain of the anti-σ factor (site-1 proteolysis); second, the cleavage of the transmembrane helix by regulated intramembrane proteolysis; and, third, the final degradation of the cytoplasmic remainder of the anti-σ factor by the Clp protease complex, thereby ultimately releasing the active σ factor. 

2 Conformation changes of (usually cytoplasmic) anti-σ factor that release the σ factor to initiate gene transcription from its target promoters (Figure 2.6.1f). These conformational
