The best understood examples of this mode of regulation are RpoE of Rhodobacter sphaeroides, which responds to and mediates resistance against superoxide stress (Dufour et al., 2008), and SigR, which is involved in mounting the disulfide stress response of Streptomyces coelicolor (Paget et al., 2001). 

A variation of this principle – in which regulation of σ factor activity, in the absence of a cognate anti-σ factor, is achieved through conformational changes of the σ factor itself (Figure 2.6.2c) – has already been described (Thakur et $a l . ,$ 2007). 

3 Protein–protein interaction cascades that signal the presence of an extracellular substrate (inducing stimulus) through both the outer and inner membranes, ultimately leading to the activation of the σ factor, which in return facilitates the uptake of the inducing substrate (Figure 2.6.1b). This mechanism is typical for FecI-like σ factors and has been elucidated in great detail for the regulatory cascade mediating iron–siderophore uptake in E. coli (Braun and Mahren, 2005; Mettrick and Lamont, 2009). 

4 Partner-switching mechanism based on σ factor mimicry can be found in the regulatory cascades orchestrating the general stress response of α-Proteobacteria. These cascades combine an ECF σ/anti-σ–like downstream module with a twocomponent-system type upstream module (see Section 3). The unique components are anti-anti-σ factors (PhyR), which contain a receiver domain (responding to stimuli sensed by upstream histidine kinases through phosphorylation) and an “ECF σ factor–like” effector domain, which – once phosphorylated – titrates the soluble anti-σ factor (NepR) away from the σ factor (EcfG), thereby ultimately activating gene expression of large regulons mediating the general stress response. This cascade was initially identified in Methylobacterium extorquens (Gourion et al., 2008) but has meanwhile been characterized in a number of additional α-Proteobacteria, including Caulobacter crescentus (Figure 2.6.1g) (Campagne et al., 2012; Francez-Charlot et al., 2009; Lourenc¸o et al., 2011). 

5 Transcriptional activation of σ factor expression by associated two-component systems uncouples the regulation of σ factor activity from a cognate anti-σ factor (Figure 2.6.2a) (Merighi et al., 2003). Such a mode of σ factor activation has been described for SigE of S. coelicolor (Paget et al., 1999b). 

6 Conserved C-terminal extensions can be found in a number of ECF σ factors that lack an obvious anti-σ factor (Figure 2.6.2e–h). Although a role of these extensions on the regulation of σ factor activity has already been demonstrated for two novel ECF groups (Gomez-Santos´ et al., 2011; Wecke et al., 2012), the exact mechanism by 

which this is achieved remains to be determined. For ECF44, it was shown that copper binds to the C-terminal extension and that the binding of Cu(I) or Cu(II) determines DNA binding by the σ factor (Gomez-Santos ´ et al., 2011). Nevertheless, how the protein switches its binding ability between the two forms of copper occurs or how the activation occurs is not known. 

7 Degradation of the σ factor has recently been proposed as a mechanism to regulate its activity (Figure 2.6.1.d) (Mao et al., 2013). In this case, the anti-σ acts not by counteracting the activity of the σ factor but by stabilizing it. In the absence of inducing conditions, the anti-σ/σ factor complex negatively affects differentiation and production of secondary metabolites and proteases. The presence of a suitable trigger then leads to degradation of the anti-σ factor. As a consequence, secondary metabolites will then be produced, which in turn negatively affect the repression of the protease production. These will then be produced, leading to the fast degradation of the σ factor. 

This short overview already indicates that regulating ECF σ factor activity is much more diverse than originally anticipated and clearly goes beyond the “simple” σ/anti-σ pairs originally described. But the ECF classification already indicates that the mechanisms described here might just be the tip of the iceberg, and more exotic mechanisms of ECF-dependent signal transduction seem to have evolved, including serine/threonine kinase-dependent activation of ECF σ factors (Figure 2.6.2i) or even regulation of gene expression by membrane-spanning ECF σ factors, as found in the phylum Planctomycetes. But these altogether novel mechanisms of ECF regulation still await experimental validation. 

Several of these mechanisms rely on the action of an anti-σ that interacts with the σ factor and keeps it inactive. The anti-σ factor sequences are not conserved, but structural studies of E. coli RseA and R. sphaeroides ChrR resulted in the identification of a structural motif termed ASD (for anti-σ domain) in their N-terminal region (Campbell et al., 2007). Some of these ASDs contain a highly conserved $\mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { X X X } } \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { X X } } \mathrm { C }$ motif responsible for binding $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and are therefore called the ZAS (for the zinccontaining anti-σ) domain (Zdanowski et al., 2006). But not all anti-σ factors contain an ASD domain. In some of these, an Nterminal sequence of approximately 50 amino acids was identified and designated the CAS (for candidate anti-σ) domain (Staron´ et al., 2009). As for the ASDs, an overall sequence similarity was not observed for the CAS domains. But in contrast to the ASDs, structural similarity of these CAS domains still awaits experimental confirmation. 

## 2.6.3 The ECF classification

Five years ago, we performed the first comprehensive phylogenetic analysis of ECF σ factors encoded in 369 complete genome sequences and defined 66 groups based not only on sequence similarity and domain architecture of the ECF σ factors and their cognate anti-σ factors, but also on genomic context conservation and putative promoter target motifs (Staron´ et al., 2009). Since then, 28 new groups have been described (Gomez-Santos ´ et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2015; Jogler et al., 2012).

In this chapter, we have compiled the available information for each of the 94 currently defined groups in a concise manner, focusing on five major aspects: taxonomic distribution, experimentally studied members, genomic context conservation, a (proposed) signaling mechanism by which their activity is regulated, and their (putative) physiological role. The order in which the groups are described follows their designation (ECFXXX). A supporting table (Table 2.6.1) summarizes the main features of each group and thereby provides a quick overview of their characteristics. Two figures (Figures 2.6.1 and 2.6.2) cluster the 94 groups according to their regulatory and signaling mechanisms and provide a graphical representation of those mechanisms along with their genomic context conservation. A glossary table of all protein domains relevant for this chapter (Table 2.6.2) was added as a reference. Finally, we provide a comprehensive summary of all known or predicted ECF group-specific target promoter motifs (Figure 2.6.3). 

In an attempt to unify our classification, we have renamed six ECF groups to match the original logic of the classification, as indicated in Table 2.6.1: ECF57 (formerly ECF01-Gob), ECF58 (ECF01-P), ECF59 (ECFSTK 01), ECF60 (ECFSTK 02), ECF61 (ECFSTK 03), and ECF62 (ECFSTK 04). In summary, ECF01 through ECF56 and ECF101 through ECF132 maintain their original designations, while groups ECF57 through ECF62 correspond to renamed groups. Accordingly, ECF63 through ECF100 and all designations from ECF133 upward are free to accommodate newly defined groups. In order to coordinate future additions to this classification and provide a suitable ECF group number, we encourage scientists who have identified a novel ECF group to get in contact with us. 

## 2.6.4 Group descriptions

The main characteristics of each ECF group, as supported by experimental work and in silico analyses, are summarized in this section. 

## 2.6.4.1 ECF01

Taxonomical distribution – ECF01 is one of the phylogenetically most diverse groups and contains proteins from at least nine different phyla: Acidobacteria, Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Chlorobi, Chloroflexi, Firmicutes, Plantomycetes, Proteobacteria, and Thermotogae (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – The best studied member of this group is $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ from B. subtilis along with its cognate membrane-associated anti-σ factor RsiW (Helmann, 2006). Genomic context conservation – No conservation beyond the genes encoding the ECF01 σ/anti-σ pair could be identified (Figure 2.6.1a) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Activation of these σ factors occurs by three successive proteolytic steps that cleave first the extracellular domain of the anti-σ factor, then its single transmembrane helix, and finally its cytoplasmic region, which contains a ZAS domain (Table 2.6.2) (Ellermeier and Losick, 2006). This leads to the release of the ECF σ factor from the inhibitory grip of the anti-σ factor, allowing it to recruit RNA polymerase to initiate transcription from its specific target promoters (Figure 2.6.1a). ECF01 proteins are phylogenetically closely related to σ-factors of groups ECF02–ECF04, as well as ECF57 and ECF58. Physiological function – Based on the experimentally validated members of this group, ECF01 proteins are thought to play a role in envelope stress response, antimicrobial compound production, and their detoxification (Helmann, 2006). 

## 2.6.4.2 ECF02

Taxonomical distribution – ECF σ factors belonging to this group are exclusively found in Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – The best studied examples are the E. coli σ/anti-σ pair RpoE/RseA (Ades, 2004) and AlgU/MucA of Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Wood and Ohman, 2009). Genomic context conservation – There is no genomic context conservation beyond the co-transcribed gene encoding the membrane-associated anti-σ factor (Figure 2.6.1a) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Similarly to ECF σ factors of group ECF01, the ECF02 anti-σ factors are also subject to regulated proteolysis, which leads to the release of the ECF σ factor (Alba and Gross, 2004; Wood and Ohman, 2009). The σ factor is then free to interact with the RNA polymerase and direct transcription from its target promoters (Figure 2.6.1a). These membrane-associated anti-σ factors contain an N-terminal anti-σ domain (ASD) and a C-terminal RseA domain (Table 2.6.2) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Physiological function – RpoE and AlgU play a role in envelope stress response and alginate production, respectively (Alba and Gross, 2004; Wood and Ohman, 2009). 

## 2.6.4.3 ECF03

Taxonomical distribution – This small ECF group is primarily restricted to the phylum Bacteroidetes, with the exception of a Chloroflexi ECF σ factor (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Similarly to the previously described groups, there is also no genomic context conservation beyond the genes encoding the σ/anti-σ pair (Figure 2.6.1a) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Given the similarity between members of this group and members of groups ECF01 and ECF02, it is postulated that ECF03 σ factors are also released from the inhibitory grip of their membrane-associated anti-σ factor. The latter contain an N-terminal CAS domain (Table 2.6.2) (Staron´ et al., 2009), which is subject to regulated proteolysis (Figure 2.6.1a). But this hypothesis needs experimental validation. Physiological function – Unknown.

## 2.6.4.4 ECF04

Taxonomical distribution –ECF04 is also a small group of ECF σ factors that belong primarily to Chloroflexi, with only one member from another phylum, Bacteroidetes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – No genomic context conservation was observed beyond the genes encoding the ECF σ/anti-σ pair (Figure 2.6.1a) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Given their similarity with members of the groups ECF01–ECF03 and the presence of a short transmembrane anti-σ factor, which contains an N-terminal CAS domain (Table 2.6.2) (Staron´ et al., 2009), it is hypothesized that the activity of these σ factors is also controlled by regulated proteolysis (Figure 2.6.1a). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.5 ECF05

Taxonomical distribution – Members of the ECF group ECF05 are restricted to Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – The two best studied members of this group are E. coli FecI (Braun and Mahren, 2005) and Bordetella pertussis HurI (Vanderpool and Armstrong, 2003). Genomic context conservation – Members of this group show extended genomic context conservation, with genes encoding outer membrane proteins located downstream of the transcriptional unit encoding the ECF σ/anti-σ factor (Figure 2.6.1b) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – In this group, regulation of ECF σ factor activity is achieved through protein– protein interaction cascades. In the absence of the inducing stimulus, the ECF σ factor is kept inactive by its cognate membrane-associated anti-σ factor, which contains an Nterminal ASD and a C-terminal FecR domain (Table 2.6.2) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Under inducing conditions (i.e., when a substrate is bound to the corresponding outer membrane protein), the σ factor is released from the anti-σ factor and is then free to initiate transcription from its target promoters (Figure 2.6.1b) (Braun and Mahren, 2005). Remarkably, and in contrast to most other ECF σ factors, members of this group do not seem to autoregulate their own expression. Instead, expression of these ECF σ factors is under the control of the Fur master regulator, which coordinates the cellular responses to intracellular iron limitation in which these ECF σ factors play a role (Escolar et al., 1999). Group ECF05 is highly similar to groups ECF06–ECF08 and ECF10, and many features described for this group also hold true for the phylogenetically related groups, including lack of autoregulation, genomic context conservation, and the target promoter motif. Physiological function – These extensively studied ECF σ factors are involved in siderophore-mediated iron uptake (Mettrick and Lamont, 2009). 

## 2.6.4.6 ECF06

Taxonomical distribution – ECF σ factors belonging to the ECF06 group are also only present in Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genomic context conservation in this group follows that described for group ECF05, that is, genes coding for outer membrane proteins are usually located downstream of those coding for the σ/anti-σ pair (Figure 2.6.1b) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – The regulation proposed for ECF06 σ factors is the same as that proposed for ECF05 σ factors and is presumably based on protein–protein interactions between outer membrane proteins, membrane-associated anti-σ factors, which also contain an N-terminal ASD and a Cterminal FecR domain (Table 2.6.2) (Staron´ et al., 2009), and σ factors (Figure 2.6.1b). Physiological function – No function was so far attributed to these ECF σ factors, although, given the extensive similarity between them and those of group ECF05, a role in iron acquisition can be hypothesized. 

## 2.6.4.7 ECF07

Taxonomical distribution – ECF07 σ factors are restricted to Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – The ECF σ factor HasI from Serratia marcescens (Biville et al., 2004) has already been experimentally investigated. Genomic context conservation – Again, genes encoding outer membrane proteins can be found adjacent to those encoding the σ and the membrane-associated anti-σ factor, which also contain an N-terminal ASD and a C-terminal FecR domain (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1b) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Again, the proposed mechanism of activity regulation presumably depends on a cascade of protein–protein interactions as described for group ECF05 (Figure 2.6.1b) (Biville et al., 2004). Physiological function – From the data collected for HasI, a general role in iron uptake for the members of this group seems likely (Biville et al., 2004). 

## 2.6.4.8 ECF08

Taxonomical distribution – As with the three groups ECF05– ECF07, ECF08 σ factors have so far only been found in organisms belonging to the phylum Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – ECF08 VreI from P. aeruginosa has already been studied (Faure et al., 2013). 

Genomic context conservation – In contrast to the situation for groups ECF05 to ECF07, no extended genomic context conservation can be observed for group ECF08 (Figure 2.6.1b) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Given the similarity between σ factors of this group and those of groups ECF05–ECF07 and the fact that the identified anti-σ factors also contain an N-terminal ASD and a FecR domain (Table 2.6.2) (Staron´ et al., 2009), protein–protein interaction cascades can be hypothesized despite the lack of obvious candidate proteins (Figure 2.6.1b). Physiological function – P. aeruginosa VreI has a role in the adaptive response to phosphate-limiting conditions (Faure et al., 2013). 

## 2.6.4.9 ECF09

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors belonging to the ECF09 group have only been found in Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – PbrA from Pseudomonas fluorescens (Sexton et al., 1996) and PvdS from P. aeruginosa (Leoni et al., 2000) have already been experimentally investigated. Genomic context conservation – Remarkably, an anti-σ factor-coding gene cannot be identified in the vicinity of the σ factor gene (Figure 2.6.2d). Instead, genes encoding MbtH-like proteins have been found adjacent to ECF09 genes, at least in the pseudomonads (Staron´ et al., 2009). MbtH-like proteins have been shown to be required for the synthesis of antibiotics, siderophores, and glycopeptidolipids (Lautru et al., 2007; Tatham et al., 2012). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.2d). Physiological function – These ECF σ factors also seem to play a role in iron uptake (Leoni et al., 2000; Sexton et al., 1996). 

## 2.6.4.10 ECF10

Taxonomical distribution – The vast majority of ECF10 σ factors are found in the phylum Bacteroidetes. Two members of this group have also been found in Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – σ factors of this group are encoded in an operon with genes encoding a membrane-associated anti-σ factor and outer membrane proteins (Figure 2.6.1b), as is the case for members of groups ECF05 to ECF07 (Staron´ et al., 2009). Moreover, downstream genes encoding one or more putative glycosyl hydrolases and other carbohydrate metabolism enzymes are regularly found further downstream. Signaling mechanism – It has been hypothesized that the mechanism by which these ECF σ factors are activated is comparable to that of groups ECF05 to ECF07. Hence, activation of the σ factor depends on a protein–protein interaction cascade involving the cognate outer membrane proteins along with the σ and anti-σ proteins (Figure 2.6.1b). As for groups ECF05–ECF08, the vast majority of these anti-σ factors contain an N-terminal ASD and a C-terminal FecR domain (Table 2.6.2) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Physiological function – These ECF σ factors are thought to be involved in mobilizing complex carbohydrates from the gut environment (Xu et al., 2004). 

## 2.6.4.11 ECF11

Taxonomical distribution – ECF σ factors that belong to group ECF11 are found in organisms belonging to the phylum Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – The paradigmatic RpoE from R. sphaeroides belongs to this group and has already been extensively experimentally investigated (Dufour et al., 2008). Genomic context conservation – Genes coding for ECF11-type ECF σ factors are associated with genes encoding the cognate soluble anti-σ factor, which contain an N-terminal ZAS domain and a C-terminal Cupin domain (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1f) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – The C-terminal domain of the anti-σ factor senses the stimulus (e.g., redox stress) through a mechanism involving disulfide bridge formation of conserved cysteine residues. This leads to a conformational change that is passed on to the N-terminal domain of the anti-σ factor. This domain represents a classical ZAS domain (Table 2.6.2). Upon the conformational changes, the cognate σ factor is released from the complex with the anti-σ factor and can then initiate transcription from its target promoters. In contrast to the regulated proteolysis described for groups ECF01–ECF05, which leads to an irreversible inactivation of the anti-σ factor, the conformational changes of ECF11 anti-σ factors are reversible (Figure 2.6.1f) (Greenwell et al., 2011; Zdanowski et al., 2006). Physiological function – RpoE of R. sphaeroides orchestrates the response to superoxide stress (Dufour et al., 2008). In general, members of this group are implicated in oxidative stress responses. 

## 2.6.4.12 ECF12

Taxonomical distribution – ECF12 σ factors show a broad taxonomical distribution and can be found in the phyla Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Chlorobi, Planctomycetes, and Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – Three members of the ECF12 group have already been studied in detail: S. coelicolor SigR (Paget et al., 2001), Myxococcus xanthus RpoE1 (Ward et al., 1998), and Corynebacterium glutamicum SigH (Busche et al., 2012). Genomic context conservation – No extended conserved genomic context could be found beyond the genes encoding the σ/anti-σ pair (Figure 2.6.1f) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – The proposed activation mechanism for ECF12 σ factors is very similar to that described for ECF11 proteins. Briefly, the N-terminal domain of the soluble anti-σ factor reversibly binds Zn2+, which determines binding to the cognate anti-σ factor. Upon perceiving redox stress, the anti-σ factor changes its conformation and releases its cognate σ factor (Figure 2.6.1f) (Kang et al., 1999). Physiological function – Members of this group play a role in disulfide stress response (Paget et al., 2001), mycothiol metabolism (Newton and Fahey, 2008), and heat and oxidative stress (Kim et al., 2005). 

## 2.6.4.13 ECF13

Taxonomical distribution – ECF σ factors of group ECF13 have been found exclusively in Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). 

Experimentally studied examples – The Ecf protein of Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gunesekere et al., 2006) belongs to the ECF13 group and has already been experimentally addressed. Genomic context conservation – There is no genomic context conservation beyond the co-transcribed gene encoding the anti-σ factor (Figure 2.6.1f) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – The small soluble anti-σ factors of group ECF13 also contain an Nterminal ZAS domain (Table 2.6.2) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Binding of $\mathrm { Z n ^ { 2 + } }$ to this domain is determined by the redox state of coordinating cysteine residues and imposes conformational changes in the protein (Zdanowski et al., 2006) that ultimately determine the binding or release of the σ factor (Figure 2.6.1f). Physiological function – ECF13 σ factors are presumably also involved in oxidative stress responses (Gunesekere et al., 2006). 

## 2.6.4.14 ECF14

Taxonomical distribution – This group is restricted to Actinobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – SigE from Mycobacterium avium (Wu et al., 1997) and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Barik et al., 2010) are the best studied members of this group. Genomic context conservation – The conserved genomic context of the genes encoding ECF14 σ factors extends beyond those encoding the σ/anti-σ pair to include genes encoding O-methyltransferases (Figure 2.6.1f) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – The cognate soluble anti-σ factor of ECF14 proteins also contains a ZAS domain (Table 2.6.2), which is required for the redox-dependent interaction between the two proteins (Figure 2.6.1f). Additionally, it has already been demonstrated in M. tuberculosis that PknB, a Ser/Thr protein kinase, phosphorylates the ECF14 anti-σ factor and that this phosphorylation is required for proteolytic cleavage of the anti-σ factor and hence the activation of the σ factor (Barik et al., 2010). Physiological function – These σ factors are involved in heat, acid, oxidative, and detergent stress responses (Wu et al., 1997). 

## 2.6.4.15 ECF15

Taxonomical distribution – This group is restricted to Proteobacteria, more specifically α-Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – Five members of this group have already been studied: M. extorquens EcfG1 (Francez-Charlot et al., 2009), C. crescentus SigT (Alvarez-Martinez et al., 2007), Bradyrhizobium japonicum EcfG (Gourion et al., 2009), Rhizobium etli RpoE4 (Mart´ınez-Salazar et al., 2009), and Sinorhizobium meliloti RpoE2 (Sauviac et al., 2007). Genomic context conservation – In this group, the conserved genomic context extends to a NepR-like anti-σ factor encoding gene, a distinct type of PhyR-like response regulator, and a sensor histidine kinase belonging to the HisKA 2/HWE type (Figure 2.6.1g) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Regulation of ECF15 σ factor activity is achieved through a mechanism of phosphorylation-dependent competitive partner switching, so-called σ factor mimicry (Figure 2.6.1g): In the presence of an inducing stimulus, the sensor histidine kinase phosphorylates the PhyR-like response regulator, which contains an N-terminal σ factor-like domain in addition to the Cterminal receiver domain. The response regulator then binds the anti-σ factor, hence acting as an anti-anti-σ factor. By this partner switch, the σ factor is released from the inhibitory grip of the anti-σ factor and is then available to initiate transcription from its target promoters (Campagne et al., 2012; Francez-Charlot et al., 2009). Physiological function – The ECF σ factors of group ECF15 play a central role in mounting the general stress response of α-Proteobacteria (Alvarez-Martinez et al., 2007; Francez-Charlot et al., 2009; Gourion et al., 2009; Mart´ınez-Salazar et al., 2009; Sauviac et al., 2007). 

## 2.6.4.16 ECF16

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of group ECF16 are only found in organisms belonging to phylum Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – The representatives of this group are SigF from C. crescentus (Alvarez-Martinez et al., 2006) and EcfF from B. japonicum (Masloboeva et al., 2012). Genomic context conservation – In this group, the conserved genomic context does not extend beyond the σ/anti-σ factors pair (Figure 2.6.1.e) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – The mechanism of activation of these σ factors is not known. Nevertheless, it is worth noting that the cognate anti-σ factors are unusual in that they contain six transmembrane helices that form a DUF1109 domain of unknown function (Figure 2.6.1.e). It has recently been demonstrated that two conserved cysteine residues, located in the extracytoplasmic face of transmembrane helices 4 and 5, are required for anti-σ factor activity (Kohler et al., 2012). This is indicative of a unique signaling mechanism. Physiological function – A function of these σ factors in mediating oxidative stress response and heavy metal stress has been proposed for C. crescentus SigF (Alvarez-Martinez et al., 2006; Kohler et al., 2012) and can be hypothesized for the remaining members of the group. 

## 2.6.4.17 ECF17

Taxonomical distribution – This is an Actinobacterial-specific group (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – Two ECF17 σ factors have already been experimentally addressed, S. coelicolor SigU (Gordon et al., 2008) and SigL of M. tuberculosis (Hahn et al., 2005). Genomic context conservation – In this group, the genomic context conservation does not extend beyond the genes encoding the σ/anti-σ pair (Figure 2.6.1a) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – The activation mechanism of these ECF σ factors depends on the regulated extracytoplasmic and intramembrane proteolysis of the cognate membrane-associated anti-σ factor as well as conformational changes of its ZAS domain–containing cytoplasmic region, which interacts with the σ factor (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1a) (Jaiswal et al., 2013; Thakur et al., 2010). Physiological function – These ECF σ factors have been reported to have a role in protein secretion and modification (Gordon et al., 2008) as well as cell envelope lipid synthesis (Hahn et al., 2005). 

## 2.6.4.18 ECF18

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors belonging to the ECF18 group are predominantly derived from Proteobacterial genomes, but can also be found in some organisms belonging to the phylum Acidobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – The biology of ECF18 RpoT from Pseudomonas putida (Duque et al., 2007) has already been experimentally investigated. Genomic context conservation – In this group, conservation of the genomic context does not go beyond the σ/anti-σ factors pair (Figure 2.6.1e) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – The cognate anti-σ factors of ECF18 proteins are transmembrane proteins with an N-terminal ASD and a Cterminal RskA (from anti-σK factor RskA) domain (Table 2.6.2) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Their signaling mechanism is still unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – RpoT from P. putida was implicated in the tolerance to toluene and other organic solvents (Duque et al., 2007). 

## 2.6.4.19 ECF19

Taxonomical distribution – This group is restricted to Actinobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – The ECF19 SigK from Mycobacterium bovis (Veyrier et al., 2008) and M. tuberculosis (Shukla et al., 2014) have been experimentally addressed. Genomic context conservation – In this group, the genomic context conservation is restricted to the transcriptional unit encoding the σ/anti-σ pair (Figure 2.6.1b) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – It has recently been demonstrated that a disulfide bridge in the σ4 region of the σ factor influences the stability of the interaction between the σ factor and its cognate membrane-associated anti-σ factor, which contains an N-terminal ASD and a C-terminal RskA domain (Table 2.6.2) (Shukla et al., 2014; Staron´ et al., 2009). This protein–protein interaction therefore determines the availability of the σ factor to initiate transcription from its target promoters (Figure 2.6.1b). Physiological function – SigK from M. bovis has a function in regulating the expression of antigenic proteins (Charlet et al., 2005). 

## 2.6.4.20 ECF20

Taxonomical distribution – The large majority of ECF20 proteins belong to organisms of the phylum Proteobacteria. But a few ECF20 σ factors have also been identified in organisms of the phylum Acidobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – Two members of this group, CnrH from Cupriavidus metallidurans (Grosse et al., 2007) and MibX from Microbispora coralina (Foulston and Bibb, 2011), have been experimentally addressed so far. Genomic context conservation – The genes coding for ECF20 σ factors are associated with genes encoding small membrane-anchored CAS domain containing anti-σ factors or, alternatively in some cases, longer genes encoding proteins containing von Willebrand factor type A domains (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1c) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signalingmechanism – In the presence of the inducing stimulus, which in the case of the CnrH anti-σ factor CnrX is the binding of cobalt or zinc to its extracytoplasmic domain, the anti-σ factor undergoes a conformational change that ultimately leads to the release of the σ factor (Grosse et al., 2007). This, in turn, is free to initiate transcription from its target promoters (Figure 2.6.1c). Remarkably, the CnrH/CnrX interaction structurally resembles that of the NepR/EcfG pair of group ECF15, indicating a similar inhibitory mechanism (Maillard et al., 2014). Physiological function – In C. metallidurans, CnrH has been implicated in nickel resistance (Grosse et al., 2007), whereas MibX in M. coralina has a role in antibiotic production (Foulston and Bibb, 2011). 

## 2.6.4.21 ECF21

Taxonomical distribution – Members of this group are largely encoded in the genomes of organisms that belong to the phylum Bacteroidetes, with a few examples that are encoded in genomes of the phylum Chlorobi (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples –EcfO from Bacteroides fragilis has already been experimentally investigated (Ndamukong et al., 2013). Genomic context conservation – There is no genomic context conservation beyond the co-transcribed gene encoding the membrane-associated CAS domain–containing anti-σ factor (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1e) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – The mechanism by which these σ factors are regulated is still not known (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – B. fragilis EcfO has been implicated in oxidative stress responses (Ndamukong et al., 2013). 

## 2.6.4.22 ECF22

Taxonomical distribution – The majority of this group is encoded in the genomes of organisms of the phylum Bacteroidetes. But ECF22 σ factors have also been found in genomes of the phyla Acidobacteria, Plantomycetes, and Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genomic context conservation has not been observed in this group, and a putative anti-σ factor has also not been identified (Figure 2.6.2d) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Unknown. (Figure 2.6.2d). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.23 ECF23

Taxonomical distribution – This group is restricted to organisms of the phylum Firmicutes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – In this group, the genomic context conservation is restricted to the transcriptional unit encoding the σ/anti-σ pair (Figure 2.6.1e). The anti-σ factor contains an N-terminal CAS domain (Table 2.6.2) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.24 ECF24

Taxonomical distribution – This group has been found in a broad spectrum of organisms belonging to the phyla Proteobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Actinobacteria, Firmicutes, and Plantomycetes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genomic context conservation in members of this group has not been observed, and no putative anti-σ factor has been identified (Figure 2.6.2d) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.2d). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.25 ECF25

Taxonomical distribution – This group is restricted to Cyanobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Conservation in this group does not extend beyond the genes encoding the σ factor and its cognate membrane-associated ASDcontaining anti-σ factor (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1e) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.26 ECF26

Taxonomical distribution – ECF26 σ factors are found primarily in the phylum Proteobacteria but have also been identified in the phylum Acidobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – SigE from Starkeya novella (Kappler et al., 2001) and PrtI from P. fluorescens (Okrent et al., 2014) have already been studied. Genomic context conservation – σ factors of group ECF26 possess a genomic context conservation that extends beyond the genes encoding the σ/anti-σ factor (Staron´ et al., 2009). Three different arrangements have been observed (Figure 2.6.1e): The genes encoding the σ/membrane-associated ASD-containing anti-σ pair (i) form a putative operon with upstream genes encoding lipoproteins, (ii) have a cytochrome c oxidase and a metallophosphoesterase encoded in their immediate vicinity, or (iii) are encoded next to a putative catalase and a type c cytochrome. Signaling mechanism – The mechanism by which ECF26 σ factors are activated is not known (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – SigE from S. novella has been implicated in playing a role in thiosulfate oxidation (Kappler et al., 2001), and PstI from P. fluorescences has a role in pathogenesis (Okrent et al., 2014). It is not clear if the remaining members of this group have a similar function or if they are involved in other processes, given the differences in genomic context conservation. The role of the neighboring genes indicates an overall role in redox processes. 

## 2.6.4.27 ECF27

Taxonomical distribution – This group is restricted to Actinobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – Two ECF27 σ factors have already been investigated, SigT from S. coelicolor (Mao et al., 2013) and SigM from C. glutamicum (Nakunst et al., 2007). Genomic context conservation – In this group, the conservation of genomic context extends beyond the σ/anti-σ coding genes. ECF27-encoding genes are located downstream of those encoding two conserved membrane-associated hypothetical proteins and upstream of those coding for thioredoxin and thioredoxin reductase (Figure 2.6.1d). Signaling mechanism – The signaling mechanism by which the ECF27 σ factors are regulated seems to involve proteolysis of both the σ and its cognate membrane-associated ASD-containing anti-σ factors (see section 2.6.2, Table 2.6.2, and Figure 2.6.1d) (Mao et al., 2013). Physiological function – The ECF27 σ factors investigated have been found to be involved in cellular responses to heat and cold shock and disulfide stress in the presence of diamide (Nakunst et al., 2007) as well as differentiation (Mao et al., 2009) and actinorhodin production (Feng et al., 2011). 

## 2.6.4.28 ECF28

Taxonomical distribution – ECF28 σ factors have only been identified in Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – No genomic context conservation has been observed in this group that extends beyond the genes encoding the σ factor and its cognate membrane-associated anti-σ (Figure 2.6.1.e) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1.e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.29 ECF29

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of group ECF29 are found predominantly in the phylum Proteobacteria, but they have also been identified in organisms belonging to the phyla Acidobacteria and Bacteroidetes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genes encoding a putative anti-σ factor have not been identified in the vicinity of those encoding the ECF29 σ factors. Nonetheless, it has been possible to identify two conserved gene organizations (Figure 2.6.2d): In one, genes encoding an outer membrane protein and a blue copper protein are found next to the ECF29 genes; and, in the second arrangement, the σ factor gene is located next to genes encoding a putative ferritin-like exported protein and a cytochrome c protein. Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.2d). Physiological function – No function has so far been proposed for σ factors of this group. The genomic context might indicate a role in redox processes, potentially involving an altogether novel signaling mechanism that does not involve classical anti-σ factors. 

## 2.6.4.30 ECF30

Taxonomical distribution – ECF30 proteins are found predominately in organisms of the phylum Firmicutes but can also be found in Actinobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – B. subtilis SigV is a member of the ECF30 group and has already been experimentally addressed (Zellmeier et al., 2005). Genomic context conservation – Half of the ECF30-coding genes are located next to genes encoding putative membrane-associated CAS domain–containing anti-σ factors (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1e), whereas a smaller number seems to be associated with transcriptional regulators (Figure 2.6.2a) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – The genomic context conservation in this group suggests the coexistence of two mechanisms of σ factor activity: one dependent on a membrane-bound anti-σ factor (Figure 2.6.1e) (Hastie et al., 2013), and another dependent on transcriptional control (Figure 2.6.2a). The latter awaits experimental verification. Physiological function – B. subtilis SigV has a role in resistance to lysozyme (Hastie et al., 2013). 

## 2.6.4.31 ECF31

Taxonomical distribution – This comparatively small group of ECF σ factors has members in four different phyla: Actinobacteria, Firmicutes, Spirochaetes, and Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – This group includes B. subtilis SigY (Cao et al., 2003). Genomic context conservation – No genomic context conservation has been observed beyond the genes encoding the membrane-associated ASD-containing anti-σ factors (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1e) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – B. subtilis SigY has been shown to play a regulatory role in sublancin production (Mendez et al., 2012). 

## 2.6.4.32 ECF32

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of group ECF32 can only be found in the genomes of organisms belonging to phylum Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – This group includes the experimentally analyzed HrpL σ factors of Erwinia amylovora (Wei and Beer, 1995), Pantoea stewartii (Merighi et al., 2003), and Pseudomonas syringae (Ferreira et al., 2006). Genomic context conservation – The σ factors from this group lack an anti-σ factor. Instead, their coding genes are in some cases linked to genes encoding a sensor kinase and a response regulator (Figure 2.6.2a) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – The activity of these σ factors is regulated at the transcriptional level by the activity of a twocomponent system (Figure 2.6.2a) (Nizan-Koren et al., 2003). Physiological function – Members of this group have been found to be involved in regulating the expression of a type III secretion system required to elicit hypersensitive response and pathogenicity in plant pathogens (Ferreira et al., 2006). 

## 2.6.4.33 ECF33

Taxonomical distribution – This ECF group only contains proteins from the phylum Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – ECF30 EcfQ from B. japonicum has already been experimentally addressed (Masloboeva et al., 2012). Genomic context conservation – In this group, the genomic context conservation does not extend beyond the genes encoding the σ and the membrane-associated anti-σ factors (Figure 2.6.1e) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – It has been demonstrated that EcfQ from B. japonicum plays a role in oxidative stress response (Masloboeva et al., 2012). 

## 2.6.4.34 ECF34

Taxonomical distribution – ECF34 σ factors are present predominately in organisms of the phylum Cyanobacteria, but can occasionally be found in organisms belonging to other phyla, such as Acidobacteria, Actinobacteria, Chloroflexi, and Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – As in many other groups, the genomic context conservation does not extend beyond the genes encoding the σ factor and its cognate membrane-associated anti-σ factor, which contain an Nterminal CAS domain and C-terminal RskA domain (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1e) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.35 ECF35

Taxonomical distribution – This group of σ factors has only been found in organisms of the phylum Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – In addition to being associated with their cognate membrane-associated CAS domain– containing anti-σ factors, genes encoding ECF35 σ factors are also associated with comparatively large proteins containing von Willebrand factor type A domains (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1e). The function of these proteins is well investigated in eukaryotes, where they play important roles in cell adhesion, migration, and signal transduction (Ruggeri and Ware, 1993), but is still elusive in prokaryotes. Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.36 ECF36

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of group ECF36 are only found in Actinobacterial genomes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – The σ factor SigC from M. tuberculosis is a member of this group (Karls et al., 2006). Genomic context conservation – Genomic context conservation has not been observed for this group, and no genes encoding putative anti-σ factors were identified in the vicinity of ECF36 genes (Figure 2.6.2c) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – The mechanism by which the activity of these σ factors is regulated depends on the interaction between the conserved regions $\sigma _ { 2 }$ and $\sigma _ { 4 }$ of the σ factor (Figure 2.6.2c) (Thakur et al., 2007). Physiological function – M. tuberculosis SigC has been implicated in pathogenesis and adaptive survival in the host (Karls et al., 2006). 

## 2.6.4.37 ECF37

Taxonomical distribution – This group is restricted to Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – No extended genomic context conservation has been identified. Nevertheless, the genes encoding the σ factors are linked to those coding for a putative membrane-associated CAS domain–containing anti-σ factor (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1e) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – No data are available concerning how the activity of these σ factors is regulated (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.38 ECF38

Taxonomical distribution – This group is limited to Actinobacterial proteins (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – The genomic context conservation in this group does not extend beyond the genes encoding the σ factor and the putative membrane-associated CAS domain–containing anti-σ factor (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1e) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.39 ECF39

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of group ECF39 have been found only in Actinobacterial genomes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – SigE from S. coelicolor (Paget et al., 1999a) and Sig25 from Streptomyces avermitilis (Luo et al., 2014) belong to this group and have already been experimentally investigated. Genomic context conservation – This group does not show any strong extended genomic context conservation, but genes encoding ECF39 σ factors are sometimes located close to either genes encoding two-component systems or putative membrane-associated CAS domain–containing anti-σ factors (Table 2.6.2 and Figures 2.6.1e and 2.6.2a) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – Some members of this group are regulated at the level of transcription (Figure 2.6.2a) by a two-component system (Paget et al., 1999b), as is the case for members of groups ECF30 and ECF32. Nonetheless, there are also ECF39 σ factors that seem to be associated with unusual putative anti-σ factors (Figure 2.6.1e) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Physiological function – S. coelicolor SigE is involved in cell envelope stress response (Paget et al., 1999a), whereas S. avermitilis Sig25 is involved in avermectin and oligomycin biosynthesis (Luo et al., 2014). 

## 2.6.4.40 ECF40

Taxonomical distribution – This group is also restricted to the phylum Actinobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – The ECF40 protein SigD from M. tuberculosis has already been experimentally analyzed (Calamita et al., 2005). Genomic context conservation – The genes encoding ECF40 σ factors are genetically linked to the genes that code for their cognate membrane-associated anti-σ factors. The genomic context conservation does not extend beyond this point (Figure 2.6.1a) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – The activity of these σ factors is regulated through regulated proteolysis of their cognate anti-σ factors (Figure 2.6.1a) (Jaiswal et al., 2013; Schneider et al., 2014). Physiological function – SigD from M. tuberculosis has been linked to pathogenesis as well as regulation of a small set of ribosomal genes and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) transporters (Calamita et al., 2005). 

## 2.6.4.41 ECF41

Taxonomical distribution – This large group of σ factors contains predominantly Actinobacterial and Proteobacterial proteins, but a few ECF41 σ factors have been found to be encoded in the genomes of organisms from the phyla Acidobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Chloroflexi, Cyanobacteria, Firmicutes, Spirochaetes, Verrucomicrobia, and Gemmatimonadetes (Wecke et al., 2012). Experimentally studied examples – SigJ from M. tuberculosis (Hu et al., 2004) and Ecf41 from both Bacillus licheniformis and R. sphaeroides (Wecke et al., 2012) have already been experimentally addressed. Genomic context conservation – None of the genes encoding ECF41 σ factors has a putative anti-σ factor encoded in their vicinity. Instead, they are found immediately up- or downstream of genes encoding one of three proteins: a carboxy-muconolactone, an oxidoreductase, or an epimerase (Figure 2.6.2e) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – It was demonstrated that the long, characteristic, and highly conserved C-terminal extension of these σ factors is crucial for the σ factor activity. The extension seems to play a dual role, contributing to both the activation and the inactivation of the σ factor (Figure 2.6.2e) (Wecke et al., 2012). Physiological function – M. tuberculosis SigJ has been implicated in resistance to hydrogen peroxide (Hu et al., 2004). This seems not to be shared by the other members of the group, for which the physiological role still needs to be determined (Wecke et al., 2012). 

## 2.6.4.42 ECF42

Taxonomical distribution – Genes encoding σ factors that belong to the ECF42 group can be found in genomes of the phyla Acidobacteria, Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Cyanobacteria, Plantomycetes, and Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – Except for ECF-10 from P. putida (Tettmann et al., 2014), none of the σ factors belonging to this group has been so far experimentally analyzed. Genomic context conservation – It has not been possible to identify genes encoding a putative anti-σ factor in the vicinity of their cognate ECF42 genes. However, the large majority of the analyzed genes are located in the immediate vicinity of genes encoding “YCII-related domain”–containing proteins (Table 2.6.2). The function of these proteins is still unknown (Figure 2.6.2f) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – σ factors from this group are unusual because of their long C-terminal extension, which contains tetratricopeptide repeats (Table 2.6.2). The latter are usually involved in mediating protein–protein interactions and assembly of multiprotein complexes (Blatch and Lassle, 1999). This raises the hypothesis that oligomerization¨ of these proteins might regulate their activity. Alternatively, it could also be possible that regulating σ factor activity is based on the interaction between the tetratricopeptide repeats in the 

C-terminal extension of the σ factors and the “YCII-related domain”–containing proteins (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.2f). These hypotheses will require future experimental validations. Physiological function – P. putida ECF-10 has been implicated in stress resistance and biofilm formation (Tettmann et al., 2014). 

## 2.6.4.43 ECF43

Taxonomical distribution – ECF43 σ factors can be found in the genomes from the phyla Acidobacteria, Cyanobacteria, Plantomycetes, and Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – ECF43 σ factor genes are linked to those encoding Ser/Thr protein kinases (Figure 2.6.2i) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Signaling mechanism – The mechanism by which the activity of σ factors from this group is regulated is still elusive. Nevertheless, it is tempting to speculate that their activity is regulated through phosphorylation by their neighbor Ser/Thr kinases (Figure 2.6.2i) (Mascher, 2013). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.44 ECF44

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors from this group have been identified in organisms of the phyla Acidobacteria, Nitrospira, Proteobacteria, and Verrucomicrobia (Gomez-Santos ´ et al., 2011). Experimentally studied examples – The ECF44 σ factor CorE of M. xanthus has been studied regarding both its physiological role and the mechanism of signal transduction (Gomez- ´ Santos et al., 2011). Genomic context conservation – Genes encoding the ECF44 σ factors are not linked to any obvious anti-σ factors. They lack strong genomic context conservation but are usually associated with genes encoding proteins putatively involved in copper handling and trafficking (Figure 2.6.2e) (Gomez-Santos´ et al., 2011). Signaling mechanism – These σ factors contain a C-terminal extension that, similarly to what was demonstrated for ECF41 σ factors, seems to play a dual role, contributing to both their activation and inactivation (Figure 2.6.2e). The C-terminal extension of CorE senses the redox state of copper by a mechanism not yet completely understood and regulates σ factor activity (Gomez-Santos ´ et al., 2011). Physiological function – These σ factors are involved in regulating copper ion homeostasis (Gomez-Santos ´ et al., 2011). 

## 2.6.4.45 ECF45

Taxonomical distribution – ECF45 σ factors are found in organisms from seven phyla: Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Deinococcus-Thermus, Firmicutes, Plantomycetes, Proteobacteria, and Spirochaetes (Jogler et al., 2012). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – These σ factors were not found to be encoded in the vicinity of putative anti-σ factor genes, and no extended conserved genomic context has been detected (Figure 2.6.2h) (Jogler et al., 2012). Signaling mechanism – ECF45 σ factors contain a Cterminal extension, but the mechanism by which their activity is regulated is still unknown (Figure 2.6.2h). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.46 ECF46

Taxonomical distribution – This group of σ factors is restricted to the Plantomycetes (Jogler et al., 2012). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – ECF46 σ factor–encoding genes are genomically linked to membrane-associated anti-σ factors similar to those of groups ECF05–ECF08 and ECF10 (i.e., they contain an N-terminal ASD and a C-terminal FecR domain) (Table 2.6.2). However, neither genes encoding outer membrane proteins nor any other conserved genes were found in their vicinity (Figure 2.6.1b) (Jogler et al., 2012). Signaling mechanism – The mechanisms by which the activity of these σ factors is regulated is not known. But it is tempting to propose protein–protein interaction cascades, as is the case for the related ECF05–ECF08 σ factors (Figure 2.6.1b). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.47 ECF47

Taxonomical distribution – This group is restricted to Actinobacteria (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – σ factors of this group are putatively co-transcribed with their cognate anti-σ factors, but the genomic context conservation does not go beyond the σ/anti-σ pair (Figure 2.6.1e) (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism – These anti-σ factors are predicted membrane-spanning proteins that contain an N-terminal ASD (Table 2.6.2) and show a weak similarity to M. tuberculosis RskA (regulator of SigK, which belongs to group ECF19) (Huang et al., 2015). No further details are available regarding the molecular mechanism controlling the activation of ECF47 σ factors (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.48 ECF48

Taxonomical distribution – This group is also restricted to the phylum Actinobacteria (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – No gene coding for an anti-σ factor has been identified in the vicinity of ECF48 genes, and no additional genomic context conservation has been detected (Figure 2.6.2g) (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism – ECF48 σ factors possess a long Cterminal extension that contains one predicted transmembrane domain. The predicted cytoplasmic portion of that extension contains a ZAS domain (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.2g) (Huang et al., 2015). It is therefore attractive to hypothesize that the C-terminal ZAS domain keeps the N-terminal ECF domains inactive in the absence of a suitable trigger. In the presence of the inducing stimulus, a conformational change either alters the conformation of the ZAS domain or exposes a proteolytic cleavage site that would ultimately result in the release of an active σ factor. Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.49 ECF49

Taxonomical distribution – ECF49 σ factors have only been identified in genomes of organisms belonging to the phylum Actinobacteria (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – In this group, the genomic context conservation does not extend beyond the genes encoding the σ/anti-σ pair (Figure 2.6.1e) (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism – The ECF49 anti-σ factors are predicted transmembrane proteins with a weak similarity to ECF19 anti-σ factors (Huang et al., 2015). Nothing is known about the mechanism underlying ECF49 σ factor activation (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.50 ECF50

Taxonomical distribution – This group is restricted to Actinobacteria (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – In this group, the genomic context conservation does not go beyond the genes coding for the σ/anti-σ proteins (Figure 2.6.1e) (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism – Except for the presence of a putative membrane-associated anti-σ factor, nothing is known about the mechanisms by which these σ factors are activated (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.51 ECF51

Taxonomical distribution – ECF51 σ factors are only found in Actinobacterial genomes, and their vast majority can be found in members of the families Micromonosporaceae and Streptomycetacea (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genomic context conservation is limited to the genes encoding the σ factor and its cognate membrane-associated anti-σ factor (Figure 2.6.1e) (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism – The anti-σ factor has a weak similarity to those of group ECF19, but nothing else is known about the mechanism responsible for σ factor activation (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.52 ECF52

Taxonomical distribution – This group is also restricted to the phylum Actinobacteria (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – ECF52 σ factors have not yet been experimentally studied. Genomic context conservation – Genes encoding ECF52 σ factors do not share a strongly conserved genomic context, as seen in many other groups, but are located in regions encoding several proteins involved in carbohydrate metabolism. Putative anti-σ factor genes have not been found in their vicinity (Figure 2.6.2g) (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism – ECF52 σ factors contain a large C-terminal extension. This extension contains a cytoplasmic-located ZAS domain, two predicted transmembrane helices, and a putative cytoplasmic carbohydrate-binding domain (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.2g) (Huang et al., 2015). Given this architecture, it can be speculated that the binding of carbohydrates either triggers a regulated proteolytic cascade or induces a conformational change that inactivates the ZAS domain to ultimately release an active form of the σ factor. Physiological function – Given the genomic context conservation and the domain architecture, a role of ECF52 proteins in regulating an aspect of carbohydrate metabolism can be envisioned. 

## 2.6.4.53 ECF53

Taxonomical distribution – ECF53 σ factors have a very narrow taxonomical distribution. They are almost exclusively found in organisms that belong to the family Streptomycetacea (phylum Actinobacteria) (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – This group does not show any conservation of genomic context (Figure 2.6.2g) (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism – ECF53 σ factors constitute an unusual group, since they possess a conserved $\sigma _ { 2 }$ region but not a well-conserved $\sigma _ { 4 }$ region. Moreover, their C-terminal extension contains a ZAS domain (Table 2.6.2) and one of several distinct conserved protein domains associated with enzymatic activities (e.g., glycosyl hydrolases and alpha-L-arabinofuranosidases) (Figure 2.6.2g) (Huang et al., 2015). While the presence of a linked ZAS domain might again suggest a conformational change that exposes a proteolytic cleavage site, the function of the variable domain is unclear. Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.54 ECF54

Taxonomical distribution – This group of σ factors is also restricted to Actinobacteria (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – ECF54 σ factor coding genes are located in the immediate vicinity of (i) a gene encoding a hypothetical protein containing a “carboxypeptidase regulatory-like” domain, (ii) a gene coding for a peptidase S8/S53, and (iii) a larger gene that encodes a protein with a C-terminal CHAT (caspase HetF associated with Tprs) domain and three poorly conserved tetratricopeptide repeats (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.2b) (Huang et al., 2015). No putative anti-σ factor has been identified. Signaling mechanism – The genomic context in which ECF54 coding genes are located suggests either that the peptidase together with its associated proteins are directly involved in the regulation of the σ factor activity or that the peptidase and the associated proteins are simply the target genes of ECF54 σ factors (Figure 2.6.2b). Experimental validations will be necessary to test these hypotheses. Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.55 ECF55

Taxonomical distribution – ECF55 σ factors can be found in organisms belonging to the phyla Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, and Firmicutes (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – No genomic context conservation has been observed in the vicinity of the genes encoding ECF55 σ factors (Figure 2.6.2d) (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.2d). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.56 ECF56

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors from group ECF56 have been identified in the genomes of organisms of the phyla Actinobacteria, Gemmatimonadetes, and Proteobacteria (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genomic context conservation was not observed in the vicinity of genes encoding ECF56 σ factors (Figure 2.6.2h) (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism – ECF56 σ factors contain a highly conserved C-terminal extension (Figure 2.6.2h), which contains a Snoal 2 domain that is widespread in bacteria. No putative anti-σ factor has so far been identified (Huang et al., 2015). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.57 ECF57 (formerly ECF01-Gob)

Taxonomical distribution – This ECF group contains more than half of all ECF σ factors encoded in the genome of the planctomycete Gemmata obscuriglobus but cannot be found in any other organism (Jogler et al., 2012). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Conservation of the flanking genes of those encoding ECF57 proteins has not been identified (Figure 2.6.2f). Signaling mechanism – ECF σ factors from this group share sequence similarity with those of group ECF01 but in addition harbor very large and diverse Cterminal extensions that frequently contain WD40 repeats (Figure 2.6.2f) (Jogler et al., 2012). These repeats are thought to be involved in assembling multiprotein complexes and are suggestive of a regulation by protein–protein interactions (Stirnimann et al., 2010). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.58 ECF58 (formerly ECF01-P)

Taxonomical distribution – The proteins of this group are restricted to the phylum Plantomycetes. The group contains one ECF01-like protein from each Plantomycetes species analyzed, which most likely represent direct orthologs conserved within this phylum (Jogler et al., 2012). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – No conservation was observed among the genes located in the vicinity of those encoding ECF58 proteins (Figure 2.6.2d). Signaling mechanism – Members of this group lack an obvious anti-σ factor, and the mechanism by which their activity is regulated is still elusive (Figure 2.6.2d). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.59 ECF59 (formerly ECFSTK–01)

Taxonomical distribution – These ECF σ factors can only be found in the phylum Plantomycetes (Jogler et al., 2012). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – The ECF59 coding genes are linked to genes encoding Ser/Thr protein kinases (Figure 2.6.2i) (Jogler et al., 2012). Such a genomic congruence between ECF σ factors and 

Ser/Thr kinases can also be found in groups ECF60–ECF62 (discussed next in this section). Signaling mechanism – The link between ECF59 σ factors and Ser/Thr protein kinases suggests that the latter might be regulating the function of the former through phosphorylation (Figure 2.6.2i) (Jogler et al., 2012). This hypothesis awaits experimental verification. Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.60 ECF60 (formerly ECFSTK–02)

Taxonomical distribution – ECF60 σ factors are only found in organisms from the phylum Plantomycetes (Jogler et al., 2012). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genes encoding Ser/Thr protein kinases are located downstream of those encoding ECF60 σ factors (Figure 2.6.2i) (Jogler et al., 2012). Signaling mechanism – Similarly to group ECF59, it can be hypothesized that the activity of these σ factors is regulated through phosphorylation by the cognate Ser/Thr protein kinases (Figure 2.6.2i) (Jogler et al., 2012). However, experimental evidence supporting this hypothesis is still missing. Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.61 ECF61 (formerly ECFSTK–03)

Taxonomical distribution – This small group of σ factors is restricted to Plantomycetes (Jogler et al., 2012). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genes encoding σ factors of group ECF61 are most likely cotranscribed with genes encoding a Ser/Thr protein kinase and a hypothetical protein (Figure 2.6.2i). Signaling mechanism – As suggested for the groups ECF59 and ECF60, the activity of these σ factors might again be regulated by phosphorylation by the action of the cognate Ser/Thr protein kinases (Figure 2.6.2i) (Jogler et al., 2012). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.62 ECF62 (formerly ECFSTK–04)

Taxonomical distribution – Plantomycetes are the only organisms encoding ECF62 σ factors (Jogler et al., 2012). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genes encoding these ECF σ factors are again linked to those coding for Ser/Thr protein kinases (Figure 2.6.2i) (Jogler et al., 2012). Signaling mechanism – Despite the lack of experimental evidence supporting this hypothesis, it can again be proposed that activity of these σ factors is regulated by phosphorylation mediated by the co-transcribed Ser/Thr protein kinases, as already suggested for the previous three groups (Figure 2.6.2i) (Jogler et al., 2012). Physiological function – Unknown. 

All subsequent groups were initially described as “minor groups” due to the low number of identified members. For those, the numbering was started at ECF101. The issues arising from this separation between major and minor groups will be discussed in Sections 2.6.7 and 2.6.8. 

## 2.6.4.63 ECF101

Taxonomical distribution – ECF101 σ factors have been found in members of the phyla Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – In this group, genomic context conservation does not extend beyond those genes encoding the σ factor and its cognate anti-σ factor (Figure 2.6.1f). Signaling mechanism – The cognate anti-σ factors of ECF101 σ factors are predicted soluble proteins that contain a ZAS domain (Table 2.6.2) (Staron´ et al., 2009). This domain coordinates the binding of $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ to the protein and is responsible for conformational changes that depend on the binding of the ion (Zdanowski et al., 2006). This suggests that the activity of ECF101 σ factors is regulated through conformational changes of the soluble anti-σ factors (Figure 2.6.1f). Experimental evidence to support this hypothesis is still missing for this ECF group. Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.64 ECF102

Taxonomical distribution – ECF102 σ factors are restricted to Proteobacteria and are mostly found in Pseudomonas spp. (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – P. aeruginosa and P. fluorescens SigX proteins have already been studied (Brinkman et al., 1999; Duchesne et al., 2013; Gicquel et al., 2013). Genomic context conservation – The genes encoding ECF102 σ factors are located downstream of four genes encoding (i) RraA, a ribonuclease activity regulator protein; (ii) CmaX, an $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } }$ influx system protein; (iii) CrfX, the putative soluble CAS domain–containing anti-σ factor (Table 2.6.2); and (iv) CmpX, a mechanosensitive ion channel. The gene encoding OprF, a porin and demonstrated target of SigX in Pseudomonas spp., is consistently found downstream of the ECF102 genes (Figure 2.6.1h) (Brinkman et al., 1999). Signaling mechanism – The mechanism by which the σ factors of this group are activated is not known (Figure 2.6.1h). Physiological function – Pseudomonas spp. SigX has been implicated in virulence (Gicquel et al., 2013) as well as outer membrane composition and homeostasis (Duchesne et al., 2013). 

## 2.6.4.65 ECF103

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of this group have been found in Acidobacteria, Actinobacteria, Chloroflexi, and Firmicutes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – A number of conserved genes are located downstream of the gene encoding the ECF103 σ factors: a putative membrane-associated anti-σ factor, a multidrug ABC transporter ATPase, and a multicopper enzyme maturation ABC transporter permease (Figure 2.6.1c). Signaling mechanism – The ECF103 σ factor cognate anti-σ factor is a membrane-associated protein containing a ZAS domain (Table 2.6.2) in its cytoplasmic region (Staron´ et al., 2009). This suggests that conformational changes or regulated proteolysis of the membrane-associated anti-σ factor might activate the ECF103 σ factors (Figure 2.6.1c). However, experimental evidence supporting this hypothesis is still lacking. Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.66 ECF104

Taxonomical distribution – ECF104 σ factors have so far only been identified in Staphylococcus spp. (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – In Staphylococcus aureus, the ECF104 σ factor has already been studied (Morikawa et al., 2003). Genomic context conservation – The genes encoding the ECF104 σ factors are preceded by those encoding a serine acetyltransferase-like protein, a cysteinyl–tRNA synthetase, a tRNA/rRNA methyltransferase, and two proteins of unknown function (Figure 2.6.2d). Signaling mechanism – The activation mechanism of these σ factors is not understood (Figure 2.6.2d). Physiological function – In Staphylococcus spp., ECF104 σ factors seem to play a role in competence regulation (Morikawa et al., 2003). 

## 2.6.4.67 ECF105

Taxonomical distribution – ECF105 σ factors are found in Firmicutes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – SigW from Bacillus thuringiensis has already been studied to some extent (Espinasse et al., 2004). Genomic context conservation – Genes encoding ECF105 σ factors are followed by those encoding a putative anti-σ factor and two membraneassociated proteins, one with 11 and another with three transmembrane regions (Figure 2.6.1c). Signaling mechanism – The ECF105 anti-σ factors are membrane-associated proteins containing a ZAS domain (Table 2.6.2) in their cytoplasmic regions (Staron´ et al., 2009). This suggests that conformational changes or regulated proteolysis might be involved in the regulation of the σ factor activity (Figure 2.6.1c). Nonetheless, experimental evidence supporting this hypothesis is still missing. Physiological function – In B. thuringiensis, SigW plays a role in betaexotoxin I production (Espinasse et al., 2004). 

## 2.6.4.68 ECF106

Taxonomical distribution – These ECF σ factors are found in Firmicutes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – The genes encoding ECF106 σ factors are located upstream of those encoding the cognate anti-σ factor (Figure 2.6.1e). Signaling mechanism – The activity of ECF106 σ factors is probably controlled by their cognate membrane-associated anti-σ factors (Figure 2.6.1e). Additional details on how the regulation is achieved are not yet known. Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.69 ECF107

Taxonomical distribution – ECF107 σ factors are found in Firmicutes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None of the members of this group have so far been experimentally investigated. Genomic context conservation – Two genes, both annotated as putatively encoding membraneassociated ASD-containing anti-σ factors (Table 2.6.2), follow those encoding ECF107 σ factors (Figure 2.6.1e). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.70 ECF108

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of group ECF108 have been identified in Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – The genomic context conservation in this group does not extend beyond the genes encoding the σ/anti-σ factor (Figure 2.6.1e). Signaling mechanism – The putative anti-σ factors of ECF108 σ factors are predicted to be membraneassociated proteins (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.71 ECF109

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of this group can only be found in the phylum Bacteroidetes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – The genes encoding the ECF109 σ factors are co-transcribed with genes encoding a putative membraneassociated anti-σ factor (Staron´ et al., 2009) and a gene encoding a leucine-rich repeat-containing protein (Table 2.6.2). In a divergent transcriptional unit is also a conserved hypothetical protein (Figure 2.6.1e). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.72 ECF110

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of ECF group ECF110 could be identified in the phyla Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – In this group, the genomic context conservation does not extend beyond the genes encoding for the σ/anti-σ pair (Figure 2.6.1e). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.73 ECF111

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of ECF111 group can be found in Cyanobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – The ECF111 encoding genes form a putative operon with two other genes encoding the cognate membrane-associated ASD-containing anti-σ factor and a LTXXQ motif family protein (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1e). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – These σ factors are associated with a LTXXQ motif family protein. This protein is similar to CpxP, which is a regulator of the Cpx envelope stress response in E. coli and has also been indicated as a possible chaperone involved in resistance to extracytoplasmic stress (Danese and Silhavy, 1998). While this might suggest a role of ECF111 in stress response, experimental evidence to support this hypothesis is currently missing. 

## 2.6.4.74 ECF112

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of this group have been identified in organisms belonging to the phylum Firmicutes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – In this group, the genomic context conservation does not extend beyond those genes encoding the σ/anti-σ pair (Figure 2.6.1e). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.75 ECF113

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of group ECF113 have only been identified in organisms of the phylum Deinococcus-Thermus (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genomic context conservation has not been observed in this group (Figure 2.6.2d). Signaling mechanism –ECF113 σ factors lack an obvious anti-σ factor (Figure 2.6.2d). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.76 ECF114

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of the ECF114 group have only been identified in Bacteroidetes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – Porphyromonas gingivalis SigH has been experimentally addressed (Yanamandra et al., 2012). Genomic context conservation – No genomic context conservation has been observed (Figure 2.6.2d). Signaling mechanism – The regulation of these σ factors is elusive. No obvious anti-σ factor has been identified (Figure 2.6.2d). Physiological function – In P. gingivalis, SigH plays a role in oxidative stress response (Yanamandra et al., 2012). 

## 2.6.4.77 ECF115

Taxonomical distribution – This group of σ factors represents an extremely narrow taxonomical distribution, being so far only identified in Bacillus spp. (phylum Firmicutes) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – The genes encoding ECF115 σ factors are most likely co-transcribed with a gene encoding the proteolytic subunit ClpP of the ATP-dependent Clp protease (Figure 2.6.2b). Signaling mechanism – The ECF115 σ factors lack an obvious anti-σ factor but are putatively co-transcribed with a peptidase. It is tempting to hypothesize that proteolysis might play a role in the regulation of these σ factors (Figure 2.6.2b). Nevertheless, no experimental evidence is currently available to support this hypothesis. Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.78 ECF116

Taxonomical distribution – ECF116 σ factors are restricted to Firmicutes (Staron´ et al., 2009).
