Experimentally studied examples – ECF116 σ factor SigX from B. subtilis has already been investigated (Cao and Helmann, 2004). Genomic context conservation – In this group, the genomic context conservation does not extend beyond those genes encoding the σ/anti-σ pair (Figure 2.6.1e). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – B. subtilis SigX plays a role in modification of the cell envelope and resistance to cationic antimicrobial peptides (Cao and Helmann, 2004). 

## 2.6.4.79 ECF117

Taxonomical distribution – This group of σ factors is restricted to Bacteroidetes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – The ECF117 σ factors are putatively co-transcribed with their cognate anti-σ factors, but the genomic context conservation does not extend beyond these (Figure 2.6.1f). Signaling mechanism – The putative ECF117 cognate anti-σ factor is a soluble protein containing a ZAS domain (Staron´ et al., 2009), indicative of a regulatory mechanism relying on conformational changes (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1f). Nevertheless, experimental evidence supporting this hypothesis has so far not been gathered. Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.80 ECF118

Taxonomical distribution – This group is restricted to σ factors encoded in Actinobacterial genomes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genes coding for these σ factors are located upstream of those encoding their cognate anti-σ factors. Moreover, they are linked to genes encoding an ATPase component of an ABC transporter and one or two additional proteins with a high number of predicted transmembrane helices (Figure 2.6.1e). Signaling mechanism – These anti-σ factors resemble those of ECF16 σ factors. They have six predicted transmembrane helices and a ZAS domain in the N-terminal cytoplasmic region (Table 2.6.2) (Staron´ et al., 2009). The regulation of the activity of these σ factors is not known but might depend on conformational changes of the anti-σ factor (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.81 ECF119

Taxonomical distribution – Members of this group have only been identified in Bacteroidetes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genes encoding ECF119 σ factors are part of an operon encoding four other proteins: a CDP-diacylglycerol-glycerol-3- phosphate 3-phosphatidyltransferase, a phosphatidate cytidylyltransferase, a hypothetical protein containing an acyltransferase domain, and a putative membrane-associated ASD-containing anti-σ factor (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1e). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.82 ECF120

Taxonomical distribution – This group of σ factors is also restricted to Bacteroidetes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genes encoding ECF120 σ factors are encoded in a putative operon encoding three other proteins: a putative membraneassociated ASD-containing anti-σ factor and two proteins of unknown function (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.1e). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.83 ECF121

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of group ECF121 have been identified in organisms of the phyla Actinobacteria and Chloroflexi (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – None (Figure 2.6.2d). Signaling mechanism –Unknown (Figure 2.6.2d). The putative anti-σ factors identified are membrane-associated proteins with an N-terminal CAS domain (Table 2.6.2) (Staron´ et al., 2009). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.84 ECF122

Taxonomical distribution – This group is restricted to Actinobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genes encoding these σ factors are usually located upstream of a gene encoding a methylated-DNA/protein-Cys methyltransferase (Figure 2.6.2d). Signaling mechanism – No cognate anti-σ factor has been identified (Staron´ et al., 2009), and the regulation of ECF122 σ factors is unknown (Figure 2.6.2d). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.85 ECF123

Taxonomical distribution – This group of σ factors is also restricted to Actinobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – These σ factors are putatively co-transcribed with their cognate membrane-associated anti-σ factors, but the genomic context conservation does not go beyond this (Figure 2.6.1e). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.86 ECF124

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of group ECF124 have only been identified in Firmicutes (Staron´ et al., 2009). Experimentally studied examples – B. subtilis SigM is the best understood member of this group (Eiamphungporn and Helmann, 2008; Horsburgh and Moir, 1999; Thackray and Moir, 2003). Genomic context conservation – The operon encoding for ECF124 σ factors also encodes a membrane-associated anti-σ factor (YhdL in B. subtilis), and a membrane-associated accessory protein that acts together with the anti-σ to negatively regulate the σ factor (YhdK in B. subtilis) (Figure 2.6.1e). Signaling mechanism – Additional mechanistic details of how the anti-σ factor and the accessory protein negatively affect the activity of ECF124 σ factors are still missing (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – B. subtilis SigM was demonstrated to be essential for growth and survival in high concentrations of salt (Horsburgh and Moir, 1999) and to be activated in response to cell wall antibiotics, ethanol, heat, acid, and superoxide stress (Eiamphungporn and Helmann, 2008; Thackray and Moir, 2003). 

## 2.6.4.87 ECF125

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of group ECF125 are restricted to organisms of phylum Actinobacteria (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genes encoding ECF125 σ factors are located upstream of a gene encoding a putative metalloprotein from the “glyoxalase/bleomycin resistance protein/dioxygenase” superfamily (Figure 2.6.2d). Moreover, genes coding for transcriptional regulators can also be frequently found in the vicinity of the ECF125 encoding genes (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.2d). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.88 ECF126

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of this group can only be found in organisms of the phylum Actinobacteria (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – ECF126 σ factor–encoding genes are frequently located in the immediate vicinity of those encoding their cognate anti-σ factor, a putative anti-anti-σ factor, and a calcium-binding protein (Figure 2.6.1f) (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism – The ECF126 cognate putative anti-σ factors are long and soluble proteins, containing an N-terminal ZAS domain and a C-terminal domain similar to the N-terminal domain of the mycothiol maleylpyruvate isomerase (Table 2.6.2) (Huang et al., 2015). This is suggestive of regulation of σ factor activity based on conformational changes of a soluble anti-σ factor (Figure 2.6.1f). Nevertheless, experimental evidence to support this hypothesis is still missing. Physiological function – The physiological function of these σ factors remains elusive. 

## 2.6.4.89 ECF127

Taxonomical distribution – ECF127 σ factors have been identified in organisms of the phyla Actinobacteria and Chloroflexi (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genes encoding ECF127 σ factors are found upstream of those encoding Rieske proteins (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.2d). These proteins are iron–sulfur proteins that are part of cytochrome complexes (Schneider and Schmidt, 2005). In contrast, genes encoding putative anti-σ factors could not be identified in the vicinity of those encoding the σ factors (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.2d). Physiological function – Given the link between ECF127 σ factors and Rieske proteins (Table 2.6.2), it is tempting to hypothesize a role of these σ factors in the responses to energy stress. But this hypothesis needs to be experimentally verified. 

## 2.6.4.90 ECF128

Taxonomical distribution – These σ factors are restricted to Actinobacteria (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genes encoding σ factors of group ECF128 are usually flanked by those encoding membrane-associated proteins of unknown function and a sortase (Figure 2.6.2d) (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism –Unknown (Figure 2.6.2d). Physiological function – No data are currently available concerning the function of these σ factors. However, the genomic context conservation suggests a role in protein export. 

## 2.6.4.91 ECF129

Taxonomical distribution – Up to now, σ factors of this group have only been identified in organisms of the phylum Actinobacteria (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – None (Figure 2.6.2d) (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.2d). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.92 ECF130

Taxonomical distribution – This group of σ factors is so far restricted to Actinobacteria (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Genes encoding these σ factors are usually located between a gene encoding a small putative soluble ASD-containing anti-σ factor and a gene encoding a larger protein of unknown function (Table 2.6.2 and Figure 2.6.12c) (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.1h). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.93 ECF131

Taxonomical distribution – σ factors of the ECF131 group have only been identified in Actinobacteria (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – None (Figure 2.6.2d) (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism – Unknown (Figure 2.6.2d). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.4.94 ECF132

Taxonomical distribution – ECF132 σ factors are restricted to Actinobacteria (Huang et al., 2015). Experimentally studied examples – None. Genomic context conservation – Gene coding for ECF132 σ factors are co-transcribed with a membraneassociated ASD-containing anti-σ factor (Table 2.6.2). The genomic context conservation does not extend beyond the σ/anti-σ factors pair (Figure 2.6.1e) (Huang et al., 2015). Signaling mechanism –Unknown (Figure 2.6.1e). Physiological function – Unknown. 

## 2.6.5 Group-specific ECF target promoter motifs

ECF σ factors bind to alternative promoter motifs and drive the expression of alternative sets of genes, whose products are only required under specific (e.g., stress) conditions. Due to the extensive sequence similarity shared by ECF σ factors from within the same group, it is to be expected that σ factors of the same group bind identical promoter sequences, as already demonstrated for σ factors of the groups ECF02 (Rhodius et al., 2006) and ECF11 (Dufour et al., 2008). 

Most ECF σ factors are subject to positive autoregulation, which enhances their activating effect as long as the inducing stimulus is present (Helmann, 2002). This fact could be exploited to identify group-specific target promoter motifs from the sequences upstream of the genes encoding the σ factors by searching for overrepresented bipartite sequence patterns (Rhodius et al., 2013; Staron´ et al., 2009). So far, (putative) target promoter sequences could be identified for 56 of the 94 ECF σ factor groups (Figure 2.6.3). 

Traditionally, a conserved AAC motif in the -35 region has been described as the hallmark feature of an ECF target promoter (Helmann, 2002). This characteristic – which was derived from the target promoters identified for the paradigmatic ECF σ factors – is challenged by the ECF classification, since only approximately one-fifth of all putative ECF σ factor target motifs identified by comparative genomics (and subsequently verified experimentally; Rhodius et al., 2013) harbor this motif, including the target promoters of ECF groups ECF01, ECF02, ECF03, ECF15, ECF16, ECF17, ECF25, ECF29, ECF30, ECF31, and ECF32 (Figure 2.6.3). 

ECF19 group-specific target promoters are unusual since they appear like an inverted hallmark promoter with a C-rich -35 region and a highly conserved GAA motif in the -10 region (Staron´ et al., 2009). A similar “inverted” pattern can be found in promoters of groups ECF57 and ECF58, two Plantomycetesspecific ECF groups (Jogler et al., 2012). This pattern is even more remarkable in light of the close relationship of ECF57 and ECF58 with prototypical ECF01 σ factors. 

Target promoters of ECF15 σ factors are also remarkable, since their consensus sequence represents a perfect inverted repeat, with a highly conserved AAC -35 motif followed by a highly conserved GTT -10 motif. This pattern is of regulatory relevance, because these σ factors direct the expression of two divergent transcriptional units: those that encode (i) the EcfGlike σ factor and its cognate NepR-like anti-σ factor, and (ii) the PhyR-like anti-anti-σ factor. Indeed, it has already been proposed that this motif can function as a bidirectional promoter (Staron´ et al., 2009). 

Approximately 25% of the ECF groups identified so far are restricted to the phylum Actinobacteria. The high GC content of these Gram-positive bacteria is also reflected in the predicted group-specific target promoter motifs, as exemplified for groups ECF48 or ECF52 (Figure 2.6.3). 

In summary, the ECF classification indicates a remarkable diversity of ECF target promoter motifs that reflects the diversity of this group of alternative σ factors.

The classical hallmark features of ECF σ factors (see Section 2.6.1) have been derived based on only a small number of well-investigated examples (Helmann, 2002), such as E. coli

Comparative genomics has become a powerful approach to analyze the ever-increasing numbers of sequenced genomes. Such an approach was the foundation for the ECF classification summarized in this chapter. It resulted in a massive expansion of the number of ECF σ factors that are now known and also provides insights and hypotheses that can subsequently be experimentally addressed. The findings derived from these studies also challenge the hallmark features and indicate that we need to rethink and modify the “textbook concepts” of ECF σ factors in the light of the newly available information. 

“Extracytoplasmic function” σ factors are named after a small group of alternative σ factors that regulate some aspects of cell surface and transport processes (Lonetto et al., 1994; see also Section 4). However, 30 ECF groups lack discernible membraneassociated anti-σ factors, but instead are regulated by soluble anti-σ factors, C-terminal cytoplasmic extensions, or unknown mechanisms (Table 2.6.1). For example, ECF σ factors of groups ECF11–ECF14 have soluble anti-σ factors and monitor the internal state of the cell (e.g., oxidative stress). Therefore, although the majority of ECF σ factors seem to respond to extracellular cues, their name needs to be taken with a grain of salt. 

Another hallmark feature states that the activity of ECF σ factors is regulated by usually co-expressed anti-σ factors. But this statement only holds true for about half of all ECF groups. ECF σ factors can also be controlled by an increasing number of additional (proposed) mechanisms, including transcriptional activation (ECF30, ECF32, and ECF39), conformational changes (ECF41 and ECF44), or protein–protein interactions (ECF57 and ECF42). 

Two additional aspects, which require some reconsideration, focus on the ECF target promoters. As mentioned in Section 2.6.5, the initially proposed typical ECF promoter contains a conserved AAC -35 motif and a CGT-type signature in the -10 region. But such a motif only occurs in about 20% of the putative target promoters identified so far. Likewise, the proposed autoregulation of the ECF-encoding operon does not hold true for an increasing number of ECF groups. Autoregulation has not been observed in the FecI-like groups ECF05–ECF10 and for those groups whose regulation is based on transcriptional activation of the ECF σ factors (ECF30, ECF32, and ECF39). Moreover, no overrepresented promoter signature could so far be identified upstream of the ECF-encoding operons of groups ECF04, ECF13, ECF20, ECF23, ECF28, ECF34, ECF35, ECF36, ECF40, and ECF43 (Rhodius et al., 2013; Staron´ et al., 2009). This finding is indicative of the absence of autoregulation in those cases. 

Taken together, ECF σ factors are a distinct group of proteins from within the $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ protein family that can be defined by their characteristic domain architecture: They only contain two conserved domains, $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 4 }$ , which are sufficient for promoter recognition and binding to the RNA polymerase core enzyme. Beyond this core feature, ECF σ factors represent a very diverse group with respect to their target promoter motifs, and an ever-increasing number of different mechanisms regulating their activity to orchestrate a huge variety of physiological responses. 

## 2.6.7 The concept of major and minor groups

In the original classification, based on 369 bacterial genomes, minor ECF groups were defined as those containing fewer than 10 proteins, whereas major groups contained 10 or more proteins (Staron´ et al., 2009). Based on this definition, major groups were assigned the numbers between 01 and 43, and minor group numbers start with 101. 

As was already recognized at that time, the set of publicly available genomes is heavily biased toward Firmicutes and Proteobacteria as well as pathogenic and industrially relevant species. Since then, the number of completed genome sequences in the public databases has increased at an ever-accelerating pace. Currently, the number of available microbial genome sequences is close to 30,000, that is, almost two orders of magnitude higher than the dataset initially available for the ECF classification. This fast increase in sequence space has important consequences on the ECF classification, since it will (i) generate new major ECF groups; (ii) increase the number of proteins in minor groups, thereby “upgrading” them to major group status; and (iii) group initially unclassified ECF σ factors into new minor or even major groups. This effect has already been observed with the analyses of only nine Planctomycetes genomes, which identified six novel major groups (Jogler et al., 2012). Likewise, the recent analysis of more than 150 Actinobacterial genomes resulted in the addition of 10 new major groups (Huang et al., 2015). Moreover, three of the previous minor groups are now major groups, since they contain more than 10 proteins. 

In light of the genomics dynamics, the concept of major and minor groups is therefore rather arbitrary and should be discontinued. To avoid confusion, the initial ECF group numbers will be maintained (Table 2.6.1). But we suggest that newly identified groups (irrespective of their initial size) will be added to the classification starting with the designation ECF63. The numbers up to ECF100 should be filled up, and additional groups should then simply be added starting with the identifier ECF133 (i.e., at the end of the initial minor groups). 

## 2.6.8 Group size and phylogenetic distribution as an indicator of the evolutionary history of ECF ?? factors

The size of an ECF group (initially used as a means to distinguish major and minor groups) very often reflects the phylogenetic distribution of its members: The vast majority of smaller ECF groups (but also some of the larger ones) is restricted to one phylum (Table 2.6.1). This distribution can be interpreted as an indication that these ECF σ factors are evolutionarily younger. While some old ECF variants seem to even predate the separation into bacterial phyla and have been conserved ever since (e.g., groups ECF01, ECF34, or ECF41–ECF45), most distinct ECF groups developed within a phylum and are hence evolutionarily younger. Yet others, often found in “minor groups,” are much younger and can sometimes be found only in closely related species of one genus (e.g., ECF104, which is restricted to Staphylococcus spp.) (Staron´ et al., 2009). The most extreme case is represented by group ECF57, whose members are restricted to one particular species, the planctomycete Gemmata obscuriglobus (Jogler et al., 2012). Despite this restriction and short evolutionary history, this group contains over 30 sequences that – while highly homologous in the conserved domains – show a surprising variety of the regulatory C-terminal extension. This indicates that this particular ECF type has indeed duplicated and diversified significantly, despite a relative short time to evolve (Jogler et al., 2012; Mascher, 2013).

The examples discussed in Section 2.6.8 raise the question of what determines an ECF group. Normally, protein paralogs or highly similar orthologs in very closely related species should not constitute a group, given that they would simply represent duplications of basically identical and hence not yet completely diversified sequences. But group ECF57 is a fine example to demonstrate that this view is oversimplified, as highlighted by the very diverse C-terminal extensions that indicate that these proteins have evolved different physiological roles.

We therefore suggest that any group of closely related ECF σ factors with conserved features that occur at the genus level or above justifies the definition of a novel ECF group. Similar ECF proteins within one species or found only in different strains of the same species should be considered as paralogs or orthologs, unless a significant diversification in some of the features relevant for the ECF classification (e.g., genomic context, anti-σ factor, and protein extensions) has been observed, as is the case for group ECF57.

Comparative genomics is a very powerful tool to identify or characterize new protein families, as exemplified by the ECF classification discussed in this chapter. It was initially based on 369 complete genome sequences of organisms belonging to 11 phyla: Acidobacteria, Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Chlorobi, Chloroflexi, Cyanobacteria, Firmicutes, Plantomycetes, Proteobacteria, Spirochaetes, and Thermotogae (Staron´ et al., 2009). These phyla represent 90% of all sequenced genomes in the databases and are again unevenly distributed, since the vast majority of those genomes derive from only three of the above phyla, namely, Actinobacteria, Firmicutes, and most of all Proteobacteria. More importantly, the remaining 10% of sequenced genomes are derived from organisms of 18 different phyla with only a low number of genome sequences per group (see the NCBI Genome database at http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genome/).

This situation, together with the continuously increasing number of microbial genomes in the databases, has two major implications for future work on expanding the ECF classification: (i) the exploitation of more and more genomes of the overrepresented phyla will presumably not increase the diversity of ECF groups to be found; and (ii) however, the careful analysis of the genomes from underrepresented phyla might in fact expose a great deal of new ECF variants, possibly with new characteristics, new architectures, new mechanisms of regulation, or new target promoters. The analysis of only nine genome sequences from the phylum Planctomycetes has clearly demonstrated the potential of this approach (Jogler et al., 2012). It is in the underrepresented phyla that the hidden potential for novel ECF-dependent regulation is to be expected. And we are curious what future research in this direction will ultimately uncover.

## Yoshihiro Yamaguchi1,2 and Masayori Inouye3



1The OCU Advanced Research Institute for Natural Science and Technology (OCARINA), Sumiyoshi-ku, Osaka, Japan

## 2.7.1 Introduction

Regulation of cell death is essential for living organisms. In the eukaryotes, apoptotic cell death is crucial for the developmental process, for maintenance of normal cell homeostasis, as well as for elimination of cells damaged by stress or pathogen infection (Orrenius, 2006). In bacteria, the regulation of cell growth and cell death is also important under various stress conditions. Indeed, almost all bacteria contain genes encoding a small toxin protein consisting of around 100 amino acid residues that targets various cellular functions, including DNA stability, DNA replication, messenger RNA (mRNA) stability, protein synthesis, cell wall biosynthesis, and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthesis to inhibit cell growth (Pandey and Gerdes, 2005; Schuster and Bertram, 2013; Shao et al., 2011; Yamaguchi et al., 2011). In normally growing cells, however, these toxins are coexpressed from an operon with their cognate antitoxins forming a stable toxin–antitoxin (TA) complex so that the toxicity of the toxins cannot be exerted under normal growth conditions. This growth-regulatory system is called a TA system (see Section 6). 

The TA systems are not essential for normal cell growth, but they prevail widely in bacteria and archaea (Pandey and Gerdes, 2005; Yamaguchi et al., 2011). This fact suggests that they may have been playing subtle, advantageous roles for cells to survive in their natural habitats, for example in cellular adaptation to ever-changing natural habitats by reducing the growth rate, completely inhibiting cell growth, or leading some cells to die. A TA system was first identified on a plasmid, which plays an essential role in plasmid maintenance (Thisted et al., 1994). When a plasmid encoding the TA system is lost from a cell, the toxin is released from the TA complex, since the antitoxin is more unstable than the toxin, resulting in cell growth inhibition and eventual cell death. This phenomenon is termed “postsegregation killing” (Gerdes et al., 1986). Since this discovery, a number of different TA systems have been identified that are encoded by bacterial genomes (see Section 6). The toxins from these TA systems are proposed to be associated with various cellular functions in regulating gene expression, bacterial population control, and programmed cell death (Yamaguchi et al., 2011). 

To date, a total of 29 TA systems have been characterized in Escherichia coli. In addition, at least eight more novel TA systems have been identified on the E. coli genome (Yamaguchi and Inouye, unpublished data). To date, about 50 different types of TA systems have been identified in bacteria. It is interesting to note that Mycobacterium tuberculosis contains more than 80 putative TA systems, whereas its nonpathogenic counterpart, Mycobacterium smegmatis, has only two putative TA systems (Pandey and Gerdes, 2005). It seems that the number of TA systems may be related to the pathogenicity of M. tuberculosis, and the TA systems in this pathogen may play important roles in the maintenance of the extremely long dormancy of this bacterium inside the macrophage (Wayne, 1994). On the basis of this consideration, it is perhaps surprising that E. coli also contains a comparatively large number of TA systems (see Section 6). 

As described in this chapter, the cellular targets of toxins encoded by TA systems are of high variety, and they appear to be induced under different stress conditions, suggesting that they play highly diverse roles in the cell. Therefore, deciphering the functions and cellular targets of these TA systems is of fundamental importance for our understanding of their roles in bacterial physiology and pathogenicity. Among bacteria, there is a group called symbiotic bacteria such as Chlamydia muridarum and Mycoplasma gallisepticum, which live inside eukaryotic cells. An earlier analysis of then-available bacterial genomes led to the conclusion that symbiotic bacteria do not contain any TA systems (Pandey and Gerdes, 2005). However, as more genomic data became available, at present at least 20 genomic sequences of symbiotic bacteria have been determined, and a computational analysis using the PostgreSQL program reveals that most of these symbiotic bacteria, indeed, contain TA systems (Yamaguchi et al., 2011). In addition to bacteria, many archaea also contain TA systems. We found that at least 86 different archaea species contain TA systems homologous to those in bacterial systems. It was also thought that TA systems do not exist in eukaryotes based on an earlier analysis of then-available genomes (Pandey and Gerdes, 2005). However, when a BLAST search is performed on the currently available genomic data, 14 DNA sequences (that may encode Doc toxin homologs) and six DNA sequences (that may encode the MazF toxin) are found in eukaryote genomic DNA such as fungal genomes (Yamaguchi and Inouye, unpublished results). These Doc homologs have 26–33% identity and 42–51% homology to E. coli Doc, and the MazF homologs have 25–49% identity and 50–66% homology to E. coli MazF. At present, it is not known if these loci are indeed expressed to produce toxin-like proteins; whether these proteins, if expressed, are toxic; and whether they have cognate antitoxins. The fact that the TA systems are widely distributed not only in bacteria and archaea but also in some fungi, animals, and plants raises intriguing questions about their roles: how do they function in the highly diverse natural habitats of these organisms, and have they played advantageous roles during evolution? 

Since these TA systems have likely been maintained throughout evolution, one may speculate that each one of them might have played a positive role in survival of the bacterium under harsh natural environments, compared to those cells that had fewer or no TA systems. Characterization of these TA systems, including the identification of their cellular targets, the mechanisms of their toxic actions, and the regulatory mechanisms of their expression, therefore, is essential for our understanding of the roles of the TA systems in bacterial physiology, pathogenicity, and evolution. In this review, we describe all the known features of TA systems so far identified in bacteria and archaea (see also Chapters 6.1, 6.2, 6.5). 

## 2.7.2 Classification of TA systems

The TA systems have been classified into six different types, Types I–VI, according to the nature of the antitoxins and the composition of the TA systems (Figure 2.7.1). In the Type I TA system, the toxin gene expression is regulated by an antisense RNA transcribed from the same toxin locus in the reverse orientation (Fozo et al., 2008a; Gerdes et al., 2005). In the Type II TA system, both toxins and antitoxins consist of proteins, and the function of the toxin is neutralized by forming a stable complex with its cognate antitoxin (Yamaguchi et al., 2011; Yamaguchi and Inouye, 2011; see Chapter 6.4). In the Type III TA system, RNA antitoxin inhibits toxin function by directly interacting with the toxin protein by forming an RNA–protein complex (Fineran et al., 2009). Notably, the RNA antitoxin is not an antisense RNA, and therefore it does not inhibit the translation of the toxin mRNA like the Type I TA system. The ToxN antitoxin RNA is the first such example of the Type III TA system (Fineran et al., 2009). The CbtA–CbeA (YeeV–YeeU) TA system is the first TA system to be identified as a Type IV TA system (Masuda et al., 2012). In the Type IV TA system, an antitoxin protein does not form a complex with its cognate toxin protein. Instead, the antitoxin indirectly neutralizes the toxicity of the toxin by enhancing the target protein activity that is inhibited by the toxin. As a result, both the toxin and the antitoxin act on the same target protein. In the Type V TA system, the antitoxin is a sequence-specific ribonuclease, cleaving the toxin mRNA to repress the toxin expression (Wang et al., 2012). Very recently, the Type VI TA system has been proposed, in which the toxin is unstable so that it is readily degraded by ClpXP protease. However, for this toxin degradation, the antitoxin is required as an adapter for ClpXP. Therefore, without the antitoxin, the toxin cannot be degraded to maintain the toxicity (Aakre et al., 2013). 

## 2.7.2.1 Type I TA system

In a Type I TA system such as RdlD–LdrA (Kawano et al., 2002; Yamaguchi et al., 2014), SymR–SymE (Kawano et al., 2007), and IstR–TisB (Unoson and Wagner, 2008; Vogel et al., 2004), the toxin gene expression is regulated by an antisense RNA transcribed from the same site for the toxin gene in the reverse orientation (Figure 2.7.1a) (Fozo et al., 2008b; Gerdes and Wagner, 2007). The RNA antitoxins bind to the toxin mRNAs, forming a double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), which is considered to stimulate the degradation of the toxin mRNAs by RNase III, a specific RNase for dsRNAs, resulting in the inhibition of toxin expression (Gerdes and Wagner, 2007). All of the toxins of the Type I TA system except the RalR–RalA and SymR–SymE TA systems consist of a very small hydrophobic polypeptide made up of 19 to 38 amino acid residues (Fozo et al., 2008a). For example, overexpression of LdrA, one of the Type I TA toxins, has been demonstrated to disturb the cytoplasmic membrane structure to inhibit ATP synthesis (Yamaguchi et al., 2014). Almost all the toxins so far characterized in the Type I TA system in E. coli are predicted to have an identical secondary structure consisting of a long α-helical structure, and to be localized in the inner membrane, likely forming a pore to destroy the membrane potential inhibiting ATP synthesis (Fozo et al., 2008b; Kawano et al., 2002, 2007; Unoson and Wagner, 2008; Yamaguchi et al., 2014). RalR from E. coli is the only toxin inhibiting DNA stability but not ATP synthesis. RalR is a non-sequencespecific endodeoxyribonuclease cleaving both methylated and unmethylated DNA (Guo et al., 2014). To repress the expression of RalR toxin, the Hfq RNA chaperone is required for RalA antitoxin activity and seems to stabilize RalA antitoxin RNA (Guo et al., 2014). 

## 2.7.2.2 Type II TA system

In the Type II TA system, each TA system is encoded by two small genes, which usually overlap by a few bases or, in some instances, are separated by a few bases (Figure 2.7.1b) (Yamaguchi et al., 2011). A toxin and its cognate antitoxin form a stable TA complex, which blocks the function of the toxin (see Chapter 6.4). Under stress conditions, however, antitoxins are preferentially digested by stress-induced proteases such as Lon, ClpAP, and/or ClpXP, resulting in the release of toxins from the TA complexes causing cell growth arrest or cell death (Aizenman et al., 1996; Christensen and Gerdes, 2003; Christensen et al., 2004). Since a Type II antitoxin contains a DNA-binding region in addition to the separate toxinbinding site, both the antitoxin and the TA complex, the TA complex is much stronger and functions as the repressor for the TA operon transcription by binding a palindromic sequence in the promoter region. Therefore, when the antitoxin is degraded by stress-induced proteases, the expression of the TA operon is de-repressed to produce more antitoxin and toxin, resulting in a higher concentration of the TA complex, which then functions as a repressor for the TA operon. Under this condition, the concentration of the free toxin in the cells increases, since the antitoxin is more unstable than its cognate toxin, causing cell growth arrest and/or cell death (Marianovsky et al., 2001). In this manner, the expression of the TA operon is autoregulated, and thus the Type II system is also termed as the addiction module (Yarmolinsky, 1995). In most of the Type II TA systems, the antitoxin genes are located upstream of their cognate toxin genes so that the antitoxins appear to have an advantage for their production over their cognate toxins. However, there are many exceptional cases in which the toxin genes are located upstream of their cognate antitoxin genes (Jorgensen et al., 2009; Yamaguchi et al., 2009). These differences in the gene order may have subtle effects on the toxin–antitoxin ratio in the cell, which in turn regulates the toxin function. It is also interesting to note that the isoelectric point (pI) values of the toxin proteins tend to be basic, whereas those for their cognate antitoxin proteins are acidic, which appears to facilitate the formation of stable TA complexes. 

## 2.7.2.3 Type III TA system

The ToxI–ToxN TA system from a plasmid in the plant pathogen Pectobacterium atrosepticum was the first example identified as a Type III TA system, in which an RNA antitoxin, ToxI-RNA (36 nucleotides), directly inhibits the toxicity of ToxN (Figure 2.7.1c) (Fineran et al., 2009). The X-ray structure of the ToxI-RNA–ToxN complex has been determined, in which three ToxI-RNA molecules bind individually to three ToxN monomers, forming a trimeric ToxN–ToxI complex (Blower et al., 2011). 

The genes for ToxN homologs have been found in other plasmids and the chromosomes of diverse bacteria, including human and animal pathogens, and soil and marine bacteria (Fineran et al., 2009). It is not known whether these ToxN genes are also regulated by antitoxin RNAs. It has also been shown that ToxN has an endoribonuclease activity, but it is not known at present if this endoribonuclease activity indeed causes the ToxN toxicity. Recent in silico analyses suggest three different Type III TA families are distributed in a range of different prokaryotic phyla (Blower et al., 2012). 

## 2.7.2.4 Type IV TA system

Recently, the Type IV TA system has been found in E. coli (Masuda et al., 2012). In this system, the toxin protein CbtA (YeeV) inhibits polymerization of the cytoskeleton proteins, FtsZ and MreB, which are required for cell division and morphology. Interestingly, although CbeA (YeeU) antitoxin is a protein, it does not form a complex with its cognate toxin protein, CbtA. Instead, the CbeA antitoxin neutralizes the CbtA toxicity by accelerating the polymerization of MreB and FtsZ. Both the toxin and the antitoxin antagonistically act on the same protein (Figure 2.7.1d). Quite recently, the AbiEi–AbiEii TA system has been identified as a possible second example of the Type IV TA system. The abiE operon consists of abiEi antitoxin and abiEii toxin genes. The mechanism of the antitoxin activity has not been identified yet. However, since AbiEi appears to be unable to interact with AbiEii, this TA system cannot be classified as a Type II TA system. Furthermore, when AbiEii toxin is overexpressed with AbiEi antitoxin, this antitoxin does not display a ribonuclease activity like an antitoxin of the Type V TA system. Thus, AbiE is unlikely to be classified as a Type V system, so Dy et al. proposed that the AbiEi–AbiEii TA system should be classified as a new TA system, the Type IV TA system (Dy et al., 2014). 

## 2.7.2.5 Type V TA system

GhoS–GhoT is the only example of the Type V TA system. In the E. coli GhoS–GhoT TA system, the activity of GhoT toxin is regulated posttranscriptionally by the antitoxin, GhoS (Figure 2.7.1e) (Wang et al., 2012). GhoS antitoxin is a sequence-specific endoribonuclease cleaving the GhoT mRNA, resulting in the neutralization of the toxin. Except for this unique neutralization mechanism, the Type V TA system is quite similar to the Type II TA system. However, in contrast to the Type II TA systems, GhoS antitoxin is a stable protein and does not bind to its own promoter. In addition, GhoT toxin causes cell membrane damage, ultimately leading to cell lysis (Cheng et al., 2014). Since GhoT is predicted to be a membrane protein because of its hydrophobicity, its expression causes membrane disturbance that prevents ATP synthesis as in the case of LdrA toxin. The GhoS–GhoT TA system is conserved in Serratia and Erwinia and possibly in other organisms. Interestingly, toxin protein translation is inhibited by antisense RNA in the Type I TA system, whereas toxin protein translation in the Type V TA system is inhibited by antitoxin RNase. It is quite interesting to study the mechanisms by which the toxins are induced in these types of TA systems. 

## 2.7.2.6 Type VI TA system

Caulobacter crescentus SocA–SocB is the only example characterized as a Type VI TA system to date (Aakre et al., 2013). Toxin SocB is an unstable protein, since it is constitutively degraded by ClpXP protease. In this TA system, SocA antitoxin neutralizes SocB by acting as an accelerator for the degradation of SocB by ClpXP. SocB toxin interacts with SocA antitoxin, and the resulting SocB–SocA complex then becomes a prey for ClpXP protease (Figure 2.7.1f). This explains the fact that clpXP is essential for viability of Caulobacter. This is a quite unique mechanism to neutralize the toxicity by antitoxin, in which a protein antitoxin functions as a proteolytic adaptor to target the toxin for its degradation. SocB inhibits the elongation reaction of DNA replication by a direct interaction with DnaN, forming the sliding clamp that results in inhibiting the formation of the driving replication fork. Based on the experiment with SocB and DnaN mutants, it has been shown that SocB binds to a hydrophobic cleft in DnaN required for its binding to DNA polymerase III through the DnaN-binding motif. It has been suggested that SocB disrupts replication by outcompeting other clamp-binding proteins (Aakre et al., 2013). 

## 2.7.3 Diversity of the toxin targets

The cellular targets of the toxins encoded by TA systems are highly diverse, and the toxicity of each toxin from the different TA systems is activated under different environmental conditions (Gerdes et al., 2005; Yamaguchi et al., 2011). Therefore, deciphering the function and cellular target of each toxin is of fundamental importance for our understanding of the roles of the TA systems in bacteria and archaea. 

## 2.7.3.1 DNA

Although many toxins have been identified to work as sequencespecific RNases, toxins targeting DNA have not been found for a long time. Recently, however, RalR toxin was demonstrated to be an endodeoxyribonuclease cleaving both methylated and unmethylated DNA (Guo et al., 2014). It had been speculated that RalR is a small toxic protein. Indeed, induction of ralR in E. coli showed growth arrest. The purified RalR cleaves lambda DNA in a pattern similar to that of DNase I, an endodeoxyribonuclease that cleaves DNA nonspecifically (Kunitz, 1950; Vanecko and Laskowski, 1961). Moreover, RalR also cleaves genomic DNA of E. coli and pBR322 plasmid DNA, indicating that RalR can cleave methylated DNA as well (Guo et al., 2014). This was also confirmed by the fact that RalR is able to cleave both methylated and unmethylated lambda DNA equally well. RalA activity requires $\mathrm { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ or $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , and EDTA inhibits the RalR activity as in the case of DNase I activity (Guo et al., 2014). Notably, RalR cleaves only DNA but not RNA. 

## 2.7.3.2 DNA replication

It has been reported that two toxins, CcdB and ParE, block DNA replication by inhibiting DNA gyrase activity, which is essential for cell growth. Although both CcdB and ParE toxins inhibit DNA gyrase, there is no homology between them. ParE is a toxin encoded on plasmid RK2 (Easter et al., 1997; Jiang et al., 2002; Roberts et al., 1994), and CcdB is a toxin encoded on the F plasmid (Miki et al., 1992). The mechanism of the action of CcdB has been determined (Couturier et al., 1998). CcdB binds to the dimerization domain of GyrA, thereby preventing strand passage and the formation of functional conformation of GyrA (Loris et al., 1999). ParE from plasmid RK2 is thought to inhibit GyrA gyrase activity by stabilizing gyrase–DNA complexes similar to CcdB (Yuan et al., 2010). However, E. coli harboring a CcdB-resistant GyrA is not resistant to ParE, indicating that ParE inhibits the gyrase activity in a manner different from that of CcdB (Roberts et al., 1994). Recently, it has been shown that ParE2 encoded on the Vibrio cholerae genome requires ATP in contrast to CcdB (Aakre et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2002). This ParE2 inhibits gyrase-dependent DNA supercoiling but not DNA relaxation. 

Very recently, the SocA–SocB TA system was identified in C. crescentus (Aakre et al., 2013). Not only is the neutralization mechanism of SocB toxicity by SocA very interesting, but also the target of SocB toxin is unique. This toxin contains a DnaNbinding motif, indicating that this toxin is likely to directly bind to DnaN in a similar manner as known clamp-binding proteins and competes for binding to DnaN during DNA replication, resulting in the inhibition of DNA synthesis (Aakre et al., 2013). Further experiments are needed to clarify the inhibition mechanism of replication mediated by SocB. 

## 2.7.3.3 mRNA stability

Among the cellular targets for TA systems, mRNA is the most frequent target for toxins. Out of 29 TA systems in E. coli so far characterized, eight have been identified to regulate mRNA stability (Yamaguchi and Inouye, 2011). Since all of these eight toxins cleave cellular mRNAs, they are termed “mRNA interferases” (Yamaguchi and Inouye, 2011; Inouye, 2006). Based on how these mRNA interferases cleave mRNAs, they are classified into two different types: those that can freely cleave mRNAs in the absence of ribosomes (ribosome-independent mRNA interferases), and others that cleave mRNA only when they associate with ribosomes (ribosome-dependent mRNA interferases) (Yamaguchi and Inouye, 2009, 2011). 

Ribosome-independent mRNA interferases are sequencespecific endoribonucleases that cleave mRNA at specific RNA sequences (Yamaguchi and Inouye, 2009). The first such enzyme is MazF from E. coli that cleaves mRNA at ACA sequences to effectively inhibit protein synthesis (Zhang et al., 2003b). Since then, a large number of MazF homologs have been identified in bacteria and archaea, and some bacteria have more than one MazF homolog. MazF homologs so far identified specifically cleave mRNAs at either three-, five-, or seven-base recognition sequences (Park et al., 2011; Yamaguchi et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2003b). It is not clear at present why these cleavage sites consist of only odd base numbers, but it is interesting to see how the RNA cleavage site expands by two bases at a time from three-base sequences to five- and to seven-base sequences. The RNA recognition and cleavage specificity appear to be extended only from the 3′ end, which is particularly evident when the E. coli MazF cleavage site (AˆCA or ˆACA) is compared with the cleavage sequence of the MazF homolog (MazFhw) from a superhalophilic archaea, Haloquadrutum walsbyi (UUˆACUCA) (Yamaguchi et al., 2012). It seems that more room is available at the 3′ end on the MazF–dimer interface for RNA substrate binding on the basis of the X-ray structure of the RNA–MazF complex (Simanshu et al., 2013). 

As the recognition sequences become longer, the target mRNAs become more limited so that MazF homologs cleave more and more specific mRNA species in the cells or fewer specific cellular mRNAs. MazF-hw, a seven-base cutter from a coastal brine pool on the Sinai Peninsula in Egypt, seems to specifically cleave the rhodopsin transcriptional activator, as its mRNA contains (unusually) as many as three of the sevenbase sequences (Yamaguchi et al., 2012). It should be noted that in comparison with DNA restriction enzymes, which require a palindromic sequence for cleavage, the number of mRNA interferases, which may be called mRNA restriction enzymes, have potentially so much more, since they do not require any palindromic sequences for sequence recognition. For example, there are only a maximum of 64 DNA restriction enzymes for six-base DNA sequences, but there are as many as 4096 (= 64 × 64) possible cleavage sites for single-stranded six-base RNA sequences. Although we have found a seven-base specific mRNA interferase cleaving only one out of a total of 16,384 possible seven-base sequences, it remains to be elucidated how many other sevenbase specific mRNA interferases actually exist in nature. There could be only a few such enzymes. The cellular function of MazF homologs appears to be highly diverse, from those that eliminate almost all cellular mRNAs, such as ACA-specific E. coli MazF, to those that are highly sequence-specific such as MazF-hw that eliminate only a specific group of mRNAs in the cells (Yamaguchi et al., 2012). Recently, the X-ray structure of a UACAU-specific MazF homolog from Bacillus subtilis forming a complex with a 9-base long uncleavable substrate RNA has been described (Simanshu et al., 2013). The X-ray structure of the RNA–MazF complex provides insights into how a specific RNA sequence can be recognized by MazF. On the basis of the X-ray structure and other information, it is now possible to design MazF homologs that cleave other RNA sequences or sequence-specific RNA-binding proteins. 

Ribosome-dependent mRNA interferases have no or very weak endoribonuclease activity (Christensen et al., 2001; Yamaguchi and Inouye, 2009; Zhang and Inouye, 2009; Zhang et al., 

2009). The RelE in the RelB–RelE TA system is one of the most investigated ribosome-dependent mRNA interferases (Christensen et al., 2003). It has been documented that RelE associates with the ribosome A-site, leading to cleavage of mRNA preferentially between the second and the third nucleotides of the termination codon (Christensen et al., 2001; Pedersen et al., 2003). The X-ray structure of the RelE–ribosome complex has been determined, showing that RelE tightly interacts with 16S rRNA but not with 50S subunits and with any ribosomal proteins (Neubauer et al., 2009). In this manner, RelE effectively inhibits protein synthesis. Homologs of the RelB–RelE system have been found in other bacteria as well as in archaea, which exist either on the chromosome or on plasmids (Christensen and Gerdes, 2003; Shao et al., 2011). RelE binds to 30S ribosomes, and it is postulated that this binding stimulates an endogenous ribonuclease activity of ribosomes (Hayes and Sauer, 2003; Pedersen et al., 2003). However, at present one cannot exclude a possibility that this toxin–ribosome interaction may induce a conformational change in the RelE protein, which may activate the latent ribonuclease activity of RelE. 

YoeB is another ribosome-dependent mRNA interferase but is associated with 50S ribosomes to specifically block translation initiation, resulting in cleavage of mRNAs immediately downstream of the initiation codon (Zhang and Inouye, 2009). Since YoeB was shown to have a weak ribonuclease activity (Kamada and Hanaoka, 2005), the mRNA cleavage observed may be directly caused by YoeB protein as a result of conformational change occurring in the YoeB molecule upon its association with 50S ribosomes. As described in this chapter, the mechanism of RNA cleavage appears to be quite different for each ribosome-dependent mRNA interferase. Interestingly, YoeB and RelE share a structural similarity, but the former interacts with 50S ribosomes to inhibit translation initiation, while the latter associates with 30S ribosomes to inhibit translation elongation. 

In VapC toxin, it was shown that VapC-mt4 in M. tuberculosis is a sequence-specific RNA-binding protein that results in cell growth arrest. This toxin has endoribonuclease activity, but it is very weak. As we mentioned in this chapter, the RNase activity of toxins such as MazF, YafQ, HigB, and ChpBK inhibits translation by cleaving mRNA; however, the cleavage of mRNA is not the primary effect of VapC-mt4-mediated translation inhibition. Instead, VapC-mt4 toxicity appears to result from its stable and selective binding to RNA containing an ACGC or AC(A/U)GC consensus sequence (Sharp et al., 2012). 

## 2.7.3.4 Ribosomes

The Phd-Doc TA system is derived from bacteriophage P1 (Jensen and Gerdes, 1995). Doc toxin inhibits translation elongation through its association with the 30S ribosomal subunit (Liu et al., 2008). Doc expression inhibits cell growth by inhibiting translation but not transcription and replication. Interestingly, Doc does not cleave mRNA, as documented with other toxins like mRNA interferases. Doc appears to function in a manner similar to that of an aminoglycoside antibiotic, hygromycin B (HygB), by inhibiting translation elongation. HygB is able to block Doc binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, indicating that HygB binds to the same region on the ribosomes as Doc (Liu et al., 2008). Furthermore, a HygBresistant strain is not sensitive to the toxicity exerted by the induction of Doc protein, suggesting that the Doc-binding site is located on a highly conserved region in 16S rRNAs similar to the HygB binding site at the 30S–50S ribosome interface containing the P and A sites, which are essential for protein translation. Notably, since Doc inhibits translation elongation by binding to ribosome, cellular mRNAs become highly stable (4–10-fold) (Liu et al., 2008). Recently, it has been reported that Doc toxin is a kinase-inactivating elongation factor, EF-Tu (Cruz et al., 2014). 

## 2.7.3.4.1 Ribosomal RNA (rRNA)

Ribosomal RNAs (23S and 16S rRNA) seem to be a good target for toxins since the RNAs are the component of active center in the ribosome. Recently, it has been shown that MazFmt6, one of nine MazF homologs in M. tuberculosis (Pandey and Gerdes, 2005), targets 23 rRNAs (Schifano et al., 2013). These authors found that MazF-mt6 cleaves mRNA at UUCCU sequences. Subsequently, they also discovered that MazF-mt6 cleaves M. tuberculosis 23S rRNA at a single UUCCU site in the ribosome, resulting in the inhibition of protein translation without mRNA cleavage (Schifano et al., 2013). Notably, it has been shown that endoribonuclease toxins such as MazF have no effect on ribosomal RNAs, as it appears that rRNAs are protected by ribosomal proteins from cleavage by the toxins, and it has also been reported that E. coli MazF toxin cleaves 16S rRNA in vivo to form a subpopulation of specialized ribosomes (stress ribosomes) resulting in selective translation of leaderless mRNA (Vesper et al., 2011) The cleavage of 23S rRNA mediated by MazF-mt6 results in the inhibition of protein synthesis as well as 50S–30S ribosome subunit association. 

## 2.7.3.4.2 Transfer RNA (tRNA)

The VapB–VapC TA system is composed of VapB antitoxin and VapC toxin. All the VapC toxins from M. tuberculosis are classified together into a group since all of them contain a PIN (PilT N-terminal) domain. This domain contains a conserved quartet of acidic residues and a fifth invariant serine or threonine residue responsible for coordinating a Mg2+ ion(s) in the catalytic center (Arcus et al., 2011). VapC proteins in Shigella flexneri 2a virulence plasmid pMYSH6000 and Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium LT2 are site-specific endonucleases cleaving Nformylmethionine (tRNAfMet) at the anticodon stem–loop site both in vivo and in vitro (Winther and Gerdes, 2011). Thus, VapC inhibits translation both in vivo and in vitro. Inhibited translation reactions can be reactivated by the addition of VapB and extra charged tRNAfMet. Similarly, ectopic production of tRNAfMet counteracts VapC function in vivo. Thus, one can conclude that tRNAfMet is the only cellular target of VapC. Since 

VapC-mt4 does not cleave tRNAfMet, caution should be taken for the identification of the target of VapC homologs in bacteria. 

## Aminoacyl-tRNA synthase

HipA in E. coli is a kinase that has been proposed to inhibit translation by the phosphorylation of the essential translation factor EF-Tu, resulting in inhibition of cell growth and induction of persistence (Schumacher et al., 2009). However, recently, another inhibitory mechanism has been proposed, as the target of HipA is glutamyl-tRNA synthetase (GltX) but not EF-Tu, so that the overexpression of GltX suppresses the HipA toxicity (Germain et al., 2013). Moreover, HipA phosphorylates its conserved Ser239. Note that Ser239 belongs to the conserved KLSKR motif, which is the characteristic sequence motif of ATP-binding sites of type I aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, existing near the active center of GltX. The serine phosphorylation inhibits the aminoacylation reaction of glutamyl tRNA and thus the GltX activity (Sekine et al., 2003). It has been suggested that the phosphorylation causes a conformational change of GltX, which may lead to the catalytic inactivation of GltX. This is a unique example of the inhibition of an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase by a toxin of the TA systems (Germain et al., 2013). The effects of HipA expression on persistence are not clearly explained by the previous EF-Tu targeting models. In the new GltX targeting model, GltX is active without HipA, so that translation proceeds normally. However, when HipA becomes active, the GltX activity is inhibited by its phosphorylation, resulting in the accumulation of uncharged tRNAGlu, which increases the frequency of hungry A site codons in ribosome. As a result, uncharged tRNAGlu enters the ribosomal A site, resulting in the activation of RelA, a ppGpp synthase. RelA activation leads to an increased (p)ppGpp that conjures the inhibition of translation, transcription, replication, and cell wall synthesis, thereby leading to slow growth, multidrug tolerance, and persistence (Magnusson et al., 2005; Maisonneuve et al., 2013; Srivatsan and Wang, 2008; see Chapter 6.3). 

## 2.7.3.5 Cell division

Recently, it was found that CbtA (YeeV) toxin inhibits cell division, which alters the cell morphology from rod- to lemonshaped cells in E. coli (Masuda et al., 2012). Interestingly, CbtA interacts with FtsZ, a tubulin-like protein, and MreB, a prokaryotic actin-like protein. FtsZ is a highly conserved GTPase (de Boer et al., 1992; RayChaudhuri and Park, 1992), which forms a ring structure at septa and is essential for cell division. MreB is required for maintenance of the typical rod shape of cells, and it assembles into a helical structure that coils along the cell length (Jones et al., 2001; van den Ent et al., 2001). MreB is also involved in cell division (Wachi and Matsuhashi, 1989), chromosome segregation (Kruse et al., 2003; Kruse and Gerdes, 2005), and cell polarity (Gitai et al., 2004). This is the first toxin to date that inhibits cell growth by binding to the cytoskeletal proteins (Masuda et al., 2012). E. coli has two other CbtA homologs, YpjF and YkfI (Brown and Shaw, 2003). CbtA shows 78% and 75% homology to YpjF and YkfI, respectively, suggesting that YpjF and YkfI also bind to FtsZ and MreB to inhibit cell division. Since both MreB and FtsZ are homologous to eukaryotic actin and tubulin, respectively, it is possible that CbtA and its homologs may be able to inhibit the functions of human cytoskeleton proteins. 

## 2.7.3.6 ATP synthesis

All the Type I toxins except for RalR and SymE, thus far identified, appear to inhibit ATP synthesis (Fozo et al., 2008b; Kawano et al., 2002; Unoson and Wagner, 2008; Yamaguchi et al., 2014). Overproduction of TisB or Hok is shown to inhibit cell growth and to reduce colony formation units (Gerdes et al., 1986; Unoson and Wagner, 2008). Both proteins are inserted into the inner membrane, affecting the membrane integrity to cause inhibition of ATP synthesis. Consequently, replication, transcription, and translation are severely inhibited. Overproduction of IbsC and ShoB proteins has also been shown to destroy the proton gradient across the inner membrane (Fozo et al., 2008b). Since all the Type I toxins have an identical secondary structure consisting of one α-helix, they are predicted to form a pore across the inner membrane to inhibit ATP synthesis (Fozo et al., 2008b; Kawano et al., 2002; Unoson and Wagner, 2008; Yamaguchi et al., 2014). These toxins may also interact with another inner membrane protein(s), leading to the inhibition of ATP synthesis. Previously (Dorr et al., 2010), TisB was shown to be involved in the persister phenomenon after treatment with the antibiotic ciprofloxacin. The persister mechanism caused by TisB expression is not well understood at present; however, the inhibition of ATP synthesis caused by TisB is likely to be an important factor for causing the persister phenomenon. Interestingly, several toxins in the Type I TA system (SymE, HokE, and TisB) are induced under SOS response (Courcelle et al., 2001; Fernandez De Henestrosa et al., 2000; Kawano et al., 2007; Pedersen and Gerdes, 1999; Vogel et al., 2004). It is predicted that the induction of these toxins causes growth arrest by inhibition of ATP synthesis but does not cause cell death (Dorr et al., 2010; Unoson and Wagner, 2008). It has been shown that GhoT toxin (57 amino acids) encoded by the GhoT–GhoS TA system (a Type V TA system) is predicted to be a membrane protein inhibiting ATP synthesis by affecting membrane integrity, but it does not cause cell lysis (Cheng et al., 2014). 

## 2.7.4 Application of TA systems

Many toxins have been studied not only for their physiological functions but also for their application as new tools in biotechnology and medicine. Particularly, among toxins encoded by the TA systems, sequence-specific endoribonucleases have been used for interesting biotechnological applications. The singleprotein production (SPP) system (Suzuki et al., 2005, 2006) established using MazF from E. coli has been shown to be highly useful in protein structure biology, in particular for membrane proteins (Mao et al., 2009). To solve the structure of membrane proteins, there are two fundamental problems: first, it is hard to overproduce membrane proteins; and, second, their purification is tedious and difficult. To circumvent these problems, a system called the SPP system has been developed, by which only a target membrane protein can be produced in living E. coli cells. In this system, MazF, an ACA-specific mRNA interferase from E. coli, is induced to eliminate almost all of the cellular mRNAs, creating quasi-dormant cells. The quasi-dormant cells, however, retain full metabolic activity, including the production of ATP and all the other nucleotides, amino acids biosynthesis, RNA transcription, and protein synthesis. Under this condition, one can first engineer an mRNA to eliminate all ACA sequences in the mRNA without altering the amino acid sequence of the protein encoded by the mRNA. Then, if this mRNA is induced in the MazFinduced quasi-dormant cells, the cells are able to produce only the protein encoded by that mRNA. Thus, live E. coli cells are converted into a bioreactor, producing only a target protein of interest (Suzuki et al., 2005). Importantly, this bioreactor is fully functional in a minimal medium consisting of only glucose and $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } C l . }$ . Therefore, isotope-labeled $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - g l u c o s e \ a n d \ ^ { 1 5 } N \mathrm { - N H _ { 4 } C l } }$ are directly used in the culture medium for nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) protein structural study. In addition, using proper amino acid auxotroph strains, one can also highly efficiently label a target protein with specific isotope-labeled amino acid(s) (Suzuki et al., 2006). In this approach, there are important unique features only achievable with the SPP system. Cell cultures can be highly concentrated for isotope labeling (20- to 100-fold) so that the concentration of expensive isotope-labeled amino acids can be significantly reduced, achieving significant cost saving. In addition, the cost saving for expensive $\mathrm { D } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ for the culture medium, which is essential for NMR protein structural study, is highly notable (Mao et al., 2009, 2011). 

In addition, MazF has been shown to be useful to regulate cell growth and death in mammalian cells (de la Cueva-Mendez et al., 2003; Shimazu et al., 2007, 2014; Slanchev et al., 2005). For example, MazF induction in mammalian cells causes striking degradation of cellular mRNAs to inhibit protein synthesis, leading to NBK–BIK and BAK-dependent apoptosis (Shimazu et al., 2007). This result raises the intriguing possibility that MazF or any other mRNA interferases may be used as a tool for gene therapy dealing with cancer and AIDS. Indeed, recently it has been demonstrated that CD4+ cells carrying the E. coli MazF gene under the Tar promoter from HIV-1 acquire resistance against HIV-1 infection (Chono et al., 2011b). Recently, the in vivo safety of this strategy and the persistence of the transfected CD4+ cells have been tested using monkeys (Chono et al., 2011a,b). Furthermore, the use of MazF for the treatment and prevention of infections by RNA viruses such as HIV-1 and hepatitis C virus (HCV) has been demonstrated (Park et al., 2012; Shapira et al., 2012). In these experiments, sequence-specific proteases from these viruses were utilized to activate MazF. Note that these proteases are essential for infection and assembly of virus particles (Carrere-Kremer et al., 2004; Freed, 1998). For example, the HIV-1 genome consists of a single-stranded RNA of 9749 bases in length, and when it is translated, two polyproteins are synthesized (Frankel and Young, 1998). These proteins are then further processed by a HIV-1 protease, producing essential proteins for HIV-1 infection and generation of the fully infectious viral particles. Two important features of MazF are used in this approach: (i) MazF forms a stable complex with its antitoxin, MazE (Zhang et al., 2003a), resulting in suppression of its endoribonuclease activity and, thus, its toxicity (Zhang et al., 2003b); and (ii) MazF induction in mammalian cells effectively causes Bak-dependent apoptotic cell death (Shimazu et al., 2007). In order to use MazF as a novel antivirus agent, a short C-terminal fragment of MazE was fused to the N-terminal end of MazF with a linker containing a specific sequence cleavable by the viral protease (Park et al., 2012; Shapira et al., 2012). Therefore, when the viral protease is induced in the virus-infected cells, the linker will be cleaved so that the short fragment of MazE is dissociated from MazF. MazF is thus activated, and it will then digest viral RNAs as well as cellular mRNAs, leading to apoptotic cell death of only the virus-infected cells. Thus, only those cells infected with HIV-1 or HCV will be eradicated with simultaneous disintegration of infectious viral RNA. This approach may also be applied to other pathogens such as Plasmodium vivax, as its proteases are important for its survival within the host cells (Vera et al., 2011). Another interesting aspect of mRNA interferase toxins is the recent finding of a highly sequence-specific mRNA interferase in an archaeon cleaving a specific seven-base sequence, possibly existing only once in every 16,384 bases (Yamaguchi et al., 2012). This finding clearly demonstrates that there is a novel mechanism for mRNA interference in addition to antisense RNA regulation to regulate specific gene expression by using highly sequence-specific mRNA interferases. 

Another application of a toxin is to prevent self-ligation of a cloning vector without inserting a DNA fragment to be cloned. To avoid this problem, CcdB toxin has been used (Lifescience Technology). This cloning vector contains the ccdB gene fused to the C-terminus of the LacZα fragment. Ligating a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) product into the vector results in the disruption of the expression of the lacZα–ccdB gene fusion, permitting growth of only positive recombinants upon transformation into cells. Cells that contain the non-recombinant vector are killed upon plating. Therefore, blue–white screening is not required for cloning. 

The development of novel antibiotics inhibiting the TA complex formation is also very attractive, as such antibiotics would have two synergistic effects: one to release free toxin in the cell, and the other to de-repress the TA operon expression resulting in more toxin production, as the TA complex functions as a repressor for its own operon. Thus, such antibiotics cause a synergistic toxic effect enhancing the toxicity of the TA system. 

Research on the TA systems has started only recently, and many questions remain to be elucidated. It is likely that more new TA systems will be discovered, and deciphering of the mechanisms of these new toxic functions will further provide important insights into our understanding of highly diverse roles of TA systems in cell physiology in bacteria and archaea. And, certainly, their application in biotechnology and medicine is wide open.

## 2.8.1 Introduction

Cellular RNAs are differentiated into two major classes. Class I RNAs or non-protein-coding RNAs lack open reading frames (ORFs). Class II RNAs, represented by protein-coding RNAs (messenger RNAs, or mRNAs), carry defined ORFs and are readily translated into (poly)peptides (Brosius, 2009; Brosius and Tiedge, 2004). Based on RNA size criteria, eukaryotic npcRNAs are defined as small (<500 nucleotides [nts]) and long non-protein-coding RNAs (>500 nts). Long eukaryal npcRNAs frequently are co- and post-transcriptionally processed; RNAs are often capped, spliced, and polyadenylated. Bacterial small non-protein-coding RNAs (sRNAs) commonly range between 20 and 300 nts. To date, many sRNAs have been discovered, but only a few are functionally characterized (Chinni et al., 2010; Papenfort and Vogel, 2014; Tang et al., 2002, 2005). 

The majority of sRNAs regulate gene expression by base pairing with mRNAs by cis- and trans-encoded interactions. sRNAs change the stability of corresponding mRNA or participate in the translational activation or repression of target genes by masking the ribosomal binding site (RBS). The mRNAs that are not protected by ribosomes during translation are often subjected to ribonuclease-mediated degradation. In particular, RNase E participates in endonucleolytic processing of target mRNA (Figures 2.8.1 and 2.8.2). Cis-antisense sRNAs originate from the reverse strand of target genes and hence display perfect base complementarities within the mRNA overlapping regions. 

Trans-antisense-encoded sRNAs display only limited base complementarity to multiple RNA targets (Guillier et al., 2006; Richards and Vanderpool, 2011; Sharma et al., 2007). Most trans-encoded sRNAs form ribonucleoprotein complexes with the Hfq protein, a chaperone acting as cofactor that aids in the regulatory roles of sRNA in Gram-negative bacteria (Vogel and Luisi, 2011; Zhang et al., 2003). Hfq protein plays important roles in the expression of virulence factors of pathogenic microorganisms (Sittka et al., 2007). However, the Hfq protein might also participate in the cis-antisense regulation (Chinni et al., 2010; Ross et al., 2013). Certainly, even cis-antisenseencoded sRNAs might act in trans after diffusion. Valid criteria to ultimately distinguish either mode of antisense transcription are difficult to establish. 

sRNAs participate in the transcriptional control of target mRNAs. They promote the formation of terminator or antiterminator structures within the 5′ untranslated region (5′ UTR) (Brantl, 2007). In addition, the large number of sRNAs suggests overlapping RNA transcription. This might render transcriptional interference more prevalent than assumed earlier (Georg and Hess, 2011). It has to be emphasized here that it is the process of sRNA transcription, rather than RNA-encoded mechanisms, which exerts the regulatory impact on target gene expression. Here, we discuss various regulatory roles of sRNA in the bacterial stress response. 

## 2.8.2 Metabolite and nutrient stress regulation

To adapt to the fluctuating growth conditions, bacteria implement efficient strategies to control intracellular metabolite and nutrient levels for cellular survival. Although glucose-6- phosphate (G6P) is an important intermediate for adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and nicotineamide-adenine-dinucleotide (NAD) biosynthesis, high G6P levels are toxic and inhibit cell growth severely (Irani and Maitra, 1977). 

When the G6P level is high, SgrS sRNA positively and negatively regulates the expression of several different target mRNAs in Escherichia coli. The ptsG mRNA target, which encodes EIICBglc, a protein involved in the transport of glucose and α-methylglucoside-6-phosphate, is negatively regulated via the base-pairing interaction between its ribosomal binding site (RBS) and SgrS sRNA. The resulting RNA duplex is then subject to RNase E-mediated degradation (Maki et al., 2010). Therefore, the cellular levels of phosphosugar are significantly reduced, which alleviates glucose-phosphate stress (Morita et al., 2005). 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/dbd2e36b-966a-4745-a615-c0703cb42feb/0e457d04837bde9ecc4bc9f0c797b44c9ad6f8c159e3d6c794c2929a7a6a5716.jpg)



Figure 2.8.1 Stress such as shifts in temperature, pH, and metabolite concentration cause the cis-acting sRNAs to alter the secondary structure of the target mRNA in order to modulate the accessibility of the ribosome at the RBS, which promotes or inhibits translation. The target mRNA is then subjected to degradation by ribonucleases. (Figure courtesy of Hoe et al., 2013).


In terms of positive regulation, SgrS binds yigL mRNA and stabilizes it against the degradation by RNase E. Therefore, haloacid dehalogenase (HAD)-like phosphatase levels are increased and elevate the dephosphorylation of sugarphosphates. The sugars are then utilized for growth rescue (Sun and Vanderpool, 2013). This combined trans-regulatory action of sRNAs on multiple target mRNAs eventually constitutes finetuned networks and transduces the organism’s response to cellular stress. 

Besides multiple target interactions, SgrS also encodes for the short peptide sgrT. This 43-amino acid peptide functions by inhibition of the EIICBglc activity. Subsequently, the glucose uptake is significantly reduced but leaves the ptsG mRNA stability unaltered (Wadler and Vanderpool, 2007). This peptide-encoding property challenges the “untranslated RNAs” definition of sRNA. Minimal sizes of detectable ORF length, which would lead to the classification of sRNAs candidates, have to be reevaluated, so that probably many sRNAs candidates are more appropriately classified as mRNAs.
