Figure 2.8.2 The stress response induces binding of the trans-encoded sRNAs to the RBS, which precludes the ribosomal binding at the RBS. The untranslated mRNA is usually subjected to RNase E–mediated degradation. Most of the trans-encoded sRNAs also involve Hfq protein to stabilize the interaction between the sRNA and mRNA. (Figure courtesy of Hoe et al., 2013).


Biofilm, a surface-associated microbial mode of bacterial growth, provides protection against various antimicrobial agents and as an adaptation to nutrient withdrawal (Banin et al., 2005). Biofilm formation depends on the carbon storage regulatory (Csr) system in E. coli (Romeo et al., 2013) and Serratia marcescens 2170 (Ito et al., 2014). The major component of the Csr system is the CsrA protein dimer, which negatively regulates pgaABCD mRNA expression. The latter encodes for the biofilm polysaccharide adhesin (Mercante et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2005). The activity of CsrA protein is regulated by two sRNAs: CsrB and CsrC that harbor nine and 18 CsrA binding sites, respectively. Both sRNAs sequester free CsrA protein and prevent productive interaction with the corresponding mRNA targets. Interestingly, the CsrD protein, which is also an integral part of the auto-regulatory loop of the Csr system, negatively regulates these sRNAs via RNase E–dependent degradation (Suzuki et al., 2006). 

## 2.8.3 Envelope stress regulation

The bacterial outer membrane protein (OMP) is the barrier that thwarts the influx of toxins into bacterial cells and controls the bacterial resistance by harboring bacterial surface proteins (see Section 18). Regulation of OMPs is influenced by changing environmental stimuli and is important for bacterial survival and virulence (Nikaido et al., 1994). The synthesis of misfolded OMPs triggers the expression of transcription factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ , which (i) upregulates genes to counteract the cellular damage and (ii) triggers regulatory feedback loops to abolish further synthesis of misfolded OMPs. $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ -dependent regulatory sRNAs are RybB, CyaR, and MicA. 

RybB negatively regulates ompW and ompC mRNAs by inhibitory base pairing with the target RBS (Papenfort et $a l .$ , 2010). MicA-based regulation of the target ompA mRNA requires two different types of endonucleases, RNase III and RNase E. The formation of RNA duplexes between MicA and target ompA mRNA induces cleavage mediated by RNase III, whereas RNase E cleaves the unpaired sRNA only (Viegas et al., 2011). 

## 2.8.4 Oxidative stress regulation

Oxidative stress is a condition characterized by an excess level of reactive oxygen species (ROS) due to an imbalance between its generation and elimination from cells (Lushchak, 2011). Excessive ROS can incur damage on proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids. 

Bacterial cells harbor defense mechanisms to reduce the damaging effects of high oxidative stress and maintain physiological levels of intracellular ROS (Cabiscol et al., 2000) (see Section 10). 

Two transduction proteins, SoxR and OxyR, are the key components in the regulatory circuit. The OxyR protein triggers the expression of antioxidant genes, including the OxyS sRNA (Wei et al., 2012). The sRNA is highly expressed in conditions of oxidative stress and participates in the regulation of approximately 40 downstream genes. One of its major molecular targets is fhlA, which encodes for a transcriptional activator. In the presence of formate, FhIA increases the expression of structural genes, giving rise to a formate–hydrogen lyase complex that comprises several metal cofactors. This complex metabolizes formate to dihydrogen and carbon dioxide. OxyS sRNA causes translational repression of $f h l A$ (Argaman and Altuvia, 2000). Consequently, the concentrations of the formate–hydrogen lyase complex are reduced, hence minimizing the deleterious effects of the hydrogen peroxide–induced damage that occurs in the presence of the metal cofactors (Altuvia et al., 1998). OxyS sRNA also negatively regulates the rpoS target mRNA, which encodes for stationary-phase sigma factor $( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { S } } )$ , by rendering the mRNA secondary structure nonpermissive to translation. Consequently, both the respiration and superoxide production are suppressed (Zhang et al., 1998). 

## 2.8.5 Iron stress regulation

Iron is an important cofactor of many enzymes, and it functions as catalyst in electron transport systems. High levels of iron promote the formation of ROS that are deleterious to protein, DNA, lipids, and membranes. The main regulator of cellular iron homeostasis is ferric-uptake regulator (Fur) (Seo et al., 2014). During high iron levels, Fur represses transcription of the operon that encodes for siderofors, small peptides that display high affinity for the ferric iron $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ . Under physiological conditions of low Fe level, siderophores participate in the uptake of extracellular $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ . Subsequently, $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ is reduced to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ by either free extracellular or membrane-standing ferricchelate reductases (Chu et al., 2010). Fur also acts as repressor of iron acquisition genes and RyhB sRNA transcription. RyhB sRNA regulates the synthesis of six iron-binding proteins by promoting RNase E–dependent degradation when iron levels are low (Troxell and Hassan, 2013; see Section 19). 

RyhB sRNA differentially regulates mRNAs in the polycistronic iscRSUA RNA operon (isc-operon), which encodes various proteins involved in the iron–sulfur (2Fe-2S) cluster. Iron–sulfur is vital for electron transport, metallo-enzyme catalysis, respiration, photosynthesis, and nitrogen fixation. Under low iron levels, the highly expressed RyhB sRNA interacts with the RBS of iscR mRNA and causes RNase E–mediated degradation of iscS, iscU, and iscA, respectively. However, the formation of stable secondary structures within the intergenic region between iscR and iscS protects the iscR transcript from degradation. Hence, the regulatory action of the IscR is constitutive even during iron depletion. The iscR mRNA encodes for IscR transcription factor that enables activation of suf operon. The suf operon encodes for proteins that provide similar molecular functions as IscS, IscU, and IscA. However, the suf operon becomes dominant under the iron deficiency condition, via unknown mechanisms (Mettert and Kiley, 2014). 

Besides degradation, RyhB sRNA also triggers the translation of target mRNAs. During iron starvation, sRNA RyhB interacts with shiA mRNA to promote translational initiation. The sRNA occludes the formation of inhibitory RNA structures, and thereby stimulates the translation of shiA mRNA. The ShiA protein transports Shikimate into the cells, aromatic compounds that are vital for biosynthesis of the siderophore enterochelin to correct bacterial growth (Prevost ´ et al., 2007). 

Recent studies demonstrated that paralogs of RhyB sRNA (RyhB-1 and RyhB-2) in Salmonella typhimurium are involved in nitrosative stress resistance. RhyB regulates genes that encode for cytochrome oxidases and the nitrate reductase system (Calderon et al., 2014). The role of RhyB sRNA is not limited only to iron homeostasis, but is also involved in multiple stress regulatory cascades such as nitrosative stress. Hence, RyhB sRNA is a general riboregulator that connects multiple mRNA targets associated with different biochemical pathways. 

## 2.8.6 Acidic stress regulation

The extreme environmental condition in the intestine requires metabolic adaptations of enteric pathogens to ensure survival and growth to incur infection. An essential feature of enteric pathogens is the ability to withstand high gastrointestinal acidity. E. coli utilizes the glutamate-based Gad system (Castanie-Cornet et al., 1999) to protect bacterial cells from the extremely acidic conditions of the intestine (pH 2 to 2.5) (see also Section 6). 

This Gad system depends on two glutamate decarboxylases, GadA and GadB, which, respectively, catalyze the generation of gamma-aminobutyric acid and utilize glutamate as a substrate. The synthesis consumes protons. Subsequently, GadC ensures product efflux. Therefore, the product levels remain constantly low, which stimulates ongoing synthesis. As a result, the intracellular proton levels are maintained, and pH levels are stabilized. GadX activates GadA and GadB transcription. gadX mRNA is regulated by the cis-antisense GadY sRNA, which partly overlaps with the 3′ UTR of the gadX. The resulting base pairing of the GadY sRNA with the gadX 3′ UTR increases its metabolic stability and leads to the accumulation of the mRNA (Opdyke et al., 2004). 

Additional analysis revealed that the gadW gene is located downstream of gadX. gadW is either cotranscribed with gadX or expressed independently depending on its own promoter (Figure 2.8.3) (Opdyke et al., 2011). This implies that GadY sRNA interacts not only with the 3′ UTR of the gadX mRNA but also with the transcribed intergenic sequence space located between gadX–gadW mRNA. The duplex is subject to endonuclease cleavage by RNase III and unknown RNase(s). This cleavage reaction yields two products, one of which is the gadX mRNA. GadY sRNA remains bound at the 3′ UTR of the gadX, protecting it from further degradation (Opdyke et al., 2011). Thus, apart from promoting the mRNA degradation, sRNAs can also induce the endonuclease-dependent operon cleavage and processing.

GadY sRNA base-pairs with the 3′ UTR of the gadX mRNA and the intergenic regions between gadX–gadW mRNA. The duplex formed at the intergenic region is predisposed to cleavage by RNase III and other unidentified RNAses.


## 2.8.7 Anaerobic stress regulation

The shift between aerobic and anaerobic growth conditions for facultative anaerobes requires drastic changes in its gene expression (Constantinidou et al., 2006). In the human gastrointestinal tract, where oxygen is scarce, bacterial cells produce energy from anaerobic respiration using alternative electron acceptors or sugar fermentation. Hence, reduced expression or upregulation of oxygen-dependent or -independent genes helps relieve stress (see Section 10). 

The Arc two-component system is the major circuit in response to low oxygen levels. ArcB is an aerobic respiratory control protein that senses oxygen availability and transmits signals to ArcA (Bekker et al., 2006). Under anaerobic conditions, ArcB is autophosphorylated and in turn phosphorylates ArcA. The latter elevates the expression of genes associated with respiratory and fermentative metabolism. Intriguingly, arcB mRNA overlaps with ArcZ sRNA, and the two transcripts are likely regulating each other. 

The predominant form of ArcZ sRNA (55 nts) is processed from longer precursor transcripts (120 nts). The mature RNA represents the actual 3′ terminal domain of the precursor. Under aerobic conditions, highly expressed ArcZ sRNA causes the destabilization of ArcB mRNA by RNase-mediated degradation, which in turn abrogates ArcA activation. In anaerobic conditions, phosphorylated ArcA represses arcZ transcription. As a consequence, higher expression of ArcB produces more autophosphorylated ArcA. Another ArcA-independent mechanism of ArcZ repression relies on transcriptional interference of arcB and arcZ. The regulation mediated by the ArcZ sRNA represents a branched feedback loop, where the repression of ArcZ sRNA is achieved by both ArcA activation and arcB transcription. This dual system works on the basis that if either component, the ArcZ sRNA or the ArcA–ArcB regulon, is activated, it represses the corresponding partner and ensures its own expression (Mandin and Gottesman, 2010). 

Helicobacter pylori is a Gram-negative bacterium that is able to withstand the acidic environment of the stomach. This is due to the activity of the urease apoenzyme. This enzyme is composed of UreA and UreB subunits, which are derived from adjacent transcripts of ureA and ureB. Urease activity produces $\mathrm { N H } _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { H C O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ buffers, which increase the pH of the cytoplasm and periplasmic lumen, thus maintaining the neutral pH environment (Meyer-Rosberg et al., 1996). At low pH, the histidine residue 94 of the periplasmic histidine kinase sensor ArsS is protonated to cause the phosphorylation of the response regulator ArsR. The phosphorylated ArsR binds to the promoter of the ureA gene, inducing the transcription of ureAB into the corresponding mRNA. Since the urease activity leads to overproduction of $\mathrm { N H } _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { H C O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ buffer systems that increase the pH, transcription of ureAB is negatively regulated by 5′ ureB-sRNA. In vitro assays unveiled the interaction of $5 ^ { \prime }$ ureB-sRNA and unphosphorylated ArsR, which acts as activator of sRNA expression under physiological conditions. The $5 ^ { \prime } u r e B \ – s \mathrm { R N A } .$ , which is encoded in antisense to the $5 ^ { \prime } .$ -terminus of ureB, represses ureAB by the formation of a transcriptional terminator. Subsequently, production o $\mathrm { f N H } _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { H C O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ reduces to maintain the pH at neutral (Wen et al., 2013). 

## 2.8.8 Temperature-based regulation by riboswitch: RNA thermometer

Certain RNA regulatory roles do not involve cis- or transencoded sRNAs but instead depend on elements that form the integral part of the mRNA itself. These regulatory elements are encoded within the $5 ^ { \prime } \mathrm { U T R }$ and adopt specific structural conformations in response to environmental molecular stimuli or even temperature. Collectively these elements, termed riboswitches, undergo structural changes that affect translational or transcriptional efficacy of single genes or even entire operons (Grundy and Henkin, 2006). 

RNA thermometers (RNATs) are temperature-dependent RNA-based control elements usually located within the $5 ^ { \prime }$ UTR of heat $_ { \mathrm { o r } }$ cold shock response genes (see Sections 8, 13, 15). RNATs control the expression of downstream genes based on structural changes within the RNAT. In case of heat shock response, low temperatures induce the RNA to adopt nonpermissive conformations, usually stem-loop structures that inhibit ribosome entry. Consequently, the conformation occludes ribosomal binding and subsequent translational initiation (Narberhaus et al., 2006). In contrast, increase in the temperature destabilizes the RNA secondary structure and permits translational initiation. Hence, different temperatures change the degree of RBS accessibility to ribosomal binding, which affects the translational efficacy. 

(i) fourU element-heat shock response. One well-known example of RNAT is the fourU element, which is located within the $5 ^ { \prime }$ UTR of the Salmonella agsA mRNA (Waldminghaus et al., 2007). The target mRNA encodes a molecular chaperone, which maintains folding competent states of polypeptides in stress conditions. The expression of agsA mRNA is increased at high temperature. Below $3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ , the fourU residues engage in the formation of imperfect RNA duplexes with the AGGA motif of the SD sequence. The resulting hairpin structure prevents ribosomal binding. When the temperature increases $( 4 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ , destabilized hairpin structures enable the translation of the agsA mRNA (Figure 2.8.4). Non-Watson-Crick base pairing

(ii) cspA mRNA–cold shock response. RNAT exerts positive gene regulation at cold shock response. For example, the transcription of $c s p A$ (an antiterminator) is enhanced when the temperature is lowered (Giuliodori et al., 2010). cspA mRNA contains an RNAT that allows mRNA translation at lower temperature $( 1 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ . Consequently, CspA, a single-stranded nucleic acid binding protein, is highly expressed during early growth phases at lower temperature. However, at higher temperature $( 3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ , its secondary structural conformation is destabilized, which leads to the drop in translational efficacy (Brandi et al., 1999). 





Kozak M. 1999. Initiation of translation in prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Gene 234(2): 187–208. 





(iii) Synthetic RNAT-based thermoregulation. The simple hairpin structure of RNAT that facilitates thermoregulation has been utilized in synthetic biology. As a proof of principle, thermozymes were designed with the fourU RNAT and a hammerhead ribozyme. The construct abolished gene expression at high temperature due to ribozyme-mediated cleavage (Saragliadis et al., 2013). This result further substantiates that RNAT can be employed as a synthetic modulator to control the target gene expression.

## 2.8.9 Future perspectives



Maki K, Morita T, Otaka H, Aiba H. 2010. A minimal base-pairing region of a bacterial small RNA SgrS required for translational repression of ptsG mRNA. Molecular Microbiology 76(3): 782–792. 



Base pairing between sRNA and target mRNA(s) is sufficient to repress the translational initiation that occurs via direct interactions of the 16S rRNA with the Shine-Dalgarno (SD) sequence within the $5 ^ { \prime }$ UTR of mRNAs (Kozak, 1999). Thus, sRNA-based regulation can provide a simple and rapid response to assuage detrimental effects of stress and to ensure the bacterial survival. The association of bacterial sRNAs with various stress-related molecular circuits suggests that they might be employed as diagnostic biomarkers of a disease and to monitor the progression of a treatment. Thus, a more in-depth understanding of the sRNAs will increase the efficiency of drug design or the establishment of diagnostic markers.

# Bacterial stress responses as determinants of antimicrobial resistance

Michael Fruci and Keith Poole 

Department of Biomedical and Molecular Sciences, Queen’s University, Kingston, Ontario, Canada 

## 2.9.1 Introduction

It is well known that in vivo susceptibility of bacteria to antimicrobials does not always match in vitro efficacy (Asseray et al., 2005) and that mutational expression of antimicrobial resistance mechanisms can be selected or mutants expressing them enriched in the absence of antimicrobial exposure (Fraud and Poole, 2010), indications that environmental conditions can influence bacterial susceptibility to antimicrobials. Indeed, there is increasing evidence that host-selected adaptive mutations that accumulate in bacteria during persistent infections can impact antimicrobial resistance. This is seen in Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections of the cystic fibrosis (CF) lung, where the most commonly mutated gene in CF lung isolates is the mexZ gene encoding a repressor of the mexXY multidrug efflux operon that contributes to aminoglycoside resistance (Smith et al., 2006). The implication is that the host environment is selecting for mexZ mutants, with efflux gene expression enhancing growth and survival in the CF lung but concomitantly contributing to aminoglycoside resistance. Perhaps not surprisingly, MexXY is the primary determinant of aminoglycoside resistance in CF strains of P. aeruginosa (Poole, 2005). A contribution of adaptive mutations to antimicrobial resistance has also been suggested for Burkholderia pseudomallei infections in recurrent melioidosis (Hayden et al., 2012), and adaptive mutations related to antibiotic resistance have been described in Burkholderia dolosa (Lieberman et al., 2011). Host recruitment of resistance is also seen in the mycobacteria, whose persistence in macrophages and in a zebra fish infection model depends on efflux pump(s) implicated in antibiotic efflux and resistance (Adams et al., 2011). Inducible by the macrophage intercellular environment, these pumps presumably play a role in intracellular survival while also contributing to the demonstrated multidrug resistance of the persisting organisms (Adams et al., 2011). 

A significant environmental impact on bacteria is stress, which, in effecting a myriad of adaptive and protective responses, alters gene expression patterns and cell physiology in ways that influence antimicrobial susceptibility (Poole, 2012a, 2012b). This can occur indirectly, as a result of stress-induced growth cessation or dormancy (Maisonneuve and Gerdes, 2014; Miller et al., 2004; Proctor et al., 2006), since antimicrobials typically act on growing cells (Eng et al., 1991), or directly as a result of the stress-dependent recruitment of resistance determinants (e.g., efflux (Poole, 2008)), changes to antimicrobial targets (Ishiguro and Ramey, 1980; Wu et al., 2010), amelioration of the adverse consequences of antimicrobial action (Han et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2010; Nguyen et al., 2011; Vega et al., 2013), alterations to membrane barrier functions (Meehl et al., 2007; Needham and Trent, 2013; Yang et al., 2012), generation of resistant mutations (Rosenberg et al., 2012), or promotion of resistant growth modes such as biofilms (Landini, 2009). Since antimicrobials are themselves growth-inhibiting stressors that often elicit protective responses in bacteria, these agents can provoke their own resistance-promoting responses (Cirz and Romesberg, 2007; Dorr et al., 2009; Morita et al., 2006). Stress responses, thus, have the potential to contribute significantly to antimicrobial resistance and may themselves be considered antimicrobial resistance determinants. Those stress responses with known links to antimicrobial resistance are summarized in Table 2.9.1 and are discussed in detail below. 

## 2.9.2 Nutrient limitation and stringent response-mediated antimicrobial resistance

Antibiotics generally preferentially kill rapidly replicating bacteria (Eng et al., 1991), and it has been suggested that the reduced growth and metabolic activity associated with nonoptimal (e.g., nutrient-limited) growth environments might explain resistance in these instances. Still, in many cases, nutrient deprivation is seen as a stress, and antibiotic resistance is linked to the bacterium’s response to that stress. A classic example of nutritional stress is amino acid deprivation, which activates what is known as the stringent response (Chatterji and Ojha, 2001; see Section 7). Associated with increased production of the alarmone guanosine 5′ -(tri)diphosphate, 3′ - diphosphate ((p)ppGpp) (Dalebroux and Swanson, 2012), the stringent response is characterized by reduced expression of genes typically associated with growth and increased expression of survival genes that economize the use of scarce nutrients (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). Activated by a variety of nutritional stresses (depletion of Fe, phosphate (Pi), carbon source, or fatty acids) (Sharma and Chatterji, 2010), the stringent response–mediated increase in ppGpp has a myriad of effects on bacterial cell physiology and, perhaps not surprisingly, impacts antimicrobial susceptibility (Wu et al., 2010). It has been known for some time, for example, that amino acid deprivation and the stringent response are linked to penicillin tolerance in Escherichia coli – relA mutants unable to synthesize ppGpp are more sensitive to penicillin-dependent lysis during amino acid deprivation (Kusser and Ishiguro, 1985), and the penicillin resistance of a mutant E. coli strain is similarly lost in the absence of relA (Kusser and Ishiguro, 1987). Increases in ppGpp levels provided by the cloned relA gene in an otherwise wild-type E. coli are also associated with penicillin (Rodionov and Ishiguro, 1995) as well as mecillinam (Vinella et al., 1992) resistance, and the mecillinam resistance of in vitro–selected mecillinam-resistant mutants is associated with and dependent upon elevated ppGpp (Vinella et al., 1992). Accumulation of ppGpp inhibits peptidoglycan (Ishiguro and Ramey, 1980) as well as phospholipid and fatty acid (Heath et al., 1994) synthesis, and this appears to be central to ppGpppromoted penicillin tolerance in E. coli. ppGpp inhibition of cell wall synthesis has been described in other bacteria (Streptomyces coelicolor, Bacillus subtilis, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis), where it is also linked to β-lactam tolerance (Wu et al., 2010). Recent evidence suggests, too, that the stringent response is involved in the mecA-mediated heterologous β-lactam resistance of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) strains, where a subpopulation of cells only is highly β-lactam resistant (Kim et al., 2013; Mwangi et al., 2013). The mecA gene encodes the low-affinity penicillin-binding protein PBP2A, whose expression increases in the highly resistant subpopulation (Kim et al., 2013) concomitant with mutational activation of the stringent response (Kim et al., 2013; Mwangi et al., 2013), suggesting a link between the stringent response and mecAmediated β-lactam resistance. Consistent with this, induction of the stringent response via amino acid starvation renders mecAcarrying heterogeneously resistant clinical isolates of S. aureus highly and homogeneously β-lactam resistant (Kim et al., 2013).
