The ppGpp alarmone is also linked to resistance to other antimicrobials (trimethoprim, gentamicin, and polymyxin B) – E. coli mutants deficient in ppGpp production are more susceptible to these agents (Greenway and England, 1999) (see 

Section 7). Activation of the stringent response via amino acid starvation promotes increased expression of the fluoroquinolone resistance efflux genes norA and mepA and a corresponding increase in ciprofloxacin resistance in S. aureus (Anderson et al., 2006), although the nature of the link between the stringent response and efflux gene expression or whether the efflux genes were responsible for the ciprofloxacin resistance was not assessed. Antimicrobials (mupirocin (Abranches et al., 2009), vancomycin (Abranches et al., 2009), and penicillin (Rodionov and Ishiguro, 1995)) themselves stimulate ppGpp accumulation, but this has not been correlated with any increases in antimicrobial resistance except in Enterococcus faecalis, where a mutant unable to synthesize ppGpp showed reduced tolerance to vancomycin (Abranches et al., 2009). Interestingly, the S. aureus ppGpp synthases RelP and RelQ are inducible by cell envelope stress and mediate tolerance to cell wall–active agents such as vancomycin and ampicillin (Geiger et al., 2014), providing a direct link between antibiotic activation of the stringent response and antibiotic resistance promotion. ppGpp production has also been linked to vancomycin and bacitracin resistance in S. coelicolor (Hesketh et al., 2011), and to tolerance to several antimicrobials in nutrient-limited and biofilm cells of P. aeruginosa (Nguyen et al., 2011). Nguyen and coworkers show that nutrient-limited planktonic and biofilm cells that are defective in the genes for ppGpp production are markedly less antimicrobial tolerant than their wild-type counterparts, with ppGpp-deficient biofilm cells in particular showing reduced tolerance to several classes of antimicrobials (Nguyen et al., 2011). This was explained, in part, by an observed reduction in antioxidant defenses (e.g., catalase and superoxide dismutase) in the ppGpp-deficient mutant that would otherwise protect nutrient-limited wild-type cells from the oxidative killing that is promoted by bactericidal antimicrobials. In agreement with this, the stringent response regulation of catalases and their involvement in the antimicrobial resistance of nutrient-limited biofilm P. aeruginosa were recently confirmed (Khakimova et al., 2013). ppGpp-deficient E. coli also shows enhanced reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and reduced antimicrobial tolerance relative to wild-type cells (Nguyen et al., 2011), suggesting that antimicrobial resistance resultant from a stringent response-mediated amelioration of oxidative stress may be common, at least in Gram-negative bacteria. 

## 2.9.3 Oxidative stress and antimicrobial resistance

Organisms that grow aerobically are routinely exposed to oxidative stress in the form of ROS (e.g., peroxide and superoxide (SO)) that are the unavoidable byproducts of aerobic respiration. ROS damage a variety of cellular macromolecules and, thus, elicit adaptive oxidative stress responses in bacteria that facilitate survival in the presence of this stressor (Imlay, 2013). Expression of a number of multidrug efflux systems is positively impacted by agents of oxidative stress (see Section 10); these efflux systems possibly play some role in ameliorating the adverse effects of oxidative stress. Similarly, a number of antioxidant mechanisms are recruited in response to antimicrobial exposure since antimicrobials themselves generate ROS that appear to contribute to the often-lethal effects of these agents (Kolodkin-Gal et al., 2008). As such, oxidative stress responses have the potential to contribute to antimicrobial resistance in a variety of ways. 

## 2.9.3.1 Efflux

Interestingly, a number of antimicrobial resistance determinants, particularly multidrug efflux systems, and/or their regulatory proteins are impacted by oxidative stress (Table 2.9.1; see Section 10). The SoxR regulator of the acrAB multidrug efflux operon in E. coli (Gu and Imlay, 2011), the MexR regulator of the mexAB–oprM multidrug efflux operon in P. aeruginosa (Chen et al., 2008), and the global regulators MgrA (Chen et al., 2006) and SarZ (Chen et al., 2009) that control expression of the norA (MgrA), norB, and tet38 (MgrA and SarZ) antimicrobial efflux genes in S. aureus are all sensitive to oxidation, with oxidation promoting de-repression of their target genes. Oxidative stress might, thus, be expected to enhance efflux gene expression and so promote antimicrobial resistance in these organisms, although this has yet to be tested. Oxidative stress (i.e., peroxide) induction of multidrug efflux genes has, however, been confirmed for the cmeABC and mexXY multidrug efflux operons of Campylobacter jejuni (Palyada et al., 2009) and P. aeruginosa (Fraud and Poole, 2010), respectively, although an influence of this ROS on antimicrobial resistance was either not tested or not observed. 

The MexXY–OprM efflux system is a common determinant of aminoglycoside resistance in clinical isolates of P. aeruginosa, particularly in CF lung isolates where it is the primary determinant of aminoglycoside resistance (Poole, 2011). The latter is an intriguing observation given that the CF lung is known to be rich in ROS (Ciofu et al., 2005), which may thus promote the development of MexXY-mediated aminoglycoside resistance in CF lung isolates. In agreement with this, in vitro exposure of P. aeruginosa to peroxide has been shown to enhance the frequency with which MexXY-dependent aminoglycosideresistant mutants could be recovered (Fraud and Poole, 2010). Intriguingly, the mexXY operon is also induced by antimicrobials that target the ribosome (e.g., tetracycline, chloramphenicol, erythromycin, and aminoglycosides) (Morita et al., 2006) in response specifically to ribosome disruption (Jeannot et al., 2005). Both drug and ROS induction of mexXY is mediated by the PA5471 (armZ) gene product (Fraud and Poole, 2010) that is also induced by ribosome-perturbing drugs (Morita et al., 2006) and ROS (Chang et al., 2005), and functions as an antirepressor of the mexXY repressor MexZ (Hay et al., 2013). In reconciling mexXY induction by both oxidative stress and ribosome disruption, one possibility is that oxidative stress also disrupts ribosome function or in some way perturbs translation. Alternatively, since ribosome disruption via mutation or antibiotic exposure leads to the production of aberrant polypeptides that are prone to oxidative modification in E. coli (Dukan et al., 2000), it may be that oxidatively modified or damaged proteins are the common trigger for PA5471 and mexXY induction, with MexXY–OprM possibly playing some role in ridding the cells of these damaged or aberrant polypeptides. Interestingly, serial peroxide exposure of Burkholderia vietnamiensis promotes a 16-fold increase in stable resistance to the aminoglycoside tobramycin that is associated with reduced aminoglycoside accumulation (Jassem et al., 2014), suggestive of involvement of an efflux mechanism. Although this is reminiscent of peroxide-promoted enhancement of aminoglycoside resistance in P. aeruginosa that is dependent on the MexXY– OprM efflux system, and a mexY homolog, amrB, has been identified in this organism and its overexpression is linked to aminoglycoside resistance (Jassem et al., 2014), peroxideselected aminoglycoside-resistant strains of B. vietnamiensis do not overexpress amrB (Jassem et al., 2014). Thus, although peroxide-mediated oxidative stress promotes aminoglycoside resistance in B. vietnamiensis, it does not appear to involve this efflux mechanism. 

## 2.9.3.2 Antioxidants

Despite some skepticism surrounding ROS and oxidative stress (see Section 10); being central to bacteria killing by bactericidal antimicrobials (Keren et al., 2013; Liu and Imlay, 2013), it would appear that ROS do contribute to antibiotic lethality (Dwyer et al., 2014). As such, antioxidant and oxidative stress protective responses in bacteria should promote antimicrobial resistance. Consistent with this, elimination of ROS defense genes in E. coli has been correlated with increased antimicrobial susceptibility (Goswami et al., 2006). A possible oxidative stress-protective mechanism that promotes antimicrobial resistance in E. coli involves indole, an extracellular signaling molecule whose production is promoted by exposure to antimicrobials (Han et al., 2011; see Section 10) and, possibly, oxidative stress – ROS induce the tnaA tryptophanase gene, whose product catalyzes the synthesis of indole (Kuczynska-Wisnik et al., 2010b). Interestingly, dimethyl sulfoxide, a scavenger of the ROS hydroxyl radical, reduces antimicrobial-dependent indole production in E. coli (Kuczynska-Wisnik et al., 2010a), which is consistent with indole being inducible by the ROS formed as a result of antimicrobial exposure and provides an explanation for antimicrobial induction of indole production. Significantly, indole produced endogenously or added exogenously has been shown to promote antimicrobial resistance in E. coli (Han et al., 2011). Indole production by highly antibiotic-resistant strains of E. coli has also been shown to promote resistance in otherwise susceptible members of a heterogeneous population (Lee et al., 2010). This was apparently due to its upregulation of resistance mechanisms that included oxidative stress-protective mechanisms (Lee et al., 2010). Although Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (S. Typhimurium) does not produce indole, co-culture with indole-producing E. coli or exposure to exogenously added indole increases the antibiotic tolerance of S. Typhimurium. This is dependent primarily on the oxidative stress-responsive regulator OxyR, suggesting that indole promotes antibiotic tolerance in S. Typhimurium by recruiting an oxidative stress response (Vega et al., 2013). Consistent with this, peroxide (an OxyR signal) also increases antibiotic tolerance in this organism (Vega et al., 2013). Indole has also been shown to enhance the antimicrobial resistance of P. aeruginosa (Lee et al., 2009a). 

The reduced drug susceptibility of swarm (vs. swim) cells has recently been linked to an increased oxidative stress response in swarm cells of S. Typhimurium that includes upregulation of cysteine biosynthetic genes, cysteine, or a related product apparently functioning as an antioxidant in protecting these cells from antibiotic-generated ROS (Turnbull and Surette, 2010). Consistent with this, cysteine auxotrophs show evidence of increased oxidative stress and drug susceptibility, and addition of a cys gene inducer enhances swim cell resistance to antimicrobials (Turnbull and Surette, 2010). 

## 2.9.4 Envelope stress and antimicrobial resistance

Environmental stressors that perturb the cell envelope (membranes and wall) are met with bacterial adaptive responses that ensure cell envelope integrity and ultimately permit survival (Poole, 2012a). In both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, these so-called envelope stress responses are typically regulated by two-component systems (TCSs) and alternative sigma factors that sense envelope perturbations and respond by modulating gene expression to prevent, reduce, and/or repair envelope damage (Poole, 2012a). Given that antimicrobials either target components of the cell envelope or must penetrate or cross the cell envelope to gain access to their targets, it is not surprising that the protective changes mediated by envelope stress responses are capable of compromising antimicrobial activity, and so promote resistance (Poole, 2014). 

## 2.9.4.1 Gram-negative two-component systems 2.9.4.1.1 PhoPQ and PmrAB

The cross-talking PhoPQ and PmrAB TCSs of S. Typhimurium and other Gram-negative bacteria protect against membranedisrupting cationic antimicrobial peptides (CAMPs) (e.g., polymyxin B, colistin, and CAMPs of innate immunity) in response to these antimicrobials (Poole, 2012a). CAMPs trigger an adaptive response that results in an increase in the impermeability of the outer membrane (OM) through the modification of both lipopolysaccharides (LPS) (Needham and Trent, 2013) and phosphatidylglycerol (PG) (Dalebroux et al., 2014). LPS modification involves the addition of 4-aminoarabinose (4AA) to lipid A, thereby reducing the net negative charge of LPS and limiting CAMP binding to LPS and, thus, entry into cells (Fernandez et al., 2011). In addition, increased palmitoylation of LPS and PG in the presence of CAMPs is predicted to alter the fluidity of the OM and reduce or abolish CAMP insertion into the OM (Dalebroux et al., 2014; Guo et al., 1998). Perhaps best studied in S. Typhimurium, these adaptive responses are mediated by the TCS PhoPQ, which directly regulates two loci, pmrAB and $p a g P$ (Gunn and Miller, 1996; Guo et al., 1998), whose products promote CAMP resistance. pmrAB encodes a TCS that controls expression of the LPS modification operon (pmr; also known as arn) that is involved in the addition of 4AA to lipid A (Fields et al., 1989). $p a g P$ encodes an OM phospholipase– palmitoyltransferase that is responsible for trans-palmitoylation of both lipid A (Guo et al., 1998) and PG (Dalebroux et al., 2014), and this also promotes resistance to CAMPs (Guo et al., 1998). In S. Typhimurium, CAMPs activate the PhoPQ (Richards et al., 2012; Shprung et al., 2012) and PmrAB (Gunn and Miller, 1996; Richards et al., 2012) TCSs, and mutants lacking functional PhoPQ (Shi et al., 2004) or PmrAB (Farizano et al., 2012) are more susceptible to these agents. Moreover, a number of findings have linked mutations in phoPQ and pmrAB to CAMP resistance in lab or clinical isolates of S. Typhimurium (Roland et al., 1993; Sun et al., 2009) and other Gram-negative bacteria, including Acinetobacter baumannii (Beceiro et al., 2011), Klebsiella pneumoniae (Jayol et al., 2014), E. coli (Groisman et al., 1992; Quesada et al., 2015), and P. aeruginosa (Barrow and Kwon, 2009; Lee and Ko, 2014), highlighting the contribution of these TCSs to acquired CAMP resistance. Unlike S. Typhimurium, CAMP-induced adaptive CAMP resistance in P. aeruginosa is not mediated by PhoPQ or PmrAB, but is instead mediated by the ParRS and CprRS TCSs that also regulate expression of the arn-LPS modification genes (Fernandez et al., 2010, 2012; Muller et al., 2011). In P. aeruginosa, the ParRS and CprRS TCSs are required for a full adaptive response to antimicrobial peptides as they respond to different antimicrobial peptides or differentially respond to the same antimicrobial peptides in a concentration-dependent manner (Fernandez et al., 2012). Interestingly, ParRS also promotes resistance to aminoglycosides, β-lactams, and fluoroquinolones (Muller et al., 2011), as a result of ParRS-mediated induction of the mexXY multidrug efflux operon (Guenard et al., 2014; Muller et al., 2011) and repression of the carbapenem selective porin, OprD (Muller et al., 2011). In addition, ParRS is required for aminoglycoside resistance that follows exposure of P. aeruginosa cells to subinhibitory levels of CAMPs (Fernandez et al., 2010). 

$\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } }$ and other divalent cations interact with LPS to stabilize the OM of Gram-negative bacteria (Nikaido, 2003). As such, a deficiency in $\mathrm { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ also triggers PhoPQ- or PmrAB-dependent LPS modifications that promote adaptation to the membraneperturbing lack of this divalent cation, and in so doing enhances CAMP resistance (Kato and Groisman, 2008; McPhee et al., 2006). Intriguingly, extracellular DNA, which is an integral part of the biofilm matrix (Flemming and Wingender, 2010), perturbs the membrane of P. aeruingosa by chelating divalent cations, including $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } }$ , and this promotes polymyxin resistance via upregulation of the PhoPQ–PmrAB-regulated LPS modification genes (Mulcahy et al., 2008). Under Mg2+-limiting conditions, PmrAB of P. aeruginosa also contributes to resistance to CAMPs, including polymyxin B and aminoglycosides by upregulating expression of polyamine synthesis genes whose products are responsible for generating the polyamine, spermidine (Johnson et al., 2012). Binding of spermidine to the OM or LPS masks the negative surface charge, and so limits polycationic antimicrobial binding and uptake (Johnson et al., 2012; McPhee et al., 2006). 

## CpxRA

The CpxRA TCS of E. coli and several other Gram-negative enteric bacteria responds to conditions predicted to generate misfolded envelope proteins that adversely impact the cell envelope, and it does so by regulating the expression of periplasmic chaperone proteins and proteases involved in refolding or degrading these aberrant proteins (Raivio, 2014). Activation of the Cpx response promotes resistance to aminoglycosides, several β-lactams, and novobiocin, and this is, in part, dependent upon Cpx-mediated upregulation of genes encoding for multidrug efflux pumps (Nishino et al., 2010). Intriguingly, CpxR directly represses expression of the major porin gene, ompF (a portal of entry for β-lactams) (Batchelor et al., 2005), and reduced expression of OmpF has been linked to β-lactam resistance (Jaffe et al., 1983); however, it currently remains unknown whether the observed reduction in ompF gene expression is responsible for CpxRA-promoted β-lactam resistance. The CpxRA system of E. coli is also triggered by polymyxin B and human-derived antimicrobial peptides, and promotes resistance to these antimicrobials (Audrain et al., 2013). In uropathogenic E. coli, the CpxRA system has been linked to amikacin resistance – deletion of the cpxRA genes was shown to compromise resistance to this agent (Debnath et al., 2013). In Vibrio cholera, mutational activation of CpxA promotes resistance to ampicillin, and this appears to be mediated by the VexGH and VexAB multidrug efflux systems, both of which contribute to ampicillin resistance and whose expression is positively influenced by CpxRA (Taylor et al., 2014). CpxRA of Klebsiella pneumoniae contributes to intrinsic resistance to β-lactams, chloramphenicol, and the biocide chlorhexidine, with loss of cpxRA compromising resistance to these agents (Srinivasan et al., 2012). Resistance may be, in part, dependent upon the multidrug efflux pump KpnEF, whose expression is positively regulated by CpxRA (Srinivasan et al., 2013). In S. Typhimurium, CpxRA is linked to resistance to several classes of antimicrobials, including a β-lactam (ceftriaxone), aminoglycosides (streptomycin and gentamicin), tetracycline, chloramphenicol, a macrolide (erythromycin), rifampin (Hu et al., 2011), and various CAMPs (Weatherspoon-Griffin et al., 2011). 

## AmgRS

The AmgRS TCS of P. aeruginosa is activated by aminoglycoside exposure and contributes to intrinsic aminoglycoside resistance in this organism (Krahn et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2009b). Although AmgRS shares significant sequence homology to the 

E. coli osmoregulatory OmpR–EnvZ TCS, microarray analysis has revealed that AmgRS regulates genes more reminiscent of the E. coli CpxRA envelope stress response regulon, including a number of membrane transporter and protease genes (Lee et al., 2009b). It has been proposed that AmgRS responds to and protects cells from envelope stress caused by aminoglycoside-generated mistranslated or misfolded proteins that damage the cytoplasmic membrane (Hinz et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2009b). In support of this, deletion of the amgR gene increases aminoglycoside-dependent membrane perturbation and reduces aminoglycoside resistance (Krahn et al., 2012). Moreover, amgS gain-of-function mutations promote aminoglycoside resistance in lab and clinical strains of P. aeruginosa, and this is correlated with an increase in expression of AmgRSregulated membrane proteases (Lau et al., 2013) and reduced aminoglycoside-mediated membrane damage (Lau and Poole, submitted). 

## BaeSR

The BaeSR envelope stress-responsive TCS of E. coli is involved in promoting resistance to novobiocin (Baranova and Nikaido, 2002) and β-lactams (Hirakawa et al., 2003) via BaeR-dependent upregulation of the mdtABCD (Baranova and Nikaido, 2002) and acrD (Hirakawa et al., 2003) multidrug efflux systems. In S. Typhimurium, the BaeSR system is also linked to resistance to a wide variety of antimicrobials, including β-lactams (Hu et al., 2005, 2011), aminoglycosides (gentamicin and streptomycin), tetracycline and rifampin (Hu et al., 2011), and fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) (Guerrero et al., 2013), with a ΔbaeRS mutant demonstrating increased susceptibility to these agents. Finally, the BaeSR TCS of Acinetobacter baumannii promotes resistance to the glycylcycline, tigecycline, through its positive regulation of the efflux pump genes, adeAB (Lin et al., 2014). 

## RcsCDB/F

Originally identified as a regulator of capsule synthesis in E. coli, the RcsCDB/F phosphorelay system that is widely distributed in the Enterobacteriaceae has been linked to envelope stress and antimicrobial resistance (Ize et al., 2004; Laubacher and Ades, 2008). The majority of signals that induce the Rcs regulon appear to perturb extracellular and/or cell envelope–associated processes or compromise the integrity of the peptidoglycan layer (Clarke, 2010). The Rsc system of E. coli, which responds to peptidoglycan stress and is thus activated by β-lactams, contributes to intrinsic resistance to these agents (Laubacher and Ades, 2008; Sailer et al., 2003), and this is independent of capsule synthesis (Laubacher and Ades, 2008). The Rcs system of S. Typhimurium is activated by CAMPs, including the polymyxin antimicrobials (Farris et al., 2010), and has been linked to polymyxin B resistance in this organism – rcsC (Detweiler et al., 2003), rcsD, and rcsB (Erickson and Detweiler, 2006) null mutants demonstrate an increase in susceptibility to polymyxin B. 

## 2.9.4.2 Gram-positive two-component systems

## 2.9.4.2.1 BceRS-AB four-component system

The BceRS TCS is found almost exclusively in Firmicutes bacteria, where it functions with one or more ABC transporters to form a TCS–ABC antimicrobial peptide (e.g., bacitracin (Rietkotter et al., 2008), lantibiotics, and CAMPs (Staron et al., 2011) detoxification system (Dintner et al., 2011). In B. subtilis, the BceRS-AB four-component system is composed of the BceRS TCS and the BceAB transporter, both of which contribute to intrinsic resistance to bacitracin (Kingston et al., 2014). BceRS-AB is strongly induced by sublethal levels of bacitracin (Rietkotter et al., 2008), and mutational inactivation of either BceR (Mascher et al., 2003) or BceAB (Ohki et al., 2003) enhances the susceptibility of B. subtilis to this agent. While originally identified as a bacitracin-specific resistance determinant, BceRS-AB also responds to and mediates modest levels of resistance to other membrane-active agents, including the lantibiotics and the CAMP plectasin (Staron et al., 2011). BceRS is also capable of cross-activating the paralogous PsdRS-AB TCS– ABC bacitracin resistance system in B. subtilis (Rietkotter et al., 2008; Staron et al., 2011), which is inducible by bacitracin, several lantibiotics, and the lipopeptide antibiotic enduracidin (Staron et al., 2011). Like the BceRS-AB system, PsdRS-AB promotes resistance to these antimicrobial inducers via the PsdAB ABC transporter (Staron et al., 2011). Homologs of the BceRS-AB system have also been described in other Gram-positive bacteria, including Streptococcus mutans (Ouyang et al., 2010), Streptococcus thermophilus (Thevenard et al., 2014), Lactobacillus casei (Revilla-Guarinos et al., 2013), and Enterococcus faecalis (Gebhard et al., 2014) where they also contribute to bacitracin resistance. 

## 2.9.4.2.2 CroRS

The croRS operon encodes an envelope stress-responsive TCS in E. faecalis that contributes to intrinsic β-lactam resistance and is inducible by β-lactams as well as inhibitors of both early (fosfomycin and cycloserine) and late (vancomycin, moenomycin, ramoplanin, and bacitracin) steps of peptidoglycan synthesis (Comenge et al., 2003). More recently, the nutritional status of E. faecalis has been linked to intrinsic β-lactam resistance in a CroR-dependent manner (Snyder et al., 2014). Growth of E. facealis on carbon sources such as pyruvate or citrate resulted in enhanced β-lactam resistance when compared to growth on glucose or N-acetylglucosamine, and this was dependent on CroR (Snyder et al., 2014). 

## 2.9.4.2.3 GraRS

GraSR (also known as Aps) is an envelope stress-responsive TCS in S. aureus that is activated by daptomycin (Mensa et al., 2014), CAMPs of innate immunity (Yang et al., 2012), polymyxin B (Yang et al., 2012), and colistin (Falord et al., 2012), and it confers resistance to polymyxins as well as to glycopeptides (vancomycin and teicoplanin) (Howden et al., 2008; Meehl et al., 2007). In agreement with this, mutational inactivation of graRS increases the susceptibility of S. aureus to vancomycin, polymyxin B, antistaphylococcal CAMPs (Yang et al., 2012), and colistin (Falord et al., 2012). Resistance to CAMPs is mediated by the products of the GraRS-regulated dltABCD operon and the mprF gene (Yang et al., 2012). DltABCD is involved in D-alanylation of teichoic acids, while MprF lysylinates phosphatidylglycerol; together, these modifications increase the bacterial surface positive charge leading to the electrostatic repulsion of CAMPs (Yang et al., 2012). The graRS genes have been shown to be upregulated in vancomycin-intermediate S. aureus (VISA) strains (Meehl et al., 2007), and expression of the VISAderived graR or graS genes in vancomycin-susceptible S. aureus (VSSA) enhances resistance to vancomycin (Cui et al., 2005; Meehl et al., 2007). Indeed, mutations in graRS are commonly found in VISA isolates (Hafer et al., 2012; Howden et al., 2008; Neoh et al., 2008), and their recapitulation in VSSA strains enhances resistance to vancomycin (Neoh et al., 2008). Expression of a mutated graR gene in VSSA also promoted resistance to daptomycin (Neoh et al., 2008). 

## 2.9.4.2.4 BraRS

Initially identified in three separate studies, BraRS (Hiron et al., 2011) (also known as NsaRS (Kolar et al., 2011) or BceRS (Yoshida et al., 2011)) of S. aureus is induced by cell wall/cell envelope–active antimicrobials, including β-lactams, phosphomycin, gramicidin, lantibiotics (e.g., nisin) (Kolar et al., 2011), daptomycin (Muthaiyan et al., 2008), and the polypeptide antibiotic bacitracin (Hiron et al., 2011), and this TCS regulates a variety of genes, some of which are involved in cell wall synthesis (Kolar et al., 2011). Although BraRS is induced by several cell envelope/cell wall–active agents, this system confers resistance to only a limited number of its inducing agents, including bacitracin and lantibiotics (Hiron et al., 2011; Yoshida et al., 2011). Resistance to these agents is mediated by the BraRS-regulated ABC transporter VraDE (Kawada-Matsuo et al., 2013). A braS point mutation has been reported in a nisin-resistant S. aureus strain, and introduction of this mutation into a wild-type strain promoted resistance to this agent (Blake et al., 2011). 

## 2.9.4.2.5 LiaFRS

The cell envelope stress-responsive LiaFRS three-component system is highly conserved among the Firmicutes bacteria, and all homologs studied thus far respond to cell wall–active antibiotics. This system consists of the classical TCS, LiaRS, and the accessory protein LiaF, which acts as a negative regulator of LiaRS-dependent signal transduction (Jordan et al., 2006). In the case of B. subtilis, LiaRS is thought to act as a cell wall damage-sensing TCS (Wolf et al., 2012) that strongly responds to lipid II cycle inhibitors (nisin, ramoplanin, bacitracin, and vancomycin; Mascher et al., 2004), daptomycin, and CAMPs of innate immunity (Wecke et al., 2009). The LiaFRS system of S. mutans is similarly cell envelope stress-responsive, regulates many cell wall and cell envelope genes in response to bacitracin, and has been linked to bacitracin, vancomycin, and chlorhexidine resistance (Suntharalingam et al., 2009). In Streptococcus gordonii, the LiaRS system is induced by polymyxin B and promotes resistance to this agent by increasing the bacterial surface positive charge via direct upregulation of the dltABCD operon whose products are involved in D-alanylation of teichoic acids (McCormick et al., 2011). A liaF codon deletion that is, in part, responsible for daptomycin resistance (Munita et al., 2013) has been described in lab (Munita et al., 2013) and clinical (Arias et al., 2011; Munita et al., 2013) isolates of E. faecalis. In E. faecium, mutations in at least one of the genes of the liaFRS system are commonly found in clinical isolates with enhanced resistance to daptomycin (Diaz et al., 2014; Munita et al., 2012). Microarray analysis of a liaS null mutant of L. monocytogenes revealed that this TCS regulates genes encoding putative membrane-associated and secreted proteins whose expression is inducible by cell wall/cell envelope-active antibiotics (vancomycin, fosfomycin, bacitracin, and polymyxin B) (Fritsch et al., 2011), and this mutant demonstrated an increase in susceptibility to several antimicrobials and disinfectants (Collins et al., 2012). 

The LiaRS homolog in S. aureus, VraSR, is also induced by cell wall–active antibiotics, including bacitracin, β-lactams (McAleese et al., 2006), glycopeptides (Kuroda et al., 2003; McAleese et al., 2006), the lipoglycopeptide telavancin (Song et al., 2012), the lantibiotic nukacin ISK1 (Kawada-Matsuo et al., 2013), daptomycin (Muthaiyan et al., 2008), and CAMPs (Pietiainen et al., 2009), and it regulates many genes involved in cell wall synthesis (Kuroda et al., 2003). Exposure of S. aureus to epigallocatechin gallate, a plant-derived cell wall/membrane– targeting agent, induced vraR gene expression, with this increase in vraR expression partly responsible for tolerance to oxacillin and ampicillin (Levinger et al., 2012). In a methicillin-sensitive S. aureus strain, deletion of vraRS increased susceptibility to bacitracin, teicoplanin, β-lactams, and some CAMPs (Pietiainen et al., 2009), whereas mutational inactivation of vraRS in methicillin-resistant strains resulted in an increase in susceptibility to β-lactams (Gardete et al., 2006; Kuroda et al., 2003), vancomycin (Gardete et al., 2006), teicoplanin, bacitracin, and fosfomycin (Kuroda et al., 2003), highlighting the contribution of this TCS to intrinsic and acquired antimicrobial resistance. Mutations in vraRS also have been identified in clinical isolates of S. aureus showing enhanced teicoplanin (Kato et al., 2010) and daptomycin resistance (Mehta et al., 2012). vraRS mutations are also commonly found in VISA strains (Hafer et al., 2012) and heterogeneously resistant VISA subpopulations (Katayama et al., 2009), and these mutations appear to be important for intermediate vancomycin resistance in some VISA isolates (Doddangoudar et al., 2011, 2012). Upregulation of vraRS and vraRS-controlled cell wall synthesis genes has also been linked to intermediate vancomycin resistance in clinical VISA isolates (McAleese et al., 2006). Recently, two mutations in vraS were shown to be sufficient to convert a vancomycin-susceptible lab strain into a VISA-like strain (Berscheid et al., 2014). 

## 2.9.4.3 Sigma factors: Gram-negative bacteria

The alternative sigma factor σE (RpoE) of Gram-negative bacteria regulates the envelope stress response to extra-cytoplasmic unfolded proteins, and there are several examples where it has been linked to antimicrobial resistance (Crouch et al., 2005; Fraud et al., 2008; Haines-Menges et al., 2014). In S. Typhimurium, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ expression is inducible by CAMPs of innate immunity and is required for resistance to these agents (Crouch et al., 2005) as well as to polymyxin B (Humphreys et al., 1999). Similarly, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ of Vibrio parahaemolyticus contributes to polymyxin B resistance – loss of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ compromises resistance to this agent (Haines-Menges et al., 2014). Interestingly, overexpression of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ leads to higher levels of vesiculation in E. coli (Macdonald and Kuehn, 2013), with increased vesiculation improving E. coli survival following polymyxin B exposure (Schaar et al., 2011). This is consistent with reports of envelope stress–induced formation of outer membrane vesicles that have been linked directly to antimicrobial resistance (Manning and Kuehn, 2011; Schaar et al., 2011). P. aeruginosa harbors a functionally equivalent homolog of the E. coli $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } } ,$ , known as AlgU, which was first described as a regulator of alginate biosynthesis in P. aeruginosa (Ades, 2004). AlgU has been shown to mediate the induction of the multidrug efflux operon mexCD–oprJ in response to the biocide chlorhexidine and several other membrane-active agents (e.g., CAMPs, detergents, and organic solvents), with AlgU-dependent chlorhexidine induction of mexCD–oprJ efflux genes contributing to chlorhexidine resistance (Fraud et al., 2008). 

## 2.9.4.4 Sigma factors: Gram-positive bacteria

Several cell envelope stress–responsive sigma factors, including SigM, SigW, SigX, SigB, SigS, and SigE, have been linked to antimicrobial resistance in Gram-positive bacteria. These alternate sigma factors are activated by cell envelope–targeting agents and confer resistance to these by regulating unique, as well as partially overlapping regulons involved in cell envelope homeostasis and, ultimately, antimicrobial resistance. The SigM regulon of B. subtilis is induced by vancomycin, bacitracin, fosfomycin (Thackray and Moir, 2003), and CAMPs (Pietiainen et al., 2005), and contributes to the intrinsic resistance of B. subtilis to lantibiotics (Kingston et al., 2013), β-lactams, bacitracin, and moenomycin (Mascher et al., 2007). The SigW regulon of B. subtilis is induced by cell wall–active antibiotics (Cao et al., 2002a, 2002b; Mascher et al., 2003), and CAMPs of innate immunity (Pietiainen et al., 2005) and mutants lacking SigW demonstrate increased sensitivity to fosfomycin, vancomycin, ampicillin (Mascher et al., 2007), and lantibiotics (Kingston et al., 2013). Peptidoglycan synthesis inhibitors induce the B. subtilis SigX regulon of B. subtilis, which includes genes involved in peptidoglycan turnover and regulation of the cell surface charge (Cao and Helmann, 2004), and deletion of sigX results in an increase in sensitivity to CAMPs (Cao and Helmann, 2004; Mascher et al., 2007), lantibiotics (Kingston et al., 2013), ampicillin, and bacitracin (Mascher et al., 2007). 

While SigM is the major sigma factor contributing to intrinsic β-lactam resistance in B. subtilis, SigX also contributes to β-lactam resistance, but this is apparent only in strains lacking sigM (Luo et al., 2012). The SigB general stress response sigma factor of B. subtilis and related Gram-positive bacteria responds to a variety of stresses, including those elicited by cell wall– active antibiotics (Lee and Helmann, 2014; van der Veen and Abee, 2010). In B. subtilis, bacitracin, vancomycin (Mascher et al., 2003), and rifampin (Bandow et al., 2002) induce the SigB regulon, whereas loss of SigB function compromises resistance to rifampin (Bandow et al., 2002). SigB also has been linked to β-lactam resistance in B. subtilis – a point mutation in the major sigma factor, sigA, promoted resistance to cefuroxime, and this was mediated by SigA-dependent upregulation of sigB (Lee and Helmann, 2014). In Listeria monocytogenes, SigB is activated by vancomycin (Shin et al., 2010) and confers resistance to the disinfectants benzalkonium chloride and peracetic acid (van der Veen and Abee, 2010). SigB of L. monocytogenes also contributes to tolerance to tetracycline, gentamicin (Zhou et al., 2012), and cell envelope–targeting agents, including nisin (Begley et al., 2006), and β–lactams (Begley et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2012), with sigB mutants demonstrating impaired survival in the presence of these agents. In S. aureus, subinhibitory concentrations of vancomycin, ampicillin, and sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim induced SigB activity in vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (Chen et al., 2011), and activation of SigB has been linked to CAMP (Zhang et al., 2005), teicoplanin (Bischoff et al., 2001), and β-lactam (Morikawa et al., 2001) resistance. Mutational inactivation of sigB in MRSA leads to increased oxacillin susceptibility, whereas mutations in sigB in glycopeptide-intermediate S. aureus (GISA) strains lead to increased vancomycin susceptibility (Singh et al., 2003), further highlighting the role of this sigma factor in antimicrobial resistance in this organism. More recently, SigS of S. aureus was shown to be inducible by ciprofloxacin and β-lactams, and to promote resistance to these agents (Miller et al., 2012). The SigE-regulated stress response of Streptomyces coelicolor is triggered by a variety of cell envelope–targeting agents, including glycopeptides, bacitracin (Hesketh et al., 2011; Hong et al., 2002), and β-lactams (Hong et al., 2002), and a sigE mutant is more sensitive to bacitracin and vancomycin (Hesketh et al., 2011). SigE also contributes to nalidixic acid, penicillin, and vancomycin resistance in Corynebacterium glutamicum (Park et al., 2008). 

## 2.9.5 Heat shock and antimicrobial resistance

Aminoglycoside induction of heat shock genes has been reported in E. coli (Van Bogelen and Neidhardt, 1990), Acinetiobacter baumannii (Cardoso et al., 2010), and P. aeruginosa (Kindrachuk et al., 2011). In the case of P. aeruginosa, this is mediated by the alternate Lon protease AsrA, whose expression is induced in response to tobramycin or heat shock, dependent upon the RpoH heat shock sigma factor (Kindrachuk et al., 2011). Intriguingly, asrA overexpression in P. aeruginosa has a modest positive impact on aminoglycoside resistance (Kindrachuk et al., 2011), raising the possibility that the heat shock response might provide some protection against aminoglycoside challenge. This appears to be the case in A. baumannii, where it has been shown that pretreatment of the organism at $4 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 30 min renders it better able to withstand a subsequent streptomycin challenge as compared to cells pretreated at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (Cardoso et al., 2010). A possible explanation for the link between heat shock and aminoglycoside resistance is that components of the heat shock response that are responsible for eliminating misfolded proteins target the aberrant mistranslated polypeptides that are produced by aminoglycoside-disrupted ribosomes and that are proposed to insert into and disrupt bacterial membranes (Davis et al., 1986). Aminoglycosidepromoted membrane damage has been reported and is a key step in the lethal activity of these agents (Kohanski et al., 2008) and so elimination of membrane-damaging aberrant polypeptides would certainly reduce their toxicity to cells. Consistent with this, overexpression of the heat shock chaperonins GroEL and GroES in E. coli was shown to counter aminoglycoside-mediated protein misfolding, membrane perturbation, and cell killing, whereas inhibition of chaperonin expression sensitized bacteria to aminoglycosides and to aminoglycoside-promoted membrane perturbation (Goltermann et al., 2013). 

## 2.9.6 Stress-induced mutagenesis and antimicrobial resistance

In the face of “growth-limiting” stress owing to nutrient starvation, hypoxia, low pH, increased osmotic pressure, extreme temperature shifts, or antimicrobial exposure, bacteria activate a stress-induced increase in the mutation rate (Galhardo et al., 2007; Rosenberg et al., 2012). Also called adaptive mutagenesis, stress-induced mutagenesis (SIM) is dependent on the presence of double-stranded breaks in chromosomal DNA (Shee et al., 2011; see Chapter 2.14) and their activation of the SOS response that typically follows DNA damage (Galhardo et al., 2009), and the stress-dependent activation of the RpoS (σS)-mediated general stress response (Lombardo et al., 2004). Double-stranded breaks occur spontaneously in bacteria and are typically repaired using high-fidelity DNA polymerase III, but under stress conditions there is an RpoS-dependent switch to a mutagenic repair process involving error-prone DNA polymerases such as DNA polymerase IV (Ponder et al., 2005; Rosenberg et al., 2012). Presumably, the increased mutation rate enhances the likelihood that mutations permitting adaptation to the stressor will arise. Since the stress-induced mutations should be random, however, and unrelated to the initial stress that triggered mutagenesis, nonselected mutations, including those that impact antimicrobial resistance, can also arise (Cirz and Romesberg, 2007). While studied predominantly in E. coli, evidence for SIM is also seen in B. subtilis, Pseudomonas putida, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Cirz and Romesberg, 2007), and an SOS response–dependent drug-induced (i.e., FQ) mutation typical of SIM has been demonstrated in S. aureus, P. aeruginosa, S. Typhimurium, and Vibrio cholerae (Baharoglu and Mazel, 2011; Cirz and Romesberg, 2007; Mesak and Davies, 2009) 

FQ (e.g., ciprofloxacin) promotion of ciprofloxacin resistance development as a result of the induction of the SOS response and error-prone mutagenic pathway is well documented (Cirz and Romesberg, 2007), and there are reports of these agents promoting SOS response pathway-dependent development of β-lactam resistance as well (Tattevin et al., 2009), highlighting the potential for SIM to promote antimicrobial resistance development. Addressing criticisms of SIM that the mutations being selected were directly related to the stressor and, so, might be selected versus induced (Roth et al., 2006), Rosenberg’s group has confirmed SIM-dependent antibiotic resistance development in response to non-antibiotic stressors. Lac− E. coli starved of lactose, for example, shows an increase in β-lactam (Petrosino et al., 2009) and tetracycline (Bull et al., 2001; Shee et al., 2011) resistance frequency, dependent on the SOS and RpoS responses. Still, some antimicrobial resistance-promoting mutations (for nalidixic acid and rifampicin) have been shown to provide a fitness or growth advantage in the absence of any antimicrobial (Heath et al., 2001; Wrande et al., 2008), and, as such, their increased frequency in growth-stressed cells may not be explained by SIM but, rather, simple natural selection and enrichment of the growth-advantaged drug-resistant mutants. Further complicating the SIM picture is a recent report that stressed cells do not show the expected overall increase in mutation frequency relative to unstressed cells. Comparing aging colonies of E. coli (growth limited) with young colonies (growth proficient), Katz and Hershberg (2013) showed that although aging colonies generated a higher frequency of drug-resistant mutants than did young colonies, the overall mutation rate in the aging colony–derived drug-resistant mutants, as ascertained by whole-genome sequencing, was substantially less than predicted by the SIM model. Thus, while stress does seem to enhance the recovery of antimicrobial-resistant mutants, the mechanism(s) are not fully elucidated, and despite the potential for SIM to promote antimicrobial resistance development, there are minimal data supporting its contribution to this in vitro or in vivo. 

## 2.9.7 Persisters

The ability of a small subpopulation of an apparently susceptible and genetically homogeneous population of bacteria to survive antibiotic exposure has been known for some time. These socalled persisters (Cohen et al., 2013; Maisonneuve and Gerdes, 2014) ultimately increase the fitness of a bacterial population in stressful environments by ensuring that a proportion of its members are able to survive insults (e.g., antimicrobial exposure) that would otherwise eradicate a phenotypically homogeneous population. An example of the phenotypic heterogeneity that exists naturally within genetically homogeneous microbial populations, persisters are suggested to either arise stochastically (randomly) and continuously during population growth or form in response to an external (i.e., environmental) trigger (Cohen et al., 2013; Maisonneuve and Gerdes, 2014). Persisters typically exhibit a slow-growth or dormant phenotype, which is often cited as the major determinant of their antimicrobial resistance since antimicrobials tend to target metabolically active, rapidly growing bacteria (Maisonneuve and Gerdes, 2014). Still, active resistance mechanisms (e.g., detoxification and efflux) can also contribute to persister resistance, and there is increasing evidence that persistence is a regulated and actively maintained state (Cohen et al., 2013). Recent data suggest that toxin– antitoxin (TA) gene pairs or modules play an important role in persister formation (Gerdes et al., 2012; Maisonneuve and Gerdes, 2014; Maisonneuve et al., 2011). Apparently, the toxin components of these modules target key constituents of macromolecular synthesis and in shutting them down compromise growth (but not viability) (Gerdes et al., 2012; Maisonneuve and Gerdes, 2014; Maisonneuve et al., 2011). Thus, stochastic or stress-mediated increases in toxin levels would promote dormancy and, so, formation of antibiotic-tolerant persisters. 

Recent evidence indicates that ppGpp, the signaling nucleotide that controls the stringent response (see Chapter 7.1), plays a major role in persister formation, ultimately regulating antitoxin turnover and, so, toxin-mediated growth cessation and dormancy (Maisonneuve et al., 2013). While stochastic variation in ppGpp levels in bacterial populations might, thus, explain stochastic persister formation (Maisonneuve et al., 2013), stress-induced (e.g., nutrient limitation) activation of the stringent response should also promote persister formation. Indeed, nutrient limitation of planktonic (Bernier et al., 2013) and biofilm (Amato and Brynildsen, 2014; Bernier et al., 2013) cells has been shown to promote the formation of drug-resistant persisters in E. coli, concomitant with increases in ppGpp levels (Bernier et al., 2013) and dependent on ppGpp production (Amato and Brynildsen, 2014; Bernier et al., 2013). Nutrient limitation of V. cholerae also has been linked to adoption of a persister phenotype by this organism, although antibiotic resistance was not specifically tested (Jubair et al., 2012). Similarly, nutrient limitation promotes persister-like dormancy in E. coli that is mediated by the RelE toxin, whose activation has been shown to enhance the formation of antibiotic-resistant persisters (Tashiro et al., 2012). It has been suggested, too, that persister formation attributed to stochastic increases in ppGpp levels may, in fact, be stress induced, with the subset of cells that form persisters experiencing localized nutrient starvation (socalled microstarvation) (Maisonneuve et al., 2013). Certainly, the heterogeneity of biofilms dictates that biofilm bacteria have differential access to nutrients, with those experiencing starvation or limitation exhibiting a dormant or resistance phenotype reminiscent of persisters (Kim et al., 2009). 

Beyond nutrient limitation, a variety of stresses also have been shown to drive persister formation in bacteria. Oxidative stress and recruitment of the SOS response promote recovery of FQ-resistant persisters in E. coli (Wu et al., 2012). The formation of FQ-resistant persisters in nutrient-starved biofilms of E. coli also has been shown to require the SOS response (Bernier et al., 2013), as does the ciprofloxacin-driven development of ciprofloxacin-resistant E. coli persisters (Dorr et al., 2009). In the latter instance, persister formation is dependent on the SOSinducible TA locus tisAB–istR (Dorr et al., 2010). Exposure of E. coli (Vega et al., 2012) or S. Typhimurium (Vega et al., 2013) to peroxide or indole, both inducers of the oxidative stress response, also increases the levels of drug-resistant persisters, and this is dependent on the oxidative stress–responsive regulator OxyR. Pyocyanin, a P. aeruginosa pigment that stimulates ROS production and an attendant antioxidant response in A. baumannii, also promotes drug (amikacin and carbenicillin)- resistant persister formation in this organism (Bhargava et al., 2014). Highlighting the relevance of in vivo conditions to persister formation, internalization of salmonella by macrophages has been shown to induce formation of nonreplicating persisters (Helaine et al., 2014). Thus, the host environment (vacuolar acidification and nutrient deprivation) itself can drive persister formation and, so, promote resistance. 

## 2.9.8 Stress-induced biofilm formation

Bacteria commonly occur in biofilms in nature and in the infected host (Lopez et al., 2010), and these structures provide a variety of benefits including resistance to antimicrobials (de la Fuente-Nunez et al., 2013; Hoiby et al., 2010; Van Acker et al., 2013; see Section 22). As such, environmental factors that stimulate bacterial biofilm formation will promote antimicrobial resistance. A variety of stresses have been linked to biofilm formation, with biofilm formation itself likely a stress response (de la Fuente-Nunez et al., 2013; Landini, 2009). In support of this, inactivating mutations in the rpoS gene encoding the general stress response sigma factor hamper biofilm formation by E. coli (Ito et al., 2008; Landini, 2009). Nutrient limitation (i.e., nutrient stress) also has been linked to bacterial biofilm formation. Fe limitation has, for example, been shown to promote biofilm formation by S. aureus (Johnson et al., 2008) and Legionella pneumophila (Hindre et al., 2008), whereas Mg2+ limitation positively impacts P. aeruginosa biofilm formation (Mulcahy et al., 2011), although the regulatory pathways have not been elucidated. Stress in the form of high toxic metal levels also has a positive impact on biofilm formation by a variety of bacteria (Harrison et al., 2007), but again the regulator(s) involved are unknown. Finally, oxygen deprivation has been shown to stimulate biofilm gene expression and biofilm formation in Actinobacillus pleuropneumoniae (Li et al., 2014). 

## 2.9.9 SOS response and antimicrobial resistance

The SOS response, classically defined as a broad regulatory network that deals with DNA damage resulting from exposure to various stresses (Baharoglu and Mazel, 2014), is linked to resistance to a variety of antimicrobials, independent of its role in SIM. β-lactam stimulation of the SOS response in E. coli, for example, promotes survival in the face of a lethal β-lactam challenge, apparently as a result of an SOS response–promoted transient halt in cell division (Miller et al., 2004). β-lactams only act on growing cells, and, thus, the halt in cell division is protective. Expression of qnrB, one of several plasmid-borne quinoloneresistance (qnr) genes commonly found in the Enterobacteriaceae, is ciprofloxacin-inducible, dependent on the drug’s induction of the SOS response (Da Re et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2009). Activation of the SOS response has been shown recently to be important for ciprofloxacin and rifampicin resistance development in E. coli, with suppression of this response blocking emergence of resistance to these agents in vitro (Cirz et al., 2005) and enhancing FQ killing of wild-type, drug-resistant, biofilm and persister cells of E. coli (Lu and Collins, 2009). Finally, exposure to ciprofloxacin activates the SOS response in Burkholderia thailandensis, and this appears to contribute to ciprofloxacin resistance – an SOS response–deficient mutant shows enhanced susceptibility to ciprofloxacin (Ulrich et al., 2013). The expression and, so, activity of integron-encoded recombinases, dubbed integrases, are also enhanced under circumstances that activate the SOS response (Guerin et al., 2009). Integrons are mobile genetic elements that typically carry multiple antibiotic resistance genes or cassettes, with integrases catalyzing recombination events that result in the capture of new resistance genes or cassettes or the reshuffling of integron-resident resistance genes to promote their expression (Gillings, 2014). As such, the SOS response can promote acquisition and expression of resistance genes by integron elements, thereby promoting resistance development. In a recent report of ceftazidime resistance development in P. aeruginosa infecting a patient being treated with metronidazole (for another condition) and ceftazidime, resistance was shown to result from metronidazole activation of the SOS response in P. aeruginosa and subsequent stimulation of an integrase-dependent excision event that yielded expression of an integron-resident β-lactamase gene (Hocquet et al., 2012). 

## 2.9.10 Stress-induced resistance gene transfer

Stress can also contribute to resistance development by promoting the spread of resistance genes. A variety of stressors, including antibiotics, induce competence in Gram-positive bacteria (Claverys et al., 2006), including Streptococcus pneumonia (Prudhomme et al., 2006), promoting transformation and, possibly, acquisition of resistance genes. Antibiotics that target DNA replication have been shown to increase the copy number of genes at or near the origin of replication (oriC) in S. pneumonia, including genes for competence, thereby increasing transformation (Slager et al., 2014) and, so, the potential for resistance gene acquisition. Horizontal transfer of antibiotic resistance plasmids between E. coli and S. Typhimurium promoted by nanoalumina (known to damage bacterial membranes and promote oxidative stress) (Qiu et al., 2012) and food preservation stresses (i.e., high or low temperature, high salt, and low pH) (Mc Mahon et al., 2007) also has been demonstrated, although the mechanisms are as yet unknown. In a mouse model of colitis, S. Typhimurium– driven gut inflammation enhanced plasmid transfer between S. Typhimurium and E. coli (Stecher et al., 2012), apparently by transiently increasing the numbers of these organisms available for conjugation. This raises the specter of plasmid-borne resistance genes being spread between pathogens and commensal organisms during mammalian gut infections. Finally, activation of the SOS response in V. cholerae by ciprofloxacin as well as other stresses induces transfer of an antimicrobial resistance gene carrying an integrative conjugative element (ICE) called STX (Beaber et al., 2004). 

## 2.9.11 Concluding remarks

In the face of stress, bacteria upregulate adaptive responses that enhance survival, and when these responses impact antibiotic activity, they have the potential to contribute to resistance. Thus, stress-promoted biofilm formation and stress-induced dormancy provide for reversible stress-mediated resistance to antimicrobials. More commonly, however, stress response contributions to resistance are manifest as a result of environmental selection of adaptive stress response mutations, with mutational activation of stress responses promoting resistance. In some instances at least, these are driven by non-antimicrobial stresses (e.g., oxidative stress selection of aminoglycoside-resistant P. aeruginosa, or animal model selection of multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa and M. tuberculosis). Environmental stress selection of antimicrobial resistance is likely to be particularly significant in the case of chronic infections where long-term exposure of pathogenic organisms to such stresses will provide ample opportunity for enrichment of resistant organisms. The specter of resistance development in the absence of antimicrobial selective pressure has potentially profound implications for prescribing practices and antimicrobial stewardship, since removal of an antimicrobial from a formulary may not impact resistance that is being driven by other, environmental pressures. While in some cases the mechanisms of stress-promoted antimicrobial resistance are understood, in others they are not. Despite the stress inducibility of many of the multidrug exporters of P. aeruginosa, for example (Poole, 2014), their roles in the corresponding stress responses and the identities of the inducing signaling or effector molecules remain a mystery. This has important ramifications since the in vivo generation of these effectors at a site of infection has the potential to adversely impact antimicrobial susceptibility and, so, antimicrobial chemotherapy. 

The connection of stress–stress responses and antimicrobial resistance may also explain, in some instances at least, the controversial link between biocide use and antibiotic resistance development (Davin-Regli and Pages, 2012) (i.e., biocide-driven stresses may be recruiting antimicrobial-resistance-promoting stress responses). The biocide formaldehyde, a lipid-, protein-, and DNA-reactive cytotoxin, has been shown, for example, to induce the mexEF–oprN efflux operon in P. putida, with MexEF–OprN contributing to formaldehyde resistance (Roca et al., 2008). Although a contribution to antibiotic resistance was not assessed, its homolog in P. aeruginosa promotes resistance to several antimicrobials, including FQs (Kohler et al., 1997). Similarly, the biocide chlorine dioxide (collapses membrane potential) stimulates biofilm formation in B. subtilis (Shemesh et al., 2010), an example of a membrane-active stressor promoting expression of a resistance mechanism. Finally, a DNA array study of E. coli showed that monochloramine, a Cl-releasing biocide, causes oxidative damage to cells and induces an oxidative stress response that includes upregulation of antibiotic efflux and other resistance genes (Holder et al., 2013). 

The fact that antimicrobials themselves are growthcompromising agents that activate bacterial stress responses also has important implications for antimicrobial resistance development, given the link between stress and resistance. Stress response pathways may, thus, be appropriate targets for therapeutic intervention. In support of this, inactivation of the SOS response compromises FQ-promoted persister formation by E. coli (Dorr et al., 2009) and renders cells more susceptible to FQs (Lu et al., 2009), inactivation of the AmgRS regulator of an envelope stress response in P. aeruginosa increases susceptibility to aminoglycosides (Lee et al., 2009b), and loss of the AlgU envelope stress response sigma factor reverses the multidrug resistance of P. aeruginosa hyperexpressing MexCD–OprJ (Fraud et al., 2008). Given the role of stress responses in biofilm formation and the significance of biofilms as determinants of antimicrobial resistance, anti-biofilm approaches based on the disruption of biofilm-inducing stress responses are also being investigated. de la Fuente-Nunez and colleagues (de la Fuente-Nunez et al., 2014), for example, have recently described an anti-biofilm peptide that both blocks biofilm formation and promotes dispersal of established biofilms by targeting the stringent response alarmone ppGpp. Production of ppGpp contributes to biofilm formation and maintenance in Grampositive and Gram-negative bacteria (de la Fuente-Nunez et al., 2014), and so peptide-mediated ppGpp turnover prevented biofilm formation and dispersed biofilms formed by a variety of Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens (de la Fuente-Nunez et al., 2014). Relacin, a drug that targets the RelA ppGpp synthase and, so, also compromises ppGpp production, has similarly been shown to reduce biofilm formation in B. subtilis (Wexselblatt et al., 2012). Because ppGpp and the stringent response contribute to persister formation, these agents may also be useful in blocking the formation of persisters. While more study is clearly needed to unravel the details of stress recruitment of resistance mechanisms in bacteria and to ascertain the degree to which stress responses contribute to intrinsic and acquired antimicrobial resistance in pathogenic bacteria, the breadth of stress responses that can impact resistance points to these responses as likely being underappreciated contributors to antimicrobial resistance.

# Transposable elements: a toolkit for stress and environmental adaptation in bacteria

Anna Ullastres, Miriam Merenciano, Lain Guio, and Josefa Gonzalez ´ 

Institute of Evolutionary Biology (CSIC-Universitat Pompeu Fabra), Barcelona, Spain 

## 2.10.1 Introduction

Bacteria are known for their extraordinary ability to adapt to a wide range of environments. Countless mechanisms are related to survival, tolerance, and utilization of diverse resources that allow bacteria to live under different environmental conditions, including the most extreme ones (Mathema et al., 2011; van Wolferen et al., 2013). Among the myriad of environmental adaptation mechanisms, a variety of them are supported by transposable elements (TEs). 

TEs are powerful mutagens that generate genomic variation upon which natural selection can act (Oliver and Greene, 2009). Nutrient limitation, toxic compounds, and temperature are examples of environmental stressors that impose new selective pressures and trigger selection of adaptive genetic variants. Although most TE-induced mutations have deleterious effects, numerous studies provide evidence of the role of TEinduced mutations in environmental stress adaptation both in prokaryotes and in eukaryotes (Casacuberta and Gonzalez 2013; Guio et al., 2014; Magwire et al., 2011; Mateo et al., 2014; Nojiri et al., 2004; Touchon et al., 2014). TE-induced mutations can increase host fitness through different molecular mechanisms: from interrupting promoter sequences to generating large genomic rearrangements involving several genes. Besides acting as active and passive agents of mutation, TEs also increase genetic variation when they move from cell to cell by horizontal gene transfer (HGT) (Aminov, 2011; Ochman et al., 2000). Indeed, HGT is considered a major force in prokaryotic evolution and plays a crucial role in processes such as antibiotic resistance and detoxification, among others (Rankin et al., 2011). 

In this chapter, we start by reviewing the variety of TEs and other mobile genetic elements present in bacteria. We then analyze the different mechanisms by which TEs modify genome structure and genome regulation when environmental stressors are present. Finally, we also describe how TEs participate in horizontal gene transfer and its implications in the acquisition of new adaptive phenotypes. 

## 2.10.2 TEs are a diverse component of prokaryote genomes

The recent availability of next-generation sequencing techniques has broadened our capacity to discover TEs. TEs are present in 80% of the prokaryotic genomes that have been sequenced (Hua-Van et al., 2011; Touchon and Rocha 2007). Although not as abundant as in eukaryotes, TEs and other mobile genetic elements constitute up to 46.7% of some prokaryote genomes (Nakayama et al., 2008). The proportion of the genome that is composed of TEs varies according to the species and the type of TE (Florek et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2011; Monier et al., 2013). For example, insertion sequence (IS) elements account for 0.16% of the genome in Pyrococcus sp. and 20.53% in Halobacterium salinarum (Filee et al., 2007). 

In Table 2.10.1, we list all the different types of TEs described to date (Campbell et al., 1979; Krupovic et al., 2014; Roberts et al., 2008). IS are the best-known TEs in bacteria and are present in most but not all prokaryotes that have been analyzed (Siguier et al., 2006a, 2006b; Touchon and Rocha, 2007; Zhou et al., 2008). IS elements are often more abundant in organisms living in extreme environments (Lin et al., 2011), and some authors agree that they facilitate adaptation to new environments and new niches (Bickhart et al., 2009; Leavis et al., 2007; Qiu et al., 2010). 

Bacterial transposons include different types of TEs, such as composite transposons and conjugative transposons (Table 2.10.1). Both transposons and IS elements can induce chromosome instability and genomic rearrangements. Additionally, transposons can add accessory genes to the host genome that can increase cell adaptability and fitness (Darmon and Leach, 2014). 


Table 2.10.1 Transposable elements (TEs) present in prokaryotes. A total of 13 types of TEs have been described in bacteria, including introns group I, which are considered both TEs and self-splicing elements, and introns group II, which are considered as TEs, self-splicing elements, and retrolements. IR, inverted repeat; RE, right external; PU, palindromic unit; RI, right internal; LI, left internal; LE, Left external; LIR, long inverted repeat; k, l, m, and n are conjugation genes; attL, left attachment site; attR, right attachment site; RDF, recombination directionary factor or excisionase; TIR, terminal inverted repeats; Cas1, caspase 1; HEG, homing endonuclease genes.

Other TEs that add genetic material to the host genome are genomic islands (GIs), transposable bacteriophages, and satellite bacteriophages (Table 2.10.1) (Bellanger et al., 2014; Bondy-Denomy and Davidson, 2014). GIs have been related with many different phenotypes and are often named according to their associated phenotypic advantages, such as pathogenicity islands (PAIs) and fitness islands. Interestingly, the same or similar GI may show different functions in different species or even in the same cell when the environment changes (Darmon and Leach, 2014). Cell environment and background also may affect the disposition for transference of GIs. For example, environmental stimuli such as temperature changes and osmolarity affect the excision rate of PAI in Escherichia coli. This ability to modulate GI stability could be essential during host infection (Middendorf et al., 2004). Recently, a new superfamily of prokaryotic TEs has been discovered: casposons (Krupovic et al., 2014). Among the proteins encoded by casposons, Cas1 endonuclease is the key element of the CRISPR–Cas (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat–CRISPRassociated protein) system involved in the defense of prokaryotic cells against bacteriophages and plasmids (see Chapter 2.11). Krupovic et al. (2014) suggested that Cas1 endonucleases appeared first in mobile elements, and latter prokaryotic cells coopted these proteins for their own hereditary and adaptive immune defense. Moreover, Cas9, which is the key protein of type II CRISPR–Cas systems, has also evolved from a distinct class of transposon proteins (Chylinski et al., 2014). Besides immunity, the CRISPR–Cas system has potentially been involved in other adaptive traits, such as increased pathogenicity (Chylinski et al., 2014). 


Figure 2.10.1 Diversity of mobile genetic elements present in prokaryotes. Mobile genetic elements are genomic elements capable of translocating themselves within or between genomes (Binnewies et al., 2006). Mobile genetic elements can be classified in transposable elements (TEs), self-splicing elements, and retroelements. Besides these three groups, gene cassettes and plasmids are also mobile genetic elements.


![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/dbd2e36b-966a-4745-a615-c0703cb42feb/84491c18f982bbec4d3a947fa9ae92b6bcf550baeb290ea4c5527332082f00f1.jpg)


Besides the above-described TEs, prokaryotes have other types of mobile genetic elements: self-splicing elements, retroelements, gene cassettes, and plasmids (Figure 2.10.1). Group I and group II introns are both TEs and self-splicing elements. Self-splicing elements are genetic fragments that can excise by themselves after transcription or translation, and usually can move to a new DNA locus by homing (Darmon and Leach, 2014; Haugen et al., 2005; Robart and Zimmerly, 2005). Group II introns are also considered retroelements. Prokaryotic retroelements are relatively simple genetic elements that basically encode a reverse transcriptase enzyme. To date, only group II introns have been reported to transpose, whereas no proof of mobilization has been found for retrons or diversitygenerating retroelements (DGRs) (Figure 2.10.1). Although only these three groups have been characterized, there is bioinformatic evidence of at least 17 novel lineages of retroelements in prokaryotes (Kojima and Kanehisa, 2008; Simon and Zimmerly, 2008). These results suggest that many types of prokaryotic retroelements remain to be characterized. 

Finally, gene cassettes usually contain one gene and a recombination site, and can be found as circular DNA or incorporated in integrons (Hall, 2012). Integrons can incorporate one or more gene cassettes, and there are several examples in which they have been related to multidrug resistance and pathogenicity (Iyer et al., 2013; Naas et al., 2001) (Figure 2.10.1). 

## 2.10.3 Molecular mechanisms underlying TE-induced environmental adaptations

TEs trigger adaptation to environmental changes by using different mutational mechanisms such as disrupting regulatory sequences or adding new promoters (Figure 2.10.2a–c), inducing genomic rearrangements (Figure 2.10.2d–h), or embedding genes necessary for survival that can be horizontally transferred (Figure 2.10.2g,h). Here, we describe several examples from recent publications showing the role of TEs in stress response and environmental adaptation and illustrating the different mechanisms of TE-induced mutations. 

## 2.10.3.1 Insertional mutations

Changes in the regulation of key genes can increase the fitness of bacteria under stress conditions. TE insertions can influence gene regulation by affecting existing regulatory sequences, introducing new ones, or truncating gene sequences (Figure 2.10.2a–c). Most of the findings on the role of TEs in stress response come from experimental evolution studies: bacteria are exposed to stressful conditions, and after a given number of generations the evolved bacteria are analyzed (Adams and Rosenzweig, 2014). When inserted in regulatory regions, TEs can inactivate gene expression (Chen et al., 171; Gaffe et al., 2011), or they can interrupt a silencer region, thus activating gene expression (Alvarez et al., 2010; Lee and Palsson, 2010). Sometimes, even a single insertion can affect gene regulation of two different operons. This is the case with an IS5 insertion that disrupted the regulatory sequence located between the fucPIK and the fucAO operons in E. coli. As a result, the fucPIK operon was silenced and the fucAO operon was constitutively activated, allowing the bacteria to grow using a nonnative carbon source (Chen et al., 171; Lee and Palsson, 2010). TEs can also add regulatory sequences in the insertion sites. These sequences can harbor promoters that activate or upregulate the expression of nearby genes (Chou et al., 2009; Luque et al., 2006; Stoebel et al., 2009; Treves et al., 1998). Besides introducing new promoter sequences, TEs can also add regulatory sequences that respond to specific substances present in the environment. An example is ISTosp1, an IS element that introduces a target site for a nitrogen-responsive transcription factor in Tolypothrix sp. (Luque et al., 2006). As a result, transcription of the nearby gene is nitrogen regulated. Gene inactivation by sequence truncation is also a common consequence of transposition that can lead to adaptation (Hottes et al., 2013). For example, the inactivation of the srpS repressor gene by the ISPpu21 insertion leads to the constitutive expression of SrpABC in Pseudomonas putida (Sun and Dennis, 2009). Studies in natural bacterial populations have described similar examples of TE insertions involved in environmental adaptation, such as interruption of regulatory regions and addition of new regulatory sequences (Hall, 1999; Safi et al., 2004). Hall (1999) described the first evidence of TEs activating cryptic genes in an E. coli population. They observed an increase of IS elements transposition when nutrients in the environment were limited. This was associated with an increase in fitness under specific conditions. Analysis of the genome sequence revealed that IS insertions interrupted regulatory regions, thus activating cryptic (silent) catabolic operons in starved cells (Hall, 1999). The activation of cryptic operons under nonstressful conditions is deleterious, but it is beneficial when their substrates are the only available sources of carbon and energy. 

In some cases, promoter sequences present in the TE respond to specific environmental stressors, such as the host immune response. Safi et al. (2004) described an IS element in Mycobacterium tuberculosis that introduced a promoter activating the transcription of downstream genes during growth in human monocytes. Survival and growth in human monocytes are main factors in the success of M. tuberculosis as a pathogen. 

## 2.10.3.2 Genomic rearrangements

TEs can also generate mutations by inducing genomic rearrangements (Gaffe et al., 2011). For example, IS elements provide inverted repeats that can trigger ectopic recombination, leading to deletions, duplications, and inversions (Gray, 2000). de Visser et al. (2004) characterized seven IS981-mediated mutations in different colonies of Lactococcus lactis that had evolved for 1000 generations under oxygen stress and/or starvation stress conditions. Specifically, they described five deletions and two insertions, each affecting different genomic regions, which improved the fitness of evolved cultures compared to their common ancestor. Experimental evolution in E. coli also revealed adaptive IS-induced genome deletions (Gaffe et al., 2011). After experimental evolution limiting glucose or phosphate availability, several clones were sampled from 10 different chemostats. Among other types of mutations, they identified several IS-related mutations. Two of the IS-related mutations occurred in different clones independently, suggesting parallel evolution. One of these mutations was an IS5-related deletion, shared between one evolved clone from the glucose-limited chemostat and eight evolved clones from the phosphate-limited chemostat. This deletion contained 20 genes, including mutY, which is involved in DNA repair, and glcABCDEFG, which is involved in glycolate use. 

TEs can also produce gene duplication events. IS elements were reported to be responsible for a duplication in E. coli clones evolving under heat stress conditions (Riehle et al., 2001). As a consequence, stress and starvation response genes harbored in the duplicated region were overexpressed, leading to increased survival. 

Recombination events between different copies of TEs in the genome can also lead to chromosomal inversions. Genomic inversions in Campylobacter jejuni involving large genomic regions were responsible for the acquisition of bacteriophage resistance (Scott et al., 2007). Those inversions arose in response to exposure to CP34, a virulent bacteriophage in avian gut. Scott et al. (2007) showed that the origin of this rearrangement was recombination between two copies of CampMu prophages present in the C. jejuni genome. This rearrangement enabled the excision of CampMu bacteriophages and led to resistance to the virulent phage CP34, most probably because of receptor saturation with endogenous CampMu prophages. The authors also showed that the rearrangement has an important negative fitness effect, and the resistant phenotype easily reverts to bacteriophage sensitive (Scott et al., 2007). 

Large chromosomal inversions induced by IS elements in Pseudomonas aeruginosa also have been associated with adaptation to cystic fibrosis lung environments (Kresse et al., 2003, 2006). 

Overall, these examples highlight how the generation of new genomic organizations induced by TEs increases genome plasticity, thus allowing bacteria to survive in changing environments. 

## 2.10.3.3 Burst of transposition events

Environmental stress and genomic stress (e.g., interspecific hybridization) can trigger a burst of TE transpositions. These events are associated with major evolutionary events and have been suggested to play a crucial role in expanding genetic diversity and forming new taxonomic groups (Belyayev, 2014). A few studies report a burst of transposition in response to stress in bacteria. In Burkholderia multivorans, growth under heat shock conditions, but not oxidative or starvation stresses, increased the transposition rate of several IS elements (Ohtsubo et al., 2005). In Burkholderia cenocepacia, a bacterium causing serious infections in patients with cystic fibrosis, a burst of transposition of the ISBcen20 element was observed under oxidative stress conditions, but not heat stress (Drevinek et al., 2010). Both studies report a change in the IS element pattern after stress in mutant colonies. Further analyses should be performed to characterize the type of mutations generated and to confirm their role in adaptation. 

## 2.10.3.4 Horizontal gene transfer

TEs can be transferred horizontally and can also facilitate HGT of new genetic content (Frost et al., 2005). TEs and genes can be horizontally transferred in three main ways: transformation, in which naked DNA is taken up from the local environment; transduction, in which DNA is transferred through a bacteriophage vector; and conjugation, in which DNA is transferred through cell-to-cell contact often mediated by plasmids (Figure 2.10.3). Conjugation has been suggested to be the main mechanism for HGT (Norman et al., 2009; Wozniak and Waldor, 2010). 

Transferred sequences often encode fitness-related genes such as antibiotic resistance, detoxification genes, and virulence factors that confer a selective advantage to the new host, thus increasing survival and spread (Hacker and Carniel, 2001). 

One of the most relevant traits acquired by HGT is antibiotic resistance. Iyer et al. (2013) reviewed examples of natural bacterial strains from different environments carrying transposon and integron insertions associated with antibiotic resistance.
