Figure 2.10.3 Horizontal gene transfer mechanisms. (a) The donor cell liberates DNA sequences that other bacteria can incorporate in their genome. (b) Infected cells can liberate bacteriophages that act as vectors and transfer genetic material to other cells. (c) A region in the genome containing genes and other elements like TEs can excise and form a circular DNA molecule. Bacteria can connect with other cells through the pilus, and the genetic material is replicated and incorporated into the genome of the acceptor cell.


In some cases, it has been experimentally shown that antibiotic resistance driven by plasmids or transposons has no fitness impact in mutant cells, thus facilitating the prevalence of these mutations in the population (Enne et al., 2005). 

Integrative and conjugative elements (ICEs) are transferred by conjugation, and they can also contribute to environmental adaptation by the transmission of advantageous characteristics. Legionella pneumophila contains an ICE (ICE-ßox) that increases the resistance to ß-lactam antibiotics and bleach. In addition, this ICE-ßox makes L. pneumophila strains more resistant to macrophages that carry phagocyte oxidase. For this reason, this element can increase the fitness of L. pneumophila present not only in natural and in engineered waters but also in humans (Flynn and Swanson, 2014). 

Resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics is also mediated by an IS element inserted in a plasmid. The IS1 element downregulates the $b l a _ { C T X - M - 3 2 }$ gene and confers resistance to this type of antibiotics. The plasmid containing this insertion was detected in different strains of the Enterobacteriaceae family that were isolated from the same patient, suggesting that HGT might be responsible for the presence of this plasmid in the different strains (Fernandez et al., 2007). 

Tn6061, a member of the Tn3 family of transposons, has also been connected with multidrug resistance acquisition (Coyne et al., 2010). Tn6061 was chromosomally located in six P. aeruginosa strains and plasmid-borne in another isolate, suggesting the incorporation of the transposon carrying resistance from the plasmid to genomic regions. In this work, they also show the role of IS-mediated large inversions in Tn6061 evolution, giving another example of how rearrangements are involved in phenotypic adaptation to changing environments. 

Antibiotic resistance is strongly linked to heavy metal resistance. Resistance mechanisms against these substances are coupled both physiologically (cross-resistance) and genetically (coresistance). Thus, exposure to antibiotics and heavy metals increases the chances of selection and co-selection of antibiotic resistance (Seiler and Berendonk, 2012). Cadmium, mercury, copper, and zinc are heavy metals that accumulate in the environment and are moderately to highly toxic to bacteria. One of the best-known examples of heavy metal resistance in bacteria is the case of the mer operon, which carries resistance for mercury and is often found in mobile genetic elements (Mathema et al., 2011). Several studies report the acquisition of mercury resistance by mer operon activity embedded in transposons in several bacteria, suggesting that it has been horizontally transferred (Dziewit et al., 2013; Smalla et al., 2006; Soge et al., 2008; Mathema et al., 2011). 

The characterization of IS insertions in Cupriavidus metallidurans CH34 after exposure to several heavy metals revealed that those were associated with genomic island mobilizations, gene inactivation, and other genomic rearrangements (Mijnendonckx et al., 2011). These changes modified the autotrophic growth capacities, thus allowing cells to survive in environments with high heavy metal content. 

Some of these IS insertions had 100% conserved equivalents in other bacteria species that live in similar contaminated environments, suggesting a recent interaction and HGT among these species (Mijnendonckx et al., 2011). 

Besides heavy metals, TEs are also involved in the detoxification of other xenobiotics such as organophosphorous compounds. This is, for example, the case of the Tnmph composite transposon involved in the degradation of organophosphorous in Pseudomonas putida (Wei et al., 2009). Tnmph contains the gene methyl parathion hydrolase (MPH) and is flanked by two isocopies of IS6100, which mediated replicative transposition to the host genome. MPH and IS6100 also have been found linked to several phylogenetically divergent bacteria, suggesting that Tnmph might have mediated organophosphorus adaptation in different bacteria through HGT (Wei et al., 2009). 

Pathogenic bacteria have to adapt to the host environment and to the host defense mechanisms. PAIs are important contributors to the ability of bacteria to thrive in the host environment by encoding several virulence factors that can be horizontally transferred. Yersinia high-pathogenicity islands are one of the most widely distributed PAIs (reviewed in Benedek and Schubert, 2007). In this case, the mobilization of PAIs from cell to cell is mediated by a P4 bacteriophage-related integrase (int) and a P4-related excision factor (xis). The comparison of highpathogenicity islands present in different species of the Enterobacteriaceae family shows high sequence conservation, evidencing horizontal transfer (Schubert et al., 2004). 

Mobilization of toxic genes can also be mediated by IS elements, thus spreading virulent characteristics among bacteria. Plasmid-borne toxic genes are strongly associated with IS elements in Clostridium perfringens (Brynestad et al., 1997; Sayeed et al., 2010). Possible circular transposition intermediates carrying toxic genes and IS elements were detected in C. perfringens type B, consistent with IS-mediated mobilization of toxic genes (Sayeed et al., 2010).

## 2.10.4 Concluding remarks



Enne VI, Delsol AA, Davis GR, Hayward SL, Roe JM, et al. 2005. Assessment of the fitness impacts on Escherichia coli of acquisition of antibiotic resistance genes encoded by different types of genetic element. Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy 56:544–551. 





Oliver KR, Greene WK. 2009. Transposable elements: powerful facilitators of evolution. Bioessays 31:703–714. 



From their central role as horizontal gene transfer vectors to their ability to affect gene expression and genome structure through different molecular mechanisms, mobile genetic elements play a significant role in the ability of bacteria to adapt to changing environments. Moreover, TEs are also responsible for some of the major evolutionary innovations as exemplified by the Casposon superfamily of TEs that are key in the only adaptive immune system discovered in prokaryotes to date (Krupovic et al., 2014). With the increase in the number of bacterial sequenced genomes, we anticipate that previously unnoticed TEs and other mobile genetic elements will continue to be discovered, and likely new mechanisms through which these TEs affect bacterial evolution will be uncovered.

# CRISPR–Cas system: a new paradigm for bacterial stress response through genome rearrangement

Joseph A. Hakim1, Hyunmin Koo1, Jan D. van Elsas2, Jack T. Trevors3, and Asim K. Bej1 

1Department of Biology, University of Alabama at Birmingham, Birmingham, Alabama, USA 

2Biological Center, University of Groningen, Groningen, The Netherlands 

3Laboratory of Microbiology, School of Environmental Sciences, University of Guelph, Guelph, Ontario, Canada 

## 2.11.1 Introduction

Bacteria are the most abundant and diverse group of organisms inhabiting the Earth. As bacterial communities are integrated and sometimes interdependent within their environments, the privations or impositions accompanying both existing and new environments pose challenges to their survival (for reviews, see Cary et al., 2010; Fierer and Jackson, 2006; Kostic et al., 2013; Kristjansson and Hreggvidsson, 1995;´ Schrenk et al., 2010; Torsvik and Øvreas, 2002). Addition-˚ ally, dynamic ecosystems with fluctuating ecophysico-chemical parameters cause stresses that can exceed the ranges of bacterial functions. Some of these parameters include pH, temperature, water, gases, depleted and/or limited nutrients leading to nutrient starvation, light–dark cycles, irradiation, cell envelope perturbation or disruption, and cohabiting bacteriophage populations (Buckling and Rainey, 2002; Burgess et al., 1999; Gomez ´ and Buckling, 2011; Middelboe et al., 2001). To counter bacteriophage attack, some bacteria have restriction modification systems (Tock and Dryden, 2005; see Chapter 2.10). In addition, genome rearrangements or reprogramming cellular functions (i.e., evolution) conducive to their fitness in the ecosystem has been proposed (Gurung et al., 2001; Rubin and Leff, 2007; Spano and Massa, 2006). 

Some of the known genetic-based mechanisms (e.g., transformation, conjugation, transduction, and recombination) contributing to genome rearrangements are considered to be the means for bacterial cells evolving with the constraints of environmental stresses. However, recently discovered clustered regularly-interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) and the CRISPR-associated proteins (Cas) (Jansen et al., 2002) are recognized as a unique strategy utilized by certain bacterial species. 

Initial recognition of the CRISPR–Cas array occurred in 1987 through the work of Ishino et al. (1987) while characterizing the alkaline phosphatase isozyme gene (iap) in Escherichia coli. It was discovered that the $3 ^ { j }$ end of the amplified segment of genome containing iap consisted of a series of homologous repeats of nucleotides, arranged in dyadic symmetry. Additionally, it was reported that these repeats were interspaced among sequences of 32 nucleotides that contained no homology within the genome (Ishino et al., 1987). Although the functional significance of the repeat sequences was not apparent in their discovery, a predictive role was suggested for messenger RNA (mRNA) stability, due to an appearance of the internal posttranscriptional folding of the RNA. Jansen et al. (2002) offered an insight into the structure and function of the loci, and coined the terms “CRISPR” and “Cas”, collectively referred to as the CRISPR–Cas system (Figure 2.11.1). 

In subsequent research, the presence of “structural artifacts” was acknowledged, characterizing a species-conserved leader sequence upstream of the repeat region, and four closely located cas genes synchronous with the CRISPR (Jansen et al., 2002). The amino acid sequence alignment of Cas1 proteins from various strains of E. coli showed significant homology, whereas Cas1 from various species of Streptococcus exhibited poor homology, depicting the species-specific conservativeness of this protein toward its target CRISPR sequences (this study) (Figure2.11.2a,b). 

Similar results were observed when the amino acid residues of Cas1 proteins from Myxococcus xanthus and Pectobacterium atrosepticum were aligned (data not shown). The comparison of the amino acid residues of the Cas2 protein of E. coli displayed a better homology as compared to various species of Streptococcus (this study) (Figure 2.11.3a,b). Evolution of interspecies diversity of the Cas1 and Cas2 proteins was further supported by the poor homologies obtained from the alignment of the amino acid residues of E. coli, M. xanthus, P. atrosepticum, and various Streptococcus species (this study) (Figures 2.11.4a,b). 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/dbd2e36b-966a-4745-a615-c0703cb42feb/84fc15706ce1e7f21f2da50a2d9e8afcea5f461529be182ccd9371d720e484e0.jpg)



Figure 2.11.1 Schematic diagram for the CRISPR–Cas system in bacteria. Extraneous mobile genetic elements enter the recipient bacterial cells through various mechanisms (transformation, transduction, and/or conjugation). The process follows three steps: (i) Once inside the cell, Cas proteins target foreign stretch of nucleotides, excising a portion of the strand (protospacer) to be incorporated into the CRISPR array, at a location adjacent to the leader sequence in most bacteria. This process is hypothesized to depend on Cas1 and Cas2 proteins for acquisition of the protospacer. (ii) Transcription of the CRISPR array initiates at an upstream AT-rich region upon infection by foreign nucleotides. Long pre–CRISPR RNA (pre-crRNA) is refined into crRNA, and stabilized through dyadic symmetry of the repeat region. CRISPR–Cas Type I and III systems utilize Cas endonucleases, yet CRISPR–Cas II utilizes a trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA), which complements the pre-crRNA and initiates cleavage through RNase III or Cas9. (iii) Spacer matching foreign nucleotide strand is incorporated into a Cas complex, which acts as a guide to locate nucleotides belonging to a repeated invasion by mobile genetic elements. In CRISPR–Cas Type III, this complex includes tracrRNA. This targeting initiates fragmentation of foreign genetic material.


Later, research on Yersinia pestis, Streptococcus thermophilus, and Streptococcus vestibularis determined the nonrepetitive spacer region to be segments of exogenous DNA, from bacteriophage and plasmid origin, that was integrated into the host cell genome in a polar fashion, adjacent to the leader sequence (Bolotin et al., 2005; Pourcel et al., 2005). Recently, the polar addition scheme of spacer integration was questioned, as some archaea, namely Sulfolobus solfataricus, have been experimentally shown to integrate spacers at random locations internally, as opposed to locations near the leader sequence in the CRISPR array (Erdmann and Garrett, 2012). Nonetheless, there appears to be a loss of a previously embedded spacer in the array after integration of new spacer content, as in the CRISPR I array in Streptococcus agalactiae (Lopez-Sanchez et al., 2012), suggesting a dynamic nature of spacer content, a mechanism that assists in response to changing environments of mobile genetic elements. 

Extrapolating from these research milestones, further genome-mapping efforts have revealed CRISPR–Cas to be present in many prokaryotes, with the current estimate at >40% for bacteria and, remarkably, >90% in archaeal species (Grissa et al., 2007). Interestingly, there also exists an intraspecies incongruity of CRISPR arrays, as some strains may harbor the CRISPR–Cas system within their genome, and others may not. The absence of the CRISPR spacer repeats is typically accompanied by a lack of associated cas genes, leading to the assignment of functional interdependency of the artifacts in the interference of exogenous DNA (Touchon et al., 2011). The number of spacer sequences within any particular strain appears to be finite, as spacer quantity is maintained through removal of internal spacer sequences after integration of new spacers (Reyes et al., 2008). This knowledge has been used as a means to subtype species on the basis of spacer count, coined “spoligotyping,” as in “spacer typing” (Van der Zanden et al., 2002). Intraspecies variation is further compounded as the nature, number, and arrangement of the Cas and other CRISPRassociated genes may vary across a single species (Pourcel and Drevet, 2013). Even the number of CRISPR–Cas systems in a genome may differ across the same species of bacterium (Carte et al., 2014).

Figure 2.11.3 Multiple sequence alignment of the amino acid residues of the Cas2 protein sequences from (a) Escherichia coli strains; and (b) Streptococcus species. The Cas2 protein sequences were downloaded from the NCBI protein database (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/protein/) and aligned with MAFFT alignment (MAFFT version 7, http://mafft.cbrc.jp/alignment/server/). The aligned protein sequences were managed and edited using BioEdit (Hall, 1999). The identical sequences are shadowed by dark gray, and similar sequences are shadowed by light gray. The alignment result showed that Cas2 protein sequences aligned well among various E. coli strains, whereas the Streptococcus species exhibited poor sequence homology.

Although 12 subtypes have been recognized across bacterial species, it is generally agreed that three major types of CRISPR– Cas systems occur in bacteria, designated as Types I, II, and III – with Type I considered to be the most common (Makarova et al., 2011a,b, 2013). Each type exemplifies a distinctive architecture of cas genes, varying in gene location relative to the CRISPR array, gene structure, and combinations of various cas genes (Makarova et al., 2011b). Among all of the cas genes identified thus far, cas1 and cas2 have been recognized to be present in all CRISPR–Cas systems, with cas1–cas6 considered the core genes of the CRISPR–Cas system (Haft et al., 2005; Horvath and Barrangou, 2010). The target of the CRISPR–Cas mechanism is typically, but not always, double-stranded DNA, as it has been discovered that the Type III-B subtypes found in Thermus thermophilus target exogenous RNAs (Sorek et al., 2013; Staals et al., 2013). 

## 2.11.2 Mechanism

## 2.11.2.1 The integration of spacer content

The CRISPR–Cas system functions as adaptive immunity through the complementation of a CRISPR RNA (crRNA) to an invading DNA element, typically of viral or plasmid origin. This causes the disruption of the foreign DNA through a series of nuclease-related events (Brouns et al., 2008). Within the CRISPR array, crRNA is first transcribed as a long singlestranded product, and then processed by the Cas and CRISPRrelated proteins, to produce short RNA sequences, which are 57 nucleotides in E. coli (Brouns et al., 2008). This sequence is embedded into the Cas proteins (in which the specific Cas or CRISPR-related proteins will differ across bacterial species) and functions as a “guide” to locate complementary sequences on foreign DNA, perhaps introduced by a bacteriophage or a plasmid (Brouns et al., 2008). The process from spacer acquisition to the RNA-mediated “immunity” or “protection” from the invading DNA occurs in three stages: (i) adaptation, (ii) expression, and (iii) interference (Figure 2.11.1) (Iranzo et al., 2013; Van Der Oost et al., 2009). 

## 2.11.2.2 Adaptation

The acquisition of spacer content is dependent on invasion of foreign exogenous genetic elements, termed protospacers prior to integration, and is a fundamental requisite for the immunity of the CRISPR–Cas system (Bolotin et al., 2005; Mojica et al., 2005, 2009; Pourcel et al., 2005). Of the three stages, evidence of the mechanism of initiation, as well as the underlining process of protospacer target and integration, has largely been inscrutable (Yosef et al., 2012). This seems to be due to difficulties with recreating the adaptation stage under laboratory conditions, which contrasts the proficient and abundant integration of spacers under natural conditions (Andersson and Banfield, 2008; Tyson and Banfield, 2008; Weinberger et al., 2012; Westra and Brouns, 2012). Some evidence has been forthcoming through investigation of Pectobacterium atrosepticum and E. coli (Datsenko et al., 2012; Swarts et al., 2012; Yosef et al., 2012), strongly associating Cas1 and Cas2 as the hypothesized universal proteins responsible for spacer acquisition (Datsenko et al., 2012; Yosef et al., 2012). This is supported by evidence that both Cas1 and Cas2 proteins function in the absence of other CRISPR-related proteins to target and acquire spacers (Yosef et al., 2012). In E. coli, Cas1 and Cas2 have been shown to form a complex that, once dissociated, will terminate spacer acquisition (Nunez˜ et al., 2014). Additionally, a specialized 2 to 5 nt motif accompanying the foreign DNA has been observed to be a target for spacer acquisition: the protospacer adjacent motif (PAM), a recognizable sequence that has been observed to be a target across various bacterial CRISPR systems, and is hypothesized to be organism specific (Bolotin et al., 2005; Mojica et al., 2009, Shah et al., 2013). This mode of adaptation has been termed the “na¨ıve method”, as the spacer acquisition occurs de novo (Fineran et al., 2014). 

Another type of adaptation has been observed within the K12 strain of E. coli, in which spacer acquisition was demonstrated to be associated with bacteriophage stress (see Chapter 2.10). As bacteria have evolved CRISPR–Cas systems of adaptive immunity, so too have phages and mobile elements to evade disruption. Specifically, mutations in the PAM sequence adjacent to protospacer regions allow for the avoidance of CRISPRmediated immunity. As a mechanism, once a spacer sequence becomes ineffective as a crRNA for immunity through homologous complementation, the same sequence will act as a guide to partially complement stretches of genomic content on foreign mobile genetic elements (Fineran et al., 2014). It has been observed that while utilizing CRISPR-associated proteins, namely Cas1, Cas2, and Cas3, alongside a guide RNA from the original spacer and an additional Cascade protein, the CRISPR machinery will recognize stretches of foreign DNA and select fragments to be incorporated as new spacer content (Datsenko et al., 2012; Fineran et al., 2014). This mechanism of adaptation has been designated the “priming” method of spacer acquisition (Fineran et al., 2014), and it has recently begun to hold validity across other bacterial species, such as Haloarcula hispanica (Li et al., 2014). As observed in E. coli, once the sequence has been acquired, insertion of the protospacer occurs through a staggered cleavage, followed by ligation, at the junction between the leader sequence and the first repeat, through the catalytic potential of the metal-binding core of Cas1 in the Cas1–Cas2 complex (Arslan et al., 2014). The use of bioinformatics tools revealed that occasionally the spacer sequences can be inserted internally within the CRISPR array, which was found to be unique as compared to the conventional process of the polar addition of spacers at the $5 ^ { \prime }$ end of the CRISPR array (Erdmann and Garrett, 2012). 

## 2.11.2.3 Expression

Although some mechanistic variation exists among the three types of CRISPR–Cas, there are common elements shared by all types, such as the transcription of the long pre-crRNA product, initiated at the upstream AT-rich region, followed by maturation of the transcript into short crRNA through cleavage internal to the repeat sequence (Horvath and Barrangou, 2010). Types I and III show a similarity in processing of the pre-crRNA product, as cas genes encoding endoribonucleases are responsible for cleavage, whereas Type II is dependent on a transactivating RNA (tracrRNA), which complements regions on the pre-crRNA and initiates cleavage through RNase III and Cas9 activity (Westra et al., 2014). 

## 2.11.2.4 Immunity

The CRISPR–Cas immunity occurs when crRNA is ushered by Cas proteins to complement stretches of nucleotides belonging to the mobile genetic elements of repeat invasions (Brouns et al., 2008). As observed in the CRISPR–Cas Cse-subtype of E. coli, the matured crRNA is embedded into a complex of Cas proteins termed “CASCADE” (CRISPR-associated complex for antiviral defense), which is composed of CasA, CasB, CasC, CasD, and CasE (Brouns et al., 2008; Jore et al., 2011). After incorporation of the guide RNA into CASCADE, the complex is guided to the foreign element. Through the activity of an additional Cas protein, Cas3 (nuclease–helicase), foreign nucleotides will be fragmented (Figure 2.11.1) (Jore et al., 2011). 

## 2.11.3 Stress response of CRISPR

## 2.11.3.1 Bacteriophage stress

Interest has been placed on the CRISPR–Cas system, specifically addressing its function in adaptive immunity against predatory phages and harmful mobile genetic elements. Regarding stresses in the environment, bacteriophages have a prominent effect on shaping microbial communities in many niches, such as marine ecosystems (Mojica and Brussaard, 2014), temperate soil (Williamson et al., 2013), and even the more extreme ecosystems such as Arctic soil (Allen et al., 2010; see Chapter 10) and Antarctic lakes (Filippova et al., 2013; Lauro et al., 2010). Not surprisingly, bacteriophages imposing a lytic cycle will decrease microbial populations of susceptible species, with mortality estimates of about 50% in some environments (Fuhrman and Noble, 1995). Such an impact may affect the biotic ecosystem at a grander scale, especially when only select species are targeted. Decreases in select species may confer a shift in populations, thus leading to a change in nutrient cycling and metabolism, an occurrence that has been investigated in the context of the microbiome (Fuhrman and Noble, 1995; Koskella, 2013; Reyes et al., 2012). 

The effect of bacteriophages in causing bacterial stress is not restricted to population decline and species dynamics. Latent phages in the lysogenic life cycle, or prophages that integrate into a bacterial host as part of the life cycle, may confer a selective advantage of the host bacteria – a mechanism to increase persistence of the phage by enhancing the survivorship of the phage-harboring host (Bossi et al., 2003). Additionally, phagemediated gene trafficking, or transduction, may offer a fitness advantage to certain bacteria over others in the natural ecosystem by inserting DNA into the genome of the host that assists in metabolic function – again, conferring a fitness advantage to both the bacteria and the phage (Mann et al., 2003). Although seemingly benign, these strategies may inadvertently cause stress to cohabiting bacteria through competition, creating shifts in the microbial populations and thereby affecting the ecosystem function. 

The effect of CRISPR–Cas systems in response to lytic phages has been researched in various bacterial species, in which a fitness benefit was established (Brouns et al., 2008; Marraffini and Sontheimer, 2008; Sorek et al., 2008). However, CRISPR– Cas is not limited to protection against lytic phages, as it can interfere with the genome of lysogenic phages. In 2010, the range of CRISPR–Cas potential against invading genetic elements was investigated in E. coli in the presence of λ bacteriophage (Edgar and Qimron, 2010). A range of activity against the phage in each life cycle was observed. First, in the presence of a lysogenetic phage, CRISPR–Cas-mediated interference was shown to target segments of the phage genome, interrupting the cycle within the cell. Although segments of the phage genome responsible for lysogenization were not specifically targeted by CRISPRs, this is evidence in favor of broad CRISPR function in preserving the bacterial genome. CRISPR–Cas response to prophage integration was also investigated, as the CRISPR–Cas system was induced after the integration of the phage DNA segments. It was observed that the CRISPR harboring E. coli cleared prophage DNA in a small portion, showing that those bacteria harboring a spacer congruent with the integrated λcI857kan (kanamycin resistant temperature sensitive cI variant) prophage had a ≈500-fold increase in survival, even after the expected lytic cycle induction of the phage at a temperature increase (42 ◦C) (Edgar and Qimron, 2010). Yet largely, CRISPR–Casmediated apoptosis occurred through self-targeting, or the prophage cycle was too progressed for timely removal, leading to cell death of the bacteria affected by the prophages. In addition to the apparent function of CRISPR–Cas in response to bacteriophage stress, CRISPR–Cas systems are functional under many phage circumstances, an area that requires additional research. 

## 2.11.3.2 Fruiting body and starvation in Myxococcus xanthus

When subjected to a nutrient-deprived environment, certain bacteria have been observed to undergo colony structure adjustments to cope with starvation stresses. One such adjustment, fruiting body formation, has recently been associated with the CRISPR–Cas system in Myxococcus xanthus (Viswanathan et al., 2007a). During periods of long starvation, myxobacterial cells undergo fruiting body development through a process of cell–cell contact interaction (Kiskowski et al., 2004; Sozinova et al., 2005). The development from aggregation to sporulation, including rippling that accompanies and precedes aggregation (Shimkets and Kaiser, 1982), has been linked to the production of five intercellular signals, canonically named the A, B, C, D, and E factors (Boysen et al., 2002; Downard et al., 1993; Kim et al., 1992). Crucial to the fruiting body process, the A factor signal is initiated by starvation, which induces the transcription of the FruA DNA-binding response regulator (Ellehauge et al., 1998; Viswanathan et al., 2007b). Additionally, cell–cell contact will initiate the C factor, encoded by csgA gene (Kaiser et al., 2010), which will activate FruA to induce devR and devS genes (Jelsbak and Søgaard-Andersen, 2000). The devRS genes have been identified to be a part of a larger locus that includes devT gene – which stimulates FruA synthesis to positively regulate devR and devS genes (Boysen et al., 2002). 

Recent analysis of the dev genes of M. xanthus revealed an association between the dev locus and the CRISPR–Cas array. Specifically, genome mapping has placed the locus as nested within the arrangement of the cas genes of M. xanthus, and has determined devT, devR, and devS genes to be cas8, cas7, and cas5, respectively (Boysen et al., 2002; Jelsbak and Søgaard-Andersen, 2000). The consequential transcription of the dev genes in response to starvation occurs alongside the cas genes (Boysen et al., 2002), with only a portion of the CRISPR repeat segment transcribing with the dev locus. This CRISPR array portion contains a spacer corresponding to an integrase enzyme, necessary for the lysogenization of the Mx8 bacteriophage into the genome (Viswanathan et al., 2007a). An interesting hypothesis proposed by Viswanathan et al. (2007a,b) was that, mechanistically, the Mx8 spacer is transcribed as a crRNA in defense against the Mx8 bacteriophage, as the M. xanthus may be particularly susceptible to lysogenization during starvation periods. Little evidence exists to verify the physiological importance of transcription of the Mx8 spacer. However, considering the cotranscription of the dev and cas genes, and the genetic architecture of the dev locus in relation to the CRISPR–Cas array, there may be an association of the two systems in response to environmental stresses, but the precise role of the system remains unknown. 

## 2.11.3.3 DNA damage repair

Prior to adopting the Cas designation, the genes associated with the CRISPR system of exogenous DNA silencing were linked with DNA repair, an observation that came through the genomic analysis of thermophilic bacteria (Makarova et al., 2002). Generally, extremophile bacteria inhabiting harsh niches will have a phenotype and underlying genotype that confer survival under the stress of DNA-damaging conditions (Stan-Lotter and Fendrihan, 2012). For example, desiccation, UV, and gamma radiation are common DNA-damaging agents in Antarctica, yet bacteria such as Pseudomonas syringae Lz4W can repair excessively damaged DNA and otherwise lethal amounts of genome fragmentation (Pavankumar et al., 2010; Sinha and Hader, 2002;¨ see Section 8). 

A gene association exists between the Cas genes and DNA repair enzymes in the E. coli CRISPR–Cas type I-E (Babu et al., 2011). Analysis of the Cas1 protein (YgbT in E. coli) revealed a multifaceted nuclease activity capable of processing substrates of branched DNA, such as 5′ flaps, Holiday junctions, and replication forks (Babu et al., 2011). In the same research, co-purification of Cas1 revealed an association of Cas1 with RuvB, a helicase that functions in the RuvAB complex, which migrates Holiday junctions for the eventual RuvCmediated double-stranded break of the target DNA (West, 1996). Additionally observed was an association of Cas1 with RecB and RecC, two enzymes that are crucial to the recombinational restoration of template imperfections in DNA (Kowalczykowski, 2000). RecB and RecC will form a complex with RecD, which inserts at the nicks induced by the RuvABC system, to initiate the homologous recombination of DNA (Kowalczykowski, 2000). RecBCD-mediated DNA repair was also identified, and examined, in the extremophile Antarctic bacteria P. syringae Lz4W (Pavankumar et al., 2010). In P. syringae, deletion of the RecBCD led to increased susceptibility to DNA damage by UV radiation, as well as decreased viability when exposed to low temperatures (4 ◦C) (Pavankumar et al., 2010; Regha et al., 2005). 

In addition to its observed function in the CRISPR–Cas system of immunity, the E. coli Cas1 (YgbT) interacts with RecB to repair DNA. Many CRISPR–Cas-containing bacteria possess the Cas4 gene (Haft et al., 2005), and in certain species such as M. xanthus, the Cas1 and Cas4 gene sequences appear overlapping with one another, emphasizing the association of the two gene products (Zhang et al., 2012). E. coli does not contain the Cas4 gene per se, yet there is a homology between the Cas4 and the RecB exonuclease, and an apparent association of the two proteins in DNA repair (Jansen et al., 2002). Cas3 was discovered to contain functional domains consistent with helicases belonging to superfamily 2 of DNA and RNA metabolism (Jansen et al., 2002). Although the CRISPR array of spacer repeats has not been verified to function in DNA repair, interestingly, the RecBCD system has previously been implicated in the interruption of foreign linear DNA, a characteristic of CRISPR–Cas immunity (Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008). This is a noteworthy observation implicating a dual functionality of the cas genes in both immunity and host DNA repair. 

## 2.11.3.4 Envelope stress as a trigger for CRISPR–Cas induction

Central to coping with environmental stress is the DnaK protein, which, in E. coli, is correlated with the heat stress response (see Section 13). Tilly et al. (1983) investigated the DnaK protein and its production during temperature increases in E. coli; and, in 1984, Bardwell and Craig (1984) reported their findings, classifying the protein as a heat shock protein (HSP) due to its previously described homology to known HSPs across many eukaryotic and prokaryotic genomes. Subsequent investigations elucidated the role and function of DnaK in folding and chaperoning of newly synthesized proteins in the cytosol (Perez-Rodr ´ ´ıguez et al., 2007), for export across the cytoplasmic membrane via the Tat (twin-arginine translocation) pathway (Graubner et al., 2007). Crucial to envelope integrity is the efficient transport of folded proteins and the avoidance of amassing misfolded or unfolded proteins in the periplasm (Raivio, 2005). 

To test the association of the CRISPR–Cas system with the DnaK chaperone protein in the context of envelope stress (see Section 18), the involvement of CasE of E. coli in response to extracellular stress has been reported (Perez-Rodr´ ´ıguez et al., 2011). Plasmids containing sstorA fused to gfp (sstorA-gfp) were transformed into a DnaK-deficient (ΔDnaK) E. coli culture – which causes the accumulation of insoluble unfolded ssTorA product, conferring envelope stress (Deuerling et al., 1999; Lim et al., 2009). ssTorA is a bacterial Tat-specific E. coli trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) reductase (TorA) signal peptide, plus the first four residues of mature TorA (ssTorA), that helps reduce TMAO into trimethylamine (TMA) as part of the electron transport chain (Fisher et al., 2006). It was discovered that endogenous sequences consisting of spacers homologous to sstorA silenced the plasmid and subdued expression of the misfolded protein (Perez-Rodr ´ ´ıguez et al., 2011). Attention was placed on the BaeSR regulatory system, in which BaeS resides in the membrane and phosphorylates the BaeR transcription activator in the event of envelope stress (MacRitchie et al., 2008). BaeR is a response regulator of the putative BaeSR two-component signal transduction system for regulation of E. coli multidrug transporter genes (Baranova and Nikaido, 2002). As BaeR was known to activate CasA in E. coli (Baranova and Nikaido, 2002), the binding of BaeR to CasA in the envelope stress due to inefficient protein translocation was inspected, and it was observed that BaeR binds internal to the CasA gene. This association with membrane-maintaining components has elucidated a potential role of CRISPR–Cas in membrane preservation. 

An additional association of CRISPR–Cas to membrane integrity was investigated in the pathogen Francisella novicida, where membrane stress was offset by the CRISPR–Cas system, specifically through the function of Cas9 (Sampson et al., 2014). F. novicida must cope with many antimicrobial agents residing within the target host organism and the macrophages that engulf the bacteria (Jones et al., 2012). Unique to this bacterium is its ability to survive exposure to certain antimicrobials, namely those that are cationic peptides (Balagopal et al., 2006). In their research, polymyxin B, a membrane-acting antimicrobial agent used to study the effect of cationic peptide antimicrobials (Mohapatra et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2006), was administered to F. novicida lacking the Cas9 gene. It was observed that at low doses (100 μg/mL as compared to the lethal dose of 800 μg/mL), the ΔCas9 bacteria displayed a susceptibility to the antimicrobial as compared to the wild-type strain (Sampson et al., 2014). In addition, two small RNAs that associate with Cas9, tracrRNA and small Cajal body–specific RNA (scaRNA), were also investigated. It was determined that, upon deletion of the two RNA products, a similar susceptibility to that of Cas9 mutants was observed. 

Besides the observed association of Cas9 to membrane stress in F. novicida, the Cas9 gene of Streptococcus pyogenes (SpCas9) is a crucial factor in the Type II CRISPR–Cas system, coding for an RNA-guided DNA endonuclease enzyme. This SpCas9 enzyme has been reported to perform efficient RNA-guided sequence-specific DNA cleavage. By modifying the SpCas9 and the CRISPR system to create a gene-editing tool, it has become possible to utilize a predetermined RNA guide strand to target a specific location in the genome of a target cell’s DNA, effectively utilizing the Cas9 endonuclease property to nick the target and nontarget strand of a double-stranded DNA (Cong et al., 2013). This could be used either to disrupt a gene for knockout study or to allow the cell’s innate excision repair mechanism to incorporate a new strand of DNA, which may be introduced by the researcher to the system, allowing the DNA to integrate at the location of the site of cleavage (Jinek et al., 2012; Mali et al., 2013). Recently, the comparatively smaller Cas9 protein of the Type II CRISPR–Cas system of Staphylococcus aureus (SaCas9) was proposed as a more effective nuclease for the RNA-guided genome-editing strategy (Ran et al., 2015). Homologous Cas9 genes are related, and the degree of their similarity is dependent on the CRISPR–Cas subtype: Type II-A, Type II-B, or Type II-C (Fonfara et al., 2013). Conserved across these homologs are the amino acids of the NHN and RuvC domains, which nick the target and nontarget strand, respectively (Fonfara et al., 2013; Jinek et al., 2012). However, between the catalytic domains are a variability of amino acids (Chylinski et al., 2014; Fonfara et al., 2013). A study by Fonfara et al. (2013), using S. pyogenes (CRISPR–Cas Type II-A) as the model bacteria, demonstrated that only the Cas9 genes belonging to bacteria that possess a closely related Type II-A system can be interchanged while still maintaining CRISPR–Cas functionality. Particularly, it was shown that the key differences in the Cas9 protein functionality across the various Type II subtypes were in the maturing crRNA, as well as the stabilization in the tracrRNA and pre-crRNA duplex, which is the eventual complex that targets invading foreign genetic elements (Fonfara et al., 2013). The striking diversity in the structure and gene-editing efficiency of the Cas9 between the two aforementioned bacteria reveals an evolutionary divergence, potentially tailoring to the immunity requirements of the bacteria, as it is targeted by species-specific phage infection. 

As the evidence implicating the CRISPR–Cas system in envelope stress amasses, speculation has arisen regarding the involvement of membrane cues to trigger the CRISPR–Cas system. The role of heat-stable nucleoid structuring (H-NS) protein in the suppressive function of CasA transcription in the E. coli CRISPR–Cas system has been reported (Pul et al., 2010). The leucine response transcription factor, LeuO, was found to be a positive regulator of CasA (Westra et al., 2010). The H-NS– LeuO regulation function was later observed in Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (Medina-Aparicio et al., 2011). An additional regulatory function of H-NS has been proposed indicating that the protein is sequestered from the CRISPR–Cas array in the event of exogenous genetic penetration, promoting the transcription of the CRISPR–Cas system (Navarre et al., 2006, 2007). With this information pooled, Tracy Raivio (2011) summarized a potential mechanism for the initiation of CRISPR–Cas induction. It was hypothesized that a signal exists at the membrane, which is triggered through either the penetration of exogenous DNA or the production of atypical protein products through foreign DNA. This signal initiates the phosphorylation of BaeR by BaeS at the membrane, which then transfers to the CRISPR–Cas system for transcription initiation. Additional positive regulation of the CRISPR–Cas locus through LeuO will occur as H-NS binds with exogenous DNA. Although key components in the cascade are yet to be determined, this offers a deeper look into the CRISPR–Cas system, elucidating the induction of CRISPR– Cas in the event of membrane stress, and thereupon providing insight into the initiation of CRISPR–Cas as it pertains to cell immunity (Raivio, 2011). 

## 2.11.3.5 Cas1 and Cas2 are toxin–antitoxin systems leading to dormancy

The overexpression of the toxin of a toxin–antitoxin (TA) system has been observed to induce cell dormancy (see Chapter 2.7), and eventual cell death in the advent of stress. It has also been hypothesized to assist in survivability of cells, as shown in E. coli, where the RelE and ChpAK toxins induce a static state of cell metabolism, allowing for metabolic halt until the antitoxin is expressed (Pedersen et al., 2002). In a vegetative cell, the toxin and its associated antitoxin are co-expressed, forming a stable complex that subdues the activity of the toxin (Van Melderen and De Bast, 2009; Yamaguchi et al., 2011). In the context of phage stress, the TA system, mainly the toxin, has been linked to abortive phage infection, neutralizing both phage and host cell transcripts, leading to cell suicide and phage elimination (Cook et al., 2013; Fineran et al., 2009). 

Interestingly, Makarova et al. (2012) linked the CRISPR–Cas system of E. coli immunity to a TA system, specifically addressing the role of Cas1 and Cas2 genes as key genes for inducing dormancy and/or abortive phage infection in the event of bacteriophage infection. They hypothesized that as a cell is invaded by a phage, cell dormancy is triggered to allow time for adequate CRISPR–Cas immunity, and/or to induce apoptosis to prevent integration and spread of the viral genetic material. Their assumption was based on the observation that Cas1 and Cas2 are universal across many CRISPR–Cas systems, and that Cas2 shares homology to the mRNA-cleaving VapD (Daines et al., 2004; Kwon et al., 2012), acting as a toxin that induces dormancy and/or death following infection. The antitoxin, Cas1, forms a complex with Cas2 in the nonstressed cell, and in the event of bacteriophage infection, Cas2 is presumably degraded, allowing for Cas1 (toxin) accumulation. However, the link of the cas genes to this area of stress coping requires more investigation, and it is highly theoretical (Westra et al., 2014), as a sufficient link between the two systems is yet to be determined. This is an intriguing association in the realm of stress response and CRISPR–Cas. 

## Conclusion

As CRISPR–Cas is in the early stages of investigation, the scope of functionality has yet to be fully comprehended. As a means to adaptive immunity (i.e., evolution in progress), the CRISPR–Cas system has been observed to combat bacteriophage infection, in addition to other types of foreign genetic material in bacteria. This is an important function conferring survivorship to targeted bacterial cells, as phages have been observed to cohabit many ecological niches with bacteria, with the major observable effect being population decrease due to lysing as part of the bacteriophage life cycle (Ashelford et al., 2003; Bergh et al., 1989; D´ıaz-Munoz and Koskella, 2014; Mojica and Brussaard, 2014;˜ Proctor and Fuhrman, 1990; Williamson et al., 2013). Alternate roles of CRISPR–Cas have been investigated, as components of the CRISPR–Cas pathway appear to be involved in other bacterial stress responses.

1Department of Plant and Environmental Science, University of Copenhagen, Frederiksberg, Denmark 

2Key Lab of Urban Environment and Health, Institute of Urban Environment, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Xiamen, People’s Republic of China

## 2.12.1 Introduction: copper bioavailability in Earth’s history

## 2.12.1.1 Great oxidation event through cyanobacteria

There is no doubt that early life on Earth evolved in an anoxic environment. While the origin of photosynthesis is not clear, it is assumed that early photosynthesis was anoxygenic. However, at a certain point, cyanobacteria started producing oxygen as part of photosynthesis (Blankenship, 2010; Blankenship et al., 1998; Buick, 2008; Farquhar et al., 2011; Sessions et al., 2009; Shih, 2015). 

This production of oxygen slowly led to an oxygenation of the atmosphere that as a consequence made multicellular life possible but also led to the extinction of many microbes. The presence of oxygen also changed the bioavailability of many metals, including copper, zinc, and iron. Whereas iron became much less bioavailable due to the low solubility of Fe(III), copper and zinc became much more bioavailable due to the increasing oxidation of metal sulfides as well as the higher solubility of Cu(II) compared to Cu(I) (Hong Enriquez et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2003). Since Cu(I) is a strong soft metal that will attack Fe–S clusters and strongly binds to molecules containing sulfhydryl groups, the cytoplasm had to be protected from Cu(I). This led to the development of a copper homeostasis system, as described in this chapter. At some time during the process of oxygenation, eukaryotes as we know them today evolved (Hedges et al., 2001), having mitochondria and the ability for phagocytosis. The early eukaryotes preyed on bacteria and archaea, and therefore needed a fast and reliable way to kill and digest them. Since life had developed under reductive, anaerobic conditions, the processes vulnerable to oxygen and soft metals present the Achilles heel to attack. Therefore, it appears consistent with this theory that macrophages use both an oxidative burst and copper shock to kill potential pathogens (Achard et al., 2012; Festa et al., 2014; 

German et al., 2013; Hodgkinson and Petris, 2012; Neyrolles et al., 2015; White et al., 2009). Although it has not been proven, one can assume early eukaryotes and present-day predatory protozoa to use these weapons as well. This would then indicate that selective pressure to keep copper resistance mechanisms came from both the increased presence of copper in the environment and the use of copper as a weapon in predation in early eukaryotes (German et al., 2013; Hao et al., 2015). 

## 2.12.1.2 Copper homeostasis and trafficking in cyanobacteria

Although most prokaryotes have their copper-containing enzymes located in the periplasm and cytoplasmic membrane, cyanobacteria are unique in that they require copper in the active center of plastocyanin (photosynthesis) and caa3-type cytochrome oxidase (respiration), both of which are located in the thylakoid membranes (see Chapters 20.3 and 20.4). Therefore, copper has to be transported through the cytoplasm of the cell to reach the target. Several systems dealing with copper trafficking have been identified in cyanobacteria. Due to the Gram-negative cell envelope of cyanobacteria, Cu(II) from the environment enters the periplasm, most likely through porins. Additionally, a TonB-dependent transporter has been identified, allowing for transport of ligand-bound copper ions across the outer membrane into the periplasm (Nicolaisen et al., 2010). While much is still unknown regarding copper uptake (as Cu(II) or Cu(I)) from the periplasmic space into the cytoplasm in bacteria in general, transporters that might be involved in copper uptake in some cyanobacteria have recently been identified. Nostoc punctiforme contains two genes encoding for transporters of the ZIP/SLC39 family (Hudek et al., 2013). Although the proteins share 100% sequence identity, the expression of the two genes differs under different metal treatments, suggesting involvement in uptake of different metal ions, including copper (Hudek et al., 2013). Bacterial members of this protein family have previously been shown to allow for uptake of a wide range of trace metals, including copper (Grass et al., 2005; Taudte and Grass, 2010). 

Once in the cytoplasm, Cu(I) is bound by the cytoplasmic copper chaperone Atx1 (Tottey et al., 2001, 2002, 2012). $\mathrm { { A t x 1 } [ \mathrm { { C u } ( I ) ] } }$ is able to interact with the two Cu(I)-transporting $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B } } – \mathrm { A T P a s e s }$ , CtaA and PacS, transferring Cu(I) onto the transporter via the formation of a Cu(I) complexing heterodimer as shown via nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) analysis for the interaction between Atx1[Cu(I)] and $\mathrm { P a c S } _ { N }$ (Banci et al., 2006). $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B } } – \mathrm { A T P a s e s }$ of the FixI–CopA2 subgroup have been shown to export Cu(I) at low rates and are involved in assembling cuproproteins (Arguello ¨ et al., 2011; Gonzalez-Guerrero et $a l .$ , 2010; Raimunda et al., 2011). Both $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B } } – \mathrm { A T P a s e s }$ are required to properly bind copper to CucA, a periplasmic copper-containing protein (Waldron et al., 2010; Tottey et al., 2008), while plastocyanin, located in the thylakoids, requires the presence of CtaA, although this transport protein is located in the cytoplasmic membrane (Tottey et al., 2002). Also important for periplasmic copper handling in cyanobacteria is FutA2, an iron-binding protein (Waldron et al., 2007). 

Two operons, copMRS and copBAC, have been identified in Synechocystis to be involved in copper detoxification (Giner-Lamia et al., 2012, 2015). CopM is a periplasmic copper-binding protein, and the expression of copMRS is regulated by the twocomponent regulatory system CopRS, encoded on the same operon (Giner-Lamia et al., 2012). It has also been found that CopM is secreted not just into the periplasm but also into the environment, where it might bind Cu(II), decreasing the copper stress to the cell (Giner-Lamia et al., 2015). Although copMRS has been identified on the chromosome of Synechocystis, a second copy of the operon is located on plasmid pSYSX. Also located on plasmid pSYSX is cusBAC; its expression is also regulated by CopRS (Giner-Lamia et al., 2012, 2015). CusBAC forms a tripartite protein complex exporting Cu(I) from the periplasm in a proton-dependent fashion. 

Like any other organism living in the presence of oxygen, cyanobacteria have to counteract the effects of reactive oxygen species (ROS; see Section 10). One type of enzymes involved in these detoxification processes is superoxide dismutases (SOD). Based on the catalytic metal, different isoforms (FeSOD, MnSOD, Cu/ZnSOD, and NiSOD) of the enzyme can be distinguished. Whereas NiSODs are the only isoform found in members of the genus Prochlorococcus, FeSODs and MnSODs are found in higher orders of cyanobacteria. In comparison, Cu/ZnSODs are rare among members of this phylum (Priya et al., 2007). 

## 2.12.2 Copper transport and homeostasis

## 2.12.2.1 Gram-positive bacteria

Several strains of Gram-positive bacteria (e.g., members of the genus Bacillus) have been identified for a possible application in heavy and transition metal adsorption, including copper, from contaminated areas (Ahmady-Asbchin, 2015; Allievi et al., 2011; Oves et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2008). The metal ions interact, and can subsequently be removed, with the cell wall surface of the bacteria. As with other prokaryotes, proteins containing copper cofactors are located outside of the cytoplasm. While no outer membrane inhibits the direct interaction of the copper ions in the medium with cytoplasmic membrane– associated proteins, incorporation of the copper ions into the cuproproteins requires uptake of Cu and subsequent export. In Gram-negative bacteria (see Section 2.12.2.2), ABC transporters as well as members of the ZIP family have been shown to be involved in copper uptake. While members of both types of transporters can be identified within Gram-positive bacteria, none has to date been characterized for their involvement in copper uptake within this group of bacteria. In Bacillus cereus, coproporphyrin III, a copper chelator, has been identified and might play a role in copper uptake (Yamada-Ankei et al., 1977a,b). 

In Bacillus subtilis, YcnJ, a CopCD (to be discussed in Section 2.12.2.2) fusion protein, has been shown to be involved in copper uptake (Chillappagari et al., 2009). This membrane transporter contains an N-terminal Cu(II)-binding site (predicted to be located on the outside of the cell membrane) for binding of the copper ions from the medium and their subsequent transport into the cytoplasm (Chillappagari et al., 2009). Since copper seems to be taken up as Cu(II), it would have to be reduced to Cu(I) once in the cytoplasm. A basic local alignment search tool (BLAST) search identified YcnJ to be common among Bacillus but failed to identify this type of uptake system within other classes of Firmicutes as well as Actinobacteria. Expression of ycnJ is regulated via the repressor YcnK, which in the presence of Cu(I) binds to the operator site of the intergenic region between ycnL and ycnKJI, thereby blocking transcription (Hirooka et al., 2012). Under copper limitation, the repressor is released and YcnJ is synthesized, allowing for copper uptake. Once inside the cytoplasm, Cu(I)/Cu(II) is usually bound by chaperones, CopZ, or regulatory proteins, such as CsoR or CopY, which in the presence of Cu(I) are released from their respective operator sites and allow for the expression of genes encoding copper export systems, or YcnK, which in the presence of Cu(I) blocks further expression of ycnKJI and therefore limits additional copper uptake (Hirooka et al., 2012). 

$\mathrm { P _ { 1 B } } – \mathrm { A T P a s e s }$ (whose old name is CPx-ATPases, for the sequence motive in transmembrane helix (TMH) VI) involved in copper homeostasis in Gram-positive bacteria were first identified in Enterococcus hirae (Odermatt et al., 1992, 1993, 1994; Solioz and Odermatt, 1995). While CopA was initially described as a copper uptake system, later analysis identified CopA of E. hirae as a member of the FixI/CopA2-like ATPases subgroup of the Cu(I)-transporting $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } \mathrm { - A T } }$ Pases subfamily. This type of $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } }$ -ATPases exports Cu(I) at low rates and has been deemed to be responsible for proper assembly of membrane-bound Cucontaining enzymes under physiological conditions (Arguello¨ et al., 2011; Gonzalez-Guerrero et al., 2010; Raimunda et al., 2011). 

The second $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } - A T P a s e }$ initially identified in E. hirae, CopB, belongs to the “classical” subgroup of the subfamily; it is a prevalent protein shown to be involved in export of excess Cu(I) from the cytoplasm. Delivery of Cu(I) to the $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } }$ -ATPases in Gram-positive bacteria often involves a cytoplasmic Cu chaperone, CopZ, which interacts with the N-terminal domain of the $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } }$ -ATPase and transfers Cu(I) onto the metal-binding domain of the transporter (Magnani et al., 2005; Solioz and Stoyanov, 2003). The chaperone CopZ has also been found to transfer Cu(I) onto the transcriptional repressor CopY, causing its release from the operator site and transcription of the cop operon (Strausak and Solioz, 1997). While best characterized in E. hirae, the $\mathrm { { P _ { 1 B } } } ^ { } \cdot$ ATPase-mediated copper resistance has been described in a number of Gram-positive bacteria (Gaballa et al., 2003; Reyes et al., 2006). 

## 2.12.2.2 Gram-negative bacteria

In contrast to Gram-positive bacteria, Gram-negative bacteria face the challenge of two membranes for uptake of nutrients, including metals. Copper has to enter the periplasm before it can be taken up via transport across the cytoplasmic membrane. Porins have been found to be involved in copper uptake of several Gram-negative bacteria (e.g., Methylosinus trichosporum OB3b, Escherichia coli, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa) (Balasubramanian et al., 2011; Teitzel et al., 2006; Whiting et al., 1995). Acknowledging that all Gram-negative bacteria face that same challenge with respect to copper uptake, it can be assumed that in other members of this group of bacteria, copper ions also enter the periplasm via existing porins. Once in the periplasm, copper can cross the cytoplasmic membrane via several mechanisms: ZupT, a member of the ZIP family of zinc and iron transporters, has been found to have a broad substrate spectrum in E. coli and is able to take up Cu(II) (Grass et al., 2005; Taudte and Grass, 2010). Similar to YcnJ in Gram-positive bacteria, CopCD, as two separate proteins (with CopD being located in the cytoplasmic membrane and CopC in the periplasm), can be identified in members of the Proteobacteria. Overexpression of copCD renders cells more sensitive to copper, indicating that the proteins are indeed involved in the metal uptake (Cha and Cooksey, 1993). Whereas YcnJ of B. subtilis only contains a Cu(II)- binding site, CopC has both a Cu(II)- and a Cu(I)-binding site and is able to undergo a Cu(II) → Cu(I) redox change, suggesting that copper might be taken up as Cu(I) rather than Cu(II) (Arnesano et al., 2002, 2003a, 2003b; Djoko et al., 2007). 

Additionally, uptake of chelator-bound copper has been described among several Gram-negative bacteria. First suggested in 1993 (Fitch et al., 1993), several chalkophores (Cu chelators) have been isolated (Anttila et al., 2011; DiSpirito et al., 1998; Kim et al., 2004; Zahn and DiSpirito, 1996). Methanobactin-mediated Cu uptake by methanotrophic bacteria is used in addition to passive and porin-dependent 

Cu uptake (Balasubramanian et al., 2011). Paracoccus denitrificans secretes the chalkophore coproporphyrin III (Znbound) under Cu-limiting conditions. Zn(II) can be replaced by Cu(II), and Cu-coproporphyrin III has been shown to be used as a copper source by P. denitrificans (Anttila et al., 2011; Nicolaisen et al., 2010). In cyanobacteria, siderophores have been shown to be involved in iron and copper uptake, and this phenomenon might be widely utilized by Gramnegative bacteria to satisfy their copper needs (Nicolaisen et al., 2010). 

Once across the cytoplasmic membrane, concentrations of free Cu(I) have to be kept extremely low within the cell due to the ability of copper to carry out Fenton-like reactions to produce ROS as well as its ability to destabilize Fe–S clusters (Dupont et al., 2011; Macomber and Imlay, 2009; Xu and Imlay, 2012). In cyanobacteria, Atx1 sequesters cytoplasmic Cu(I) and delivers it to the $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } }$ -ATPases (Banci et al., 2010; Tottey et al., 2001, 2002, 2012) (as discussed in this chapter). In Proteobacteria, no Atx1-like Cu(I) chaperone has been described to date. In E. coli, the transcriptional repressor CueR binds zeptomolar concentrations of Cu(I) and regulates transcription of copA, encoding a “classical” $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } - A T P a s e } ,$ as well as cueO, encoding a periplasmic multicopper oxidase (Grass and Rensing, 2001a; Outten et al., 2000, 2001; Petersen et al., 2000; Stoyanov et al., 2001). Since CueO is exported via the twin-arginine transport (TAT) system, incorporation of Cu(I) into the structural and active site occurs in the cytoplasm. Once in the periplasm, CueO has been shown to oxidize Cu(I) to Cu(II), rendering it less toxic (Djoko et al., 2010; Singh et al., 2004). In addition, CueO also oxidizes enterobactin, which is able to sequester copper (Grass et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2001). While the presence of CopA and CueO-like proteins seems common, some Gram-negative bacteria also encode a tripartite transport complex spanning both membranes and transporting Cu(I) from the periplasm into the surrounding medium (Delmar et al., 2013; Kulathila et al., 2011; Long et al., 2010, 2012; Su et al., 2011). This transport complex is composed of a member of the resistance nodulation cell division (RND) family, CusA; a membrane fusion protein (MFP), CusB; and an outer membrane factor (OMF), CusC. In E. coli, an additional gene, cusF, is part of the cusCFBA operon encoding a small periplasmic Cu(I)-binding protein (Franke et al., 2001, 2003; Grass and Rensing, 2001b; Munson et al., 2000). Expression of cusCFBA is regulated by a two-component regulatory system, CusRS, which in E. coli is encoded directly downstream and in the opposite direction of the cusCFBA operon (Munson et al., 2000). CusF has been shown to be important for full copper resistance mediated by the Cus system (Franke et al., 2003). CusF seems to act as a Cu(I) chaperone, accepting Cu(I) from CopA after transport across the cytoplasmic membrane and delivering it to the CusCBA complex via direct interaction with CusB (Bagai et al., 2008; Loftin et al., 2005, 2007; Mealman et al., 2011; Meir et al., 2015; Padilla-Benavides et al., 2014). While this arrangement has been found in E. coli and some sequences of Shigella, in strains of Erwinia, Pseudomonas, and 

Cupriavidus metallidurans CH34, CusF is encoded as part of the MFP CusB as a C-terminal fusion (Bersch et al., 2011). 

Within the Enterobacteriaceae, the presence of CueO and CopA is common among nonsymbiotic members of this family, whereas symbiotic Enterobacteriaceae lack copper transport systems. The Cus system, which is mainly responsible for copper efflux under anaerobic conditions or in the absence of CueO, is less common in this family (Rensing and Franke, 2007). 

While CueO and CusCFBA were originally identified as able to detoxify Cu(I) in the periplasm, Salmonella Typhimurium, which lacks the Cus system, has been shown to grow in the presence of up to 5.5 mM $\mathrm { C u S O _ { 4 } . }$ This copper tolerance can be attributed to the presence of the periplasmic protein CueP, which, in the absence of Cus, allows for survival under high copper concentrations and has been shown to decrease ROS (Osman et al., 2010; Pontel and Soncini, 2009; Yoon et al., 2014a,b). Expression of cueP is able to restore copper tolerance in a Δcus-deletion strain of E. coli. A BLAST analysis searching the nonredundant protein database identifies CueP mainly within the Enterobacteriaceae (genera Salmonella and Citrobacter). In addition to CuiD (CueO), CopA, and CueP, S. Typhimurium also utilizes GolT, an additional $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } - A T P a s e }$ for copper export (Checa et al., 2011; Espariz et al., 2007; Nies and Herzberg, 2013). Additionally, many strains of Enterobacteriaceae contain a 19-gene copper resistance island, discussed in Section 2.12.3.1. 

## 2.12.2.3 Archaea

The least well-characterized group within prokaryotes with respect to copper homeostasis are the archaea. Proteins showing up to 25% identity to YcnJ from B. subtilis can be identified within the Euryarchaeota and Thaumarchaeota. Similarly, members of the ZIP family of transporters, which have been shown to allow for uptake of a variety of metal ions including copper, are present within the archaea. Evidence of production of siderophores by members of the Haloarchaea (Dave et al., 2006) suggests utilization of chelated copper ions as an additional copper uptake mechanism. However, experimental evidence regarding the function and metal specificity of any of these possible uptake mechanisms is still lacking. 

Better understood are the mechanisms that archaea have in place to deal with excess copper. As within bacteria, $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } }$ -ATPases are common among archaea, although not all members of the domain contain genes encoding them. Best understood are the copper resistance mechanisms of Sulfolobus sulfataricus and Archeoglobus fulgidus. In S. sulfataricus, copper resistance is mediated by two members of the “classical” $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } - A T P a s e }$ type, CopA and CopB. The genes for both transporters are associated with genes encoding regulatory proteins and possible cytoplasmic copper chaperones (Ettema et al., 2006; Vollmecke et al., 2012). Expression of copTA, encoding the Cu-binding protein CopT and the transporter CopA, is regulated by the archaea-specific activator CopR, encoded directly upstream of copTA (Villafane et al., 2011). Located in a different region of the chromosome and flanked by IS elements is copYZ, encoding a regulatory protein and copper chaperone, respectively, and transcribed in the opposite direction of copB. Both $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } }$ -ATPases were shown to be important for copper and silver resistance in S. sulfataricus (Vollmecke et al., 2012). 

A. fulgidus also encodes two $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B } } \mathrm { - } \mathrm { A T }$ Pases. However, whereas CopA is a member of the “classical” $\mathrm { { P _ { 1 B - 1 } } } .$ -ATPases (thereby exporting Cu(I), which it receives from the cytoplasmic copper chaperone CopZ) (Arguello¨ et al., 2003; Gonzalez-Guerrero et al., 2008, 2009; Mandal et al., 2002; Padilla-Benavides et al., 2013; Rosenzweig and Arguello, 2012), CopB is identi-¨ fied as a $\mathrm { P } _ { 1 \mathrm { B } - 3 } – \mathrm { A T P a s e }$ responsible for the transport of Cu(II) (Jayakanthan et al., 2012; Mana-Capelli et al., 2003). In contrast to members of the $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } - A T P a s e }$ subfamily, which contain an N-terminal CXXC-metal-binding motif and the CPC motif in TMH VI, members of the $\mathrm { P } _ { 1 \mathrm { B } - 3 } { - } \mathrm { A T P a s } _ { }$ e subfamily have a histidine-rich N-terminus and the motif CPH in TMH VI (Raimunda et al., 2011). New studies suggest that the additional sequence motif MSXST, instead of MXXSS in $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } }$ -ATPases, might provide the Cu(II) specificity (Meloni et al., 2014). $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 3 } } -$ ATPases can be identified among archaea as well as bacteria. 

## 2.12.3 Mobile copper fitness islands

## 2.12.3.1 Copper resistance as a response to predation and highly contaminated environments

Copper homeostasis is essential in most environments, since most organisms need copper in small amounts but need protection from elevated copper concentrations inside cells. Most commonly, this is achieved by the presence of at least one $\mathrm { C u ( I ) P _ { 1 B - 1 } - }$ ATPase. However, in copper-contaminated environments, many microbes possess additional genes encoding proteins responsible for increased copper resistance. These proteins are often located in the periplasm of Gram-negative cells or outside of the cytoplasmic membrane in Gram-positive cells (Arguello¨ et al., 2013; Solioz et al., 2010). The genes are often clustered together in two or more operons and are often on mobile elements. As they are often flanked by transposable elements, they could also be classified as copper fitness islands. Initially, these copper fitness determinants could be identified in isolates from environments with elevated copper concentrations (Brown et al., 1995; Monchy et al., 2006). However, genome sequencing identified these elements increasingly in sites not contaminated by copper (Eloe et al., 2011). One possible explanation would be the use of copper by predatory protozoa to kill their prey (German et al., 2013; Hao et al., 2015). Bacteria would then harbor copper resistance elements or even complete copper fitness islands as a protection from predation. Since macrophages also use copper to kill pathogens (Achard et al., 2012; Festa et al., 2014; German et al., 2013; Hodgkinson and Petris, 2012; Neyrolles et al., 2015; White et al., 2009), copper fitness islands could also be seen as pathogenicity islands. 

## 2.12.3.2 Identification and occurrence of copper fitness islands

Heavy and transition metal resistance mechanisms can confer the carrier with an important ecological advantage compared to competitors by allowing survival under high-metal conditions. While microorganisms can encounter high copper concentrations at metal-contaminated (naturally or due to anthropogenic influence) sites, metals like copper and zinc are also utilized by phagocytic cells such as predatory protozoa as well as by macrophages and neutrophils as part of our innate immune system (Achard et al., 2012; Festa et al., 2014; German et al., 2013; Hodgkinson and Petris, 2012; Neyrolles et al., 2015; White et al., 2009). In these cells, microorganisms and potential pathogens are engulfed and exposed to a toxic mixture of metals, ROS, nitric oxide, and destructive enzymes to ultimately kill the engulfed microbe. It thus appears that utilizing additional metal resistance determinants as a pathogen can aid in survival and proliferation. 

## Copper fitness islands in Enterobacteriaceae

In Enterobacteriaceae, plasmid-bound copper resistance was first described located on plasmid pRJ1004 from E. coli (Tetaz and Luke, 1983). Sequence analysis showed that the pco system encodes for the two-component system PcoRS, the periplasmic multicopper oxidase PcoA, the outer membrane protein PcoB, the inner membrane protein PcoD, as well as two periplasmic copper-binding proteins, PcoC and PcoE (Brown et al., 1995; 

Lee et al., 2002). Expression of pcoABCD is regulated by PcoRS, while the regulatory system of pcoE is chromosomally encoded (Munson et al., 2000; Rouch and Brown, 1997; Zimmermann et al., 2012). 

In the presence of copper, membrane-bound PcoS is phosphorylated and transfers the phosphate group onto PcoR, activating transcription of the structural genes of the pco determinant. Membrane-bound PcoD interacts with periplasmic PcoC and allows for uptake of Cu(I) into the cytoplasm to be incorporated into PcoA before being transported into the periplasm, where oxidation of catechol siderophores, subsequent Cu(I) sequestration, and the possible direct oxidation of Cu(I) to Cu(II) decrease the toxic effect of access copper. PcoE is predicted to bind access Cu(I) for immediate relief of copper stress (Figure 2.12.1) (Brown et al., 1995; Djoko et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2002; Munson et al., 2000; Rouch and Brown, 1997; Zimmermann et al., 2012). 

Later sequence analysis (National Center for Biotechnology Information accession no. KC146966) showed that on pRJ1004, next to the pco determinant, genes originally described to be involved in silver resistance in S. Typhimurium harboring pMG101 (Gupta et al., 1999; McHugh et al., 1975) are located. The sil-determinant encodes for the RND-dependent efflux system SilCBA; the periplasmic chaperone SilF; the $\mathrm { { P _ { 1 B - 1 } } ^ { - } }$ ATPase SilP; the periplasmic Ag(I)-binding protein SilE; the two-component regulatory system SilRS; as well as an additional protein, now named SilG, of unknown function (Gupta et al.,

1999; Randall et al., 2015). Expression of silCFBAGP is regulated by the two-component regulatory system SilRS, while expression of silE seems to be controlled by the chromosomally encoded CusRS system (Gupta et al., 1999; Silver, 2003; Zimmermann et al., 2012). SilCBA forms a tripartite transport system transporting Ag(I) and possibly Cu(I) from the periplasm into the surrounding medium. Cytoplasmic Ag(I) and/or Cu(I) is exported across the cytoplasmic membrane via the $\mathrm { { P _ { 1 B - 1 } } ^ { - } }$ ATPase SilP, where it is thought to be taken up by SilF to be delivered to the SilCBA complex for subsequent export from the periplasm. Like PcoE, SilE is thought to act as an initial defense mechanism by binding Ag(I) or Cu(I) ions in the periplasm (Gupta et al., 1999; Silver, 2003) (Figure 2.12.1). 

Also identified in this sequence are two additional genes, pcoF and pcoG, encoding a putative copper-binding protein and a putative M23B metallopeptidase, respectively. The same 19-gene pco–sil cluster (Figure 2.12.1) has been identified in a recently sequenced copper-resistant strain of E. coli as well as three strains of S. Typhimurium isolated from copper- and zinc-fed pigs in Denmark (Luthje¨ et al., 2014; Qin et al., 2014). Here, the 19-gene pco–sil cluster is flanked by mobile elements. Within Salmonella enterica subsp. Enterica, the copper resistance locus is either part of a Tn7-like transposon (Peters et al., 2014), as shown for isolates of the serovars Heidelberg, Montevideo, Senftenberg, and Tennessee; or part of a larger conjugative element and shown for isolates of the serovars Senftenberg, Ohio, and Cubana. Recent sequencing of E. coli J53 (pMG101) indicated the transfer of the pco–sil cluster from the plasmid into the bacterial chromosome, with the cluster being flanked by Tn7-like elements (Randall et al., 2015). 

Analysis of completed genomic and plasmid sequences shows the presence of the pco–sil cluster within members of the genera Citrobacter (chromosomally encoded only), Cronobacter, Enterobacter, Escherichia, Klebsiella (plasmid encoded only), Salmonella, and Serratia (plasmid encoded only). The transfer of a plasmid carrying the copper fitness island was responsible for a nosocomial outbreak of Klebsiella pneumonia (Sandegren et al., 2012). 

In addition to the pco–sil cluster, strains encoding the yersiniabactin biosynthesis pathway have been found to be more copper tolerant (Chaturvedi et al., 2014a). Previously described as a virulence factor known to bind copper, the yersiniabactin determinant has been described in strains of K. pneumonia, Salmonella, E. coli, and Yersinia pestis (Aviv et al., 2014; Fodah et al., 2014; Rakin et al., 2012; Schubert et al., 2004). Analysis of the completed genome and plasmid sequences of Enterobacteriaceae also identified the yersiniabactin determinant in members of the genera Cronobacter and Enterobacter. In addition to binding and therefore removing Cu(II) from the environment, yersiniabactin-Cu(II) has been shown to mimic superoxide dismutase activity, removing ROS generated in the phagosome (Chaturvedi et al., 2014b). Interestingly, several of the sequenced strains of E. coli (including strains of EHEC O104:H4 and the avian pathogen APEC O1) and K. pneumonia contain both pco–sil as well as the yersiniabactin biosynthesis determinant. 

## Copper fitness islands in Pseudomonas

Members of the genus Pseudomonas range from bacteria promoting plant growth to members causing serious disease in plants, animals, or humans. Early studies identified the presence of plasmid-encoded copper resistance genes, copRS and copABCD, in the plant pathogen Pseudomonas syringae (Cha and Cooksey, 1991; Haefeli et al., 1984). Regulated by a two-component regulatory system, copABCD encodes for a periplasmic multicopper oxidase (CopA); an outer membrane (CopB); CopD, which is located in the cytoplasmic membrane; and the periplasmic protein CopC (Cha and Cooksey, 1991; Cooksey, 1993). The presence of CopCD renders cells more copper sensitive and has been described as responsible for copper uptake (Cha and Cooksey, 1993). Similar to the pco determinant described for Enterobacteriaceae, CopA and CopB are important for full copper resistance. Analysis of copper resistance in isolates of P. syringae revealed the wide presence of plasmids carrying copper resistance (Cazorla et al., 2002; Gutierrez-Barranquero et al., 2013). 

Plasmid-encoded copper resistance of strain P. syringae pv. syringae UMAF0081 (as well as others) revealed the presence of the already-mentioned copABCD operon, cusCBA, encoding the membranes spanning efflux pump CusCBA involved in detoxification of copper from the periplasm, the $\mathrm { { P _ { 1 B - 1 } } ^ { - } }$ ATPase CopG, as well as a two-component regulatory system named CopRS (Gutierrez-Barranquero et al., 2013). Interestingly, the cusCBA operon does not encode for the periplasmic protein CusF identified within the cus determinant of E. coli and other Enterobacteriaceae. However, it appears CusF is encoded as a fusion with the C-terminus of CusB. While the importance of CopABCD in copper resistance had previously been established, it could be shown that copG or cusCBA alone were able to confer partial copper resistance in P. syringae and are therefore significant for full copper resistance (Gutierrez-Barranquero et al., 2013). A BLAST analysis of the copper resistance cluster present in P. syringae pv. syringae UMAF0081, and further searching in the microbial genomic database (http://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi), identified the cop–cus cluster in six of the deposited shotgun sequences of Pseudomonas but failed to identify the genetic region within other Proteobacteria. 

Recent sequence analysis of Pseudomonas jessenii H16, isolated from Cu-contaminated soil in Denmark, revealed the presence of two copper resistance gene clusters, composed of 10 and 12 genes (Qin et al., unpublished). Since the 10-gene copper resistance cluster is also present in P. jessenii C2, isolated from pristine soil and showing lower tolerance toward copper, the high resistance levels observed in P. jessenii H16 would need to be attributed to the presence of the additional 12-gene cluster (Figure 2.12.2) (Qin et al., unpublished). Both strains contain genes encoding a multicopper oxidase, $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } }$ -ATPase; a possible Cu(I) uptake system CopCD; a copper-responsive twocomponent regulatory system CusRS; several potential Cu(I) chaperons: CopZ, CopG, and a hypothetical protein; as well as a transcriptional regulator, CopR (Qin et al., unpublished).
