The 12-gene copper resistance cluster (Figure 2.12.2) is flanked by two hypothetical proteins following a predicted thiamine biosynthesis protein, ThiF, and a CsoR-like transcriptional regulator, and it is part of a larger, approximately 50 kbp metal resistance cluster flanked by a hypothetical sulfur carrier protein and Tn7-like transposition proteins and also carrying genes predicted to be involved in nickel and mercury resistance, respectively. The 12-gene copper cluster encodes a $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } } \mathrm { - A T P a s e } ,$ , CopA, predicted to export Cu(I) from the cytoplasm into the periplasm; a CusCBA transport complex predicted to extrude Cu(I) from the periplasm in a proton motive force-dependent manner; an outer membrane protein CopB; a cytoplasmic membrane protein CopD, for Cu(I) uptake for incorporation into the periplasmic multicopper oxidase (named CueO), oxidation of Cu(I) to Cu(II), as well as oxidation of siderophores and subsequent copper sequestration; a blue copper domain containing protein, the hypothetical metal-binding protein CopG; and a two-component regulatory system CusRS, which is predicted to be involved in regulation of the expression of the genes within this copper resistance cluster (Figure 2.12.2) (Qin et al., unpublished). A BLAST analysis of the 12-gene copper cluster of P. jessenii H16 (approx. 17.6 kbp) identified this gene region within the shotgun sequences of several strains of Pseudomonas, including P. syringae and Pseudomonas fluorescens, but was unable to identify this gene cluster outside the genus Pseudomonas. 

## Copper fitness islands in Enterococcus

Not only Gram-negative bacteria but also Gram-positive pathogens face the challenges presented to them by phagocytic cells. High copper resistance in Enterococcus has been linked to plasmids, and a recent study of various isolates of Enterococcus demonstrated that copper and antibiotic resistances could in most cases be co-transferred via conjugation (Freitas et al., 2011; Hasman and Aarestrup, 2002; Silveira et al., 2014). Plasmid-mediated copper resistance in Enterococcus has been linked to the presence of tcrB, encoding a copper-transporting $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B } - A T P a s e }$ (Hasman, 2005). Sequence analysis of TcrB would predict it being a member of the $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 3 } - A T P a s e s }$ , transporting Cu(II) rather than Cu(I), due to the presence of the histidinerich N-terminus, the CPH motif in TMH VI, and the presence of the motif MSXST, suggested to provide Cu(II) specificity (Meloni et al., 2014; Raimunda et al., 2011). The gene tcrB is part of the tcrYAZB operon, encoding an additional $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B } - A T P a s e } ,$ TcrA (of the $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B - 1 } - A T P a s e }$ subfamily), for export of Cu(I); the cytoplasmic copper chaperone TcrZ; and the copper-dependent regulator TcrY (Hasman, 2005). Also associated with copper resistance is the presence of the multicopper oxidase CueO (Grass and Rensing, 2001a). Comparative analysis of transferrable copper resistance determinants in Enterococcus showed that the majority of the resistant strains harbored both tcrB and cueO, with 62% of the strains having both compared to 22% having only tcrB and 16% containing only cueO (Silveira et al., 2014). 

Recent sequencing of highly copper-resistant strains of Enterococcus faecalis and Enterococcus faecium isolated from pigs fed a copper-supplemented diet identified tcrYAZB in close proximity of cueO; genes encoding a two-component regulatory system, named CusRS; and copY, encoding a copperdependent transcriptional regulator. Multiple genes encoding possible metal-binding proteins as well as transposable element are located in close proximity to genes encoding known copper resistance proteins (Figure 2.12.3) (Song et al., unpublished; Zhang et al., 2015). Also located in close proximity to the copper resistance cluster is a gene encoding a putative prolipoprotein diacylglyceryl transferase, a protein that has been shown to be involved in virulence (Cho et al., 2013; Reffuveille et al., 2012). High-level copper resistance in Enterococcus appears to involve the tcrYAZB operon with the encoded proteins TcrA and TcrB exporting access copper, Cu(I) and Cu(II), from the cytoplasm. The cytoplasmic copper chaperone TcrZ sequesters copper in the cytoplasm and transfers it to the $\mathrm { { P _ { 1 B } } ^ { - } }$ ATPases. Expression of tcrYAZB is regulated by TcrY (Hasman, 2005). The multicopper oxidase CueO, located outside the cytoplasmic membrane, probably oxidizes Cu(I) to Cu(II), since no siderophores have been identified to be released by strains of Enterococcus, but experimental evidence for this assumption is still lacking. In close proximity of cueO are genes encoding a two-component regulatory system, CusRS, and a transcriptional regulator, CopY, both being possible candidates in regulation of cueO expression. While this is the case within the recently published sequences of copper resistance islands within Enterococcus (Zhang et al., 2015), the copper resistance island of Enterococcus faecium HF50105 (accession no. ## Conclusions



Chaturvedi KS, Hung CS, Giblin DE, Urushidani S, Austin AM, et al. 2014b. Cupric yersiniabactin is a virulence-associated superoxide dismutase mimic. ACS Chemical Biology 9: 551–561.

Tetaz TJ, Luke RK. 1983. Plasmid-controlled resistance to copper in Escherichia coli. Journal of Bacteriology 154: 1263–1268. 



Although the presence of copper homeostasis systems is common among prokaryotes, within different taxonomic groups copper resistance islands have been identified, allowing for survival under high-copper stress conditions. While many of the evolutionary pathways of development for these copper resistance mechanisms are still speculative, the presence of copper resistance genes in isolates from both metal-contaminated and uncontaminated sites suggests additional selective pressures apart from high concentrations of bioavailable copper ions that could also be responsible for the presence of copper resistance determinants. We suggest a hypothesis in which copper is used in predatory protozoans to kill engulfed bacteria. Since protozoan grazing is a major selective pressure on bacteria, the presence of copper resistance determinants would help bacteria survive. This would in turn lead to a widespread dispersal of copper resistance determinants irrespective of copper contamination in the surrounding environment.

# Ribonucleases as modulators of bacterial stress response

Catia B ´ arria ´ ∗, Vania Pobre ˆ ∗, Afonso M. Bravo, and Cec´ılia M. Arraiano 

Instituto de Tecnologia Qu´ımica e Biologica Ant ´ onio Xavier, Universidade Nova de Lisboa, Oeiras, Portugal ´ ∗These authors contributed equally to this work. 

## 2.13.1 Introduction

Bacteria have developed complex regulatory processes in order to rapidly adapt to environmental changes. RNA metabolism plays a critical role in bacterial adaptation because the continuous degradation and synthesis of prokaryotic messenger RNAs (mRNAs) promote metabolic changes that are required for cells to grow and divide. The protein level depends on the balance between translation rate and mRNA decay. Thus, RNA degradation is a fundamental process in the regulation of gene expression. Ribonucleases (RNases) play a major role in this process because these are the enzymes that process and degrade RNA and contribute to the maintenance of the optimal amount of each transcript in the bacterial cells. These enzymes are the main effectors of the posttranscriptional regulation network, directly intervening in the maturation, degradation, and quality control of all RNA molecules. In this chapter, we will focus on the role that RNases play in several bacterial stresses. 

## 2.13.1.1 Ribonucleases

RNases are RNA-specific hydrolases or phosphorylases capable of catalyzing the cleavage of the phosphodiester bonds in a reaction that, ultimately, yields monoribonucleotides essential for the synthesis of new RNA. They are divided in two main classes: exoribonucleases, which cleave RNA, one nucleotide at a time, from one extremity; and endoribonucleases, which cleave RNA internally. In Escherichia coli, the process of RNA degradation usually begins with an endonucleolytic cleavage at one or more internal sites on the RNA molecule, followed by exoribonuclease-mediated processing (Arraiano et al., 2010). In this bacterium, two endoribonucleases have been associated with the initial cleavage events: RNase III, which is specific for double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), and RNase E, which cleaves single-stranded molecules (Arraiano et al., 2010; Silva et al., 2011). 

RNase E, encoded by the rne gene, is a single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) endonuclease that primarily cleaves AU-rich regions (Arraiano et al., 2010). RNase E is essential for cell growth, and the inactivation of temperature-sensitive mutants prevents degradation of many transcripts, extending the lifetime of bulk mRNA. This endoribonuclease is primarily involved in mRNA decay, but it is also responsible for the processing of both 5S and 16S ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) and the maturation of transfer RNAs (tRNAs) (Arraiano et al., 2010). The highly conserved RNase E N-terminal contains the catalytic domain, which is essential for tRNA processing and cell viability. The C-terminal half is less conserved and deprived of enzyme activity. In fact, mutant cells with deletions on the RNase E C-terminus are viable and process both rRNAs and tRNAs normally. However, they are not able to efficiently cleave mRNAs (Viegas and Arraiano, 2008). The RNase E C-terminal domain serves as a scaffold to bind to other proteins (e.g., the RNase polynucleotide phosphorylase (PNPase), the helicase RhlB, and enolase), which will contribute to the degradation process and assemble an RNAdegrading complex called the degradosome (Saramago et al., 2014a). The C-terminal domain of RNAse E is also responsible for its membrane localization. 

In Bacillus subtilis, two proteins with cleavage activity identical to E. coli RNase E were identified: RNase J1 and RNase J2. RNase J1 is essential, while RNase J2 is not (Even et al., 2005). RNase J1 plays a major role both in the maturation of the 16S rRNA gene and in mRNA stability. In a similar fashion to E. coli RNase E, RNase J1 was reported to potentially form, together with PNPase, RNase Y, and two glycolytic enzymes, a degradosome-like complex (Arraiano et al., 2010). RNase J1 and J2 display different activities, acting as both endo- and exoribonucleases (Even et al., 2005). 

E. coli RNase G is a paralog of RNase E, sharing a high level of sequence identity (35%) and similarity (50%). However, it is neither essential to complement RNase E deletion strains under normal physiological conditions (Arraiano et al., 2010; Chung et al., 2010; Viegas and Arraiano, 2008). Nonetheless, both enzymes are required for the two-step sequential maturation reaction of the 16S rRNA 5′ end (Arraiano et al., 2010). 

RNase Y is a single-strand specific endoribonuclease present in B. subtilis, which prefers $5 ^ { \prime }$ monophosphorylated RNA substrates (Shahbabian et al., 2009). The absence of the RNase Y gene (rny) results in the accumulation of several mRNAs, including several transcriptional regulators of stress responses and biofilm formation (Lehnik-Habrink et al., 2011). In this bacterium, RNase Y was shown to interact with both RNase J1 and RNase III, thereby controlling the amount of total mRNAs (Durand et al., 2012a). Furthermore, as already mentioned, RNase Y interacts with RNase J1 in a degradosome-like complex (Commichau et al., 2009). RNase Y orthologs, despite being identified in 40% of the eubacteria, are not present in either archaea or eukaryotic organisms, except in Drosophila willistoni (Arraiano et al., 2010). 

RNase III was the first dsRNA-specific endoribonuclease to be discovered (Robertson et al., 1968). Since then, it has been shown that RNase III is widely distributed among other organisms, being the prototype of the RNase III family (Arraiano et al., 2010). Like the other members of its family, RNase III is a hydrolytic enzyme capable of degrading dsRNAs yielding both a 5′ monophosphate end and a 2 nt overhang in the 3′ hydroxyl terminus (Meng and Nicholson, 2008). In E. coli, RNase III is encoded by the rnc gene and plays an essential role not only in rRNA and tRNA maturation but also in mRNA decay (Arraiano et al., 2010). Even though RNase III is not essential in this bacterium, rnc mutant cells grow slower when compared to the wild-type strains. This RNase is involved in the formation of the 16S and 23S rRNAs by processing the 30S rRNA precursor (Arraiano et al., 2010). In similar fashion to the eukaryotic RNase III orthologs, Dicer and Drosha, the E. coli RNase III is also involved in translational silencing. However, whereas Dicer and Drosha have a role in micro-RNA (miRNA) maturation, RNase III is involved in the degradation of small RNA (sRNA)– mRNA complexes (Denli et al., 2004; Meng and Nicholson, 2008). RNase III also acts as a stress modulator controlling the steady-state level of genes involved in cellular adaptation to stress (Arraiano et al., 2010). In B. subtilis, this RNase was shown to be essential (Durand et al., 2012b). 

In E. coli, there are three main exoribonucleases involved in RNA decay: PNPase, RNase R, and RNase II. All these enzymes degrade RNA processively and nonspecifically from the 3′ end. The action of these enzymes is often stimulated by the addition of poly(A) tails to the 3′ end of the RNA molecules. 

PNPase belongs to the PDX family of exoribonucleases. This RNase is encoded by the pnp gene and has processive, sequenceindependent, phosphorolytic activity, being capable of synthesizing and degrading ssRNA, depending on the conditions (Arraiano et al., 2010). The phosphorolytic activity exerted by PNPase requires a 3′ overhang of 7–9 nt of RNA, frequently stalling in the presence of structured RNAs (Carpousis et al., 

2008). Nonetheless, folded RNAs, such as sRNAs, can also be targeted by PNPase if a 3 polyadenylated tail is present. PNPase can associate with other enzymes in the degradosome, which is capable of degrading highly structured RNAs (Arraiano et al., 2010). PNPase is known to be implicated in the posttranscriptional regulation of several sRNAs, having a preponderant role in their degradation (Andrade and Arraiano, 2008; De Lay and Gottesman, 2011), with the steady-state levels of several sRNAs being increased in pnp mutants (Saramago et al., 2014a). Moreover, E. coli PNPase is a cold shock protein (CSP), essential at low temperatures (Awano et al., 2008). 

The E. coli RNB family of enzymes is present in all domains of life and includes RNase II, RNase R, and the eukaryotic Rrp44/Dis3, Dis3L1, and Dis3L2 proteins (Lathem, 2014). These proteins have a cold shock domain (CSD) at the N-terminal region and a C-terminal S1 domain, both involved in RNA binding. They also have a central RNB domain responsible for the catalytic activity (Lathem, 2014). RNase II is encoded by the rnb gene, which can be transcribed from two promoters, P1 and P2, and terminates in a Rho-independent terminator 10 nucleotides downstream of the rnb stop codon (Arraiano et al., 2010). This enzyme hydrolyses RNA in the $3 ^ { \prime } { - } 5 ^ { \prime }$ direction in a processive way. In E. coli, RNase II is the major hydrolytic enzyme and participates in the terminal stages of mRNA degradation. However, it is not capable of cleaving secondary structures and halts when the transcript is double-stranded. Moreover, RNase II is not essential in this bacterium unless PNPase is also missing (Arraiano et al., 2010). RNase R is encoded by the rnr gene and was shown to be involved in several cellular processes. This RNase is able to unwind and degrade RNA secondary structures, a critical process at low temperatures (Barria ´ et al., 2013). RNase R takes part in the degradation of mRNAs, and plays an important role in the removal of mRNAs with stable stem loops, such as repetitive extragenic palindromic (REP) elements (Cheng and Deutscher, 2005). This RNase has an important role in RNA quality control, namely in the degradation of defective tRNAs. Together with PNPase, RNase R also eliminates aberrant fragments of the 16S and 23S rRNAs (Arraiano et al., 2010). RNase R is considered a stress response enzyme, with its levels being increased in several stresses, such as cold shock, stationary phase, and heat shock (Cairrao˜ et al., 2003; Chen and Deutscher, 2005). 

Besides the individual action of RNases, cells contain complexes that are important in RNA processing and/or degradation. The degradosome is a large multiprotein complex in which the components contribute to the efficient degradation of mRNA. 

In E. coli, the degradosome is formed by two RNases, PNPase and RNase E; the adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-dependent RhlB helicase; and the glycolytic enzyme enolase (Arraiano et al., 2010). RNase E provides the organizing scaffold for the degradosome. The C-terminal half of RNase E has four segments (A, B, C, and D) with different roles in the degradosome assembly.
